en: *Mālatīmādhava* by Bhavabhūti,
with the commentaries of Tripurāri and Jagaddhara.
Second Edition. Edited by Maṅgeśa Rāmakṛṣṇa Telang and Vāsudeva Śāstrī Paṇśīkar.
Printed and published by Tukārām Jāvajī, NSP, Bombay, 1905.
Started on: 15-03-95.
Completed on: Typed by V. SARATHA //Śrīḥ//
Mālatīmādhava. First Act.
Bhāvapradīpikā.
I worship Him whose hair is adorned with a crescent moon, who is the abode of the essence of beauty,
whose sprouts of playful side-glances are filled with the nectar of compassion,
and who is radiant with a luster that eclipses the splendor of ten million rising suns.
I bow to that splendor which wields the noose, the goad, the sugarcane-bow, and the flower-arrows of the mind.

We take refuge in that lord of elephants, whose face is radiant as streams of ichor flow from his temples and are scattered by the wind from the fans of his two ears— streams that appear like masses of obstacles to devotion being driven away.
I bow to the two lords of Kāñcīpurī, the leaders of the mountains who take up residence at the foot of the single mango tree, for the accomplishment of all desired aims.
The great poet Bhavabhūti, who was proficient in grammar, logic, and epistemology,
composed a dramatic work titled *Mālatīmādhava*.
An exposition of that [work] is being composed by the wise Bhāradvāja,
the son of Tripurāri and of the sacrificer Parvateśa.
Although there are indeed ancient commentaries on this [text],
they have not been accepted by the wise, because they either employ the doctrine of the "ineffable" (avaktavya) or abandon the doctrine of the "effable" (vaktavya).
Therefore, this *Bhāvapradīpikā*, a brief commentary on the *Mālatīmādhava* composed for the delight of connoisseurs, is being fashioned with measured words.
Let this be as enchanting as the explanation of something never seen before,
like a human woman to lovers who have never beheld celestial beauties.
Or rather, let its utility lie in its proximity to the previous commentary;
for when the sun is absent, is the lamp not to be taken up?
For those like us whose intellect does not penetrate the ancient treatises, this [work] serves as a means of access.
May the virtuous, free from envy, accept this with respect in every way; for who would show such disdain toward one who is humble and full of affection?
Or rather, what is the use of this wretchedness of ours? If he, being a connoisseur of excellence, perceives any distinction in my work, then let him accept it.
Only those like us, whose intellects have been refined by traveling the path of literature, understand this labor;
how indeed could others—those who are wicked—know it?

Then the venerable Bhavabhūti, in order to achieve the purpose of composing excellent poetry such as *kīrti* (fame) and so forth, expanded this dramatic work named *Mālatīmādhava*, a *prakaraṇa*—the preeminent among the types of *prekṣya* compositions, primarily a drama (*nāṭya*)—along with all its constituent parts. Regarding the definition of a *prakaraṇa* therein, Bharata states: "In that regard, one who composes it should create the plot-substance and the hero himself through his own poetic genius; that is to be known as a *prakaraṇa*."

The *Daśarūpaka* also states: "Now, in the *prakaraṇa*, the plot is invented and based on worldly life; one should make a minister, a brahmin, or a merchant the sole hero. He should be wise and tranquil, employing skillful means, and devoted to virtue, pleasure, and wealth. The rest—such as the junctures (*saṃdhi*), the introductory scenes (*praveśaka*), and the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*)—is like that of the *nāṭaka*. In that regard, at the commencement of the drama, the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) is performed by the actors to pacify obstacles. As it is said: "First is the *pūrvaraṅga*, and then the *prastāvanā*."

"In the commencement of all dramas, this is held to be common: that which the actors perform prior to the dramatic subject matter for the sake of pacifying obstacles on the stage is called the *pūrvaraṅga*. In that context, the *sūtradhāra*, having performed the entire set of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*) of the *pūrvaraṅga* as taught by Bharata, must employ the *nāndī*, which is a component of the recited text (*pāṭhya*). As it has been said: "Even though there are many constituent parts of the *pūrvaraṅga* in a drama..."

"For them, the *nāndī*, which is dear to Nandīśvara, must certainly be performed. As for the definition of the *nāndī*: "A verse consisting of a benediction or a salutation, uttered at the beginning of a poetic work, is called a *nāndī*; or rather, there is a fixed rule regarding its opening words. It should be auspicious, suggesting [auspicious objects] such as the conch, the discus, the lotus, the ruddy goose (*kokaka*), or the white water-lily (*kairava*); the *nāndī* is adorned with either twelve or eight words. The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) introduces the alternative position that there is no fixed rule regarding the number of words.

Thus says Vidyanatha: "By some, no fixed rule regarding the number of words in the *nāndī* has been accepted. In this context, the poet, performing the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) characterized by salutation to his chosen deity for the sake of completing the intended *prakaraṇa* without obstacle, first speaks the *nāndī*—consisting of eight words, adorned with a benediction, and employed by the *sūtradhāra*, which is a constituent part of the *pūrvaraṅga*: "Cūḍā... This *nāndī* is marked by the name of the moon, as in the phrase "saṃdigdhamugdhendavaḥ."

As it has been said: "He should be depicted marked with the name 'Candra' (Moon), for he is the treasury of the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*); when the Moon is pleased, the splendor of the *rasas* flourishes," so says Bāḷuki. This is the meaning: the connection is that "may the matted locks of the Lord of Beings protect [us]. He qualifies them with the word "cūḍā": *cūḍā* means a crest or tuft of hair; according to Amara, "the crest (*śikhā*), the tuft (*cūḍā*), and the mass of hair (*keśapāśa*) [are synonyms]. By this, the head—which serves as its locus—is indicated, because a garland of skulls is an ornament of the head. Its *āpīḍa* is a wreath bound crosswise upon it.

Hemacandra (Halāyudha) states: "The *āpīḍa*, *śekhara*, *uttasa*, and *avataṃsa* are garlands worn on the head. Although the word *āpīḍa* alone suffices to denote a head-garland, the inclusion of the word *cūḍā* (crest/topknot) is for the purpose of suggesting its proximity [to the hair]. This is like the term *karṇāvataṃsa* (ear-ornament). As they say: "Words such as *karṇāvataṃsa* are formed with terms like 'ear' (*karṇa*) for the purpose of suggesting their proximity [to that specific part]. In this context, the term refers to the skull-fragments (*kapāla*), because the *āpīḍa* is strung together from them.

In them, the streams of water from the Gaṅgā on Śambhu’s head—flowing downward as they fill their throats and pervading the entire space—are mingled with the brilliance of the bees’ eyes, which, due to their common nature, blend particularly with it like lightning. In those [streams], the charming moon is the object of doubt—whether it be a tuft of ketaka flowers or a digit of the moon—because its form and color are so similar to the soft interior of the ketaka bud.

[The phrase] "having made them into matted locks" means they were bound together and formed into a topknot (*jūṭī*). [The phrase] "scattered" refers to their being spread out; for it would be impossible for them to give rise to the suspicion that they were the tips of *ketaka* flowers, as that would entail the disappearance of a single digit of the moon. [The phrase] "by those very serpents which are creepers" means by those very coils (*valaya*) that have been encircled; that is to say, by those resembling creepers. [The phrase] "those whose topknots are bound with a garland fashioned [therefrom]" refers to those [women]. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (naturalistic description) permeated by *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *sandeha* (ambiguity). Their definitions are not written here for fear of prolixity.

Here, from the perception of the tranquil form of the Lord adorned with a mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*), the hero of the story is indicated as "steadfast and peaceful" (*dhīraśānta*). By the word *jaṭā* (matted hair), which implies a plurality of agents, the multiplicity of heroes and heroines is suggested. Through the term *bhūteśasya* (of the Lord of Beings), which functions as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) to *jaṭā*, it is indicated that the hero’s independence in accomplishing his own purpose involves dependence on others; thus, the constant exertion of ascetic women such as Kāmandakī in carrying out that task is suggested. In this way, the slight unfolding of the poetic meaning (*kāvyārtha*) is to be inferred. //1//

Considering that such obstacles are dispelled by auspiciousness alone when it is accumulated, he says "sānandam" (with joy). May the shakes of the face belonging to Vināyaka protect [us]. Since Vināyaka is the king of obstacles, the intention is that the shakes of his face are the removers of impediments.

Regarding these, he states the causal sign: when the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), whose body has contracted for the sake of achieving entry through a subtle aperture—having been made into a sacred thread after being terrified by the peacock, the vehicle of Skanda, which was summoned by the sound of the muraja drum played by Nandin during the wild dance (tāṇḍava) of the Trident-bearer (Śiva), a sound resembling the roar of thick clouds—enters joyfully into the aperture of the nose, that is, the opening of the lotus (the nostril), because at that very moment the nearby cavity is attained; what are they like?

The quarters are made resonant by swarms of bees rising from their temples; these [bees] are accompanied by "cītkāra," an imitative sound. The poetic figure here is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication). Through these two verses, the commencement of the rainy season (*jaladharasamaya*) is indicated, because its conclusion will be described in the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture), and that which is indicated in the *mukha-sandhi* (opening juncture) must necessarily be brought to completion.

Regarding this, some commentators explain that by the word "kapāla" (skull), a row of cranes is indicated; by "the dripping of water," rain; by "lightning," lightning itself; by "the crest of the ketaka," the blooming of the ketaka flower; by "the mass of matted hair bound with serpent-bracelets," the rising of clouds; by "the sound of the drum," the roar of thunder; and by "Kaumārabarhin," the joy of the peacock. Whether this is apprehended through the power of the words (*śabda-śakti*) or through the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*), only they themselves know.

It is not the case that some learned person might have the notion that these words, although restricted to the contextual meaning, convey another related meaning through the power of a different denotative function (*śakti*). Nor is it experienced by sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdayas*) that the contextual meaning itself is capable of conveying such an extraneous meaning. Rather, there is a requirement for the indication of the very elements of the plot as they are being delineated in the *mukha-sandhi* (the opening juncture) for the sake of their final resolution; however, this does not apply even to descriptions of all the seasons and so forth which are merely to be mentioned therein.
Therefore, this meaning is not even within the scope of the poet's intention; consequently, this is not the path for those who know the way of Dhvani.

The two verses beginning with "dantaśreṇiṣu" are considered interpolations by earlier commentators and have not been explained; nevertheless, as they are seen in some manuscripts, we shall provide an explanation. "Danta... [etc.]—May the waves of the river of his crest (cūḍāsravantyūrmayaḥ), which are the ripples of the river of his head, protect you! These waves are intense due to their surging from the caves of Brahma’s skull; they are produced by the rolling about of the cranium of the Creator’s head. Flowing and trickling down the rows of teeth, they are agitated by whirling and circling accompanied by a tumultuous roar.

Those [streams] which possess the sound of bubbles in the regions of the nostrils and other cavities; which, shattered by the impact against the cheeks, fall from very high places down onto uneven ground; and which consist of intense torrents of water—these are described here. The poetic figure is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //3//

"Pakṣma" (eyelash). "Tārtīyīka" means the third; the suffix *īkak* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *īkak* may be added after a word ending in *tṛtīya* to denote the same meaning (*svārthe*). May that eye of yours, which burns with passion (*madanaploṣaṇa*), protect you—what kind of eye? That which makes even the entire mass of lightning a mere fragment compared to the tawny hue of its row of eyelashes. Time (*kāla*) is the sacrificer (*yajvā*) himself. When the bud [of the eye] was slightly opened, he offered the world as an oblation into that place of the *āhavanīya* fire. Its edge resounded with a hissing sound (*śātkārin*), like iron heated by a flame being sprinkled with drops of water from the stream of nectar falling from the crescent moon on his head. This is the figure of speech known as *udātta* (the Sublime). //4//

Now, wishing to state the introduction (*prastāvanā*), he first introduces its two constituent parts, *prarocanā* (the prologue) and *mukha* (the opening), beginning with *prarocanā*: "At the end of the *nāndī*" and so forth. The meaning is as follows: when the stage-manager (*sūtradhāra*) has performed the preliminary rites (*pūrvaraṅga*), entered the stage for the first time, recited the *nāndī*, and completed the remaining collection of elements of the preliminary rites—such as the withdrawal of the audience, the cleansing, and the anointing—and has exited, another manager similar to him enters and begins the introduction.

This has been stated in the *Daśarūpaka*: "Having first performed the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) and once the *sūtradhāra* has exited, another actor enters and causes the drama (*kāvya*) to be recited in a similar manner. As for the definitions of the *prarocanā* (prologue) and *mukha* (opening): "The announcement of the work to be performed, the specification of place and time, the delighting of the assembly's mind with words that indicate the subject matter of the poem, and the praise of the poet, the work, the actors, and so forth—this is the *prarocanā*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the assembly, the plot, and the hero is intended.

"‘The *sūtradhāra* addresses the *naṭī*, the *māriṣa*, or the *vidūṣaka*; that which introduces the subject matter of his own role through striking speech is the *āmukha* (prologue). Thus, enough [of this]. This verse is spoken by one who cannot endure the playful charm (*vilāsa*) of a previous poet. He indicates the time of dawn with the word ‘*udita*’: it has risen by a large portion of its orb; the sense is that it is ‘almost risen. ‘I shall worship’ (*upatiṣṭhe*) means I shall propitiate with a hymn; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule ‘*pathyārādhanayośca*’."

He acts accordingly with the words "of auspicious things": O Viśvamūrti, O you who are the self of all! According to the Vedic revelation, "The Sun is the self of that which moves and that which stands," you are the abode of auspicious, blessed splendors. Bestow upon me the Lakṣmī that is foremost and capable of accomplishing every happiness; be gracious. By the repetition in "whatever... whatever" (yadyat), he intends the totality of all modes.

"Whatever sin exists in every form, established in me in any manner whatsoever—such sin, being in that state, I, who am bowed down, renounce; remove it, turn it back. Regarding this, they say that because the meaning expressed by the repetition (*vīpsā*) of "whatever" (*yadyat*) is itself taken up by the pronoun "that" (*tat*), which refers back to the subject at hand, a second occurrence of the word "that" is not required. Therefore, the claim that one should see two instances of the word "that" in the subsequent sentence because two instances of the word "what" (*yat*) were seen in the preceding sentence is a false interpretation.

"O Blessed One, bestow manifold auspiciousness for the sake of greater auspiciousness"—this means "grant auspicious things that are followed by further auspiciousness. This is the *bhāratī* style (*vṛtti*), consisting of speech in the form of predominantly Sanskrit, indicated by this verse which points toward the meaning of the poem. It also serves as a component of the *prarocanā* (prologue), as it indicates the plot's meaning through the perception of the avoidance of misfortune and the attainment of desired ends for the hero of the story, his friends, and others. Nevertheless, the phrase "whatever [calamities]" refers to the afflictions caused by Aghoraghaṇṭa, Śārdūla, Nandana, and so forth.

"Prosperity! Prosperity!"—thus two blessings are indicated: the attainment of Mālatī and Madayantikā. "For the sake of greater prosperity"—this indicates the rescue of Mālatī from the hands of Kapālakuṇḍalā, as well as the saving of the lives of Mādhava and Makaranda when they were seized by the guards. //5//

Regarding the term *nepathya*: *nepathya* is the area behind the stage, separated by a curtain (*yavanikā*), where the family of actors (*kuśīlava-kuṭumba*) resides for tasks such as applying makeup; this is according to the statement: "The place for the family of actors is designated as *nepathya*. *Māriṣa* refers to an actor (*naṭa*). An actor is to be addressed as *māriṣa* by the *sūtradhāra*; for it has been said: "The *sūtradhāra* [should address] the actor as *bhāva*, and he [the actor] [should address] him as *māriṣa*. *Suvihitāni* means well-prepared or properly accomplished.

Regarding the phrase "of Śambhu, the Lord Kālapriyanātha, whose abode is Mahākāla": by the expression "dwelling in various lands," he demonstrates that the assembly is conversant with all arts (*sarvakalāveditva*). For it is in the presence of a refined assembly that there is enthusiasm for manifesting skill in dramatic performance (*prayogakauśala*). "Bharatas" refers to actors who study that treatise (*tacchāstra*). To the question, "What then should they perform?", he says: "I have been commanded. "A composition possessing the specified qualities" means a work endowed with those qualities which are pleasing to a learned assembly.

"Āryas" refers to those who know all branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). "Mixed" (*miśra*) is a designation for those worthy of honor (*pūjya*). They are called "gods of the earth" (*bhūmideva*) because they are preeminent therein, because the discernment of merits and defects in an assembly depends upon them, and because they are to be propitiated as being of divine nature. By this, the assembly is praised. The question of the actor is: "What are these qualities that they proclaim? He states those very qualities with the word "abundantly" (*bhūmnā*).

The applications—that is, the dramatic performances—of the *rasas* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, which are established through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements in great abundance and profusion, are profound and impossible for those of superficial vision to comprehend. For if the objects of the *rasas* were not concealed during their manifestation, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *rasas* becoming merely subordinate; they must remain concealed, like the jar-like breasts of a passionate woman. Therefore, regarding comprehension and aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*), only those of subtle intellect who are true connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) are capable, and not those who consider themselves scholars merely because they possess knowledge of words and their meanings.

As the author of the Dhvani said: "It is not perceived merely by one who knows the science of words and their meanings; rather, it is perceived only by those who know the true essence of the meaning of poetry. By this, the quality that constitutes the very life of the composition—its exclusive devotion to *rasa* (aesthetic flavor)—is demonstrated. Likewise, "heart-stealing" (*hṛdya*) actions refer to the charming activities of the hero, his friends, and others, performed out of "friendliness" (*sauhārda*), which is disinterested affection. By this, the quality known as "being endowed with a hero who is calm and wise" (*dhīrapraśānta-nāyaka-upetatva*) is demonstrated.

Likewise, there is agitation (*auddhatya*) on the part of the hero, even though he is primarily characterized by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), when he takes as his objective the sentiments of disgust (*bībhatsa*), wonder (*adbhuta*), and fury (*raudra*), which are opposed to it. Similarly, the *Kāmasūtra* has been arranged and composed in a manner that is favorable, serving as the seed for the mutual passion between the heroine and the hero; here, "kāma" means passion. That very passion is called a "sūtra" because, being the seed of all the matters to be treated, it is like a thread (*sūtra*).

The meaning is this: even the employment of sentiments such as the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the furious (*raudra*), and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*)—which are opposed to one another—in the *Aghoraghaṇṭa* episode of the *Mahāmāṃsa* sale and elsewhere, achieves propriety precisely by avoiding contradiction through becoming subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the primary erotic sentiment, in accordance with the main purpose characterized by the attainment of Mālatī. As it has been said: "When the intended sentiment has attained its established footing, there is no flaw in the expression of opposing states that have become its subordinate members."

In this matter, the poet must indeed be attentive, such that even when introducing a conflicting sentiment (*virodhī rasa*), not even the slightest trace of impropriety finds a foothold. As it has been said: "There is no cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) other than impropriety; the composition of well-known propriety is the supreme secret of *rasa*. By this, the quality known as "possessing propriety" (*aucitya-śālitva*) is demonstrated. "Varied narratives" refers to the fact that the subject matter (*vastu*) produces wonder; thus, the variety of plot (*vṛtta-vaicitrya*) is a quality. "Eloquence in speech" refers to skillfulness in expression.

By this, the union of faultless qualities and ornaments has been demonstrated; the underlying sense is: "I have been commanded for the purpose of employing such a composition, preeminent in its qualities. //6//

"In what [work]?"—the intention is: "What kind of composition is generally observed? "It is remembered"—the sense is: "By good fortune, I have now remembered such a composition. "The Taittirīyas": the *taittirīya* is the *chandas* (Vedic text) proclaimed by Tittiri; those who study that are the Taittirīyas. "The five-fire practitioners" (*pañcāgnayaḥ*): those devoted to the service of the five fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*; that is to say, those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgnayaḥ*). "The drinkers of Soma" (*somapīthinaḥ*): those for whom the drinking of Soma exists.

The meaning is: those who perform sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; those of firm vows (*dhṛtavratāḥ*), who are devoted to austerity and self-restraint; those whose family name is Udumbara; likewise, those who discourse on Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*), who are established in the knowledge of the Self (*adhyātmaniṣṭhāḥ*). Regarding the word "they" (*te*): they are *śrotriyas*, that is, Brāhmaṇas born of distinguished lineages who are devoted to the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), the knowledge of their meaning, and the performance of the prescribed rites. The form *śrotriyaḥ* is grammatically correct by virtue of the rule "one who studies the Veda is called *śrotriyaḥ*" (*śrotriyaṃśchando'dhīte*).

For the purpose of that [attainment], which is the certainty—knowledge free from doubt—regarding reality (*tattva*), which is the ultimate nature of Brahman and the supreme human goal, specifically preceded by the removal of improbability and contrary conceptions; it is the eternal, extensive sacred learning (*bhūriśruta*).

Thinking, "A Brahmin must study and know the Veda with its six limbs," they value the constant hearing of the scriptures as it is enjoined by eternal Śruti, and not for the sake of gaining fame by crushing the pride of opponents. They value wealth for the purpose of performing sacrifices and the like, or for constructing tanks and other works, and not out of a desire for enjoyment. They take a wife for the sake of producing progeny, and not to satisfy the god of love.

They require long life for the sake of increasing their ascetic merit, but not out of a craving for existence or a fear of death. This is the figure of speech known as *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). //7//

"Of the son of such-and-such a person, born of such-and-such a family"—the suffix *phak* is applied here because [the word] belongs to the *naḍādi* class. The genitive case remains unelided (*aluk*) according to the rule: "In the forms *āmuṣyāyaṇa*, *āmuṣyaputraka*, and *āmuṣyakulika*, the elision of the sixth case-ending is to be stated as not occurring. He is one whose mark is the title "Śrīkaṇṭha"; "Bhavabhūti" is merely another name for him used in common parlance.

Out of natural affection for the Bharatas, due to his mastery of the *Nāṭya-veda*, and because of his skill in fashioning heroes and other characters for dramatic performance, the actors show such devotion to that teacher; therefore, out of his paternal fondness for them, he entrusted this work of his—abounding in such qualities as those mentioned here—to us, saying, "Let them proclaim it in public assemblies through performance. In this work, indeed, there is a style of expression where words are well-known... [the phrase] beginning with "ye nāma" and so forth.

Here, at the outset, there is the display of discipline and the manifestation of poetic skill and learning. The word "nāma" signifies renown. There are certain great souls, renowned even in comparison to me, who spread contempt for us, disparaging us by asking, "What is this? and thus holding us in low esteem.

For they, having washed away the stain of the mire of worldly tendencies from their minds with the water of solitude, contemplate the reality of the inner Self alone; viewing the entire world as if it were a blade of grass and knowing some secret reality accessible only through the Upanishads, their disregard for us—who are dependent on ignorance—is entirely justified. Therefore, this effort is not directed toward them.

What then? It is because there is no purpose for those who have passed away; because among those of the present, neither the superior nor the inferior are engaged in this task; and because one such as he—capable of composing a work of this kind—is not being mentioned here. [The opponent argues: "By the force of the context, even though the relative pronoun *yaḥ* (who) and the demonstrative *tam* (him) are not explicitly stated, both are understood in the sense that 'one similar to me will arise. To show that the arising of such a person is indeed possible, he says: "Time. [Time is] limitless and infinite. "Vast" means extensive.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is possible that in some place and at some time, even someone like me might be born as one who adopts this [view]. Alternatively, the word "nāma" is used in the sense of "kila" (indeed). The sense is: "It is indeed strange that whoever they may be, however they may be, they spread contempt even for us—who by our own greatness overwhelm the entire world—just as there might be some talk of contempt for the sun by insignificant stars. What do they know? The meaning is: nothing at all.

The sense is that because they are ignorant, there is no harm to us whatsoever by way of disregarding them. The word "api" (even) is displaced in its position; this effort is not even directed toward them, because they are beyond our reach. Toward whom, then? Because there is no purpose with those of the past and because there is currently no one like me, it is directed toward whoever may arise in the future who is like me. [Objection: How can there be someone like you arising hereafter, when such a person is not found even amidst this vast proliferation [of beings] now?

Because of this possibility, he says: "Even in time that has no limit, and in space that is undetermined, who knows whether at some time or in some place someone like me might even now arise? This is the meaning. This is the figure of speech known as *hetu* (causation). //8//

"By the qualities," and so forth. By the qualities of our venerable teachers, which are being proclaimed, what quality of mine—their disciple—has not been made manifest? The meaning is that because I have been instructed by such teachers, all [virtues] are attributed to me. He points to that very teacher with the words "yathārtha" (as it truly is). //9//

"Whatever one knows"—this refers to the Upaniṣads, which are the "heads" of the Vedas, as well as the Sāṃkhya of Kapila and the Yoga of Patañjali, which are treatises on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*). "Not indeed"—the meaning is that such knowledge does not serve the purpose of skill in the composition of poetry. What then is useful for drama? He says: it is the maturity of speech (*vacasām yatprauḍhitvam*), which is proficiency in conveying the intended meaning. This is because of the statement: "In poetry, the successful accomplishment of the intended meaning is known as maturity (*prauḍhi*)."

Or rather, it is a form of variety such as this: "The composition of the sentence-meaning within a word, and the expression of the word-meaning within the sentence-meaning; boldness, expansion, and contraction, as well as its being full of intentional significance. Or, *udāratā* (loftiness) is the beauty of the composition, or the quality of having praiseworthy content. If there exists this gravity of meaning—the capacity to convey multiple meanings in the form of profundity—then that alone is the indicator and signifier of scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), erudition (*vyutpatti*), wit (*vaidagdhya*), and the power of poetic creation (*kavitā-śakti*).
The meaning is that, having observed the merits of the composition for themselves, the learned will understand my own proficiency; it is not necessary for me to state this with my own voice. //10//

Having thus offered praise for the poet and his poem, he introduces the *āmukha* (prologue) after completing the *prarocanā* (inducement), beginning with the words "tāvat" and so forth. It should be understood that since the components (*vīthyaṅga*) of the *vithi* are optionally included in the *āmukha*, they are not explicitly mentioned here. To that extent, the *bhūmikās* (roles) have been entirely prepared; that is, those belonging to their respective groups have been taught and instructed in the adoption of the appropriate characterizations, costumes, speech, gestures, and so on, for the purpose of the various dramatic performances.

"Of the Buddhist elder nun, the aged female ascetic of the Sugata; first, that is, to be introduced at the very beginning. What follows? The word "speak" is to be supplied. Regarding "then": first, the roles of both Kāmandakī and Avalokitā have been assumed by us two. But how, or by whom, is the role of the principal heroine (nāyikā) to be taken up? This is the meaning. He gives the answer: "Kalahamsa... [and so forth].

Kalahamsa is Madhava’s servant, and Makaranda is his friend; since this assumption of Madhava’s role will occur at the very moment of their entrance, there is no need to worry about it now. By this, it is meant that everything has been well arranged by him, and nothing remains to be done. Thus, this indicates the initial entrance of Kāmandakī and Avalokitā.

However, some explain that the entry of all the characters appearing in this *prakaraṇa* is indicated at the very beginning; that is incorrect. For it is only at the specific occasion of each character's entry that their entrance should be indicated. Furthermore, it is nowhere seen in any treatise on dramatic theory (*nāṭya-śāstra*) that the entry of all the characters of an entire *prakaraṇa* must be indicated at the outset. On the contrary, the indication of each respective character is clearly observed immediately prior to their actual entry. Thus, enough of this. Regarding the word "tena" (by him):

The meaning is: "by virtue of possessing the qualities prescribed by the members of the assembly" and "because it has been studied by the various classes. Regarding the word *sāmājikān*: Amara states, "A *samāja* is for animals; otherwise, a *samāja* is for those who share a common dharma (the assembly). "Certainly" (*bāḍham*) means: "We shall do so. "This one" (*eṣaḥ*): having abandoned the form of the *sūtradhāra*, I have become Kāmandakī. "I too have become Avalokitā"—this is the *prayogātiśaya* (excellent performance), which is a limb (*aṅga*) of the *āmukha* (prologue).

As it has been said: "Because of the introduction with the words 'This is he,' following the performance of the *sūtradhāra*, where there is the entrance of another actor, this is considered *prayogātiśaya* (the excellence of performance). The entrance of another actor involves an introduction with the words "This is he. When the *sūtradhāra* himself immediately becomes the next actor, the introduction is with the words "This is I. Thus, there is not much difference between them. This concludes the *prastāvanā*. [The *sūtradhāra*] turns around and acts out his departure.

Kāmandakī and Avalokitā, dressed in the garb of nuns with robes of saffron cloth, enter seated. Having thus concluded the prologue (*prastāvanā*), he begins the mixed interlude (*miśraviṣkambha*) for the purpose of indicating the portion of the story that is to be announced—beginning with "Kāmandakī," etc. The word "speaks" (*vadati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. As for the definition of an interlude (*viṣkambha*): "An interlude is that which indicates portions of the story already occurred or yet to occur; it is concise in meaning and is performed by middle-ranking characters."

The *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) is also to be described as being of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*). It is said: "The pure is performed by middle-ranking characters; the mixed is performed by low and middle-ranking characters. Because of the extension [of rules] stating that "the rest is like the *nāṭaka*," the *viṣkambhaka* is also employed in the *prakaraṇa*. Thus they say: "In the context of the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*, one should know there is what is called the *praveśaka*; however, the *viṣkambhaka* should be used in both the *nāṭaka* and the *prakaraṇa*. [Regarding the word] *avalokitā*: "May the Blessed Lady command. [Regarding the word] *api nāma*: [End of excerpt]

The two are so described because they possess auspiciousness, blessings, and mutual suitability in terms of age, beauty, fortune, and charm. By this, it is indicated that through their mutual compatibility, Mālatī alone is the worthy bride for Mādhava, and he alone is the fitting groom for her. The word *bhūri* (abundant) suggests that, being born of a praiseworthy lineage, they are worthy of the connection between their respective families. This is further implied by the use of the copulative compound (*itaretara-dvandva*) for Mālatī and Mādhava, which conveys their companionship.

It is illuminated that there exists a mutual passion between them as its cause; the meaning is that it is desired by their kinsmen and other connoisseurs. By this, the mutual passion of Mālatī and Mādhava is indicated here in the play as the seed (*bīja*), according to the rule: "The seed is a cause for the plot, slightly introduced and expanded in many ways."

That which is initially indicated only briefly and subsequently expanded in many ways—the cause of the action or the purpose—is called the *bīja* (seed). In this context, the primary action (*kārya*) is the marriage of Mādhava and Prabhāvatī; the cause of that is their mutual passion, which is the *bīja*. The *bīja* is the first of the ten dramatic elements (*arthaprakṛti*), while the *kārya* is the fifth. Could it even be the auspicious taking of hands in marriage? What indeed might it be?

By this, the first stage, called "Initiation" (*ārambha*), is shown through the perception of eagerness for the sake of the fruit consisting of the union of Mālatī and Mādhava; as it is said: "Initiation is merely eagerness for the attainment of abundant fruit. Furthermore, because of the simultaneous presence of the seed (*bīja*) and the initiation, this is the "Opening Joint" (*mukhasandhi*). As it has been stated: "The five elements of the plot—known as the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the episode (*prakarī*), and the purpose (*kārya*)—are endowed with five stages: initiation (*ārambha*), effort (*yatna*), hope of attainment (*prāptyāśā*), certainty of attainment (*niyatāpti*), and the arrival of the fruit (*phalāgama*)."

"According to their respective order, the five junctures (saṃdhi) beginning with the *mukha* arise. In this context, the *mukha* (opening) is that juncture wherein the seed (*bīja*) possesses its purposeful distinction. And for that *mukha* juncture, the twelve constituent parts (*aṅga*), such as the *upakṣepa* (introduction) and others, must be employed in accordance with the commencement of the seed. These will be defined in due course further on, so let this suffice. "With joy" (*saharṣam*): because of obtaining an omen indicative of the fulfillment of the desired object being contemplated. He demonstrates that very point with the words "revealing" (*vivṛṇvatā*).

As if by one who understands the inner meaning, she wonders in her doubt whether this purpose will be achieved or not; thinking, "I shall dispel her uncertainty," [he acts] as if knowing our intention. Thus, while the auspiciousness is being revealed and future blessings indicated by the throbbing left eye—yet which, though being on the contrary side, is not actually adverse because it portends the success of the contemplated task—it is nevertheless accepted as being the "left" (*savya*). Furthermore, the term *savya* is also understood to mean "other than the right" (*savyetara*).
"The throbbing of the left eye in women portends auspiciousness," so say the prognosticators; this is the ornament known as *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction). //11//

Avalokitā: Great indeed is this mental agitation and heartache of the Blessed Lady, taking the form of anxiety! It is wonderful, truly wonderful! That she now wears as her only garment a patched robe made from scraps of tattered rags fallen in the streets; that her livelihood consists solely of the dropping of alms-food—mere mouthfuls of begged food—into the hollow of her belly, sufficient only for the maintenance of life.

The meaning is that whatever food is cast into a vessel, a hand, or a mouth is swallowed like medicine; it is not eaten preceded by the tasting of its flavor. Minister Bhūrivasu is employing the venerable lady—who is majestic and self-possessed—in such laborious tasks that produce suffering, such as acting as a messenger for those possessed by passion. Let him indeed employ her even in this improper activity, since he is so preoccupied with his duties and because this task would otherwise be difficult for anyone else to accomplish.

And in that effort, the very obstacle to worldly existence—which is uprooted and severed—is the hindrance to the rain of the nectar of supreme beatitude; in other words, it is an impediment to liberation. That this [obstacle] is being cast down even by you upon yourself—this is all truly wonderful. Kāmandakī: "Child," [the meaning is] "you should not speak thus. "Since he... [means]: That the venerable Bhūrivasu, who is worthy of honor, appoints me to a task—that is, to a matter requiring my execution—is the fruit of his affection and love.

This very love that is worthy of confidence is called *praṇaya*. Some say that *praṇaya* is simply sincere goodness. Its essence is its stable core. The sense is: "The commissioning of us to a task, even an improper one, out of an excess of affection is indeed appropriate for us to accept. If the duty desired by a friend can be accomplished, let it be achieved either with our lives or with penances more praiseworthy than they.

Therefore, it should be construed by repeating the phrase: "That task, which is even greater than the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), would have been performed and accomplished through our lives and ascetic penances. The sense is that the fulfillment of a friend's purpose is weightier even than liberation.

The minister Bhūrivasu, desiring to bestow his daughter Mālatī upon Mādhava—the son of Devarāta, who was his own childhood friend—was unable to grant her openly out of fear of King Nanda, the minister’s brother-in-law, who had requested her hand. Consequently, he appointed Kāmandakī to manage the affairs of arranging a secret marriage; this narrative will become clear further on. //12//

"Why this insistence that Mālatī must be given to Mādhava alone by Bhūrivasu? Or why this determination on the part of the Holy Lady that this task must be accomplished even at the cost of her life? To this he replies: "Do you not know? The implication is: "Since childhood you have been my pupil; you surely know all of this. "No" means: "Not by Bhūrivasu, nor by Devarāta, nor by me. "Sahacarya," meaning the state of being companions, [arose] through dwelling in various directions—that is, by living in many different lands.

The word "asmad" (from us) is used in the ablative plural because the friendship was established through our joint study at one time; it is precisely from us that this vow of theirs proceeded, being brought about by me alone. To the question "Which [vow]? he says: "by the two of us. Therefore, the sense is that since this was a prior agreement and Bhūrivasu was led by me, my insistence on this matter is appropriate. Furthermore, Saudāminī, as my first disciple, is a witness to this matter; hence he says: "in the presence of Saudāminī."

Because it is understood that this [incident] falls within the scope of accomplishing her purpose as well, the portion of the narrative concerning the prevention of Mālatī’s misfortune—which she will carry out at the end—is indicated. Furthermore, Bhūrivasu does not appoint me to the role of a messenger; rather, I am acting myself for the sake of fulfilling my own desired vow. Thus, it is also indicated that one should not suspect me of the slightness of being a mere messenger. Moreover, the statement "in the presence of Saudāminī and myself" would be inconsistent with the intended meaning.

And because of the rule "tyadādīni sarvair nityam," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) such as *sa ca devadattaśca tau* (he and Devadatta, those two). However, the restriction that only those ending with *dvi* belong to the *tyadādi* group is intended merely to exclude the substitution of *yat* for *tad*. Now, regarding the words *tat* and *idānīm*: *tat* refers to what was previously promised. The word *mantriṇā* (by the minister) is used to demonstrate his intellectual skill (*buddhikauśala*), showing that he sent his son here with a view toward many purposes. *Ānvīkṣikī* is the science of logic (*nyāyaśāstra*). Since the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*) is also rooted in logic, it is included within it.

"Well-arranged" means properly accomplished. He states the reasoning for this careful arrangement: "If not... Since the relationship [between Mādhava and Makaranda] was previously promised, Bhūrivasu would himself give his daughter to Mādhava; however, if Devarāta were not sent here, then due to the absence of a reminder and the passage of time, Bhūrivasu might even forget his promise. Therefore, by this dispatching of his son, the friend's promise has been brought within the range of memory.

Or, even if at some time, by the power of past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), he were to hesitate to give his daughter—though remembering her despite knowing her excellent qualities—because she possesses a beauty that transcends the world, even that [hesitation] has been dispelled. For, in order to inspire enthusiasm, to generate a desire for a relationship, and to produce mutual affection between the two youths, the son was revealed with qualities not shared by others; thus, by these two reasons, the promise made through the dispatching of the daughter is well-established. This is the meaning. //13//

Avalokitā: Why does the minister not offer Mālatī to Mādhava himself? That is why he urges the Blessed Lady toward a clandestine marriage. [The use of the genitive case for *mādhavasya* here functions in the sense of the dative. Kamandakī states the reason for not offering her herself: "Her"—meaning Nandana, the king’s boon companion and counselor of pleasure, requests that Mālatī through the king; the meaning is that he asks the king to bestow her upon Nandana. He requests it by means of the king's authority.

The intended meaning is that it is not [done] by means of praiseworthy and excellent qualities. A direct refusal, saying "I will not give her" in the presence of the king's request, would lead to the king's anger; however, this method in the form of a clandestine marriage (*cauryavivāha*) is auspicious and beautiful, because it serves as the cause for avoiding the attainment of the undesirable and achieving the desired—namely, the union with the beloved and the avoidance of the king's enmity. //14//

Avalokitā: "How wonderful, how wonderful! It appears that the minister has no regard for Mādhava, since he does not even know his name. How is it that, wishing to give his daughter to him, he acts as if he were indifferent toward that very Mādhava, as though he did not even know him? Kāmandakī: "That is a concealment; it is a masking of one's outward appearance out of fear of the king. The meaning is that he is merely acting ignorance. She says, 'Especially, however,' indicating that one must continue to act ignorant even from this point forward."

Because it occurs immediately after childhood and because its characteristics generally persist, "childhood" (*bālya*) here refers to the first stage of youth. [This state] is characterized by being devoid of the discernment between what is proper and improper, ignorant of concealing outward appearances, and entirely subservient to the command of passion. It is a time when one strives to fulfill one's desires even by transgressing against elders. Since they are in the first bloom of youth, their inner feelings are unrestrained; therefore, specifically regarding her own mind’s inclination toward mutual affection, she acts to prevent the dulling of that manifest mutual passion.

A concealment must be made; a hiding must be performed. It should be enacted so that Mālatī believes, "My father does not know that I am in love with Mādhava," and so that Mādhava understands, "The minister does not know that I am in love with his daughter. If this is done, then, their enthusiasm being unimpeded, the union of their desires will be accomplished of its own accord.

Otherwise, because our impetuosity would be known by our elders, we would feel shame; consequently, the desired marriage—arranged as a mere pretense to thwart their efforts—would not be accomplished. This is the underlying sense. Here, because the seed (bīja) of the mutual passion between the two protagonists is introduced, it is stated that this constitutes the dramatic element (aṅga) called *upakṣepa* within the opening juncture (*mukhasandhi*). As it is said: "The laying down of the seed is *upakṣepa*. //15//

Regarding the word *anurāga*: it need not even be said that this concealment is merely for the sake of hiding the fact that the minister does not know even the name of Mādhava. For, since both children are the dear friends' offspring in relation to Kāmandakī, they are referred to as "the two children" (*vatsayoḥ*). The report of their passion (*anurāga-pravādaḥ*) is "world-wide" (*sārvalaukikaḥ*), meaning known by all people. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "after *loka* and *sarvaloka*"; the vowel lengthening in both parts of the compound occurs because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* class. The sense is: even commoners (*pāmarāḥ*) know this, so what need be said of the minister?

By this, because of the multiplication of the seed (*bīja*), the juncture-element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "elaboration" (*parikara*) is stated; as it is said: "The elaboration is the expansion of that [seed]. And this being so, it results in our welfare. Why? Because, for this reason, the two sons of the king might be possible to deceive at length.

If, after our marriage has been performed, King Nandana should become angry and say, "How is it that this wretched female mendicant has acted in opposition to us? then there would be no fault on my part, for we two were united by ourselves through the power of mutual affection. And since that affection is approved by all the world, our purpose will be easily achieved; such is the meaning. //16//

And in this very way, the wise are seen to conduct themselves as if they were indifferent, appearing to others as though they were ignorant even of the news of those matters, yet accomplishing their tasks solely through the skill of their intellect; thus he says: "Externally," etc.

A wise man, though he alone knows the task to be performed and has entrusted the burden of that work to a group of many agents, yet appearing as one to others, begins—solely for the purpose of deceiving the world by concealing his own actual activities—a different mental operation external to the secret task he desires, even though it is not the primary objective; this is done through the predominance of all outward manifestations, such as appearance, speech, and conduct (the term *anubhāva* being used here with a focus on the state of being).

Acting in such a way as to be delightful through exclusive devotion to that [goal], so as to please the minds of the world, he remains day and night intent solely upon this; for he does not even know the report of any other business—this is the meaning of "acting in such a way" that it is perceived even by those who seek out his vulnerabilities.

He conceals and covers even the most minute and subtle vulnerabilities—the points where the enemy’s secret designs and stratagems may be perceived—even those that are extremely fine; thus, having deceived even a person of all-pervading discernment through guiles and acts of deception by generating false confidence, he himself, appearing as if indifferent and neutral, accomplishes his own ends and maintains silence.
The meaning is that she does not utter even a mere word outwardly regarding her desired undertaking; this is a description of the natural disposition of a clever person. //17//

Now Avalokitā speaks of the portion of the task she herself has accomplished: "By me. And by me, too, at your word, Mādhava is being led along the royal road closest to Bhūrivasu’s residence through various introductions and the employment of many kinds of seemingly innocent pretexts. The meaning is that it has been arranged so that he comes within the range of Mālatī’s vision. By mentioning his proximity, it is indicated that the excellence of all his limbs can be clearly perceived.

The fact that he is not to be suspected even when frequently traveling is indicated by the word *rājamārga* (royal road). Kāmandakī says, "We have obtained the fruit of the means employed by you," and explains: "It was told. *Dhātreyī* means the daughter of a nurse (*dhātrī*); [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*. By this, it is indicated that because she shares the drinking of breast milk and plays in the dust with her, she is a place of extreme confidence, and thus she knows everything that is in her [Mālatī's] mind. To the question "What was told?", she replies: "Furthermore... (bhūyaḥ).

Seeing Mādhava making many trips back and forth along the city street near his own residence—just as Rati, newly born after the burning [of Kāma], might behold the newly arisen Kāma—Mālatī, standing at the path of a high window above the rafters of the pleasure-palace, beheld him with longing, gazed upon him again and again, and became deeply filled with yearning, her heart’s affection being fixed solely upon him, her husband, out of her sense of fidelity.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: she "faints" or "wastes away" (*tāmyati*), meaning she withers, by means of her limbs which are "extremely turbid" due to the heat of passion (*madanasaṃtāpa*), "agitated" by the intense longing (*raṇaraṇikā*) manifested through various experiences, and "possessing lovely complexions" caused by the various stages of love (*kāmāvasthā*). Regarding the nature of this longing and its attendant moods (*anubhāvas*), the *Bhāvaprakāśikā* states: "Wherein the mind [fixes] on a woman because it perceives there the enjoyment of the pleasures of all the senses...
(and so forth).

"Poets know that longing (*utkaṇṭhā*) to be the desire for attainment accompanied by mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*). The internal resolve for union, the gazing toward various objects of hope, the languor of the limbs, the coloring of the mind, the brooding of desires, sitting with the chin resting on the arms upon the knees, a bright complexion of the face, perspiration and heat, and faltering speech—these states experienced through longing are described by those skilled in the science of emotion (*bhāva*). In this context, it should be understood that Mālatī’s longing directed toward Mādhava constitutes the first stage [of love].

For example: "Longing, attachment of the mind, resolve, praise of qualities, aversion to activity, feverish distress, pride, abandonment, madness, fainting, and death—these are the ten stages. And in this regard: "Longing (*abhilāṣa*), which is a yearning for a beautiful object when it is seen or remembered as its basis, is manifested through eagerness, perspiration, horripilation, joy, wonder, and trepidation, as well as by attendant states such as restlessness, paralysis, and bashfulness. (18)

Avalokitā: "Certainly. This means that what was said by Lavaṅgikā is indeed firm. She states another reason for its firmness: "Therefore, by her [Mālatī], a portrait of Mādhava—a likeness intended to dispel her agitation—was painted; that very portrait has today been placed in the hand of Mandārikā by Lavaṅgikā. The meaning of the word 'tāvat' (meanwhile/in due course) is that it will eventually reach the hand of Mādhava. Kāmandakī: [Reflecting].

The remainder [of the sentence] implies that [the character] reflects upon the significance of placing the picture-board in Mandārikā’s hand and then explains it. "Well-arranged" (*suvihita*), etc.: the attendant (*anucara*) is the servant (*ceṭa*). "The temple-maiden" (*vihāradāsī*) refers to Mandārikā, the attendant of the Buddhist monastery (*bauddhālaya*). "By way of the ford" (*tīrthena*) means by way of the path of descent. "For the introductory purpose" (*upoddhātāya*) means for the sake of a matter that serves as the cause for accomplishing the task at hand. And that matter is the conviction in Mādhava that "she is enamored of me"; the intention is that only when that is true will his engagement in the performance of the task be successful.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*): namely, the purpose behind placing the picture-board in Mandārikā’s hand. Avalokitā states another task she has accomplished: "In this matter, having aroused Mādhava’s curiosity, I sent him to Madanodyāna at dawn, where the great festival of Love was underway. For what purpose? Because it is said that Mālatī will go there; thus, their mutual sight will come to pass. Kāmandakī says, "Well done," and so forth.

"By that [means], namely, through the application—that is, the extreme persistence—in accomplishing what is dear to me and desired by me. Avalokitā: "Venerable lady, Saudāminī has now attained the power of the marvelous accomplishment of mantras; she observes the vow of a Kāpālika on Śrīparvata. Kāmandakī: "From where? That is to say, from whom was this learned? Avalokitā: "In this city, in the region of the great cremation ground, there is a Cāmuṇḍā named Karālā. Kāmandakī: "'There is'? Yes, she exists."

The meaning is that she is indeed heard of as being well-known. She is fond of the sacrifice of various living beings, such as humans, cattle, and so forth. By this, the offering of Mālatī in the fifth act is indicated. [She is] for those who are reckless, whose nature is characterized by daring.

Avalokitā: "In that regard, there is a female disciple named Kapālakuṇḍalā, possessed of great power, who belongs to a practitioner named Aghoraghaṇṭa—who dwells in a cremation ground not far from here, having come from Śrīparvata, and who is intent on the practice of mantras while wearing a shaven head and carrying human skulls. She comes there every evening; it is from her that this report has reached me. Kāmandakī: "All of this is possible."

By this, the wonderful feats to be accomplished by Saudāminī later on are indicated. Avalokitā: "Enough now with this; enough with this useless narration of Aghoraghaṇṭa's exploits"—this is the meaning. Venerable lady, if that Makaranda, who is Mādhava’s constant companion and childhood friend, were to marry Madayantikā, the sister of Nandana, that too would be a second joy for Mādhava.

By this, the episode of the *patākā* (the secondary plot) concerning Makaranda, the suitor, is indicated within the *garbha-saṃdhi* (the "embryo" juncture). Kāmandakī: "Appointed"—the meaning is that even this was previously considered by me. Avalokitā: "The venerable lady has acted wisely. Kāmandakī: "That"—meaning, having learned Mādhava's movements and having ascertained the news of whether or not their mutual sighting occurred in the Madana garden; let us go and see Mālatī herself.

The meaning is that she must be brought under control through familiarity, yet not so much that he does not fear this rash act of offering herself—which is unsuitable for noble maidens and has been taught by us. Kāmandakī, having reflected—having deliberated upon what kind of mission as a messenger should be performed—reaches a conclusion; this is the ellipsis. She is one whose nature is exceedingly noble and profound. And such is her profundity: "By whose power [the true] forms [of feeling] remain hidden during joy, anger, fear, and the like..."

"The profundity of those dispositions is proclaimed as being unperceivable in their manifestations"—this is the form of what has been stated. Because Mālatī, due to her exceedingly profound nature, does not herself disclose her own intention even in her final state, for that reason, the method—the course of activity—of a *nisṛṣṭārthā* (fully authorized) female messenger must be employed; it must be made the primary focus. The meaning is that it should be relied upon as the principal means.

The term *nisṛṣṭārthā* (one to whom the matter has been entrusted) is derived from the etymology: "she in whom the object—the burden of the task—has been surrendered (*nikṣiptaḥ*) or entrusted (*nisṛṣṭaḥ*) with the words, 'You yourself know all that must be done. Thus, she is called a *dūtī* who independently carries out the mission. As it has been said: "Having learned the desire in the minds of two youths whose passion is firmly rooted, she who proceeds for the sake of accomplishing what they require—even without being commanded by them—is declared by the learned to be a *nisṛṣṭārthā*, because the etymological derivation 'she in whom the burden of the task has been entrusted' is applicable."

A messenger who possesses unutterable guile and for whom treaties and the like are authoritative is one whose mission is fully empowered (*nisṛṣṭārtha*); such as the venerable one [is] for the Pāṇḍavas. Now, he hopes for the success of his own undertaking with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*). With the verse beginning "autumnal moonlight" (*śarajjyotsnā*): she is auspicious (*kalyāṇī*), endowed with a captivating form and corresponding virtues; "well-born" (*sujātam*) refers to her beloved, the lord of her life. The autumnal moonlight and the night-lotus serve as the analogy for their union in mutual passion. May she "delight him" (*nandayatu*), meaning may she cause him to be enriched with unsurpassed bliss.

By this, it is implied that the young man, having performed meritorious deeds, may achieve his purpose; that he may gladden her through their mutual and equal passion; and that she may fulfill her own duty. The particle *ca* (and) illuminates this meaning. This being so, may the Creator’s activity—which is most weighty and superior—bear fruit in the fashioning of those virtues which are mutually and perfectly suited to one another; may it be fruitful precisely by the result characterized by their union.

May he be charming and praised by all people; for the union of these two, whose forms are fashioned so as to be mutually suited, is the very fruit [of their existence]. Otherwise, it would be entirely in vain. As Kālidāsa has said in the verse beginning with "paraspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham" (their beauty was mutually desirable). Here, the figure of speech is *anyonyam* (mutuality), which is to be praised through the simile (*upamā*). In this context, the limb (*aṅga*) named *vilobhana* (enticement) occurs, because there is praise of the seed (*bīja*), namely their mutual passion, in accordance with its suitability. As it is said: "The description of its qualities is *vilobhana*. //19//

This is a *miśraviṣkambha* (mixed interlude), because it is performed by characters of low and middle status. He begins with the words "Then," etc., demonstrating what was indicated in the statement, "Mādhava’s attendant is named Kalahaṃsa. Regarding the definition of an *aṅka* (act): "The division of the plot is twofold: that which is to be revealed (*prakāśya*) and that which is to be suggested (*sūcya*). That which is to be revealed is characterized by a continuous flow of sweet and noble sentiments; one should reveal this through the *aṅkas*. The characteristics of an *aṅka* shall now be stated: it is enacted by characters present on stage and is preceded by the seed (*bīja*) and the drop (*bindu*) [of the plot]."

"A *aṅka* (act) concludes the relevant matter, is endowed with the *patākāsthāna* (the suggestive pause), and serves as the locus for sentiments (*rasa*) through the arrangement of various types of matters. One should describe therein an event occurring within a single day or a single night; it should be performed by five or six characters, who then exit at its conclusion. Thus [it is said]. He is one by whom the very picture-board, taken as an accessory, serves as the means for the sight of Mādhava.

Now, what [is this]—one by whom the majesty and gravity of Mālatī’s heart have been eclipsed, that majesty which had surpassed the pride of the God of Love and had cast aside the haughtiness of the God of Love, which was itself eclipsed by the splendor of the play of beauty and the charm of form? It should be understood that this is known through the sight of the portrait of Mādhava painted by Mālatī; for by this it is made known that Mālatī, having been targeted by the God of Love toward Mādhava, has been drawn far away and her fortitude shaken.

"I see my lord Mādhava. [She speaks with agitation and longing: "Since my lord Mādhava, suspecting an affection for Mālatī within himself, brought this picture-board—which is most worthy of being accepted—as a means of proof, he has performed a great service for his master. Where is he now? [Walking about, etc. "I am exhausted. I shall rest here in this garden grove for a moment and then look for my lord Mādhava, who is accompanied by Makaranda."

In the reading "makarandanandanam," the meaning is that he is a source of joy because he is a dear friend; the interpretation as "son" has been disregarded due to its awkwardness. By this very [word], Makaranda's entrance is indicated. He says this with the words beginning with "tataḥ" (then). "Madanodyānam" refers to a garden characterized by a temple of the god Kāmadeva; by this, its status as an excitant (*uddīpanavibhāva*) for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is stated. "Diṣṭyā" is an indeclinable resembling a word ending in the third case, signifying good fortune. "Abhivartate" (approaches).

The meaning is that she is coming toward him; the implication is that she does not see him because her mind is elsewhere. "Having observed" means having scrutinized; the word "speaks" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The phrase "of this, however" (*asya tu*) serves as a supplement to the verse and is connected with the words "the movement," and so forth. Regarding "the movement": the movement was sluggish due to the absence of a visible object, undertaken somehow even without prior desire. By this, the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called lassitude (*ālasya*) within the context of love-in-separation (*vipralambha*) is indicated. As it is said: "Lassitude is a distaste for activity."

Likewise, vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is empty when it is fixed upon the mind by means of thought (*cintā*); for that very reason, it is also empty because it lacks the fruit consisting of the discernment of its own object. As it is said regarding emptiness: "Empty vision is that which is like a cluster of stars, smooth, motionless, perceiving emptiness, grasping external objects, and dark; however, empty vision arises from thinking. By this, the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called thought (*cintā*) is manifested. For it is said: "Thought is defined as the recollection of objects preceded by an effortful application of the mind."

Likewise, "the body is unwell" means that it is devoid of strength and its hands, feet, and other limbs are incapable of their own functions; by this, the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called languor (*glāni*) is suggested, as it is said: "Languor is that which causes the activities of speech, mind, and body to cease. "Sighing excessively" means more powerful than before; by this, fatigue, despondency, delusion, and so forth are suggested, because sighing, as an ensuant (*anubhāva*), is common to many emotions. Thus, the third stage, consisting of recollection (*anusmṛti*), is shown.

For example: "He sighs again and again through the contemplation of his desires; the recollection of other matters due to aversion is thus described. What could this be? Makaranda’s conjecture is: "What indeed might be the cause of these [states] such as anxiety and lassitude? Having reflected, he determines the cause: "What else could it be? Or rather, what need is there for conjecture here? What cause other than the transformation of love (madanavikāra) could be imagined for these? The meaning is: none at all.

He states that very cause with the words "it wanders": in the world, it wanders by the command of Kandarpa; it expands unimpeded. And [this refers to] youth, whether the first or the second, because the other two stages are unsuitable here. It is "changeable," meaning its nature is to produce transformation. As for youth, it is said: "That state of being young which is capable of enduring the exertion of sexual union, and possesses an intoxication like that of a rutting elephant—that is declared to be youth."

The specific characteristics of youth have been elaborated in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* beginning with the words, "Youth, however, is of four kinds," and so forth; they should be understood from that very source. Those various states—such as the rising moon, gardens, and the like—which are graceful (*lalitāḥ*), beautiful, pleasing to the eye, sweet, and captivating, are the excitants (*uddīpanavibhāvāḥ*) that cast off or remove even the steadfastness (*dhīratām*) and fortitude (*dhairyam*) of one who is naturally composed. As for fortitude: "Unassailed by fickleness and free from boastfulness regarding all matters..."

"The natural state of the mind is called fortitude. This means that he has surely come today to Madana’s garden to witness the festival of Love; his heart is attached to someone, and he remains overwhelmed by the very condition of love. This is the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation), characterized by doubt resolved into certainty. //20//

By the words beginning with *diṣṭā*, the entrance of Mādhava is indicated. He states this with the words beginning with *tataḥ*. "As described" means his state as defined by the passage beginning with *gamanam*. Regarding the words beginning with *tām*: my mind (*cetas*), acting as the agent, having contemplated for a very long time—that is, for a great duration—that woman whose face is as charming as the moon, who was made the guest of my eyes in the preceding moment; having made her the object of meditation by means of the "foremost of goats"—that is, by the abandonment of other objects—meaning, having meditated upon her.

The meaning is: by some kind of change of state that cannot be defined as "it is like this," which has never been experienced at any time or in any way whatsoever. "It turns away" (*vyapavartate*) means it proceeds otherwise than its natural state; that is to say, it undergoes a transformation. To the question "by doing what?", he describes that very same deviation from the path: "at an untimely moment" (*akāṇḍe*), meaning at the very moment of the first sight, [she felt] shame.

What is shame (*lajjā*)? It is the contraction of the mind, thinking, "How have I engaged in an action censured by the noble ones and fit to be ridiculed by others. As it is said: "Shame is indeed the contraction of the mind resulting from the performance of what is improper. Having conquered that [shame], having cast it aside; having warded off modesty (*vinaya*), that is, humility (*vinītatā*); having uprooted—that is, having churned away—steadfastness (*dhairya*), that is, fortitude; [he acted] in such a way that his discrimination (*viveka*), which is the knowledge of what ought and ought not to be done, became sluggish (*manthara*), that is, dulled.

In this context, it should be understood that the two stages—the abandonment of shame and the loss of discernment, as well as madness—are mentioned at the very beginning in order to demonstrate the intensity of passion; alternatively, "of dull discernment" may be taken as an adjective qualifying the mind. //21//

It is a marvel! As for the phrase "by which wonder": my mind, in her presence, became stunned—motionless and with all other states extinguished—by that wonder (*vismaya*), a transitory emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) belonging to the aesthetic sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhutaraasa*) born from beholding her unprecedented beauty, which is fit for a superhuman world; it became dazed as if by plunging into the ocean of nectar or bathing in a flood of ambrosia, through an outpouring of unsurpassed bliss (*ānanda*); and it became slow, with its other mental functions restrained, being solely intent on relishing that [bliss].

That very same [heart], now that she is absent, is kissed by embers as if touched by fragments of blazing fuel; while it ought to be said that it is "burned," the tender expression "kissed" is used out of fear of burning the beloved dwelling within the mind. It remains "vyathamānam," meaning tormented. The meaning is that this extreme difference in the state of the mind, arising from the mere distinction between her presence and absence for a single moment, is truly marvelous. //22//

Makaranda, though not seeing himself because his mind was elsewhere, makes himself known and calls out by himself: "Makaranda! Friend Mādhava! This way, this way; please come," is the ellipsis. "Lalāṭatapaḥ" and so forth: the meaning is that he stands in the middle of the sky, scorching the forehead (the sun). The suffix *khac* is applied by the rule "asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ"; the augment *mum* is added by the rule "khityanavyayasya. Kalahamsa: How is it that Mādhava, the companion of Makaranda, is adorning this very young garden?

I shall show him that which brings comfort to Mālatī’s eyes, which are currently tormented by the pangs of love—for the sight of a painting yields the fruit of mere visual perception—and which is his own likeness. Or rather, let him first experience the pleasure of rest; I will show it to him later—this is the implied meaning. Makaranda: "That" refers to the sweet fragrance, cool and astringent, spreading far and wide from the filaments of blooming flowers.

Although astringency and coolness are properties of taste (*rasadharma*), they are metaphorically attributed to the fragrance because they co-inhere in the same object as that particular taste. Therefore, let us sit in the shade of this golden *cāmpeya* tree, which has perfumed the garden with its scent. Regarding the verse beginning with "sakaleta" and so forth: "of a different kind" means in a distinct state. The particle "api" is used for inquiry. "Having laughed" [is the phrase].

The remainder of the sense is as follows: when Mādhava had lowered his face due to the knowledge of what was in his own mind, [the speaker] laughed at the correspondence with his own thought—that it was indeed the transformation of love (madanavikāra) that he had inferred to be the cause of this distinctiveness—and spoke in order to loosen her bashfulness by demonstrating his own favorability. What did he say? "Mugdham" means beautiful. "What suspicion or bashfulness can there be toward me, who am no different from your own inner heart? Therefore, speak with full confidence"—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, this infatuation with Smara (the God of Love) is certainly not your own invention, as it is common to gods, demons, and humans alike. Therefore, it is not right to deny this, as if it were something entirely improper never done before by others; thus he says, "In others. [He refers to] Viśvadhātṛ, the creator of the world, the eldest of the gods (Brahmā), who desired his own daughter; to the Supreme Lord (Śiva), who has his beloved (Pārvatī) seated upon half of his body; and even to Vāmadeva, the subduer of Smara—among these and other beings, that is, among all living creatures, whose discernment is obscured by darkness and impaired by ignorance. This is the meaning.

He is equal toward both the even and the uneven, his activity unimpeded. Such as he is, this one born of the mind (Cittajanman), who dwells within your heart, is of renowned power and celebrated majesty; indeed, he brings even Brahmā and the other gods under his control—what need is there to mention others? This is the sense. Therefore, do not let there be a concealment—that is, a denial or suppression within the mind—of that cause of transformation dwelling in your heart due to shame. Cast aside your bashfulness and speak; this is the meaning. //23//

Mādhava: Friend, why should I not tell you? My intention is this: even from you, who are the object of my entire confidence, there must be no concealment. As they say: "A friend is defined as one who shares the same joys and sorrows, is the sole repository of secrets, and is skilled in providing remedies for calamity.

Having had curiosity aroused by Avalokitā—who generated an eagerness to go by saying, "Today indeed there is a great festival for the city-dwellers in Madanodyāna; therefore, you too must go to see it"—I went to the temple of Kāmadeva, the site of the festival.

There, having wandered here and there out of a longing to behold beautiful objects, a fragrance arose from his exertion caused by that wandering—a fragrance that was spreading, sweet, captivating, and like the scent of wine; it was like the scent of *kesara* flowers produced by the *jāti* plant. Drawn by that fragrance, a swarm of bees gathered together; the row of flower buds, crowded and agitated by that swarm, served as his charming ornament. He [was the one] whose [ornament] was that very row of buds.

And thus, it is in a delightful courtyard, in front of the temple of the god Kāmadeva, that he is; by this, his suitability as a place for properly observing the festival is expressed. Regarding the young *bakula* tree: because it is young, the meaning is that he is sitting there plucking its flowers. He stands at the edge of the basin (*ālavāla*), which is cool from being watered daily. "Falling incessantly" means falling densely.

At the very place where he was seated, he began to fashion a captivating garland—charming through its skillful and beautiful arrangement—by taking as many blooming flowers as required according to his whim. Immediately thereafter: the world-conquering banner, the moving ensign that serves as the emblem of victory over the three worlds, went forth before him; and following that very banner, the God of Love set out with the desire to conquer the universe.

And my intention was that I had become the first target of his arrows. Her maidenhood—her state as a girl—is manifested by the arrangement of her ornaments and attire, which is radiant, luminous, clever, refined, charming, beautiful, and suited to a child; for she is still in the bloom of her first youth. Yet, because of her age, the thought remains that it cannot be known whether she is truly a maiden. She is of a noble nature and an exceedingly profound disposition. She is most generous and most courteous.

Because of the observation that "the word *udāra* is used for both 'generous' and 'great,' as well as for the 'southern quarter,'" she is one whose retinue is [thus] noble. From that very fact, the suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (meaning "where I was standing"), because it is applicable to all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). Now, he describes her form—which first came within the range of his vision—as if it were being perceived directly even now, beginning with the word *sā*: "She. The state of being beautiful is *rāmaṇīyaka*; the suffix *vuñ* is applied here according to the rule "after a word ending in *y* and having a heavy penultimate syllable."

"Beauty" means up to this point. Its "treasure-store" (nidhi) is its repository, like a conch or a lotus; or it refers to the presiding deity thereof. Or, it is the "abode" (niketana), the temple, of beauty—the excellence of every limb. O friend, the cause and material (upādāna) for her creation was the moon and so forth, but not the physical elements. And Madana was the architect (vedhāḥ), but not an ordinary one dulled by the study of the Vedas. As it is said: "In the act of creating her, the Creator was the moon, radiant with splendor," and so on.

By this description of the heroine’s virtues, it is stated that the great passion directed toward her is also excellent; thus, through the praise of the qualities of the "seed" (bīja), the element of the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) called *vilobhana* (enticement) is expressed.
