As it is said: "Enticement is the proclamation of those [the hero's] virtues. By defining the nature of these qualities, the fourth stage (*avasthā*) of Mādhava, consisting of the praise of virtues, is demonstrated. As it is said: "In beauty, nobility, and virtues, in playful gestures, smiles, and glances, and in the sweetness of his sight and conversation, there is no woman equal to her."

"Wherever such auspicious speech may exist, that alone is the praise of virtues. Here, the transitory mental state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of deliberation (*vitarka*) is manifested; as it is said: "Deliberation (*ūha*) is called *vitarka*, which [occurs] regarding the objects of others according to one's intelligence. This is a fusion (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and concealment (*apahnava*). //24//

"Then," [it is said]. By her affectionate female attendants—who were objects of her love, standing nearby and surrounding her—she was entreated as she desired the sport of gathering heaps of flowers; though she herself wished to go, her desire was blunted by modesty, and thus she was requested by them, who sought to delight her mind, to dispel that [hesitation]. To him alone, where I stood, and to some other extraordinary [place] of hers...

I observed the transformation produced by the affliction born of love—an affliction that had been accumulating for many days and increasing over a very long period—in him whose birth was due to such a specific excellence of virtuous conduct that even the performance of rites such as the *aśvamedha* sacrifice would seem insignificant compared to it. For one of a different nature would not possess the fortune required to ascend the throne of universal sovereignty over the three worlds, which is characterized by being a fit object for such a desire. He states the signs [of this] in his upward movement: "Because..."

"Parimṛditā" means withered by gradual emaciation, like a lotus stalk or a fiber of a lotus root (*mṛṇālī*); the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied here according to the rule "jāter astrīviṣayādayopadhāt. "Glānam" means having reached a state of exhaustion. This indicates a state of emaciation belonging to the stage of love (*madanadaśā*). Regarding activities such as bathing and drinking, her engagement occurs only with great difficulty through the entreaties of her attendants—such as their coaxing words, prostrations at her feet, and other conciliatory gestures—and not out of her own natural inclination.

The state of love known as "disgust for activity" (kriyādveṣarūpā ratiḥ) has been shown. Since this can also arise from the influence of physical illness, he states another unique symptom with the words "kalayati" (it assumes) and "abhinava" (fresh). The cheek, beautiful like a freshly cut tusk of an elephant, assumes the splendor—the beauty—of the stainless moon. Even though paleness may occur due to other causes, such similarity to the spotless orb of the moon is not possible elsewhere; thus, it is a unique external manifestation (anubhāva) of the state of separation (vipralambha).

In this passage, although only the consequents (anubhāvas) such as physical exhaustion and so forth are directly expressed, nevertheless, the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas)—such as despondency, languor, numbness, dejection, longing, anxiety, delusion, and agitation—which are invariably associated with these consequents, are understood as belonging to one of great fortune throughout his life; furthermore, the excitants (vibhāvas), such as the garden of Love and others, are indicated by the reference to the "birth" [of the hero]. Thus, the erotic sentiment of love-in-separation characterized by longing (abhilāṣavipralambha-śṛṅgāra) is suggested, being fully developed through the sustenance of the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) called love, which is nourished by the excitants, consequents, and transitory emotions. //25//

"She is mine," and so forth. Like a wick made of nectar, she produces such an unsurpassed bliss that, by the mere sight of her, the excellence or pre-eminence of all other pleasures is utterly eclipsed. Furthermore, she has drawn me toward herself, as if withdrawing a transformation of iron through the mere proximity of a magnet—the "iron-attracting gem-pin"—just as it draws a piece of iron. What more need be said?

What is the purpose of this particular modification of the mind, which has arisen at that time, which—due to its infinity and because experience is its sole means of proof—is impossible to describe specifically, and can only be defined in some vague way? He states that this much has already been accomplished: "It causes torment" (*saṃtapta*). This means my mind is "constantly attached" (*sadāsakta*) in such a way that no cause for attachment—no external condition serving as a motive—has been considered or reflected upon. Furthermore, this is not something with a happy outcome (*śubhodarka*), by which it might somehow be endured at present.

However, he says that this leads exclusively to misfortune: "A continuous succession of torments" means a persisting fever itself; "the great, supreme calamity" refers to the suffering that causes death, for the sake of which [this fever exists]. This is because the medicine for quenching such torment—in the form of attaining that [liberation]—is exceedingly difficult to find. The implication is that beyond this point, death alone is the refuge.

Anticipating the objection, "If you know this to be so, why do you not restrain your mind?", he says, "For the most part," to show that we, being subject to the impressions (*vāsanā*) of past karma, possess no independence whatsoever. [The goddess] is "Bhagavatī" because she possesses majesty; for even the Lord (*Īśvara*) is dependent upon her. For it has been said: "The Blessed One indeed creates the worlds in dependence upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings. She is "all-consuming" (*sarvaṃkaṣā*), as she pervades all objects by being the cause of every effect.

For without it, not even a single effect such as breathing can come to pass. Such "destiny" (bhavitavyatā)—which is indeed the ripening of past unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa)—ordains both the auspicious and the inauspicious for every living being. Just as we are not independent in accomplishing what is desired, so too are we not independent in warding off what is undesired. The meaning is that whatever has been brought about by the power of karma must necessarily be experienced. This is the figure of speech known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). //26//

Makaranda: [It is] "affection" (*sneha*). [The phrase] "dependent on a cause" means dependent on external adjuncts (*bāhyopādhi*). The meaning is that these two properties—being affection and being adventitious (*aupādhikatva*)—are contradictory when residing in a single substratum (*dharmin*). As for the twofold nature of affection mentioned in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*: "That moisture of the mind toward objects which consists essentially of fear and apprehension is called affection. Fluidity (*drava*) of the mind is of two kinds: from touch and also from sight."

Like lac from contact with fire, or like a moonstone from its sight, that moisture and coolness which exists in the minds of two people in all circumstances—that too is declared to be affection (*sneha*). And that affection is of two kinds, consisting of the artificial and the natural. Affection based on a condition is artificial; affection free from conditions is natural. When the condition ceases, that which was produced by it also ceases.

"By such statements as 'it will be born of the nature of oiliness and will persist as long as the substance exists,' one should understand that the term 'oiliness' (sneha) is applied through a metaphorical attribution of oiliness to that which possesses an adventitious adjunct (sopādhika). This establishes that natural oiliness is indeed independent of external adjuncts. 'Behold,' etc.—the meaning is: ascertain this matter by means of an illustration. 'It intermingles'—meaning it intermingles with objects and entities, both insentient and sentient."

An internal, hidden cause—some singular factor that can only be understood through its effects and is impossible to define through mere reasoning—binds them together and brings them into union. Furthermore, their affections and attachments do not depend upon external conditions or outward causes. He provides an illustration: at the rising of the sun, the lotus blossoms; and when the moon, the cold-rayed one, has risen, the moonstone melts.

And here, no external cause is perceived other than the natural affection [of their own nature]. Likewise, the fact that someone’s inner organ blossoms and melts at the mere sight of another anywhere is the majesty of innate love; this is the meaning. This is the figure of speech known as *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). //27//

"Then, then?"—the implication is, "Tell me what happened next. Mādhava: "And then..."—that is, immediately thereafter, at that very moment. "With a play of the eyebrows"—this refers to her clever and artful female companions having looked at me. Then, following my glance, glances filled with the nectar of smiles—charming through their association with the ambrosia of gentle laughter—and casting a particular luster of intent, were exchanged and sent to one another.

The meaning is that upon seeing me, they looked at one another preceded by smiles. Now, regarding the act of looking at me, he qualifies it with the words "as if with recognition" (*sapratyabhijñamiva*). Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a cognition that grasps the identity between a previously experienced object and the one present before one's eyes. Since she is a supreme Buddha, this recognition was not perceived by me through direct perception; rather, the word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that it was merely imagined. Anticipating the question, "How did you imagine this?", he states the reason: "as if [saying] 'This is he'."

The word *nāma* is used in the sense of "renown. That Mādhava, renowned by the name "the beloved of Mālatī’s life," who is celebrated in the conversations of her friends—it is as if there were a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) here, the seed of which is the conceptual identification (*utprekṣā*) that distinguishes between the aspects of "that-ness" and "this-ness" (*tattedantāṃśāvaccheda*), thinking, "This is he indeed. Yet, since even that [recognition]—consisting of verbal expression through the words "that" and "this"—is absent at that moment, and because the form of a cognition is not itself perceptible, he indicates with the word *iva* that this too is merely imagined. Anticipating the question, "How is even that inferred? he states its clear indicative mark (*liṅga*) with the phrase "with the play of her eyebrows."

The playfulness of the eyebrows is their movement. The meaning expressed by such an action—namely, "This very person who was the thief of our lady’s heart during social gatherings, the one named Mādhava, is this very same man"—is the skillful raising of the creeper-like brows. Together with that, the movement of the eyebrows manifests *tattedantā* (the identity of "that-ness" and "this-ness"), characterized by the former experience and the presence before the eyes; for such movement takes the form of a dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the object. Thus, the meaning is that by means of that [movement], through the specific attribute of delimiting "that-ness" and "this-ness," their recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding me is inferred. This is the *bhāvika* ornament. //28//

Makaranda—(To himself: How so? The word "nāma" (by name) is used here in the sense of possibility. The reflection is: how could there be a recognition of them when it has never been experienced before? This should be understood as directed toward himself; otherwise, Mādhava would have to provide a reply. Mādhava—Now, immediately thereafter, those attendants came right before her into my presence. Upon seeing me, they turned back and [informed] her who was coming from behind. Their fingers themselves were the petals.

The description of the fingers as petals illuminates the hand’s nature as a lotus. Their "grace" (*vilāsa*) refers to refined and charming movements; it was by means of these that they spoke to me. In response to the expectation of how they returned, there are three adverbs. Among them, *salīlam* means "with grace," accompanied by playfulness (*līlā*). Grace (*līlā*) is defined as the imitation of a desired object through the movement of the outer corners of the eyes (*apāṅga*), as in: "By means of mind, sweet speech, and bodily gestures impelled by affection... [and so forth].

"Līlā" is the imitation of a beloved; it may belong to both women and men. "Uttālā" means raised. It refers to the clapping of the two hands—specifically, the striking together of the palms with fingers extended upward—which causes the series of bracelets (*kaṅkaṇa*) on the rows of bangles to tremble. Thus [the action] should be performed.

The *kalahaṃsas* are those who are startled, agitated, and intoxicated; their *vibhrama* is a distinctive wandering, and their gait is charming. Like that, the movement of her feet is delightful. By means of that, the anklets (*mañjīra*, *nūpura*) produce a pleasant tinkling sound (*raṇaraṇāyamāna*). This is interwoven with, or mingled with, the jingling (*śiñjita*) of the small bells (*kṣudraghaṇṭikā*) fixed upon her girdle (*kāñcīdāman*), making it resonant (*mukhara*). Thus [she moves].

In response to the inquiry, "What have you said?", [she replies: "O noble lady, by good fortune we are prospering! For in this very place, according to the saying, 'The very creeper that was being sought has now clung to your feet,' here before us is someone—or rather, some person. The use of the general term 'someone' (asau) is intended to conceal him, as it would be improper to point him out directly. Furthermore, the use of the phrase 'of someone' (kasyā api) instead of 'of you' (tava) is a veiled expression, as the latter would be inappropriate; it means that your beloved is standing there."

However, some, considering even the feminine gender to be inappropriate, read "kasyāpi" (of someone) and explain it as "janasya" (of a person). Makaranda: "Hanta" expresses joy. The "udbheda" (emergence) of the great, deeply rooted prior passion is its manifestation; the word "pratibhāti" (appears) is to be supplied. "Udbheda" is a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the "Mukha-saṃdhi" (opening juncture); as it is said: "Udbheda is the disclosure of what was hidden. Kalahaṃsa: Between these two, there is an uninterrupted conversation concerning women, characterized by a continuous flow of charming and delightful topics; the verb "vartate" (is occurring) is to be supplied.

Makaranda: And then? And then? Mādhava: "In the meantime," [meaning] at this juncture, the office of the preceptor of love was exercised by that large-eyed maiden. For Love alone is the preceptor in the instruction of various amorous graces bestowed upon young maidens, being one whose identity is entirely unfamiliar to them. His "office" (ācāryakam) refers to his state as a preceptor; [the suffix -vuñ is applied here] according to the rule *yopadhādgurūpottamādvuñ*. His proficiency in instructing in the various gestures of the erotic sentiment manifested—that is, it became manifest. Of what sort was it?

[It is] a state of manifoldness that transcends the entire range of modes of expression and surpasses the diversity of the power of speech; for this very reason, it is something that cannot be specifically pointed out. It is where a *vibhrama* (bewildered charm) has arisen. *Vibhrama* is a particular kind of amorous gesture (*śṛṅgāraceṣṭā*). As it is said: "The inversion of speech, bodily movement, mental disposition, dramatic representation, ornamentation, and posture, when fashioned with haste upon seeing the beloved—that is *vibhrama*."

That [object] is contemplated by the mind alone, accompanied by abundant *sāttvika* transformations—that is, a profusion of *sāttvika* states such as paralysis (*stambha*) and the like. Regarding these *sāttvika* states, it has been said: "That state of being which arises through the contemplation of that [object] in a manner conducive to it is *sattva*; those produced by that are declared to be *sāttvika*. For example: "Paralysis, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are considered the *sāttvika* states."

"Apāstadhairyam" means that the steadiness of mind has been cast off by both of them due to seeing one another. "Vijayi" means victorious or characterized by the habit of conquering; it refers to that which spreads unimpeded anywhere. Here, because there is a composition based on the experience of the full-blown erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), there is the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the erotic sentiment, complete with the presence of the objective (*ālambana*) and excitatory (*uddīpana*) determinants (*vibhāva*) through the perception of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as delusion and agitation appropriate to it. Furthermore, the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *parikara* (periphrasis). //29//

And thus, from the presence of that very object of its own focus—the long-standing, weighty, and ancient passion, accumulated through a continuous stream of verbal conceptualizations and memories, which constitutes the very essence of life—there arises, like the ocean of milk at the touch of the moon’s rays, a surging tide whose interior is filled to overflowing; and by the logic of a full jar bursting forth, it repeatedly wells up externally, attaining the state of *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) characterized by unsurpassed intensification, like a mass of billowing waves.

He says that the amorous glances, which constitute the very first manifestation [of love] and were directed toward me as their object, appeared: "Then... and so on, "stimita... and so forth. I became the manifold recipient of those specific amorous glances. As it is said: "A glance in the context of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is desired to be gracious, playful, lovely, modest, imbued with the intent of passion, and featuring moving eyebrows and side-long looks."

He qualifies [the gaze] in order to show its specific nature: [it is that of eyes] which, immediately after opening while I was standing right before them, fell upon me and remained motionless upon that very object out of a longing to see; "stimita" (fixed/still) is indeed a transformation of the erotic gaze (*śṛṅgāradṛṣṭi*). As it is said: "That which does not move from its own range is called *stimita*. Then, [there is the gaze] of those whose eyes have blossomed, perceiving every single detail within the object. The transformation of the blossomed gaze is as follows: "The blossomed gaze penetrates the specific details within the object."

Therefore, those whose creeper-like eyebrows are accompanied by the movement of the brows known as *catura*—which quiver slightly, swelling with joy born from the savoring of sensory objects; for *catura* is a name for a particular movement of the brows, as it is said: "The arrangement of the brows is sweet through a slight swelling [of joy] that is *catura*"—and by whom this modification of the gaze called *prasanna* is expressed, as it is said: "That is *prasanna* which is accompanied by the play of the brows and a smile"—[they are] thus *masṛṇānām*, meaning tender and charming due to their passion.

An example of a gentle modification of the gaze (*masṛṇadṛgvikāra*) is as follows: "That [gaze] should be known as gentle when it is suffused with passion. Then, due to being overcome by pleasure, there are eyes that are half-closed and not fully opened. By this, the "half-closed" (*mukulita*) gaze is described. And an example of the modification of the gaze called "half-closed" (*mukulita*) is as follows: "With the tips of the eyelashes slightly quivering and touching, the lids raised and turned upward, and the pupil partially opened by pleasure—this is considered the 'half-closed' (*mukula*) gaze."

"The gaze remains half-closed during dreamy, pleasant sleep"—by this, the facial expression known as *vikūṇita* (the contraction of the eyes) is described. As for *vikūṇita*: "That gaze in which three parts are contracted while the other part is expanded, being characterized by a distinct look, is called *vikūṇita*. Thereafter, [the glances] are those that possess expansion in the corners—the regions of the outer eyes—due to the desire to see again; that is to say, they are those that have fully embraced their objects.

For it is the side-long glance (*apāṅgadṛṣṭi*), falling upon that very object, which correctly discerns the object of perception. By this, two modifications of the gaze are described: the "expansive" (*vistārī*) and the "longing" (*saspṛha*). As it is said: "That by which an object is embraced is called expansive; where there is a repeated longing of the gaze, that is the longing [glance]."

Then, when the fall of my eye—sent toward him to observe his return—occurred simultaneously and directly before him, [his eyes] were slightly contracted and somewhat closed out of bashfulness. Regarding the modification of the gaze called *saṃkucita*, it is said: "That in which there is a contraction of the outer corners is *kuñcita*. By the use of the plural number, the modification of the gaze known as *lola* is indicated, as it conveys the sense of a continuous, flowing movement.

For example: "That which possesses a continuous flow [of glances] is called *lolā* (tremulous). By the word "various" (*vividha*), he includes other specific modifications of the erotic glance—such as those characterized by a longing for sweet flavors, yearning, eagerness, passion, affection, love-filled expansion, grace, and softness. Their definitions are not written here for fear of prolixity. This is the ornament (*alaṃkāra*) known as *parikara* (the preparatory). //30//

Now I have become such a vessel for her gaze. Therefore, he describes that very state once more: "Then... [he says] "Alas... Her eyes possess lashes that are thick with extremely dense eyelashes; by means of her side-long glances—defined as "the casting of the pupil toward the outer corner of the eye is called a *kaṭākṣa*"—those specific types of looks previously mentioned, my heart was left without refuge. At that time, because I was rendered powerless by a state of total dependence (*pāravaśya*), protection by another was impossible, and since she herself was absent, [I remained unprotected].

Finding no protector, it was forcibly snatched away and seized. Because of the captivating nature of her side-long glances, at that moment my mind became as if empty. Then, because my intellect had been stolen away by them, it was carried off and cast aside; due to their extreme sharpness, it was as if pierced by iron arrows (nārācas). The meaning is that it experienced pain, as if perforated by the tips of sharpened shafts.

And so, because those glances were like the heated arrows of the God of Love, my mind—having melted upon being pierced by them and dissolved right there according to the analogy of a stream of water—was as if drunk up by them. Just as water or the like that has been drunk dissolves within the drinker, the meaning is that my mind dissolved within their sidelong glances. Furthermore, fearing the potential re-sprouting of my mind even though it had dissolved into the basin of my heart, they uprooted it—that is, they pulled out its very root—rendering it incapable of arising again. This is the meaning.

This is an exaggeration (*atiśayokti*) regarding the extreme state of mental subjugation; it has been described by the poet in this way solely for the sake of enhancing his poetic maturity (*prauḍhi*). However, some explain it as follows: just as a clever man, having stolen the fruit of a coconut tree, pierces it with an iron spike, makes it perforated, drinks the water inside, and then extracts and eats the pulp within, so too these side-glances (*kaṭākṣa*), having stolen the fruit of the mind from the very tree of Mādhava, first pierce it—since it is firm due to its depth and fortitude—and make it wounded.

They explain that the simile of the coconut fruit is stated as follows: having drunk up the modesty, discipline, discernment, and so forth contained within it—which had emerged through the openings of its wounds—the [hunter] was still not satisfied by that much alone; thus, he uprooted the very root characterized by consciousness and began to devour it. To the question, "Of what kind were those side-glances? he says: "Sluggish," and so on. "Sluggish" means those cast first. "Extended before" means they were directed toward me, who was standing right in front. Then, as if out of shame upon reflection, they turned back.

*Alasā* and the others are the modifications of the gaze (*dṛṣṭi-vikāra*) in the context of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). Among these, *alasa* (the languid) is as follows: "The *alasa* is that which turns away from a desired object due to shame and other such reasons. Then there are the *valita* (turned) glances, which are cast obliquely upward out of a longing to see again. Regarding *valita*: "The *valita* is the triangular look of one who has turned back again. The definition of the triangular (*tryaśra*) is: "The triangular is that which is cast obliquely upward. Then there are the *mugdha* (innocent) glances, whose nature consists of an internal state accompanied by some pretext.

The innocent (*mugdha*) is as follows: "The innocent [gaze] is one that looks naturally, yet contains an inner emotion through artifice. Thereafter, the affectionate (*snigdha*) is that which is permeated by the state of passion (*rati*), a synonym for love; the affectionate gaze is as follows: "That which is affectionate is joined with a state of passion consisting primarily of love. Thereafter, the motionless (*niṣpanda*) does not move elsewhere from its object; the motionless is as follows: "That is motionless which does not flicker anywhere other than where it has been seen."

Consequently, they were sluggish and disinclined toward moving to other regions; by this, "sluggish vision" (*mantharadṛṣṭi*) is described, as in the phrase: "sluggish means slow-moving. [This state] leads to an expansion—characterized by the sight of an object that causes wonder and further blossoms—toward being oriented toward the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and its transitory emotions (*bhāva*). The astonishment residing within the internal organ is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the marvelous flavor (*adbhutarasa*). By means of that, they are described as "smiling," their pupils wide open with rows of quivering eyelashes.

Regarding the *smera* (smiling) gaze: "That which has trembling eyelashes and pupils is called *smera*. This very same gaze, when it manifests the sentiment of wonder (*vismaya-rasa*), is known as the *vismitā* (astonished) gaze. As it is said: "The *vismitā* gaze is remembered as being used in wonder; its pupils are dilated with astonishment, both lids are raised and curved in joy, and the gaze is even and wide-open."

Here, through the side-glances (*kaṭākṣa*) and other such *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) of that nature, there is the perception of the emotion of love (*rati-bhāva*) directed toward Mādhava, which has reached its highest intensity; and through the appropriate *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory emotions), as well as through Mādhava’s own words beginning with "my heart has been stolen," there is the perception of his deep passion for Mālatī as its object, along with the specific transitory emotions and their corresponding *anubhāvas*. Thus, there occurs a simultaneous *dhvani* (suggestive resonance) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) based on mutual objects.

For this very reason, it is said that the *mukha-sandhi-aṅga* (limb of the introductory juncture) called *parinyāsa* (the conclusion) is established, due to the full development of the "seed" (*bīja*), which is their mutual passion.
The [verse] runs as follows: "Its accomplishment is the final renunciation. //31//

"But I"—[meaning] even though she, who is enchanting in every way through her physical form, the arrangement of her limbs, the play of her glances, the movement of her body, and so forth, was already the object of my affection as conceived through the specific ways of looking previously described; and even though that very affection, being the "rasa" (the aesthetic flavor) because it is to be relished, had been brought under control—that is, made submissive—by her presence near me; and even though my sensory faculties were elsewhere withdrawn from their functions; [he is one] whose desire is to conceal his own restlessness and loss of composure from others.

He had somehow managed to finish weaving the remainder of the filigree garland he had previously begun, his mind being elsewhere due to intense absorption; thus, the meaning of the sentence beginning with "Then, when the cane was joined" is clear. The sense is that the Madana garden, like the sky from which the full moon has long since departed, or as if shrouded in blinding darkness, became in some way unfit for sight. And at the time of her departure, he states the basis of hope for her sustaining her life: "As she goes... [yāntyeti].

As she was departing—moving away even at the very moment of her departure—with her neck turned back in eager longing for a sight of me, she bore a face resembling a lotus with its stalk twisted from its base, like a full-blown white lily turned away from its bond; and though many side-glances were cast by that long-lashed-eyed woman, they were obstructed by being blocked by the dense branches of the trees, yet by chance, one single glance pierced through and was deeply, firmly embedded in my heart.

It is as if his heart has been thrust inside; by the word "deeply" (*gāḍham*), he indicates that it cannot be extracted again. The sense is that, because it is firmly attached, it remains exactly as it was even now, causing pain like a thorn within. The poetic conceit (*samādhi*) is that the archer Manmatha, having taken her very creeper-like eyebrow as his bow and her side-glance as an arrow, has driven it into the target of my mind in such a way that it can never be pulled out. What kind of side-glance is it? It is smeared with both nectar and poison.

At the moment of falling [into his power], it produces unsurpassed bliss; even now, because it is the cause of life, it is "smeared with nectar" (*amṛta*). Because it is the cause of the unbearable agony of separation, it should be seen as "smeared with poison" (*viṣa*). By this, the constituent element (*aṅga*) called *vidhāna* (the mode) is stated, according to the rule: "The mode (*vidhāna*) is that which produces pleasure and pain. The phrase "as if dug in" suggests the shaft-like nature of the side-glance due to its sharpness; thus, the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). //32//

Regarding the words "thence" (*tataḥ*) and "in the discernment" (*paricchede*): from the moment it was fixed by her side-long glance, a certain transformation or change has occurred. It stupefies the internal organ (*antaram*), rendering it devoid of comprehension; and in that very state, it produces heat—that is, it causes intense torment. This is a description of two stages of love (*madana-avasthā*): stupor (*jāḍya*) and feverish distress (*saṃjvara*). Among these, stupor is as follows: "Stupor is a constant lack of comprehension regarding all activities; one does not perceive the pleasant or the unpleasant, nor does one feel pleasure or pain."

"In response to a question, one says nothing; one neither hears nor sees; one utters cries of 'Alas! Alas!', makes sudden exclamations of 'Hum!', and the limbs become limp. Emaciation, discoloration, labored breathing, stiffness, and insensitivity to touch—these states arising from *jāḍya* (stupefaction) are attributed to the god whose banner is the fish. As for *saṃjvara* (fever): "An unbearable burning of the mind is proclaimed as *saṃjvara*, by which one feels as if one were wallowing in the midst of a river of glowing coals. Furthermore, *jāḍya* is a state of rigidity resulting from contact with extremely cold substances.

By that [glance], she stupefies; because of its extreme coolness, she stiffens; and she expands the heat—when this is said, a contradiction is perceived, for there is a contradiction between the nature of coolness and being the cause of heat. The resolution, however, lies in the fact that looking with a turned neck indicates affection. Even when now being recollected as being anointed with the nectar of intense passion, the sidelong glance makes one feel as if immersed in nectar. Yet, when contemplated through the realization of the hopelessness of attaining her again, it causes pain like poison.

Therefore, there is the figure of speech *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction). To the question "What kind of transformation (*vikāra*) is it?", he says: "beyond determination" (*paricchedātīta*). Determination (*pariccheda*) is knowledge consisting of the ascertainment that "it is this much" or "it is so great. That which is beyond this is not its object. Likewise, it is "beyond all words," meaning it is not within the range of any verbal operation, such as primary denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and so forth. By these two adjectives, its unaccessibility to both speech and mind is expressed.

And since this [transformation] cannot be compared by saying "it is like that" with any previously experienced change whatsoever, he says: "again. It is not known what was experienced in another birth, because those who do not remember their past lives (*ajātismara*) have no recollection of what occurred in a prior existence. The sense is that, in this present life, however, no such transformation has yet entered the path of experience by which this [present state] could be compared.

Likewise, because of the destruction—and thus the absolute eradication—of that discriminative knowledge (*viveka*) born from hearing the scriptures and so forth, which is the opponent of ignorance; [the forest] is "dense" (*gahana*), meaning difficult to traverse, due to that great delusion (*mahāmoha*), which is a firm error or nescience (*avidyā*). By this, the state of intoxication known as *unmāda* is indicated, as it is said: "Unmāda arising from separation is the persistent grasping at what is not that as being that; it is a state of mind that occurs everywhere, in all conditions, in every way, and at all times."

"Devoted to him, delighted by talk of him, he hates even other loved ones; he sighs deeply and repeatedly, and remains with unblinking eyes; during times of recreation, he weeps, cries out, and meditates for a moment; he becomes weary, trembles, laughs at himself, praises himself, and faints. Thus have the states born of madness been described by those skilled in drama. By these very characteristics, [the character] has been explained as "a certain person" (ko'pi). //33//

Now, he states that the effects and experiences of this transformation are immeasurable, saying: "The manifestation of determination" (*paricchedavyakti*). Even when an object is present before one, in contact with the senses, and capable of being grasped, there occurs no manifestation—that is, no clear appearance or the resulting state of patentness (*prākaṭya*)—arising from a "determination," which is a correct experience consisting of the ascertainment, "This is a jar," or "This is a cloth."

By this, it has been stated that because the mind is afflicted by modification (*vikāra*), the eye and other senses do not function toward the cognition of external objects due to their lack of stability. He says "it occurs" (*bhavati*) to show that [the mind] does not function correctly even in the case of recollection (*smaraṇa*). In the case of an unpracticed object—something grasped only once upon its sudden appearance—the experience might sometimes fail to deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Or, even if an impression were deposited, it might sometimes fail to produce recollection due to a lack of firmness. However, when an object is grasped again, because a firmer impression is deposited, there must necessarily be a recollection corresponding to the original experience.

Furthermore, in this case, even regarding an object that has been repeatedly experienced, memory does not arise in accordance with the original experience, despite the presence of causes for the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), such as the sight of similar objects. On the contrary, under the influence of defects (*doṣa*), there occurs a recollection that is discordant, distorted, and erroneous, by virtue of its being otherwise than it was. In some instances, no memory arises at all regarding what was previously experienced; rather, the meaning is that there is merely a reversal of memory (*smṛtiviparyaya*).

In a lake of snow, in a pool of frost, or in the moon whose body consists of nectar, there is no cessation of the fever. The meaning is that because it cannot be cooled by any cooling substance whatsoever, the fever does not subside. The implication is that you should not attempt any application of cold remedies at all. Nevertheless, my mind remains empty due to its persistence in this state.

The meaning is that having begun to pursue some purpose, one is unable to bring what was commenced to completion because of its utter forgetfulness in the very midst of it. He states the reason for this: "and he wanders" (*bhramati*). The meaning is that he does not remain still upon any object even for a moment. It should be understood that the expression "it numbs and spreads heat" (*jaḍayati ca tāpaṃ ca tanute*) is a repetition of those very two qualities—stupefaction and torment—already mentioned. The poetic figure is either *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction) or *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). //34//

Kalahamsa: Indeed, he has been firmly captivated by someone today. Could it possibly be Mālatī herself? For just as he does not tolerate even the mention of another woman, so too has he been seized today by someone who fell within the range of his vision at the time of the festival procession. Indeed, for two youths, a festival procession is the primary means for their first encounter—as it is said: "A procession, a public appearance, an excursion, a dream, a painting, or a conversation about love..."

"For there are means for the first glance, since passion increases between two youths. Thus, he has been captivated; his mind has been brought under her control. She is the one who draws the heart [toward her]. "Apināma" is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*); it is Mālatī herself who is considered possible. The meaning is that she alone possesses the beauty suitable for being the object of such longing. Makaranda—[speaking] to himself: when a matter is not intended to be heard by others, the term *svagataṃ* (to oneself) is employed.

As it has been said: "The subject matter (*vastu*) is proclaimed to be twofold, by way of the distinction between what is to be heard and what is not to be heard. That which is restricted to all [characters] is remembered as 'to be heard' (*śrāvya*), and that is also considered to be of two kinds. Therein, that which is 'not to be heard' (*aśrāvya*) is to be employed as 'aside' (*svagata*); one should use the term 'aside' for that. That which is audible to all is 'open' (*prakāśa*); one should use the term 'open' for that. Furthermore, that which is to be heard by a specific person alone is divided into two types with respect to dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharma*): namely, *janānta* (aside to another) and *apavārita* (aside to oneself). One should employ *janānta* when speaking to another while excluding others by means of the *tripatāka* hand gesture."

"That which is a mutual address is called *janāntika* (aside). That which is spoken in secret elsewhere, turning away [from others], is called *apavārita* (whispered). This is due to the requirements of dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharma*) for the purpose of advancing the plot. *Abhiṣaṅga* means attachment or obsession. This unprecedented intensification of mental attachment occurring all at once is called the *saṃdhyanga* (limb of the juncture) named "Paribhāvana" (Intensification), because of the onset of wonder; for it is said, "Paribhāva is the onset of wonder. Therefore, what is this? Thus now his state of madness persists.

Immediately upon that, even before the ten calamities had actually occurred, the thought arose within himself: "Shall I restrain him from this affliction? Having reflected thus, he determined that it was impossible to prevent it—saying, "Or rather: 'May he not be deluded' (mā mūmuhat). This means: "May Kāma, who is born of no other source and whose sole origin is his own mind, not delude you; may he not cause you to fall into confusion. The *luṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

"Let your mind not be so densely covered—thickly veiled—by that dark, impure, and censurable transformation known as the assault of passion, which is opposed to the three aims of life (trivarga). Such a collection of instructions would be useless and fruitless in this very state, because it leads to what ought not to be done. The word "nanu" is used here for emphasis, referring to oneself.

He states the reason for its futility: in this month of Mādhava, desire remains present—its limbs stretched wide, its sleep freshly manifest, its qualities expanding—and its activities continue to rob the lives of those separated from their lovers; furthermore, youth persists, characterized by the increasing loss of discernment and other such traits. Therefore, there is nothing at all to be instructed to him now.

Just as advice given to a traveler whose entire property has been plundered by bandits—such as, "This road is infested with thieves; therefore, you should not go by this path"—is useless, so too is the instruction "Do not fall under the power of love" directed toward one whose mind is already helplessly drawn by powerful passion. Because the opportunity has passed, such advice is entirely futile. As it is said: "What would be achieved by one who says to a man who has already finished eating, 'Do not eat'? //35//

Having thus determined that it is impossible to deny [her love] for himself, and desiring to avert her distress by fulfilling her desire, he adopts a conciliatory attitude and asks: "Aloud. "Friend, it is known from your own words and from her specific gestures that she is indeed enamored of you. What remains to be known is in what family she was born, whether she is suitable for a matrimonial alliance, and what her name is. Your question—"Is there anything you know regarding the means to achieve this?"—is directed toward that end."

Mādhava: "Listen," and so forth. Having delayed by means of the pretext of gathering flowers; [he says,] "I gather those very flowers" in the course of collecting them. Having drawn closer and become more proximate, she bows under the pretext of a flower-garland—joining her lotus-hands at the surface of her forehead as if binding a wreath upon her head—and thus pays homage. By this salutation, it is indicated that you alone shall be the husband of my mistress.

She spoke thus to me as I was about to speak. Having already learned from the mouth of Avalokitā and others of Mādhava’s proficiency in all the arts (*kalā*), she begins to speak skillfully, starting with "O noble one" (*mahābhāga*). One whose fortune (*bhāga*) or lot (*bhāgadheya*) is great is a "noble one. According to the rule "the suffix *dheya* is added after *nāman*, *rūpa*, and *bhāga*," the word *bhāga* itself becomes *bhāgadheya* when used in its own sense. The meaning is: "one whose excellence of great fortune is perceived by his very appearance."

This arrangement—the manner of arranging the flowers, the skill in weaving the garland—is delightful and captivating due to its well-knit threads and its nature as a string with well-formed knots. And our mistress is curious regarding this particular excellence in the composition of flower-garlands, which displays such supreme artistry. She is called "Bhartṛdārikā" (the daughter of the master) because the minister Bhūrivasu is equal to a king; she is so addressed to indicate great respect for her.

In her, who serves as the locus [of this activity], there exists a novel operation regarding flowers—one never before seen elsewhere, variegated, and producing a sense of wonder—in the form of weaving garlands. The meaning is that, having attained an extraordinary and unique renown in this art of floral arrangement, and having now perceived your skill in weaving garlands to be equal to her own cleverness, she remains with a mind overcome by curiosity.

Therefore, let there be the fulfillment of your cleverness—the proficiency in weaving this garland of flowers—through being cherished by that woman who is herself skilled in discerning such artistry. As it has been said: "I do not consider a mastery of performance to be truly successful until it satisfies the learned. Let the fruit of her own creation of this garland likewise consist solely in the delighting of those who recognize its beauty; the meaning is that even though individual flowers, once plucked, no longer produce their own natural fruits, let this very thing be its fruit.

Therefore, let this unfading lotus of yours—endowed with such loveliness and artistry, and offered by you with such affection—attain great value and high price by serving as a neck-ornament for the princess, through its being worn as a pendant around her neck.

Just as some supreme jewel placed upon a crown ornament of finest gold becomes of great value, so too may this Bakula-garland, which is like a jewel, become of great value by serving as a neck-ornament for the princess; such is the literal meaning. Another interpretation, however, is that this union of yours—which revolves in the minds of well-wishing friends like us and of impartial connoisseurs as something to be wished for—is merely a matter of aspiration.

In that regard, there is a novel operation of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma)—unprecedented by any lover separated from their beloved and therefore extraordinary and wondrous. The meaning is that you are being powerfully overcome by Smara (Love) on account of him. Therefore, let the fulfillment of the erudition—the mastery of all arts—of both through their mutual union come to pass.

The meaning is: "She alone in this world is worthy to know the essence of your cleverness (*vaidagdhya*), and you alone are worthy to know hers; thus, through the attainment of an object of mutual recognition suited to each other, let the cleverness of both be rendered fruitful. And the definition of cleverness is as follows: "Cleverness is proclaimed to be proficiency in thorough mastery regarding worldly matters, Vedic matters, and likewise conventional matters."

May the loveliness of the Creator’s activity—the fashioning of an emanation characterized by both [sexes]—bear fruit through the very result of the union of you two; for otherwise, the effort of the Ordainer in creating this pair of man and woman, so radiant with the excellence of such a laborious creation, would be entirely in vain. This is the intended meaning.

Therefore, may you—who are a jewel of the three worlds, full of passion, and the foremost of connoisseurs—attain great value by hanging around her neck, that is, by embracing her throat. For she alone is worthy of purchasing you, who are like a priceless gem, with the wealth of her own beauty—a wealth consisting of the pleasure of embracing your neck, which is imagined as a test for the lover Rati—and which is beyond the reach of other young women, whether poor or otherwise; no one else is so capable, such is the meaning.

In this passage, under the pretext of a prayer for a garland of flowers, there is a *patākāsthānaka* (an intermediate juncture), because it indicates—by means of another's request—the previously accomplished matter of Mālatī’s separation and the future matters that will persist until the conclusion, all witnessed by the bakula-garland. As it is said: "When past and future events of a plot are related under the guise of another's pretext, that is indeed a *patākāsthānaka*."

For this very reason, it is specifically a *bakula* garland—fragrant and capable of enduring for a long time even when withered—that has been mentioned by the poet, and not merely any other kind of flower garland. (Makaranda: The meaning is that such eloquence in speech is a marvel belonging only to her attendant’s cleverness. (Mādhava: When she was questioned—"Who is she, and whose daughter is she?"—she replied: "This one," and so forth. *Prasūtiḥ* means offspring; it does not mean she is an adopted child or of mixed caste. By this, her fitness for marriage is indicated.

"She is a ground of confidence and a vessel of trust; therefore, one should not entertain any doubt toward me"—thus it was said. By the word "dhātreyī" (the foster-sister), her own words being beyond transgression and her knowledge of all his vital secrets are indicated. Kalahamsa (with joy): [The reason for his joy is as follows: "She by whom this portrait of him was brought by me—this man is now attached to that very Mālatī; thus my efforts have now borne fruit. This is the cause of his joy. "What indeed is this 'Mālatī'?"—by this, it is stated that Mālatī is the object of his passion.

"What indeed?"—this is an interrogative exclamation (*kāku*) indicating an excess of joy. "Then, by good fortune, the divine Lord Kusumāyudha has manifested his power; we have triumphed. This means that all of us, who were occupied with the mission of messengers and intent upon our duty, have succeeded. The plural number in "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*) is used because, at the moment of my lord's life-threatening crisis, we took pride in ourselves by bringing the semblance of the medicine for his restoration and thereby saving his life. Makaranda (to himself): "O Minister... [He addresses him.]

The meaning is that the mere fact of her being the daughter of a minister is not sufficient grounds for such high esteem toward her. For she is not merely an object of great respect because she is the daughter of a minister; rather, it is also due to her possession of qualities such as a beauty that transcends the world. Therefore, the sense is that even though this transformation of passion arose in him by chance, it is indeed praiseworthy because its object is so worthy. He establishes this very insufficiency of [mere] respect with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended to indicate extreme regard; the meaning is that he himself always praises her. And [the phrase] "and her" (*tāṃ ca*)... [is used].

Even the king, though capable of procuring and bestowing a thousand maidens upon his jester-friend, accepted the role of a lowly messenger because he was unable to provide a young woman like Mālatī, who is the very object of his desire. The point is: what need is there to speak of her praiseworthiness? Mādhava: "By her," and so forth; "being pursued" means being repeatedly entreated with affectionate words.

In order to show that the garland is praiseworthy because it was worn and then discarded by his beloved, he says "from his own neck" (*ātmanaḥ kaṇṭhāt*). Regarding the passage beginning with "this one" (*asau*), the connection is as follows: with a gaze fixed upon it—meaning a gaze intent solely on that garland due to the attainment of an object difficult to obtain—he highly prizes that very garland.

Because her mind was attached elsewhere due to the sight of Mālatī, she was distracted from the task at hand; thus, with one part already woven, it was "uneven"—meaning disfigured and unattractive compared to the preceding portion—and yet she had woven another part after seeing Mālatī. The sense is that she did not hold the garland in high esteem because of its beauty, but rather because it was woven by me. For this very reason, he will say later: "Whether because it was woven by me out of affection, or because it was brought by the hand of my dear friend."

"Immediately thereafter," and so forth. [This refers to] the people of the city (*paura*) and the people of the market-town (*naigama*). The distinction between a city (*pura*) and a market-town (*nigama*) is stated as follows: "That which is situated on a mountain, in a forest, or in a kingdom, crowded with the dwellings of all people, and engaged in the business of buying and selling—that which is thus exalted is called a *pura*. That which is endowed with the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), crowded with the dwellings of all people, and engaged in many types of labor—that is designated as a *nigama*. In the phrase "in the eyes being torn apart by the crush of the crowd," the meaning is that they were separated from the range of vision, having fallen away from contact with the eyes and become obscured.

Makaranda—now, having confirmed through various signs that Mālatī’s affection for him, which had been generally known by Mādhava but was doubted due to his own lack of confidence, has become firm, speaks in order to steady her mind: "Friend," [he says]. The meaning is: since her affection for you is now perceived from your words, this task has been successfully accomplished.

Nor should it be suspected that she was already possessed of such pallor on her cheeks and other symptoms even before seeing me—therefore, that she has fixed her affection on some other youth previously seen by her, and not on me. For you alone were previously seen by her somewhere, and are the cause of this long-accumulating obsession with the transformations of love. However, one must simply know where you were previously seen by her; thus he says, beginning with "yohi... and so forth.

"How can it be determined that I alone am the cause in this matter? To this he replies: "Certainly not... Such women—resplendent with a multitude of virtues such as noble lineage and character, born of great fortune, and having obtained birth through the ripening of excellent past deeds—possess "an attraction of the eye," meaning they possess delight for the eyes. As it is said: "Noble-born and virtuous maidens, whose ornaments are their good fortune, never become vessels for the stain of infamy. Even if her heart were attached to another, she would not cast her gaze upon you."

"The mind of one woman is elsewhere and her gaze elsewhere, but this is not the case for the most excellent of women"—this is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). He says "moreover" (*api ca*) to indicate that there is yet another sign of her prior affection for you. Regarding the phrase "of those whose gazes are mutually intermingled": among her friends, whose eyes are mixed together as they look at one another's faces in order to recognize with certainty (*sapratyabhijñam*)—thinking "it is indeed he"—that some beloved of someone is present right here, this [fact] was reported.

And the "informing" (prajñāpana) of her own friend is one [point]; the meaning is that this is a sign (cihna) or mark (liṅga) for this purpose: namely, that her prior passion was indicated toward you alone by her paleness and other such symptoms.

Then Mādhava, out of eagerness—wondering whether Lavaṅgikā will or will not manifest that other sign of love which he himself had determined to be in the form of her words—and unable to endure waiting for the opportunity to hear them, asks with the word "and" (ca), implying "what else do you add? by asking: "Mādhava: And what? The particle "ca" (and) means: "What other sign of prior affection does she indicate? Makaranda replies: "Of the foster-sister. This is cleverly phrased; the ellipsis is "a sign of prior affection. //36//

Kalahaṃsa: And this—meaning, that this too is a sign of her prior affection, and thus he offers the painting as the occasion arises. Since Makaranda has only superficially understood Mālatī’s activities up to the point of the drawing of the portrait, he refers to it in general terms as "by whom. Kalahaṃsa, having reflected again, says in order to have him read it aloud: "By whom indeed her heart was stolen. Makaranda: "Is it possible?"—this is a question; the word "painted" is to be supplied. Kalahaṃsa:

Now, "atha kim" signifies agreement; the meaning is: "Certainly, by Mālatī alone. Mādhava says: "Friend," etc. "The reasoning (*tarka*) has become clear"—that is, it has become stainless due to the departure of the turbidity characterized by doubt—and the inference (*ūha*) is that she is truly enamored of you. Here, because the arrival of happiness is perceived through the certainty of Mālatī’s affection for himself resulting from the viewing of the portrait, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (subordinate element of the plot) called "Attainment" (*prāpti*) is stated. As it is said: "Attainment (*prāpti*) is a certain arrival of happiness. Makaranda:

"Kalahamsaka, from whom did you obtain this? "It was from Mandārikā’s hand; hers, in turn, from Lavaṅgikā. "Kalahamsaka, it is for the dispelling of longing. "She who is like the Kaumudī moonlight"—meaning she who, like the moonlight, brings unsurpassed satisfaction to the cakora-birds that are your eyes—"of her, you, O noble-born one, are the beloved support of the bond of desire, that is, of firm passion. Therefore, there is no doubt regarding union with her."

Since, at this very union, Fate has exerted itself through the creation of mutual suitability, and Madana has suddenly produced intense passion and launched his assault—having fixed his intent upon this encounter and girded his loins—it follows that you need not worry about it; such is the meaning. //37//

"She is to be seen": even for one as steadfast as you, she who is capable of producing such a transformation of the mind is a form to be beheld by me, possessing a beautiful appearance. By this, having dispelled Mādhava’s doubt, the establishment of the seed of mutual passion is expressed; thus, the juncture-element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "Resolution" (*samādhāna*) is stated, according to the rule: "The arrival of the seed is resolution. She is one whose form is to be seen, whose appearance is lovely. The implication is: "Who is she that has displayed proficiency in the arts? Therefore, you too should manifest your own cleverness to her under the pretext of sketching her."

Mādhava: "To my friend. [The status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established by the rule *rucyarthānām*. The ellipsis is "I shall do that. Now, in order to depict the resemblance of each of her limbs, Mādhava—having mentally scrutinized all the limbs of Mālatī and thereby experienced the involuntary emotional states (*sāttvikabhāva*) such as tears—speaks to demonstrate the unsuitability of his own visual and manual faculties for the act of painting: "Again and again," and so forth.

Having resolved, "I shall write to my beloved," whatever remembrance of her limbs—such as her eyebrows or eyes—arises at that moment, a flood of tears welling up at every instant (the word *vāra* meaning both "occasion" and "moment") repeatedly veils or covers her eyes even though they are being wiped again and again. By this, the *sāttvika* emotion known as tears (*aśru*) is expressed; as it is said: "Tears are water produced from the eyes, born of sorrow, anger, or intense joy."

By her *saṃkalpa*—that is, by her thought—a state of numbness (*jaḍimā*) was induced, by which her body attains a rigidity (*stambha*). Regarding numbness and rigidity: "Numbness is an incapacity for actions caused by anxiety, longing, fear, and so forth; rigidity is the cessation of movement caused by fear, passion, illness, and so forth. (Bharata, Nāṭyaśāstra 7.70–71).

Likewise, at the very moment of that recollection, this hand of mine becomes moist with perspiration; and during the act of drawing lines—that is, in the process of painting—it remains possessed of fingers that are tremulous and unsteady due to incessant trembling and constant quivering. What shall I do? The meaning is that it is now difficult to manifest skill in the art of painting. Regarding perspiration and trembling: "Perspiration (sveda) is the emergence of moisture from the body caused by passion, physical exertion, fatigue, and so forth;
trembling (vepathu) is the shaking of the limbs caused by passion, disease, fear, and the like. //38//

The passage beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless) is clear. Regarding the word *jagati*: in the world (*jagati*, i.e., the universe), those various entities (*bhāvāḥ*), such as the crescent of the new moon and so forth, are victorious; by acting as allies to the God of Love (*manmatha*), they are characterized by the power to subjugate those separated from their lovers. They are naturally sweet (*prakṛtimadhurāḥ*), captivating by their very nature. They are not merely established through blind tradition according to the maxim, "There is a Yakṣa under this banyan tree."

There are indeed others besides Mālatī who delight and excite the minds of those others who have not beheld the lotus-face of Mālatī or who lack discernment; this is nothing new. Let them be so. But what is the use now of those who, by comparison, are mere wretches? This is the intended meaning. According to the maxim that "the world has diverse tastes," let it be as it may for others; for me, however, she is the moonlight for my eyes, the bringer of joy to my sight.

This is stated solely according to worldly convention (*loka-prasiddhi*), and not from his own perspective. For, since the moonlight and the like are utterly insignificant compared to Mālatī, the superimposition (*āropa*) of "moonlight-ness" upon Mālatī—intended to demonstrate her excellence—is contradicted by his own words. Therefore, it should be explained that the superimposition of "moonlight-ness" is based merely on the thought, "Just as moonlight is a source of delight to the eyes for the world, so too is Mālatī to me," and not for the purpose of demonstrating her excellence.

Thus, the fault of the contradiction in meaning has been refuted. This Mālatī has become the object of [my] vision; this is stated with an emphasis on the state of being (bhāva). That she has come within the range of my sight is, in this very birth, the one and only great festival and cause of happiness throughout the entire expanse of the world; the meaning is that others, such as the crescent moon and so forth, are not. The poetic figure (alaṃkāra) is Hyperbole (atiśayokti). //39//

Having entered, she says, "Mandārikā! and, showing [the painting] to Mādhava, she hands the picture into Kalahaṃsa’s hand, saying, "Bring it back quickly. The sense is that Mandārikā, having returned from Madanodyāna, was reflecting on where the picture-board might be—since Mālatī, who was staying in the pleasure-pavilion, had today felt an intense longing for a special sight and sought to dispel it—and being agitated by its absence, she searched for Kalahaṃsa in the crowd of people; not seeing him there, she enters and speaks.

The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating agitation (*saṃbhrama*). Furthermore, the protracted vowel (*pluta*), prescribed by the rule "in the case of a formal inquiry after a reproach" (*nigṛhyānuyoge ca*), is also employed in regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*). The address "O thief! (*core*) is intended as a mockery, implying: "A picture-board was brought from my house by you, a thief. For this very reason he says: "You have been caught by following your footprints. For a thief is indeed apprehended only by following the marks of his footsteps. [He says] "with shame" (*salajjam*), because it is improper to mock him in the presence of his own master.

"How is it that those two are also here together?"—this is a respectful inquiry, saying, "Come this way," because she intends to employ them immediately in the task at hand for the sake of conciliating her. Mandārikā: Kalahaṃsaka, bring the picture-board. Kalahaṃsaka: Take this. Mandārikā (to Kalahaṃsaka): By whom was Mālatī depicted here, and for what purpose? Kalahaṃsaka:

The meaning is that Mādhava was drawn by Mālatī for that very purpose and for that very reason—that is, for the sake of dispelling her longing—and likewise, Mālatī was drawn for his sake and for that same purpose. Mandārikā says "with joy": the cause of her joy is that the mission of Kāmandakī’s attendants, such as herself, acting as messengers, is now on the verge of bearing fruit. "By good fortune, the creative power of the Lord of Creatures has manifested its fruit."

The Creator’s artistic skill in fashioning such a pair of youths has now borne fruit through the intensity of their mutual passion; the sense is that nothing remains for them to achieve beyond this point, which is the very culmination of marriage itself. Makaranda: Regarding this matter of the portrait, what your husband says—that it was drawn by Mālatī to dispel her longing—is it so? (The word *api* is used here as an interrogative particle, meaning: "Is that truly the case? Mandārikā: Noble sir, it is indeed so.

Makaranda: "Where?"—the implication being that she drew his likeness in order to dispel her longing. Mandārikā: Lavaṅgikā says he was at the window. This means he was seen through the opening of this lattice. Mandārikā: May the noble sir grant his permission.

"I shall report to Lavaṅgikā this virtuous conduct of the Lord Madana—who possesses unimpeded power over the Blessed One and whose sport consists of activities conducive to uniting such pairs as were otherwise impossible to unite—characterized by mutual passion and the creation of forms corresponding to one another’s. I have been appointed to this very task by her; therefore, I shall inform her of this event, and she will act as is appropriate. Makaranda: "She has arrived, lady?"

This refers to the occasion for reporting this portrait to Lavaṅgikā—[the portrait] of one who has been gazed upon by Mādhava, whose passion for her has been confirmed, and who intends to produce confidence in Mālatī’s mind by means of her depicted form; that is to say, it is appropriate for the occasion. *Saṃstyāya* means a dwelling or residence. Regarding the phrase beginning with *dharmāmbhaḥ* (the water of religious merit), etc.: The water of religious merit is the water used for ritual purification (*śuddhodaka*). The "fragrance of the body" (*gandhavatī tanuḥ*) refers to the body which possesses a natural fragrance. "The lotus of the face" (*vaktrapadma*) is the lotus-like face. "The moon of the heart" (*hṛdayendubimba*) is the orb of the moon that is the heart. "The stream of tears" (*aśrudhārā*) is the flow of tears. "The moonlight of the eyes" (*netracandrikā*) is the moonlight consisting of the eyes. "The rays of the teeth" (*dantarociḥ*) are the luster of the teeth. "The moonstone" (*candrakānta*) is the moonstone gem. "The moon" (*indu*) is the moon itself. "The stream of the river of heaven" (*svarganadīpravāha*) is the current of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā). "The nectar of the lips" (*adharāmṛta*) is the nectar of the lips. "The sandalwood paste of the cheeks" (*kapolasthalīmalayaja*) is the sandalwood paste applied to the surface of the cheeks. "The moon of the forehead" (*lalāṭendubimba*) is the lunar orb of the forehead. "The moonstone of the temples" (*karṇapāśacandrakānta*) is the moonstone located on the lobes of the ears. "The stream of the celestial river" (*svarganadīpravāha*) is the current of the heavenly river. "The nectar of the lips" (*adharāmṛta*) is the nectar of the lips. "The sandalwood paste of the cheeks" (*kapolasthalīmalayaja*) is the sandalwood paste on the cheeks. "The moon of the forehead" (*lalāṭendubimba*) is the lunar orb of the forehead. "The moonstone of the temples" (*karṇapāśacandrakānta*) is the moonstone on the ears. "The stream of the celestial river" (*svarganadīpravāha*) is the current of the heavenly river. "The nectar of the lips" (*adharāmṛta*) is the nectar of the lips. "The sandalwood paste of the cheeks" (*kapolasthalīmalayaja*) is the sandalwood paste on the cheeks. "The moon of the forehead" (*lalāṭendubimba*) is the lunar orb of the forehead. "The moonstone of the temples" (*karṇapāśacandrakānta*) is the moonstone on the ears. "The stream of the celestial river" (*svarganadīpravāha*) is the current of the heavenly river. "The nectar of the lips" (*adharāmṛta*) is the nectar of the lips. "The sandalwood paste of the cheeks" (*kapolasthalīmalayaja*) is the sandalwood paste on the cheeks. "The moon of the forehead" (*lalāṭendubimba*) is the lunar orb of the forehead. "The moonstone of the temples" (*karṇapāśacandrakānta*) is the moonstone on the ears. "The stream of the celestial river" (*svarganadīpravāha*) is the current of the heavenly river. "The nectar of the lips" (*adharāmṛta*) is the nectar of the lips. "The sandalwood paste of the cheeks" (*kapolasthalīmalayaja*) is the sandalwood paste on the cheeks. "The moon of the forehead" (*lalāṭendubimba*) is the lunar orb of the forehead. "The moonstone of the temples" (*karṇapāśacandrakānta*) is the moonstone on the ears. "The stream of the celestial river" (*sv

"Of her whose eyes are charming and beautiful"—this refers to the attendants, the courtesans; "the saffron on their cheeks" means the saffron applied to their cheeks. By this, a particular mode of anointing is indicated, as it is said: "That which, through skill, is fashioned upon the breasts or the cheeks, and which intoxicates the eyes—that is true anointing. "By the spreading of the clusters of drops of the water of perspiration" refers to the diffusion of the mass of sweat-drops.

I think—that is, I conjecture—that it was that very same wonderful and marvelous leaf-design (*patralekhā*) fashioned by me in the morning which has now lost its cleverness, being the very product of that skill. The sense is that by midday, the saffron on her cheeks would have had its patterns wiped away and its artistry destroyed by the force of perspiration. //40//

Then, through the power of the manifestation of his madness, even though the wind is insentient, he prays for union with it, saying "unmīlat... and so forth: "O Wind, while still embracing her, and not after delaying even a moment, touch every limb of mine—that is, every single part of my body. The sense is that even the touch of your own limbs as you embrace one's beloved is equivalent to the touch of the beloved’s limbs herself. As it is said: "Blow, O Wind, from where my beloved is; having touched her, touch me too."

"The touch of my limbs against you, and the meeting of our eyes with the moon"—thus [she speaks]. "Her" (tām) means she remembers her exactly as she was seen previously. "Slightly trembling" (īṣatpracale) means somewhat unsteady due to the influence of amorous playfulness; or else, it means she whose eyes were somewhat unsteady in order to conceal them from her friends, lest they perceive her through her unblinking gaze. She is one whose body (aṅgam) is bent (natam)—that is, bowed down—by the weight of her full breasts or by the exhaustion of separation. He qualifies the breeze: "unfolding," etc.

"Karāla" means jagged, uneven, lofty, vast, or even deformed, according to the lexicographical authority. That *kundakośa*—the expanse of the *kunda* vine—is "jagged" with buds (*mukula*) that are opening and about to blossom. From it, thick and dense drops of nectar (*makaranda*), which is the sap of the flower, flow forth; by the phrase "companion of the fragrance of that [nectar]," the state of love known as *vilāpa* (lamentation) is indicated. As it is said: "Here it was seen, here it was embraced, here it arrived, here it stayed."

"‘He has passed away here; he lies right here, adorned. Such words as these are called lamentation (*vilāpa*). Whether inside or outside, in front or behind, far or near, close at hand—he sees [the deceased] in one place, goes toward him in another, and stands still elsewhere. He sits in one spot, sleeps in another, and sometimes reproaches or rejoices. Here and there, on the street, he cries out, wanders, and runs about. Thus arise the states born of lamentation, following the power of the mind-born [god of love]. (41)

Makaranda (to himself): "He strikes"—the word *hanta* here expresses despondency, according to the observation that "the word *hanta* [is used] in joy, compassion, at the beginning of a sentence, and in despondency. He strikes repeatedly; he is unrestrained, meaning unimpeded—that is to say, difficult to ward off. The sense is: how has this utterly improper act been commenced by that most cruel wretch, the cursed god of love?

The meaning is that he is "grown" (pravṛddha) in such a way that, at the very moment of his birth, he would be destroyed as one for whom there is no opportunity for medical treatment. "Vikṛta" refers to the three *doṣas* in a state of disorder. A "transformation connected with disorder" (*vikṛtavivarta*) is a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sāṃnipātika*), consisting of the transformation of the three *doṣas* when they are aggravated. The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both this [fever] and terrible. "Kaṭhora" means extremely intense. "Kūṭapākala" is a specific disease of elephants; it is called *kūṭapākala* because, arriving suddenly through a deceptive stratagem (*kūṭa*), it strikes down the animal right then and there.

For example: "Just as a forest-dweller might strike down a herd of deer with a snare, so indeed does *kūṭapākala* kill the elephant by means of a decoy. Just as a deer is cruelly slain by hunters using a snare, so too does the elephant perish because of it; therefore, it is called *kūṭapākala*. Some explain that *kūṭapākala* is a specific type of elephant fever produced by the three *doṣas* acting in concert (*kūṭībhūya*, i.e., having come together). By this, the state of insanity (*unmādāvasthā*) is indicated. The poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is simile (*upamā*). //42//

"Therefore, here" means that there is no other way [to proceed]. This method, consisting of the *saṃprasāraṇa* (transformation) of meanings, is a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture). As it is said: "The transformation of meanings is designated as *yukti*. Mādhava, however, observing everywhere now that very same [vision] which he had seen at the time of departure, reflecting upon his own extreme state of madness within himself, says: "I see," etc. [He sees] that very same [vision] which he saw at the time of departure, now appearing in many forms.

The illusory form (*vivarta*) is a phenomenal appearance; she manifests as having a body consisting of mere appearance. He reveals her manifold nature with the words "here and there": at one time, coming close to my ear as if eager to whisper a secret, she sat alternately on both sides, her single breast bristling with horripilation from the touch of my arms; at another time, sitting directly in front of me, [she said], "Why do you remain so dejected and distressed?"

She was coaxing me like a bold woman, saying, "In every way, my life depends on you"; yet a moment later, approaching me from behind with slow steps and covering my eyes with both hands, she would divert me by asking, "Tell me, who am I?"; at other times, as if wishing to consider whether he was gazing incessantly upon another or indeed upon me alone, she would enter within me, there beholding her own self as the supreme deity to be worshipped, appearing in a different form fashioned by my own desire.

Seeing her appearing [before him], and suspecting her to be another woman, he thought, "Surely you are deceitful; I do not wish to remain in your presence. As if out of indignation, she went outside and, though grasped by the hem of his garment, she withdrew by force. At times, as if embracing a yoginī, she circled around many bodies and delighted me with manifold amorous gestures—such is the manner of the expansion of his own mental desires. Furthermore, of what sort was she?
She was bearing a face whose gaze was turned askance—slanted due to her attachment and fixation upon me—resembling a blooming, enchanting golden lotus. //43//

Thus, reporting to his friend Makaranda the very matter he had reflected upon within himself, he says: "It spreads. An indescribable [fever], whose cause is unknown to anyone, a tormenting affliction by its very nature, this fever of love—a bodily burning that immediately produces the apprehension of calamity—spreads; it exists pervading all the limbs. Thus, the characteristic of this particular state known as fever has been described.

Delusion (*pramoha*), defined as "the mind's state of bewilderment produced by pleasure, pain, and so forth," obscures—that is, destroys—the capacity of the sense organs (*karaṇa*) to perceive, which is their power to grasp their respective objects. Bearing an increase of longing (*raṇaraṇaka*), the heart, being whirled about and boiled by the fire of love—according to the statement that "whirling about is boiling"—blazes within, just as oil and the like blaze up through excessive heating.

How, then, is the sustenance of life maintained now? To this he says: "Consisting of that" (*tanmayatvam*)—that is, identity with Mālatī—is essentially like a sprinkling of nectar; the meaning is that it is the elixir of life. //44//
May this rashness which I, though being a fool, have committed,
serve for the pleasure of those great-souled ones who perceive only virtues.

Thus ends the commentary on the first act of the *Mālatīmādhava-bhāvapradīpikā*, composed by the scholar Tripurāri, the son of Parvatanātha Yāyajūka, the ornament of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Second Act.
Victorious is the unprecedented scholarship of the flower-bowed god; oh, how marvelous!
It is the sole initiator of the tradition for the entire manifold creation beginning with Brahmā.
By whom was this girl taught, that she is so bold even in matters never instructed?

Now, the poet, beginning another act, introduces the *praveśaka*—a device for suggesting the events that will occur immediately following Lavaṅgikā’s departure—in order to indicate the subsequent plot development, starting with the words "Then," and so forth. As for the *praveśaka*: "The *praveśaka* indicates portions of the story already occurred or yet to occur; it is employed at the beginning of a drama by low-ranking characters. The two *ceṭīs* are maidservants, for such characters alone are suitable for the *praveśaka*.

As it is said: "That which consists of a continuous sequence of conversations with attendants is to be known as a *praveśaka*. First: *Halā* is an address to a female friend. In the vicinity of the music hall, the venerable Kāmandakī was conversing about something with Avalokitā as her companion. Because of the frequent usage [of grammatical forms] in Prakrit, the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense is employed here even for the immediate past. The meaning is: "What did you say to her at that time? Second:

Friend, it is said that Makaranda, the dear companion of Mādhava, reported the entire incident at Madanodyāna to the venerable lady.
