Makaranda was certain that Kāmandakī is indeed our refuge; therefore, for the sake of remedying his friend’s misfortune, he reported everything to Kāmandakī, who is capable of doing so—this is what was heard from the mouth of Avalokitā.

Then, desiring to see the mistress, the venerable lady sent Avalokitā to ascertain the cause of her recent behavior and to learn the mistress’s current condition, asking, "Where is she, and how is she faring? I too told that Avalokitā that the mistress was staying in a secluded place accompanied by Lavaṅgikā.

First: Friend, Lavaṅgikā was indeed delayed right there while gathering saffron flowers; she did not come from Madanodyāna with us as we were returning. Has she arrived now? Second: Indeed so; the meaning is that she has certainly arrived.

Having caught her by the hand as she was indeed falling, and having forbidden all her attendants, she has climbed onto the upper part of the terrace situated at the edge of the outer door of the pleasure-house, above the veranda where the mistress of the house is. First [Mādhava]: "Surely she is diverting herself with conversation about that noble one. The meaning is that she dispels her longing through that very subject, asking what was said by you and what was said by him. Second [Śakuntalā]: "Sighing..."

A sigh arises from the realization of an obstacle to Mālatī’s desire. Whence indeed can she find consolation? By this extraordinary sight today, her obsession—that is, the intensity of her passion—will surely reach its ultimate limit, the highest peak. He indicates another cause for the increase of her obsession: "And at dawn, at the very time of daybreak, the Great King, seeking the hand of the princess on account of Nandana, was informed by the minister. First [Act]: "What was informed?"

"Tell me," is the ellipsis. Second [Mālatī]: "O Great King, you have authority over your own daughters," is the ellipsis for "it has been requested. Therefore, I consider that Mālatī’s passion for Mādhava, lasting until death, is indeed like a thorn smeared with the poison of the fear that her desired boon might not be granted—a thorn equal to the fruit of Love’s arrow. First [Makaranda]: "Perhaps the Blessed Lady will manifest here some aspect of her blessed nature?"

The meaning is that it is expected that Kāmandakī, who is exceedingly affectionate toward Mālatī, will manifest her greatness—consisting of her own perfection in knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and so forth—in order to fulfill her [Mālatī’s] desires. Second [act]: "O you of ungrounded desires, come! (the remainder is: "in order to pursue the task at hand").

Thus ends the introductory scene (*praveśaka*): Makaranda’s report to Kāmandakī regarding Mādhava’s condition, the arrival of Lavaṅgikā, the entrance of Mālatī and Lavaṅgikā, and subsequently Kāmandakī’s arrival to ascertain Mālatī’s state; and after she has hinted at the unfolding account of Nandana, the two maidservants exit. Then, [the text begins with] "Then," etc.; the meaning is that Mālatī and Lavaṅgikā enter, their entrance having been indicated by the statement that they are staying in a secluded place accompanied by Lavaṅgikā.

Now, one might object: since there is no entrance of a hero (nāyaka) here, and because the defining characteristic of an act (aṅka)—namely, the description of the hero's own conduct witnessed firsthand—is absent, how can this be considered an act? [Response: There is no fault, because by the term "leader" (netṛ), the heroine (nāyikā) is also included through the grammatical principle of "single remainder" (ekaśeṣa).

Furthermore, since both acts cover the activities of a single day and constitute a single juncture (*saṃdhi*), it should be understood that this second act was composed as a continuation of the first act, after the hero’s activities had been concluded for the sake of facilitating the entry and exit of the characters, and in order to facilitate the transition from the hero’s activities to the heroine’s activities. If it is asked how two acts can have a single juncture, it is said: "These [acts] are for the purpose of the subsequent parts of the story which are interconnected."

"Connection (*saṃbandha*) is said to be the juncture (*saṃdhi*) when there is a single intermediate purpose. Such is its nature. Therefore, in this context, while Mālatī and Mādhava are engaged in a single intermediate purpose—characterized by the strengthening of the seed (*bīja*) of their mutual passion—which is subsumed under the ultimate purpose of their marriage, the efforts of Kāmandakī, Avalokitā, and others on this day consist of strengthening Mālatī’s resolve through the account of the painted tablet at Madana’s garden and the introduction of Nandana as a suitor for Mādhava.

The connection of these narrative elements—namely, the proclamation of [his] lineage, character, age, beauty, and so forth—constitutes the "Opening" (Mukha) juncture along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), according to the definition stated: "The Opening is the emergence of the seed (*bīja*), from which various purposes and sentiments arise. Enough of this elaboration. Mālatī: Friend, what happened after that? What happened after that?

To Lavaṅgikā, who had said only this much—namely, her own delay in Madanodyāna, her journey to Mādhava, and her request for the Bakula garland with clever words—the King, out of an excess of curiosity to hear the subsequent events, asks with agitation. The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of indicating respect; the ellipsis is "tell me the subsequent event. Lavaṅgikā: Then this Bakula garland was brought by that noble one. Mālatī: (Having gazed at it with respect and looked closely.)

Friend, this arrangement is uneven on one side. Lavaṅgikā: In its lack of beauty, you yourself are at fault. Mālatī: How so? The meaning is: how can I be the cause of the unevenness on one side of the garland being fashioned by Mādhava? Lavaṅgikā: Because he, whose limbs are dark as durva grass, was thus rendered disconcerted; in reality, his hands were made unsteady during the act of stringing it.
By the very wealth of your own beauty, you drew in even that profound mind and rendered his hand incapable of the task at hand; hence this disparity in the composition [of the verse].

The sense is: "He has been born. Mālatī: "Friend Lavaṅgikā, you are always inclined toward consolation. You say this merely to comfort me; the sense is that his affection for me is considered impossible. Lavaṅgikā: "Friend, what kind of 'inclination toward consolation' is this? What is the point of my lack of trust when the matter is established by direct perception? The meaning is: "Indeed, I am saying it; he too has been witnessed by my dear friend herself"—this is how the connection ends. The sense is: "It is not by me alone [that this is known]."

With her two eyes—which possess the grace of blooming white lotuses stirred by a gentle breeze and which are wide open due to the force rooted in the concealment of the physical transformations born from beholding you under the pretext of beginning to arrange a garland of *bakula* flowers; "balāmoḍi" being a regional term for "force"—[the gaze is] skilled in the playful agitation of the arrows of the God of Love, as manifested by the graceful movement of her creeper-like brows, which quiver with the charm of a long, steady, and expanding gaze of wonder.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "vibhāvita" means manifested; "anaṅgaśarasaṃrambha" (the impetuosity of the arrows of the bodiless god of love) refers to the agitation caused by the arrows of Kāma; "vibhrama" is the resulting confusion or charm; "vidagdha" means cleverly or artfully; "locanaprānta" refers to the corners of the eyes; "pariyantraṇā" is the restraint or regulation; "vilāsa" is the grace arising from that very restraint; "ullasita" means shimmering; "bhrūlatā" refers to the creeper-like eyebrows; "stimita" means motionless; "dīrgha" means long or extended; "vismaya" is wonder; "adbhutarasatāmāpādyamāna" means being brought to the state of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*); "vijṛmbhamāṇa" means expanding or unfolding; and "avalokayan" means looking at or beholding as if it were directly perceived. [In summary: He was beholding [her] in such a way as to be cleverly manifested by the playful movement of his creeper-like eyebrows—which were shimmering due to the very restraint of the long, wide corners of his eyes, which were rendered motionless by the wonder arising as he experienced the marvelous sentiment unfolding before him—and which thus revealed the impetuous assault of the arrows of the bodiless god of love. It was as if he were seeing her with his own eyes.

The sense is that his passion for you is discernible through those very longing glances. Mālatī: [Embracing her. The cause for the embrace is the joy born from demonstrating a direct correspondence with the events of her own heart. Regarding "Ām" (Yes): some say it signifies agreement; the meaning is that what was already present in my mind has been spoken by you as well, and indeed it is exactly so.

Dear friend, are those playful charms—which appear for a mere moment to that person who is present for only an instant, whose feet are covered in dust, and who is ignorant of their specific nature—merely deceptive, intended to delude him? Or is it as my dear friend imagines? That is to say: have we been deceived by his innate charms due to our lack of familiarity with them, or are they, as you suggest, truly indicative of his passion? Lavaṅgikā:

"Even though she has reached a certainty, she merely says 'this is doubtful'—smiling thus, and with indignation saying, 'Even when a matter is certain, why is it being concealed from me? [This is the implied sense]. The indeclinable *sāvajñam* denotes affectionate anger. You too, by your very nature, on that occasion were made to dance *asaṃgītakaṃ*, meaning devoid of the singing of women; for there is a saying: 'The singing of women seated in the theater is considered *saṃgītakaṃ*.'"

"If you have been deceived by his innate charms, then your own charms must also be natural and deceptive of him; they cannot be born of affection. This is a counter-argument used to determine the point at hand. Mālatī: (With shame, as she is unable to conceal anything further) "Hum" (in response to the question). Then what?—meaning, "Tell me the rest that remains to be said. Lavaṅgikā:

Then, when Mādhava had been hidden by the crowd of people returning from their journey, I went to Mandārikā’s house. That morning, her picture-board had been taken into my hands and deposited with me as a trust. Mālatī: For what reason? Lavaṅgikā: Kalahaṃsaka, a follower of Mādhava, is in love with her; it was given into her hand for the purpose that she might show it to him. Thus, Mandārikā has become a messenger of pleasant tidings. Mālatī: (To herself)

"Surely that Kalahaṃsaka must have shown this portrait of himself to his master; otherwise, how could Mandārikā be a bearer of such pleasant news? This is the underlying thought. [Aloud: "Friend, what is it now that is pleasing to you? That which has been reported by Mandārikā," is the meaning. Lavaṅgikā:

Indeed, this portrait of yours is a means of cooling for a moment my heart—which is scorched by an unbearable distress born from the intensity of longing for you, that very object so difficult to attain, which causes me torment as I am already consumed by the heat of not having obtained you—so much so that it provides relief even for a single instant. "It is now dear to me," is the implied conclusion.

The sense is this: it is precisely this that is dear to me—that because you were unable to live without seeing her, you drew a portrait so that you might sustain your life even by the sight of a painting; and that he likewise drew a likeness of you. For from this arises the certainty of the seed of their union, which is the intensity of mutual passion. Mālatī (with a sigh of joyful relief): This is a source of consolation, for it confirms my beloved’s absolute passion for me, since he has seen the likeness of himself drawn by her.

Joy and consolation: according to the definition, "joy (*harṣa*) is the clarity of mind resulting from the attainment of what is desired, praise, and so forth. In some versions, the reading is "with joy and trepidation" (*saharṣasādhvasam*). In that case, the cause of trepidation is the thought: "To whose eyes among my kinsmen would this reach, revealing my affection for another man—a thing unbecoming of a maiden? Alas! Even now there is no consolation for my heart, since even this reassurance is suspected to be a deception. How can it even be words?

The word "are seen" is to be supplied [as the verb]. "Jagatī" has been explained previously. Regarding "with joy": the contemplation of the meaning of the verse is the cause of that joy. "O highly fortunate one, your speech is indeed worthy of your creation"; the meaning is that the sweetness of your creation and the sweetness of your speech are exactly equal. Furthermore, the sight of you is enchanting at that moment, yet in the long run—at the time when you are no longer visible—it is terrible with the pain of longing. Truly blessed are those women who do not behold you.

Only by the power of merit do some women, even if they somehow behold you, have the capacity to reach their own hearts. Those who do not see you are unfortunate because their very birth is fruitless; and those who, though seeing you, are distracted by other thoughts, are likewise unfortunate because you are not worthy of their regard due to being like mere beasts. Thus, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast) is suggested. Lavaṅgikā: Friend, even though you have been consoled in this way, there is no consolation for you. Mālatī: How so?

"What now is this sign of consolation seen that is not otherwise accounted for?"—this question is asked even though it has already been understood from those very words. Lavaṅgikā: For the sake of which you, bearing a heart like an *aśoka* sprout whose bonds are severed and whose roots are cut away, wither away—exceedingly delicate and unable to endure even a fresh *navamālikā* flower—you are being wasted by the flower-armed god [Kāma], and have reached such a state of emaciation; he too has been made known to the venerable Love-god as one who suffers torment.

The meaning is that his state of being difficult to endure arises from the verse written there; for just as it was for you, the very perception of his deep passion is the cause of consolation. Mālatī: Friend, may it be well with that one of great power now. But for me, consolation is extremely difficult to obtain. May my own final state come upon me this very moment! May he not fall into a condition similar to mine. The meaning is that such a person, an ornament of the three worlds, is rare in birth. (Weeps.)

Because sensation is so difficult to endure, there is a fear of immediate calamity, and thus it is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Regarding the phrase "relying on the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*): as they say—``Even for courtesans, celestial nymphs, and the foremost queens in the inner apartments, something conditioned may be appropriate when occasion demands it. Thus, Mālatī is included among the women of the inner apartments; for this very reason, she is addressed as "the daughter of the master. Regarding the term "mental affliction" (*manoroga*): like poison, it spreads incessantly and without ceasing, pervading all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

This is the disease of love, characterized by the affliction of the god of love; it is violent, agitating, and brings about immediate ruin. Like a smokeless fire that has been fanned and kindled, it blazes forth. Thus, like a severe fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (*sāṃnipātika*), it strikes and torments every limb, moving hither and thither within and without all the members of the body.

Therefore, my father, though overcome by affection for his offspring, is unable to rescue me from this insurmountable calamity because he is so intent on pleasing the king. Furthermore, although a mother’s heart is more intensely overwhelmed by boundless love for her daughters—since a father’s affection is greater toward male children—even so, Mother is dependent upon her husband and is not capable of protecting me.

Even my female friends, who share my joys and sorrows through playing in the dust together and so forth, and who are no different from my own mind compared even to my mother—nevertheless, because they lack independence regarding me, they are not capable of protecting me. However, if there were one capable of protecting me, he alone would be like the nectar-restoring herb, Mādhava; yet since he is difficult for me to attain, death alone is now my refuge, and nothing else. This is the meaning.

The employment of these three similes—poison, a blazing fire, and fever—is for the purpose of indicating an excellence, showing that this [defilement] cannot be compared by means of just one. Furthermore, fever (*saṃjvara*) and madness (*unmāda*) are mentioned by him; their definitions have already been stated previously. //1//

Lavaṅgikā: It is even so. Meetings with virtuous people bestow happiness that is directly perceived, yet they are difficult to endure when one is out of their sight. It is no wonder that there is distress here. To provide the reason for this, she says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). "Dear friend": you whose physical condition—due to seeing him at the window for even a moment—has become like a full moonrise that acts as a fiercely blazing fire, and whose life is endangered by the merciless operations of Love. (The word *bhavati* [you are] is to be supplied.)

That you are now grieving today because of the sight of his particular excellence—what more need be said here? Therefore, dear friend, we know this much alone: that for the world of living beings, the fruit of a longed-for desire regarding an unattainable object—which consists in its fulfillment—is precisely this: a union with a noble beloved that is worthy and corresponding to a profound mutual bond of love and deep affection.

Whoever attains what fruit immediately after separation from the body—Śiva alone knows that. However, for those living beings who desire the fulfillment of their own birth, if they obtain a circle of dear friends who are equally devoted and noble due to the excellence of their own virtuous deeds in previous lives, then, by whatever means possible, union with them is indeed the praiseworthy fruit of one's desires; this is the conclusion agreed upon by all people. —Mālatī.

Friend, you who propose such a rash act regarding the life of my beloved Mālatī, begone! To me, my very life is the most beloved and dear thing. Therefore, out of greed for my life, you yourself are proposing this rash act of giving yourself away—a stain upon our family, contrary to the custom of maidens, and one whose intent was never accepted by my most venerable kinsmen. You must not advise me thus. Hence, the prohibition should be stated as: "Withdraw from this advice of rashness. My life is dear only to you; it is not dear to my elders or others.

Therefore, the implied injunction is: "You yourself must instruct me in such a way that my mind becomes free from the thorns of doubt regarding my life. Regarding the word "with tears": even if you, out of mere affection, offer this reckless advice, it will not bear fruit through mere instruction alone; it would only result in a rash determination to transgress the commands of my elders. Consequently, the fruit of my own immodesty must be experienced by me alone.

The meaning is that they say while weeping, "What is to be done by you in this matter? Alternatively: "I myself, looking at him again and again many times—supplying the word 'him' (tam)—have committed an offense, being lightened by my own ill-bred conduct due to the absence of shame as my heart has melted far away; for it was with a heart whose support and reliance was its fortitude, which had been established [against him] but was now restrained and fixed [upon him] as he fled."

The sense is that, having repeatedly disregarded the bounds of propriety for young maidens of noble family by gazing at him, this affliction of mine is not particularly grave. It should be understood that by "gazing," visual delight is expressed; by "fleeing," mental attachment; and by "melting away from afar," the destruction of shame is described. Nevertheless, dear friend, let it burn, and so forth.

Night after night, throughout all the nights of both the bright and dark fortnights, having abandoned his own regular schedule due to enmity toward me, let the moon—ever possessing its full digits, entangled in a mass of flames under the guise of its perfect orb which blazes like a heap of fuel for the life-force of those separated from their lovers—burn as a fire, designated by the name "Cool-rayed" through the figure of irony (viparītalakṣaṇā), marked by the smoke named "Moon" which is actually the sin of slaying women separated from their husbands; let it burn me alone as its fuel according to its will.

Taking that very fire, let Madana himself burn me. What more, or what else, will these two do beyond death—that is, after dying? And that death has been accepted by me alone; thus, the sense is that the exhaustion [of my life] is not a fault because it was voluntarily accepted. For me, moreover, my father is praiseworthy, his virtues being worthy of praise by all people; my mother is beloved, born of a stainless lineage; and my family is beloved, remaining untainted for so long as to be free from even a trace of blemish.

Furthermore, this person named Mādhava is not only more dear than even the life residing in my heart because he is so desirable; he is to be ranked as the very first [object of affection]. Thus, without him, I am like a wretch; and because I do not collapse even when resolved upon the reckless act of abandoning him, I am exceedingly ungrateful. For this very reason, even life, which was acquired later, is not dear—this is the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*). As for the underlying sentiment (*bhāva*), although it flashes forth in many ways, it has not been written down here for fear of prolixity; it should be inferred by those with sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*). //2//

Lavaṅgikā (to herself): What means is there now? She did not accept the advice on rash action that I suggested, and the final stage [of her life] is imminent. The meaning is: "What should be done here? While Lavaṅgikā is thus reflecting, "What means is there now?", the female door-keeper, who has half-entered from the tiring-room, speaks as if instructing her in a means under the pretext of overhearing: "Here is the venerable Kāmandakī. It was not stated that she understood the connection by thinking, "What means is there now? because that understanding was already established.

For this very reason, Mālatī and Lavaṅgikā ask: "What does the venerable lady command?"—the meaning being that she is arriving. The female door-keeper says: "She has come desiring to see the princess. Both [girls] say: "Why is there such delay? She is already outside"—the word "by her" (*bhavatyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Lavaṅgikā [says to herself]: "It has indeed become well-ordered; a blessing has been accomplished, since the venerable lady has arrived at this very moment. Kāmandakī [says]: "Excellent," and so forth.

"Not opposed to either world" means not inconsistent with both worlds—this world and the next—and being composed of both truth and falsehood by way of equivocal speech. For instance: "Indeed, our entire family is Your Majesty’s retinue; therefore, Your Majesty has authority over the maiden folk, who are your own and may be employed as you wish. This is not opposed to this world because it serves as a cause for worldly happiness through pleasing the king's mind. [And yet: "Your Majesty has authority only over your own maiden folk."

However, because it was stated that "it is not mine," which is the truth itself, and because of the avoidance of the sin of breaking a previously made promise regarding friendship and kinship, there is no contradiction with the world beyond. This is the sense: if, when requested by the king, one were to say "I will not give it" and thus verbally refuse, one would be subject to punishment for the visible fault of violating the king's command.

Now, if one were to say "I give [her] out of deference to the King," having decided so while intending to fulfill a promise made to a friend or relative by acting through another's mouth and thus undertaking the effort of a marriage, there would be sin due to the fault of speaking otherwise. However, speaking thus through deception, he has spoken what is contrary to both worlds; or rather, it is not contrary to both worlds—that is, to the two modes of worldly conduct consisting of the feigned marriage and the pursuit of joy.

Through the revelation of historical narratives such as the account of Śakuntalā, the course of action and the proper path to be followed have been explained. Thus, because a partiality is perceived otherwise, even that Sūtra which has been praised would describe the manifold qualities of the Leader according to her own preference. Hereafter, only this much remains to be done: she must be made to cultivate such an intimacy—a love that, by making her worthy of confidence, causes her to act without hesitation and with immediate trust even in an improper undertaking. as it is said: "The means (*karaṇa*) is the commencement of the subject matter. //13//
The words of the poet Bhavabhūti are victorious, delighting through the excellence of their essence which flows with the nectar of immortality;
they are sweet, noble, and profound.

"Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; Mālatī will go to the temple of Śaṅkara together with her mother. For it is said that by doing so, one's good fortune increases. Therefore, under the pretext of gathering flowers with her own hands for the purpose of worshipping the deity, she will bring Mālatī—who is accompanied by Lavaṅgikā—to that very Kusumākarodyāna garden. [The implication is: 'The venerable lady herself [will be there]. From this, a mutual meeting will take place. But as for you, where are you going? Buddharakṣitā:

I have indeed been invited and summoned by my dear friend Madayantika, who is already set out for Śaṅkara’s city; therefore, having paid homage at the feet of the Venerable Lady, I shall go right there. Avalokitā: Regarding that matter for which you were appointed by the Venerable Lady—the union of Madayantika and Makaranda—what is the news? (The word *vartate*—"is it proceeding?"—is to be supplied. Buddharakṣitā:

Indeed, by the command of the Blessed One, during various confidential conversations, I have so greatly elevated my dear friend Madayantika’s secret passion for Makaranda—describing it as being such and such—that even her heart's desire has reached the point of thinking, "I must see him. Avalokitā: Excellent, Buddharakṣitā! Excellent! Come, let us go. (They both exit. [End of Interlude. Then Kāmandakī enters, her entrance signaled by Avalokitā.

Kāmandakī: "So be it. In that manner, although Mālatī was humble and bowed down with a modesty characterized by devotion and faith appropriate for elders, and possessed a natural disposition befitting a girl of noble family, I—by means of various stratagems—secured her constant presence near him through many methods such as arranging her tresses with clever artistry, painting decorative patterns on the surfaces of her bud-like breasts and cheeks, diverting her with dice-play and playful jests, and presenting her with rare objects.

In just a few days, she has been brought—that is, led—to a state of service and endearment through an excellence of affection characterized by such things as the disclosure of all the secrets of her heart to her friends, Lavaṅgikā and others, after casting aside timidity, shame, and apprehension; the acceptance even of the loss of life as spoken by me; and the inability to endure separation from me for even a moment. "Bhajana" (service/devotion) in this context means precisely the form of endearment; the meaning is that she has been brought [to that state]. //1//

He demonstrates trust itself by saying "she goes": in our absence, she undergoes *vaicitrya*—that is, mental agitation or distress of mind; she departs [from her composure]. But in our presence, she becomes serene, her inner being becoming tranquil. She delights in private, spending long periods of time playing by revealing secrets of jesting (*narma*) such as she would never tell even to her friends. Out of affection, she gives voice—that is, she always speaks only what is pleasant, and never otherwise.

In the reading "deyaṃ dadāti," the meaning is that she gives what is to be given, such as camphor and other items as a gift of affection; likewise, she attends to him with favor by rising to meet him, offering a seat, and so forth.

Likewise, on the occasion of my departure from her side toward the monastery, she—her arms entwined like a noose around my neck—repeatedly restrained me; yet when I insisted that I must go by all means, she immediately turned back. At that very moment, she bound me with many irrefutable oaths regarding my return, saying: "If you do not come this very instant, then you have killed your own teacher with your own hand, and you have acted toward me with a contrary intent."
Having prostrated with words of authoritative testimony, he thus entreats me; that is to say, he makes a request. //2//

"And this" refers to what is about to be stated, which is a stronger—that is, more firm—basis or cause for hope, specifically the hope that "he will certainly do as I have said. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Śākuntala and so forth."

Having heard from my friends—whom I have either prompted myself or been incited by them—those legendary tales beginning with the story of Śakuntalā, which were introduced by means of words that appeared on the surface to be directed toward others (i.e., beyond the scope of our immediate presence) but were in fact intended solely for my instruction; [having heard these], she has placed her limbs upon my lap. This person is now at your disposal to be employed as you wish; therefore, whether it be death or life, it is yours.

As if announcing, "I am entirely dependent on you," she casts her body into my lap; for a long time, she has attained a state of stillness and motionlessness through anxiety—pondering, "How should I act like Śakuntalā and others? and through deliberation, "What indeed is the means here? This is the most excellent basis for hope. This very meaning of these two verses was stated in the *Ratirahasya* during the description of the heroine who has been brought under the power of a female messenger (*dūtī*).

For example: "When he behaves in this manner, his disposition should be observed: having seen her, he speaks with a smile; he sits down close by; he asks about her food and bed; he offers a story in private or meets with her in secret; he sighs and yawns; he gives her some of his own wealth or something else; when she is leaving, he says, 'You shall come again,' and thus he becomes conciliatory," and so forth. (3)

"Regarding that": we shall now commence the subsequent series of tasks immediately following Mādhava's presence. The passage beginning with "In the tiring-room" and ending with "I shall see him again" has already been explained. Lavaṅgikā:

Friend, this [tree] indeed—because of the tumultuous clamor of the flocks of cuckoos, which is exceedingly sweet due to their playful act of devouring the flower-clusters that are thoroughly moistened by the sweet nectar; and because of the agitation caused by the swarms of restless bees that have flown up in terror from the top of the mango tree; and because its formidable, jagged leaves are torn upward with their petals spread wide by the crushing impact—[stands there].

According to the statement, "The word *karāla* is used for that which is jagged, high, vast, and also for that which is blossomed," [the mountain] is captivating due to the fragrance of the *campaka* flowers, that is, the *cāmpeya* blossoms. It is "like a swan" (*marāla*), meaning like a symmetrical (*samavṛtta*) swan; according to the statement, "The word *marāla* refers to a symmetrical [form]."

The garden breeze of Kusumākara embraces you—its cool touch acting as sandalwood paste for your lovely moon-like face, which is radiant with droplets of nectar in the form of perspiration brought forth by your faltering and uneven gait; a gait slowed by the burden of supporting the expansive curve of your hips and made unsteady by the weight of your thighs. Therefore, let us proceed from here.

"Mādhava has gone there"—thus indicated, Mādhava enters. Mādhava: "Hanta! (expressing joy). "Parāgatā" means she has come toward him; here the prefix *para-* indicates the sense of being face-to-face. "Appearing": my inner heart, which had become almost like a memory because I had lost all hope of seeing my beloved again, now—by her first appearing and becoming manifest—makes it breathe with relief and restores it to life, as she is the omen of my lover's arrival.

How is it so? It is like the lightning (*aciraprabhā*), appearing before the peacock scorched by the summer heat, which indicates that rain is imminent; thus, there is a simile. In this context, Mādhava’s longing to see Mālatī is the "Bindu" (the drop), because it serves as the cause for their meeting again after the interruption caused by the events concerning Mālatī and Nandana described in the second act. As it is said: "The Bindu is the cause of non-interruption when there is an interruption in the intermediate plot."

And here, through the third and fourth acts—which delineate a portion of the unified plot (*ekabhāvikathā*) composed of intermediate purposes consisting of mutual sightings—the *bindu* (the "drop" or central motif) previously indicated is brought into connection with the effort that will be described in the fourth act: "Therefore, by every means, I must exert myself toward their reunion, even at the cost of my life. From this conjunction arises [the following]: "Therefore, please be seated..."

Beginning with "I wish to tell something that must be told" and ending with "if there were a bond of affection directed toward him," Kāmandakī and Lavaṅgikā describe the intensity of the amorous suffering of Mādhava and Mālatī; thus, the seed of their mutual passion—which was previously latent—is here brought to light. This process of manifestation is further characterized by the presence of dramatic elements such as *vilāsa* (graceful dalliance), which will be developed subsequently, while the subsequent narrative of Śārdūla’s story and the news of Nandana’s decision to marry [Mālatī] serve as intervening obstacles that momentarily obscure it.

The *pratimukha-sandhi* (the intermediate juncture) is now defined. Its characteristic is as follows: "The manifestation of the seed (*bīja*) through being both manifest and unmanifest constitutes the *pratimukha*; the *bindu* arises from effort, and there are thirteen constituent parts (*aṅga*) herein. //4//

"By good fortune, Mālatī too is coming accompanied by Lavaṅgikā"—this is the ellipsis. "It is a marvel! [He says this because] due to the proximity (*sāṃnidhyāt*) of the face of that lotus-eyed one—which is itself a stainless moon free from blemish—my mind, though naturally devoid of fluidity (melting) and lacking any adventitious cause for it, has repeatedly attained a state of dullness (*jaḍimānam*), a state of inertia characterized as "incompetence in action" (*kriyāsvapāṭavam*). This occurs through the medium of the moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*), which is mountain-born, pure by its very nature, and produced from a pristine source.

The meaning is that upon reaching a shrine (*caitya*) which has water as its essential nature (*jalaprakṛtika*), a transformation consisting of fluidity—that is, the state of melting—is maintained. This "melting" of the mind is what is meant by "wonder. By the phrase "of the mountain by means of the moonstone," there is the perception of one's own similarity to a mountain; thus, the cause of wonder is that even my mind, though firm like a mountain, melts away. //5//

"Saṃprati" (now) means that, in comparison with her previously seen state, because the obstacles of separation have become manifest and because it has been ascertained that they pertain to her very self, Mālatī remains exceedingly beautiful; this is the meaning. The word "yataḥ" (since) is to be supplied. Regarding "jvalayati" (she inflames): the "villāsa" (grace) of the "parimṛditā" (crushed), i.e., the faded *campakāvalī* (garland of *campaka* flowers)—the excellence of its luster—is like that [of Mālatī]; by that, she is "lulitaiḥ," meaning turbid or, more precisely, pervaded.

With limbs languid and averse to all activities, she kindles and inflames the fire of love; she intoxicates her heart, making it subject to joy, and she fulfills the purpose of her eyes by providing the ultimate object of sight. Thus, experiencing this state of separation determined to be caused by me, she agitates my inner mind with both bliss and the pangs of passion. This is the meaning. The poetic figure employed here is *kārakadīpaka* (the illuminator of grammatical factors). //6//

Mālatī: Friend, in this thicket of the bower, because of our short stature, we were gathering flowers from the creepers and shrubs whose blossoms could be plucked by our own hands. Mādhava: "The first"—by hearing these words of my beloved, never heard before, I am now experiencing a particular state of the *kadamba* tree: one whose buds are formed by the momentary joy arising from being sprinkled by fresh drops of water from a line of clouds, and which is characterized by a thrill of horripilation (*pulaka*) quivering upon me as I hear her dear speech.

The meaning is that [something] is being imitated. Here, because the effort of approaching him and so forth is understood through its conformity with the desire for enjoyment (saṃbhoga) implied [in the speech], and through the curiosity to hear those words, this is the element of the *pratimukha-sandhi* called *vilāsa*. As it is said: "Effort (*samīhā*) for the sake of enjoying love is proclaimed as *vilāsa*. //7//

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, let us do so. Mādhava: The venerable lady’s mastery—the skill in instructing the science of love—is such that its wonders are immeasurable and beyond definition. By her grace, I now stand here, though hidden, beholding my beloved without hesitation as she busies herself gathering flowers; with her silken garment slipping loose, the beauty of every limb is clearly revealed, and thus I feel as if I am submerged in a lake of nectar.

By this, the dramatic element named *parisarpa* (the winding) is stated, because of the subsequent pursuit of Mālatī, who was previously seen and then her sight of whom was interrupted. As it is said: "The *parisarpa*, however, is the pursuit of that which was seen and then lost. Mālatī: Friend, let us gather [flowers] in another place than this one; in a different region.

Then Kāmandakī, having brought Mālatī by some means into the presence of Mādhava who was stationed nearby in concealment, spoke in order to detain her right there and prevent her from wishing to go elsewhere: Kāmandakī—“O friend! [She has become] exhausted, incapable of wandering about. Why? To this she says: “she causes [my feet] to stumble,” O fair-browed one!

Although the term *subhrū* (O fair-browed one) lacks the designation of *nadī* because it occupies the position of *uvaṅ*, and thus the rule "the short vowel is substituted for *ambā*-type words and *nadī* stems" (*ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ*) does not apply, the correctness of the word *subhrū* is to be understood from the observation of its usage by great poets, such as in the verse: "O fair-browed one, whence comes this disrespect in your father’s house? (*vimānanā subhrū kutaḥ piturgṛhe*). *Kheda* is the fatigue produced by gathering flowers; according to the statement: "Fatigue (*kheda*) is the exhaustion of mind and body resulting from excessive exertion."

It shines forth in every possible way as if identical to the gaze of a passionate woman who, through the sight of her beloved—which has the beloved as its object—is filled with intense longing. This is a playful remark (narmagarbhokti) implying that those very expressions of emotion seen in the woman as she gazes upon her lover are now visible in you as well, due to the influence of her fatigue. Furthermore, there is the perception that [your state] coexists with the gaze performed by the beloved hidden behind the creepers—being identical in terms of both time and the object of focus.

Furthermore, these emotional manifestations (*anubhāvas*) are produced solely by the glances of her beloved and do not arise from the effects of fatigue; thus, even for one who was unaware that her beloved was looking at her, such a transformation occurs through the mere touch of his side-long glance—just as a moonstone undergoes change through the mere contact with moonbeams. "Oh, how profound is your passion!"—this is the suggestion (*dhvani*) of hyperbole (*apahnuti-atiśayokti*) directed toward Mālatī, who is being addressed.

"Thus, although she was guarded by thousands of sentries, I alone have brought her back within the range of my beloved's sight through a stratagem, and not you"—this is an implied message directed at Lavaṅgikā; she has been led into the path of your gaze.

"Behold her confidence"—this is addressed to Mādhava as a bystander; for although she does not know that you are present here, these emotional transformations belong to her as she gazes at you with passion. "Oh, how skilled you are at captivating the hearts of young women!"—thus he expresses himself toward him alone. Although it would have been possible to illustrate the manifold suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) in every verse and even at every word, we have omitted them here for fear of prolixity.

In response to the inquiry as to how there is equality [between the two], he states the similarity of their effects regarding fatigue (*śrama*) and the sight of the beloved (*priyadarśana*): "It causes her speech to falter and makes it stammer. Speech also becomes faltering due to fatigue; likewise, from the sight of the beloved, the *sāttvika* emotion known as stammering (*gadgada*) arises. As it is said: "The experts know stammering to be a paralysis of speech caused by intoxication, joy, shame, and so forth. It "takes refuge in limb after limb," meaning it pervades and exists within all the individual parts of the body.

In the interpretation where it refers to the sight of the beloved, however, "the body" (*aṅga*) is the agent; it takes refuge in another part of the body (*avayavāntara*), which serves as the object, due to exhaustion. This is said to be the *sāttvika* emotion known as exhaustion (*śrama*). Its definition has already been stated. In this reading, because the initial agent—the sight of the beloved—has been abandoned in favor of a different agent, the phrase "equal to the sight of the beloved" functions as a *sahokti* (simultaneity) figure. Nor should it be argued that this is not a fault because the meaning is merely suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

The word "equal" (*tulyam*) implies that, by virtue of the term *sahārtha-tulya* (meaning "equal to [her]"), both [the lover's and the beloved's actions] are expressed directly (*vācya*) and thus lack the status of being suggested (*vyaṅgya*). For it is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), manifested through the transitory states (*anubhāva*) produced by the sight of the beloved, that is suggested; not, however, the act of seeing the beloved herself. Therefore, the reading "sraṃsayati" is superior. It means "she causes each limb to sag," i.e., she makes it droop; by this, the sinking of the limbs (*aṅgasāda*) is expressed, and that is indeed common to both [the lover and the beloved]. Furthermore, the moon-like face produces drops of perspiration characterized by their shining nature.

By this, perspiration common to both is indicated; as it is said: "Perspiration is the emergence of water from the body caused by the heat of passion, fatigue, and so forth. And she closes her eyes; as it is said: "Sighing, perspiration, hissing sounds, and the contraction of the face and eyes—these are the manifesting effects (anubhāvas) of fatigue. Furthermore, in another sense, the closing of the eyes due to the helplessness of pleasure reveals the *sāttvika* emotion known as paralysis (*stambha*). This is a combination (*saṃkara*) of the figures of speech *sahokti* (simultaneity) and *dīpaka* (illumination). //8//

Lavaṅgikā: "The Blessed One has given a most excellent command. Mādhava: "A jest is a word of sport. By this, the dramatic element (*aṅga*) called *narma* (jesting) is mentioned; as it is said: "A word of jest is *narma*. Kāmandakī: "Therefore, please be seated," and so forth. "Something" means only a very small thing that must be told. [She] says [this], having raised up the chin—the lower part of the face—which was bent down by shame; "says" is the ellipsis. "Listen," and so forth.

The citation of a passage from the *Ratirahasya* by Kāmandakī is intended to indicate that the intensity of the hero’s separation about to be described is established by the scriptures as a function of the female messenger (*dūtī*). As it is said: "Having produced a state of cheerfulness, she should say: 'O fortunate one, listen to this wonder! What is so wonderful? This youth, delicate as a flower, has been bitten by the serpent of your glance; O friend, he has fallen into a state of doubt. He pants, perspires, and faints; his fever is likewise irresistible.'"

"Without obtaining the nectar-essence of the moon of your face, she could not have remained alive; O fortunate one, never even in a dream did such a transformation come upon him. The address "O fortunate one" (subhage) clearly implies that your good fortune is such that Mādhava—the sole son of his parents and the very support of his lineage—has come here at the mere mention of your name and remains here alone. Mālatī: I am attentive. Kāmandakī: Incidentally, regarding the statement made by Avalokitā that Mādhava’s body was unwell.

"Binding of the mind": it is called "binding" because it binds [the mind], preventing its movement elsewhere and making it dependent solely upon itself; that is, it is a place of rest. The meaning is "a vessel of affection. Lavaṅgikā: "We remember. Kāmandakī: "He... [referring to Mādhava]. "Acting as if dejected" means acting as if his mind were distressed. "Dependent on another" means under the control of another. By the phrase "at the festival of the Madana-grove," the delight of the eyes (*cakṣuḥprīti*) is expressed, as this refers to their initial mutual sighting. "Acting as if dejected" indicates attachment of the heart (*cittāsaṅga*).

To report that he has been reduced to various such states by Madana on account of you, he describes his other conditions as well, beginning with "When [he beholds] the moon": When this man does not experience joy—that is, a particular state of bliss—either upon seeing the moon, whose body consists of nectar and who delights all the worlds; or when seeing a beloved person, a vessel of unsurpassed affection; then, though he is exceedingly steadfast and possessed of fortitude, he manifests—that is, reveals—an internal heat that is most difficult to endure. By this, two conditions known as "restlessness" (arati) and "feverish heat" (saṃtāpa) have been described.

Likewise, although he possesses a natural bodily luster with limbs as dark as the *phalinī* creeper and the *priyaṅgu* plant, and is thus not pale—despite being marked by the paleness born of separation—he nevertheless bears a body that is exceedingly emaciated and sweet, endowed with the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya*). The definition of sweetness is: "In all conditions, sweetness is the softness of one's movements. He bears a body that has become utterly thin.

And this emaciation, paleness, and so forth, is not caused by disease; thus he says: "He is lovely, and his form remains captivating due to the mere residue of its radiance. Emaciation (kārśya) is mentioned here as a specific state. This is a combination of the two figures of speech: inference (anumāna) and contradiction (virodha). //9//

Lavaṅgikā: This too was reported by Avalokitā at that time, as she was urging the venerable lady to hurry, saying, "Mādhava’s body is restored to health. Kāmandakī: "As far as... [meaning] having heard from ear to ear that the madness caused by Love had been dispelled, I too concluded it to be exactly so; for otherwise, his steadfastness would not have wavered—this is the sense. Regarding the word "experience" (*anubhavam*): with the words "this one," she points to Mālatī’s face while grasping it by the chin.

The moon of his face—present in the mind by virtue of being the subject under discussion, yet hidden from view by a creeper—attained the state of being experienced, reaching the range of direct perception. It is established with certainty and beyond doubt that the sight of the moon of your face has become the cause for the ripening of such a miserable condition for him in every respect.

For, like the water of the great ocean—which is of profound depth, steady, and waveless—his mind has become agitated by longing, tremulous with surges, disturbed, robbed of its fortitude, and overflowed. Just as the ocean is stirred at the very sight of the moon before it even becomes silent, so too, in the agitation of Mādhava’s mind, the sole cause is the sight of your moon-like face; thus, from the effect, the cause is inferred. This is the meaning. The poetic figure is an inference (anumāna) blended through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements between metaphor (rūpaka) and simile (upamā). //10//

Mādhava: "Aho!"—this refers to the purity of the presentation, that is, the manner of exposition being free from defects such as internal contradictions. Regarding the attribution of greatness, the "basis" (*nibandhana*) for the effort involved in superimposing upon me the likeness of the ocean—which does not actually exist in me—is the reason for this comparison. Alternatively, this is no cause for wonder in those such as these. Why? To this he says: "In the scripture" (*śāstre*). This refers to a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), which is a state of perfect realization (*pariniṣṭhiti*) consisting of right knowledge free from the bristles of doubt.

Innate (*sahaja*) is natural understanding—a wisdom characterized by spontaneous flow even toward subtle objects of knowledge and their secrets; or it is boldness, the skill of mature expression, or as it is said: "Boldness is the state of being entirely free from timidity even during performances. Such is the speech (*vāṇī*) which possesses cultivated qualities (*guṇa*)—such as clarity (*prasāda*) and sweetness (*mādhurya*)—that are acquired through effort; and it observes the requirements of time, that is, it watches for the appropriate occasion for speaking.

The quality of being possessed of *pratibhāna* (creative intuition) consists in possessing an intuition characterized by ever-new manifestations that are identical with [the object]. These qualities are like wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadughā*) that fulfill desires regarding the actions one wishes to accomplish. Therefore, the meaning is: what wonder is there in the purity of the introduction and other aspects of this Blessed Lady, who is preeminent in these qualities? //11//

Kāmandakī: "Since... [means: because you, being terrified of life, find it impossible to live without her; thus, for one possessed by such agitation, there is nothing—even what is difficult for a person in separation—that is not done. However, the meaning is that everything is indeed performed by him who hates life. She says this very thing: "For instance... he bears... [means: when the tree is budding, i.e., covered with buds, which, by virtue of their sharp points, have become the arrows of the God of Love (Manmatha).

By the phrase "raṇatkokila" (resounding with cuckoos), it is said that because of the chatter of the flocks of cuckoos—which act like the clamor of the army of Kandarpa—it is impossible even to approach the vicinity as long as that sound is heard, let alone to see him. She fixes her gaze upon that mango tree (*sahakāra*), a particular species of tree charming by its youthfulness, as if it were a serpent whose very look is poison; the meaning is that she casts her glance [upon it] thinking, "Let what is to be happen."

Furthermore, why does he cast his body—as if into a region where enemies stand close by amidst the falling showers of arrows encountered during the time of battle—into the path of the wind that carries the fragrance of saffron flowers and blows gently from the Sandal Mountain? "What is the use of this body so mercilessly subjected to the experience of suffering?"—thus it is considered, and he is touched but once. Likewise, for the sake of allaying his fever, he has as his only covering merely the moist lotus leaves placed there by his attendants; he is one whose physical form is fainting and succumbing to exhaustion.

Since this fever cannot be extinguished by any cooling remedy, today the very affliction of the forest-fire’s flames is the medicine for its quenching, according to the maxim that "heat is pacified by heat. Thus, regarding the forest as the most effective means for the immediate abandonment of the body—being required at that moment—she out of love and partiality takes refuge in death, seeking the rays of the moon which, like the flames of a forest fire to those separated from their lovers, cause her life-breath to depart at that instant.

Thus, the meaning is this: although he performs an exceedingly difficult feat, disregarding his own life, he becomes a vessel for the suspicion of ill omen because he incessantly holds within his heart you alone—the medicinal herb that paralyzes all poisons, fires, and the like—despite his rashness. Here, since many actions such as seeing the blossoming young mango tree and so forth are combined as means for a single effect characterized by death, there is the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation). As it is said: "Accumulation (*samuccaya*) is the simultaneity of qualities and actions. //12//

Mālatī: He performs such a difficult task! Kāmandakī: Thus, in the manner described, even death can be endured by him, since he is by nature delicate and possesses the highest degree of delicacy. As it is said: "Delicacy is divided into three types—superior, middling, and inferior—in descending order. That which cannot endure the touch of a flower or a sprout is the superior. Because he has previously experienced [the intensity of] passion, its unbearable nature was mentioned as being "perhaps" [the case]. This poor soul is truly pitiable.

Or rather, he is a "tapasvin" (an ascetic) because he performs a most difficult penance characterized by the experience of the pain of separation from you, solely for the sake of the great human goal (*puruṣārtha*) of union with you. By the word "Kumāra," his state of not yet having taken a wife and the well-being of his parents are implied. Mālatī: Friend, because of him—who is the ornament of the mortal world—I am apprehensive about something and, as if possessed by a spirit, I do not know what he will do. She indicates death by the word "something."

"I do not know what answer should be given to the words of the Blessed Lady; you yourself should provide the appropriate reply, such as reporting my condition," was her intention. Mādhava: "By good fortune! By the power of fate, I have been favored by the Blessed Lady who has revealed my own state. Or rather, because she was separated from me only by the creeper, these words were heard by Mādhava standing nearby; this utterance is made out of joy at hearing her speech. Lavaṅgikā:

The Blessed One is thus described. Our lady, having frequently beheld him as he adorned the street near our residence for a moment, has experienced a delight of the eyes; this is what is meant by "joy of the sight. Though she is made beautiful by the intense experience of amorous longing, manifested by the lovely beauty of her limbs which resemble the tender root of a lotus embraced by the rays of the sun, she causes her attendants to grieve. Her physical exhaustion and paleness have been mentioned. She takes no pleasure in artistic diversions—namely, the arts such as dancing, singing, and so forth.

Discontent has been described; she merely passes her days with the circles of her cheeks resting upon her fading, lovely hands. Anxiety has been indicated; moreover, she languishes at the breeze from the edge of the palace garden, which is beautiful with the trickling nectar of blossoming lotuses and carries a mass of honey-drops from slightly opened *kunda* and *mākanda* flowers. This is an expression of the intensity of the pain produced by the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).

Furthermore, from that day forward—when the commencement of his youth, which was most praiseworthy and indeed to be accomplished, was brought about by the various amorous sports (*vibhrama*) and playful charms (*vilāsa*) of that Mādhava—who had assumed a physical form on that very day to witness the prosperity of his own great festival, like the divine Madana, the ornament of the forest of desire (*kāmakānana*), and who was characterized by a continuous flow of passion and an intensity of longing directed toward a suitable beloved—the [festival] became exceedingly laudable. "That whose commencement of youth is such" is the meaning.

At that moment of deception through the casting of glances at one another, Mālatī attained the joy of mutual gazing, which delighted her circle of friends; for her mind was feverish and distressed, while her limbs—agitated by a sudden curiosity yet rendered motionless by a paralysis born of trepidation—were overcome by the involuntary states (sāttvikabhāva) of perspiration, horripilation, and trembling.

From that time forth, experiencing a transformation of her state that is fierce and intense due to the expansion of an especially unbearable exhaustion, she withers away like a young lotus-plant at the rising of the full moon. Nevertheless, I know that for a mere moment, by fixing the imagined union with her beloved within her heart, she becomes cool, like the earth being drenched by a heavy downpour of rain.

[He beheld a face] exceptionally beautified by the splendor of rows of pearl-like teeth shining from lips quivering with joy; with clusters of tears of incessant bliss rolling upon cheeks downy with hair standing on end; (if the reading is *bāhadhevam*, *dheva* means a drop); charming with a crescent moon of a forehead marked by beautiful drops of perspiration breaking forth continuously, and with blue-lotus eyes slightly askance, motionless, languid, upturned, smooth, and closing like buds; "niṭila" means the forehead.

She bears a charming lotus-face, and her maidenhood has become a subject of doubt in the minds of her clever female companions; for this reason, her virginity has been cast into a state of uncertainty within the hearts of those skillful friends by signs of sexual enjoyment, such as the throbbing of the lips, horripilation, tears of joy, specific changes in the eyes, perspiration, and so forth.

"How is it that this maiden, though still a girl, appears as if she has been enjoyed by a skilled lover and is adorned with the marks of sexual union?"—thus she becomes filled with doubt. For that reason, one should understand that she has been "extinguished" (satisfied) by the fullness of the enjoyment of her beloved, who was fashioned [by her own mind] and placed within her heart. All of this has already been explained by us in the commentary on the verse beginning with "nīvībandha," and so it is not elaborated upon here.

Furthermore, she passes her nights as if they were wide awake—having demonstrated a state of vigilance—as she wears a necklace of moonstones from which flows a continuous stream kissed by the mass of the unrestrained rays of the moon; as her bed consists of young plantain leaves bristling with a profuse shower of drops from the spray of especially cool sandalwood juice mixed with abundant camphor; and as she possesses a palm-leaf fan moistened with lotus petals brought to her by a company of female companions eager to perform services such as massaging her feet. Thus, the state of wakefulness is shown.

Having somehow attained sleep, she found that sleep itself was a pleasure because it brought about a union with her beloved in a dream; this very point he expresses as follows: she was one by whom the mass of *piṇḍālaktaka* dye was vomited forth—that is, discharged—from her two sprout-like feet, which were washed by incessant streams of perspiration. *Tharatharāyanti* is a regional word (*deśīya*) denoting trembling. She was one whose knot of the lower garment (*nīvībandhana*) had slipped away—that is, loosened—from the sides of her thick thighs, which were shaking.

The meaning is that through the tossing of her trembling vine-like arms over their breasts—which were heaving in many uneven ways with sighs from the surging waves within her agitated heart, and which were covered in downy hair and bristling with thrills—she experienced the bliss of a firm embrace from her beloved during a dream-union; this was evidenced by the loosening of her girdle due to perspiration and trembling, her sighing, her horripilation, and the encircling of her vine-like arms.

She is one whose eyes are closed due to the delusion produced by that bed—upon which the hero was once present, but which has now become empty of consciousness because he has been released from her sidelong glance at the moment of sudden awakening, and because it is devoid of the hero whose neck was once embraced within such an arm-lasso.

She is one whose hope for life was produced by the long sighs that issued forth all at once after being suppressed for a long time—at the moment when her fainting fit was broken by the efforts of her circle of friends, who were agitated and distressed, and who employed means such as fanning with fans and sprinkling with cool sand; she thus causes her circle of friends—who were previously bewildered as to what should be done, who had first sought the end of their own lives, and whose only activity was the censuring of the irresistible play of fate—to act [in a certain way].

Let the Blessed Lady observe this: regarding these limbs, which are exceedingly delicate and tender due to a creation abounding in beauty, how long—after what period of time—will there be a "successful conclusion," meaning a happy ending, for the God of Love who has manifested therein? This is the sense remaining [in the verse]. The meaning is: when, after this moment, will the cruel-acting Smara (the God of Love) act with skill upon Mālatī’s limbs by means of a reunion with her beloved?

And how? These dawns possess the veils of darkness shattered by the unrestrained and bold moonlight—moonlight that is overflowing and stainless, as tender as the cheeks of a Kerala woman whose cheeks have put forth sprouts through the passion of anger (koparāga) brought on by playful quarrels with her lover; and these [dawns] have the courtyards of the sky washed by the brilliance of moonlight, white and radiant like a surging stream of milk.

The ends of the night bring misfortune to my dear friend in all ten directions, stirred up by the Malaya breeze—which is smooth, glossy, and robust through its blending with the outpouring of abundant fragrance produced by the crushing of the pāṭala buds that have already begun to emit their scent. Such are the beginnings of the night for my dear friend, and such are the endings of the night.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "May the Blessed Lady also see how or in what manner they become sources of misfortune. In the reading "they do not exist" (*na bhavanti*), the meaning is: "How could they not be sources of misfortune? They certainly are. By showing that both the beginning and the end of the night are causes of misfortune, it is demonstrated that the entire day and night are of such a nature. Kāmandakī: "If... (yadīti).

If this bond of affection is a deep attachment, and if its object is Mādhava—that is, if it has Mādhava as its support—then this very thing is clearly evident. The word *hi* (for) has the sense of *eva* (indeed). My heart, which was gladdened by this stability of affection and filled with joy because of the favorability of the task already begun, is being rent asunder by this cruel state of yours described [by you]. The meaning is that, due to her delicacy, fearing the sudden onset of misfortune, it becomes as if torn apart. //13//

Mādhava: "Exultation" (*abhyullāsa*) refers to the agitation of the heart due to the apprehension of something undesirable; the meaning is that it is "appropriate" (*sthāne*). Kāmandakī: "Negligence" (*pramāda*) means our own lack of attention. "Oh, what a marvel!"—the meaning is that even now, while I am still in doubt, I am delaying the reunion with Mālatī even at the cost of my life. She expresses the impropriety of this delay: "By nature graceful" (*prakṛtyā lalitam*). "Graceful" (*lalita*) is defined as a physical posture suited to the erotic sentiment arising from the onset of youth.

As it is said: "The graceful (*lalita*) movement of women is described as having a delicate arrangement of limbs, with actions of the eyebrows, eyes, and lips that are neither excessive nor coarse, but smooth. Because of its connection with this [grace], her body has *saukumārya* (delicacy) as its sole essence; *saukumārya* alone is the stable constituent part of this body, meaning there is no other connection to physical strength (*sattva*). By the statement, "That which cannot endure the touch of flowers or tender shoots is the highest," it is this highest *saukumārya* that is intended here.

Moreover, this five-arrowed one [Kāma] is cruel and his activity is most terrible; let that be as it may. But how is it that even this season has now arrived—possessing the lovely moon as its crest-ornament, with clusters of mango blossoms shaken by the fragrant breeze blowing slowly from the Candanācala mountain, and free from the obstruction of frost, clouds, and the like? Alas! A succession of misfortunes has converged. By this, the dramatic element named *vidhūta* (agitation) is expressed, as it is said: "Agitation (*vidhūta*) is the distress of two youths arising from the failure to attain sexual union. //14//

Lavaṅgikā: Furthermore, let the venerable lady know this as well. This picture-board, which contains the likeness of Mādhava—meaning that this too, which demonstrates the intensity of Mādhava’s passion, must be known by the venerable lady. As for the breast-cloth, it was for the purpose of looking at the garland suspended from his neck. This Bakula wreath suspended from her own neck is also the very one fashioned by his own hand; it is the "reviver" of my dear friend.

Thus, there should be no doubt whatsoever regarding the Blessed Lady’s affection for Mādhava; the intention is that some means of union must be employed immediately by any possible way. Mādhava: "Victory! (conquered!)—that is, [the obstacle has been overcome].

Friend Bakulāvalī, who was formerly draped around my neck and has now become an intimate companion at the neck of my beloved—being thus solely intent on accomplishing my purpose—you have become my friend. In this entire world, in every realm of existence, you alone have triumphed; you have attained a preeminent excellence that surpasses all others, since you have become the darling of this beloved woman.

For how might I become the object of her longing gaze that betokens passion for me; how might I attain the bliss of satiety born from the touch of her body; and how might my life find its fulfillment through the great festival of embracing her neck even for a moment? That which I have thus constantly yearned for has been realized by you, who serve as the ornament to the circle of her breasts and who incessantly gaze upon and contemplate them with longing—you who have become the very support of my life.

The sense is that, being constantly hailed as "dear friend," her good fortune has increased a thousandfold—alas, what an excellence of your beauty! He demonstrates this very point through the following qualification: the expansion of the breasts, which is as pale as the joint (*kāṇḍa*) of a mature lotus stalk—that is, the region of its nodes—is a *vaijayantī*, a banner, signifying the manifestation of their grace and illuminating their preeminence.

By this—namely, by Madhava’s knowledge that the bakula garland fashioned with his own hands has become an ornament upon the neck of his beloved—the experience of joy is realized and the state of restlessness (arati) is pacified; thus, the dramatic element called *śama* (tranquility) is expressed. As it is said: "The pacification of restlessness is tranquility (*śama*). The poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) here is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality). //15//

Having thus nourished the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa through the mutual expression of affection and the communication of each other’s conditions, he introduces the *arthopakṣepa* (plot-indication) called *cūlikā* in order to conceal it with another *rasa*. [The stage direction: "In the tiring-room" (*nepathye*). The definition of *cūlikā* is: "An indication of the matter of the *cūlikā* by those stationed behind the inner curtain. "O you country-folk dwelling in the city of Śaṅkara! Indeed, these two—intolerance and anger—which are filled with the onset of youth and difficult to endure, as well as impatience and wrath—"

Alternatively, there are two types of anger: persistent anger (*sthirakrodha*) and immediate wrath (*tātkālikakopa*). As they say: "Krodha is that which, directed toward those who have committed an offense, assumes the state of enduring resentment; roṣa is immediate wrath. Through the *vyatikara*—the blending or union—of these two, there is a forceful compulsion. By that force, his fetters (*nigala*), which were previously broken—that is, shattered—and subsequently opened—that is, with the door-fastenings removed—became stuck, adhered, and melted right within that iron cage. Thus, he is one whose shackles have slipped from his own feet.

He whose bodily form was adorned with unrestrained ferocity—formidable, difficult to behold, terrifying, and fierce—was characterized by a lofty, high, and beloved tail-tuft that served as a strange banner (vaijayantikā); this tail, like a staff for a young elephant, had been raised upward and extended out in sport and at will, having finally attained its own natural freedom after a long time due to the removal of the confinement of his cage and shackles.

Having departed from the monastery, at that very moment of departure, his cavernous mouth—the hollow of the face made jagged by fangs as hard as saws—was making a *kaṭakaṭā* sound through the gnashing produced by the crushing of those harsh, rough fragments of bone belonging to the many bodies of embodied beings that had been greedily swallowed. He was one whose mouth-cavern was formidable with such fangs.

Likewise, that which is "vikaṭa" refers to a yawning or a movement; by that, he is "uddāmadāruṇaḥ," meaning fiercely terrifying. A "capeṭa" is a hand with its fingers spread apart. As Amara states: "In the sense of a hand, *capeṭa*, *pratala*, and *prahasta* [are used] when the fingers are spread. By that [hand], it was "āmoṭita," meaning crushed or rubbed. This form [is derived] from the root *muṭ* in the sense of "crushing."

That whose throat-cavity is filled—meaning completely full—with the excessive vomiting (udgāra) of the flesh of men and horses gathered from all sides, which is lean and bloody; and which possesses a deep, gurgling sound (*gharghara*) within that cavity. *Rallī* is a regional word (*deśīpada*) used to denote a long and sweet sound.

He was one by whom the vault of the sky was filled with the vast expanse of a long, sweet, and gurgling sound—a throat-roar produced by the very species of a tiger enraged at the time of devouring meat. Furthermore, he was one whose host consisted of all those people who had been slain, some crushed and ground to powder, some vanished and rendered invisible, and some brought to their end, led to the ultimate limit of safety.

In some versions, the reading is "bhīṣitanaṣṭaniṣṭhāpitāḥ. In that case, it should be explained as follows: first they were terrified; afterwards they perished, having passed beyond the range of vision; and finally they were brought to rest, having been led to a place of safety. Likewise, the wicked tiger—whose path of movement is mired in the blood flowing from the limbs of creatures torn apart and dragged away by his hard claws acting like shards—is performing the sport of Death (Kṛtānta). Therefore, protect your own lives according to your ability! [Thus speaks] Buddharakṣitā.

"Save her! This sister of our dear friend, the minister’s son Nandana—Madayantika—is being overwhelmed by this wicked tiger, while her attendants have been struck down and scattered. Mālatī: "Friend Lavaṅgikā, oh, what a great calamity! It was improper for us to remain so long alone in this desolate forest. Now, who will save us? (This is the sense. Mādhava: "Where is he? I shall slay him this very moment and release your friend. (This is the meaning.)

Mālatī (with joy and trepidation): [Thus: There is joy because Mādhava has discovered right here, while present in this very place, the entire account of the painting-board depicting the pain of her own separation and the story of Bakulāvalī, which was reported to him by Lavaṅgikā; and there is trepidation because, having seen him in this secluded spot, someone might report it to my father. Ah! Oh, what a lapse of care! [The word] *ahmahe* is employed in the sense of anxiety accompanied by negligence. According to the rule: "The specific verbal form *ahmahe* should be used by speakers specifically in the context of anxious negligence."

This too occurs right here. Mādhava: The verse beginning with "yad" (since) serves as a supplement to this. Regarding the word *aviralam* (densely): by this [Mālatī], the agent, who is overwhelmed by wonder and joy (*ullasita*) due to that sight of me which has arrived unexpectedly (*atarkitopanatam*), without suspicion (*aśaṅkitam*), and by force (*haṭhāt*), her eyes—expanded (*sphāritena*) according to the definition: "Expanded is said to be long and with trembling pupils"—acting as the instrument, have bound her, as it were, densely with a cord (*dāmnā*) made of white lotuses (*pauṇḍarīka*).

The word "I" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And the state of being a tethering rope (*dāmatva*) for her side-long glances arises from their falling down in close succession, forming a continuous line. By showing himself to be bound, he manifests the *sāttvika* emotion known as paralysis (*stambha*). Likewise, he is as if bathed by an overflowing, full stream of milk; through this bathing in a flood of milk, he expresses the excellence of his own satiation.

I have been swallowed whole—entirely engulfed and taken in by her glance, as if drawn into my very heart due to the excellence of the sweetness of the object. This suggests that she remains unsatisfied even after gazing at me for a long time. She is like one sprinkled by a thick cloud raining down nectar; by this, the operation of the gaze known as *lola* (the "rolling" glance) is described, according to the principle of a continuous downpour of rain. As it is said: "That whose movement proceeds in a continuous stream is called *lola*. Thus, there is the poetic figure of *mālōpamā* (the string of similes). //16//

Buddharakṣitā: Noble sir, he is indeed at the entrance of the street outside the garden. Mādhava: (Pompously and with agitation) He is vigilant and attentive. Mālatī: Lavaṅgikā, a doubt has truly arisen—there is a suspicion whether he will emerge from the jaws of death by the tiger or not. Alas! (The sense is: "Fie! Mādhava: (With loathing and disgust) [He] says... (the verb "says" is understood). Aha! (expressing wonder). Regarding the word *saṃsakta*:...

The path of the claw-armed tiger bears and displays extreme ferocity and terrifyingness. Of what sort is it? It is strewn and crowded with networks of entrails—first caught upon creepers and the like, then severed and cut, and finally twisted and cast upon the ground—and it is where there are quivering, radiant, displaced, and overturned fragments of headless trunks, that is, severed pieces of skulls.
Likewise, it is that place where there is mud reaching up to the ankles due to the mingling—that is, the mixing—of *kīlāla*, which is blood. //17//

"Ah, what negligence! It is a marvel that the attendants of Madayantikā have been so inattentive, in the sense that she has fallen into a peril from which there is no remedy. He explains this very lack of remedy: "As for us... We, for our part, remain at a distance; but the maiden has come within the range of the beast. The meaning is that she stands in a place reachable by a single step. The exclamation "Hā! indicates the calamity of a beloved person. Mādhava’s state of joy arises from both the slaying of the tiger and the saving of the woman.

Kāmandakī’s state of being "pregnant with meaning" (*sākūtatvam*) arises because Makaranda’s assistance in saving Madayantika’s life is conducive to the union of the two lovers. How so? Makaranda suddenly arrives in a state of agitation from [the scene] where he was struck down—that is, killed—by that tiger. The phrase "from a certain man with a weapon in hand" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. He is one by whom a weapon has been "attained" (*adhigatam*), meaning he has seized the weapon held in the hand of the soldier slain by it.

The meaning is that he, appearing unexpectedly between Madayantikā and the tiger, has become her support. The others [say]: "Well done! Great manliness has been displayed"—this is the ellipsis. "Firmly": Makaranda struck and slew the beast so as to make it firm [in its death]. And by this Makaranda, that beast was deprived of life (made *vyasu*), crushed (*pramathita*), and—according to some readings—"fanged" (*daṃṣṭrāyudha*). "Mutilated" (*khaṇḍita*): the meaning is the tiger. //18//

The others: "A calamity" means a great danger; the word "presented" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Kāmandakī: The reason for her being filled with significance has been stated. A "vyāla" is a cruel beast. Like a staff fixed to the surface of the earth with one end firmly planted, he remained motionless by leaning upon—that is, supporting himself by—the "sword-blade," meaning that despite being struck powerfully, due to his great heroism he remained standing while clutching his own weapon, rather than falling.

He was supported by Madayantika, who was bewildered and distressed, as she extended her hand to him for support. The others: "Alas! Woe! The noble one is fainting from the severity of his wounds!
