Mādhava: "What? Is Makaranda unconscious, having fallen into a swoon? O Blessed One, save him! It should be understood that he speaks thus because, due to the calamity befalling his friend, he himself seems to have become unconscious. Kāmandakī: "You are overly timid. Why do you fear so much for this reason alone? 'Nanu' is used here as a form of address."

"Come, let us see Makaranda; we shall see how he is faring"—this is the meaning. And this constitutes an *aṅkāvatāra* (transition between acts), because the matter of the subsequent act is introduced at the end of the preceding act, since the two acts possess a connected narrative. As it is said: "An *aṅkāvatāra* is the entry of the next act at the end of an act without a break in the continuity; it is desired as the entrance of a future act following the interruption of the story stated at the conclusion of the previous act."
If there exists in some rare scholars the skill to savor the aesthetic essence of Bhavabhūti’s poetic compositions, [then they may understand this work].

Thus ends the commentary on the third act of the *Mālatīmādhava-bhāvapradīpikā*, composed by the venerable Tripurāri Sūri, the son of Parvatanātha Yāyajūka, the ornament of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Act Four.
I bow to Kāmākṣī— the left-eyed lady on the left side of Śambhu— who has bestowed her favor for the purpose of granting the bliss of love, so that my desires may be attained.

The poet now begins the act itself, for at the end of the preceding act he had already indicated the entry of the characters and the events of this act through the *praveśaka*. [He does so] with the words beginning "Then," and so forth. Since Mādhava too is stunned by the calamity that has befallen his friend, we must observe that he finds support in the presence of Mālatī. Madayantikā: Be gracious, O Blessed One; protect the noble one, who out of compassion for those in distress has risked his life for the sake of Madayantikā.

"Madayantikā’s sign"—this is a suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the literal meaning is transferred to another sense. What is illuminated is her capacity to produce the beauty of the limbs that cause the loss of life for a supreme leader among extraordinary men. "The others": Alas! What is there now for us to behold here? Makaranda: Friend, you are far too timid. What is this? The meaning is that even for one as steadfast as you, this is improper. "Nanu" is used as an address: am I not indeed composed, not bewildered? Madayantikā:

Ah! Makaranda has now awakened. By the attribution of "full moon" (*pūrṇacandra*), he indicates the intensity of his passion, for it brings delight to his own heart. Mālatī places her hand upon Mādhava’s forehead; this placement of the hand on the forehead is intended to instantly dispel his fainting spell through the touch of his body, which is like a sprinkling of nectar. One should not suspect such audacity on the part of Mālatī.

In such a time of calamity, because performing appropriate services for everyone everywhere is not manifested in the world as a sign of worldly wisdom (*dārṣṭya*). Kāmandakī: [The act of] smelling the head is a manifestation of affection toward the children of venerable elders. She is one whose two dear ones—the objects of her affection—are like her own offspring, though they are still living. The others: "A pleasant thing has happened to us. Buddharakṣitā: Friend Madayantikā, this is indeed he.

The meaning is: this very Makaranda is the one whose unsurpassed affection for you was previously described by me. Madayantikā: Friend, I already knew it. This is indeed Mādhava, and this person is that very man. [She does not mention his name because she has determined him to be her husband. The meaning is that through the correspondence with the specific physical description mentioned by you, through his disregard for his own life and his devotion to saving my life, and through the conduct of Kāmandakī and others, it was already known that this Makaranda is devoted to me.

Buddharakṣitā: "Am I also one who speaks the truth? Does his brilliance, such as his beauty and other virtues, which I have described, appear before your very eyes or not? Madayantikā: "Indeed, those like you do not show partiality toward people like us. Friend, there is even talk of Mālatī’s affection for this noble gentleman; therefore, my heart feels that the fulfillment of my brother’s desire is difficult to attain. Kāmandakī: [Silence] (Or: [She reflects])...

It is delightful, for it is charming because it perfectly reveals the beauty of each other's limbs as their garments slip away in agitation, and because it is linked to the great festival of a firm embrace under the pretext of nervousness. It is likewise powerful, being the root of assistance that enables one to cross over a calamity otherwise difficult to surmount through fate—and not by our own efforts, since achieving such a thing would be impossible through human exertion alone. It has been brought near, that is, made present. Makaranda: "Even as he arrives," meaning even as he comes with haste.

*Avaskanda* means overcoming. I have accepted—that is, I have taken as my own—the maiden Abhijātā, a young girl whose status as a daughter of a great family is inferred from her distinguished appearance and other traits. Mālatī and Mādhava reflect; the meaning is that both of them reflect because the cause of their mental agitation is common to both, as is the case with pleasure and pain. Kāmandakī sets forth the news that causes excessive agitation in Mādhava’s mind—Kāmandakī: "By this account... [etc.]

The meaning is that the bestowal of Mālatī upon the king for his delight must be nearly accomplished. Now, having ascertained the news, they will soon come here to summon [the king] to the inner apartments; therefore, before that happens, I shall have Mādhava himself express his own intention in order to inspire confidence in Mālatī’s mind—with this in mind, he says: "Dear Mādhava, you have been made to flourish by Mālatī; you have had your consciousness restored. This is the occasion for a gift of affection, a reward."

The meaning is: "Let that be given. Mādhava says: "As for 'this'... This Mālatī, because she—out of compassion—has made me free from pain, even though I was unconscious due to the fainting fit of my friend who was wounded and mangled by a serpent (a cruel creature), is therefore at liberty to accept both my heart and my life according to her own will, without even my permission, in the manner of the *pūrṇapātra* (the full vessel); she is empowered to dispose of them as she pleases.

The *pūrṇapātra* (full vessel) is defined as jewelry, garments, and so forth, being forcibly seized by one who announces pleasant news. The intention is: "Since my heart and even my very life have long been dependent upon him, that much shall be given by me; beyond this there is nothing—what more can be given now? Because this provides a fitting reply, it is called the dramatic element (*aṅga*) named *pragamanam* (departure). As it is said: "A fitting reply is *pragamanam*. (1)

Lavaṅgikā: Indeed, this favor has been accepted by our dear friend. The meaning is that this itself is a great favor—that the life of your heart depends upon our dear friend; what more could be praiseworthy than this? Madayantikā: This noble person knows how to speak charmingly. "Charming" means speaking in a way that reveals the intentions within the mind and demonstrates skill in outward courtesy, such that it is captivating to the heart. Mālatī:

"What indeed could Makaranda have heard that would cause such distress?"—the word "to Mādhava" is to be supplied. "Entering," and so forth: "The elder" means the eldest. "By the Supreme Lord"—meaning by the King whose commands are not to be transgressed—"our entire being [is placed] in supreme trust. This signifies an unsurpassed harmony of minds between one another, demonstrating that "his is ours" and "ours is his," fit for disposal according to his will. "Bestowed" means given. "Let us honor [him]."

The meaning is that it brings about great respect through joy. And this is the limb (aṅga) called *nirodha* (suppression), because it obstructs the attainment of what is currently under discussion; as it is said: "Suppression (*nirodha*) is the obstruction of a benefit. Makaranda: "This is she"—the meaning is that she is the very same person of whom you heard the distressing report. *Vaivarṇya* is the state of being discolored, a form of the *sāttvika* emotion caused by the torment arising from the onset of an incurable calamity.

As it is said: "A change in complexion (*vaivarṇya*) or a difference in color may arise from distress, suspicion, fear, and the like. Madayantikā: Friend Mālatī, you have indeed been my dear friend and sister since we lived in the same city and played together in the dust; now, moreover, as the wife of my brother, you have become the ornament of our home. Kāmandakī: "May you prosper"—this is a statement made with a touch of irony. Madayantikā: By the grace of your blessings.

The intention is that the recovery of Mālatī is due solely to your blessings, and not from the intensity of mutual affection between the husband and wife. Friend Lavaṅgikā, our desires are fulfilled and complete. Because the recovery of Mālatī—who is accompanied by her attendants—is itself your recovery, the plural form "your" is used. Lavaṅgikā: Friend, this must be discussed among us as well. The meaning is that we too must say: "Our desires are fulfilled precisely by the recovery of those like you, who possess such praiseworthy connections."

Moreover, we ourselves must deliberate on this: that our desires will be fulfilled by your future gain in the form of obtaining Makaranda, along with your attendants. It is not for you to do so, because the acquisition of Mālatī and her retinue is certain through your mere resolve alone. Madayantikā: Friend Buddharakṣitā, come now; let us celebrate this great festival. Lavaṅgikā: [She approaches.]

Just as wonder and bliss, which are overflowing and full within the heart, emerge from it, so too do the steady glances—those glances beautiful because of that wonder and bliss, and whose steadiness is maintained for the sake of concealing their true nature—become whirled and turned; finally, they are cast about toward the corners of the eyes, moving with a variety of charming, languid, and rolling motions.

The glances of Madayantikā and Makaranda—possessing the rich hue of a blooming blue lotus—have become intermingled through their meeting face-to-face; such is the casting of their side-long looks that I believe these two have already attained the fulfillment of union through their minds alone. The meaning is that by the very manner in which their glances proceed, they are inferred to be thus. Kāmandakī says: "Nanu" (indeed), etc.; "mānasaṃ mohanam" refers to the delusion of the mind, namely, the enjoyment created by imagination.

He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that manifests this [state] with the words "tathā hi" (for thus). Regarding "īṣat" (slightly): it praises the visible sight of these two so that it may be manifest; the meaning is that it describes the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) created by their mental resolve. Of what kind was the sight? It was "uneven" (*viṣama*), meaning crooked, due to a slight oblique turning—that is, a slight upward tilt to one side. This is the erotic transformation (*śṛṅgāra-vikāra*) known as "crooked" (*vakra*). As it is said: "That movement of the limbs where there is a contraction is called 'crooked'. "Kūṇita" means having the corners of the eyes slightly contracted.

The meaning is that it is contracted at the outer corner (apāṅgadeśa) by three parts. Regarding *kūṇita* (contracted): "That gaze of which there is a contraction of three parts and an expansion of the other [parts] due to a particular emotion (*vilakṣa*) is called *vikūṇita*. And: "When there is a contraction of three parts in front through love, that becomes *kūṇita*. He points to this [gaze] as being present before him. It is *stimita* (motionless), *niṣpanda* (unwavering), *lalita* (graceful), and *premārdra* (moist with love) due to the emergence—that is, the manifestation—of love (*preman*), which is passion (*anurāga*).

Regarding *niṣpandalalita*, it is said: "That which does not move at all toward anything other than what has been seen is *niṣpanda*; that which is moist with love, blossoming within, and radiant is called *lalita*. Where the eyebrows are slightly contracted and breathing out a little, that modification of the eyebrows is called *catura*, as is the modification of the gracious glance; its definition was stated previously. It is smooth through the experience of internal intoxication and internal bliss, and colored by love.

"That [glance] should be known as smooth (*masṛṇa*), yet tinged with passion (*anurāgakaṣāyita*"); this too was stated previously. "Where the eyelashes (*pakṣman*) are drooping (*srasta*), languid (*avasanna*), motionless (*niṣkampa*), and fixed (*niścala*)," that is the *ākekarā* eye. Regarding the *ākekarā* gaze, it is said: "The *ākekarā* gaze is considered to be one whose lids are contracted, which is slightly closed for the purpose of meeting the body [of the beloved], and whose pupil (*tārā*) repeatedly rolls about. Some, however, maintain that in the phrase "the eye seen with an *ākekarā* glance," the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) itself denotes the *ākekarā* gaze.

They explain that the very nature of the sidelong glance (*ākekaradṛṣṭi*) is defined by such qualifiers as "slightly oblique" (*īṣattiryak*) and so forth; furthermore, the word *aciram* (not long) is an adverbial qualifier of the act of seeing. //2//

Madayantikā: Friend Buddharakṣitā, will this lotus-eyed one, the giver of my life, be seen again? By the repetition of "will he," an excess of longing is expressed. Buddharakṣitā: If fate is favorable. Then Mādhava, having reached the certainty that Mālatī would be given to him, speaks the verse beginning with "cirāt" (after a long time), revealing the extreme distress born of his despair.

Let the thread of hope—the very cord of expectation for attaining her, which has persisted for so long as fragile as a lotus fiber or a stalk of lotus—now break; let it be severed. The hope for union with my beloved, though weak, has endured for this length of time; the meaning is that it is now snapped. Likewise, let this great mental anguish, this very disease of the mind, now spread forth without limit and without respite.

The meaning is: having somehow endured this mental anguish while awaiting the limit characterized by the attainment of Mālatī, let it now expand without restraint due to the certainty that that limit no longer exists. Likewise, let the preeminence of the burden of restless mental agitation—in the form of despondency—attain its firm footing in me, unfeignedly, that is to say, with full confidence. The meaning is: let it reach a state of instability, like a tuft of cotton tossed by a gale, because the hope for Mālatī’s attainment—the very support for that agitation—has vanished.

In this way, let fate maintain its constancy, and let Love be one who has accomplished his purpose; for the great objective that must be achieved by both has been brought to fulfillment through great effort—this is the meaning. The sense is that life beyond this point will be difficult to obtain even for a mere moment. Since multiple causes converge toward a single effect, there is the figure of speech known as *samuccaya* (accumulation). //3//

Or rather—thus he consoles himself: "Equal"—meaning one who possesses equal love, a shared passion that is difficult to find and hard to attain because it depends on another; for me, having entreated such a person, this result—a state consisting of calamity—is entirely appropriate given that Fate’s undertaking was perverse and its effort was directed toward the contrary.

Although I resolve my heart thus, "Therefore, I must not yield to despondency," nevertheless, at this moment of hearing about the gift—specifically upon hearing the news that King [Nandana] has given Mālatī to Nandana—her face, its luster fading away, its radiance suddenly drained, and thus possessing the brilliance of the morning moon, burns me within. The meaning is: her condition is such merely by the hearing of the news; but once that purpose is accomplished, what will become of her? This alone is the cause of my agony, not the certainty of our own misfortune. //4//

Kāmandakī: Becoming despondent—that is, becoming dejected—[she says]: "That my dear child Mālatī should live without hope is itself difficult. Such a state of affairs exists that life itself is more contemptible than death. And this calamity cannot be remedied except through a deceptive stratagem; and since that is difficult, it is for this reason that my mental agitation is so intense. Very well then."

He says aloud, "I ask," in order to comfort her by resorting to boldness. By the address "O long-lived one," he indicates that while I am here, you should not entertain any doubt regarding your life. I ask because I wish to know what the cause of this extreme distress is now, compared to before. Having been certain for so long that Bhūriśravas alone would give his daughter to me, why have you maintained your life in this way? Tell me this; I ask you.

If that were so, then this excessive remorse is now appropriate, because she has been given by him to another; such is the meaning. Mādhava—(with shame): "It is only through youthful fickleness that you have become enamored of her. Having understood the intention of Kāmandakī’s words—that Bhūrivasu did not summon Mādhava here saying, "I shall give my daughter to you"—he speaks with shame. "Not at all, not at all!"—from where could there be a statement such as "I shall give her to him"? His thought is: "He does not even know our name."

Kāmandakī: In that case, Bhūrivasu has not fallen away from his former state, nor has it changed; previously, you had no hope that Bhūrivasu would give [his daughter], and now that hope is still absent. What then is the cause for this excessive distress? Your mutual passion also has not diminished from its former state; since it is by virtue of that which both of you have sustained your lives for so long, nothing new has occurred at present. This is the sense of the question: "Why is there such anguish? Makaranda:

Although Bhūrivasu did not say, "I shall give my daughter to Mādhava," nor did he remain waiting with that intention in mind, nevertheless, because Mālatī had not previously been promised to anyone by her father and because he himself imagined his own fitness [for the marriage], he remained in a state of mere hope. Now, however, having heard the report that the King, having been previously entreated, has given her to Nandana, his hopes are shattered; thus, fearing the undesirable outcome, there is a discrepancy between the earlier and later times—this is the meaning.

Kāmandakī: "I know. This report is indeed true. Nevertheless, the meaning is that one need not fear on this account, for although the King, who gave Mālatī [in marriage], lacks the authority to bestow another's property, and although her father—who does possess such authority—has not intentionally given her away, she still remains as before available for hope. Anticipating the doubt, "How is it certain that she was not given by her father? she says, "This much at least," indicating that even upon considering his words, there exists this established reputation regarding her being chosen as a bride. Makaranda: [listens].

This is so; the meaning is that I have also heard it. Kamandaki says "and today" to indicate that even the events of this very day—namely, that Mālatī was given away by the King himself and not by her father, who alone has the authority to bestow her—have indeed been heard.

Now, one might object: "Even if the land was given today by the King himself and not by Bhūrivasu, nevertheless, his consent is implied by the earlier statement, 'She has authority over it,' and so forth. Anticipating this, [the author] first demonstrates that worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), in order to state that legal purity (*vyavahāra-śuddhi*) does not arise from that statement because it was employed as a deceptive device for the purpose of fraud—beginning with the words "In that same way, my child" (*tadvatseti*). For embodied beings, *tantrāṇi* refers to family affairs in the form of worldly transactions.

"Tantra refers to household duties," says Halāyudha. Those things whose foundation or stability lies in speech—meaning they are based solely on verbal expression—are the regulations concerning the causes of merit and demerit, such as scriptural injunctions like "One should speak the truth; one should not speak falsehood. These depend entirely upon speech; that is, every practice, whether a cause of good or evil, has its root in speech alone.

But this [speech] of Bhūrivasu consists of a verbal artifice and is not "pure" (śuddhā); thus he says, "And that... Although it appears to be true at first glance due to the skill of figurative expression, when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is indeed false. To the question "Why?", he says, "Certainly not... Because of his lordship, he possesses independence even over the daughters of others; therefore he says, "the daughter... The kings are the authorities (*pramāṇa*), meaning they are the determiners; that is to say, they are independent agents.

Such is the practice of Dharma (*dharmācāra*), the conduct of the righteous; its *samaya* is the treatise that promulgates it. The ellipsis is "is not seen anywhere. Therefore, since the father does not give [the bride] and the king lacks authority, the act of giving performed by the king is contrary to both worldly custom and the scriptures; this point remains established. Thus he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The intention is that, because this discussion is merely introductory (*paspaśaprāyaka*), one should not conclude that there is no hope for a solution based on this much alone.

Furthermore, in order to inspire confidence by showing how she could not possibly go to anyone other than him while she herself was alive, she spoke with pride: "And how? (kathaṃ ca). The meaning is: "I remain ever vigilant regarding our union; therefore, you should not suspect anything undesirable. She expresses this very point in the words: "Do not [fear] for you two" (mā vām).

Whatever evil or undesirable thing might be suspected regarding her, regarding you, or between the two of you by ourselves and others—suspected even out of place according to the maxim that "love perceives dangers even where there are none"—and whatever is to be feared due to the power of affection, let that not exist even toward your rivals. For while an undesirable thing is indeed desired when it falls upon an enemy, it is not proper to expect such a thing even from them; this is an expression of the extreme misery of their current state.

Therefore, having gone to the very limit in every way, I must make an effort—even at the cost of my life—to attain union with you; this is the meaning of "must be done. And this is the second stage, known as *yatna* (effort). As it is said: "That activity directed toward a result which does not yet perceive the attainment of that result, but consists of a supreme state of longing—that is called *yatna*. //5//

Makaranda: "Moreover," and so forth. Even a mind that is detached from worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and free from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and hatred, it causes to melt—that is, it makes tender with compassion. "Compassion" (*dayā*) means pity; it is an affection characterized as love. Therefore, because your inner heart is under the sway of compassion and affection, this effort—which is contrary to and opposed to the conduct consisting of the practice of the eightfold yoga and so forth, which is easily accessible within the tradition of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) at the time of your ordination—is now forcibly and unexpectedly present.

Furthermore, beyond this, however, destiny and their respective fortunes prevail; the meaning is that you must do whatever is to be done by you. And this, being of the nature of conciliation, is the constituent element (aṅga) called "attendance" (paryupāsana). As it is said: "Conciliation is attendance. //6//

[Offstage: Venerable Kāmandakī, this queen requests that you come quickly, taking Mālatī with you. Mādhava and Mālatī gaze at one another with compassion, fearing for each other’s welfare, yet with passion as they perceive one another’s inner feelings. Mādhava: [The phrase] "of me, who am the sole vessel of sorrow" is an example of *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācyatā* (the expressed meaning being transferred to another sense).

The worldly course of life with Mālatī—consisting of mutual glances, conversation, and so forth, the conduct of those who are enamored—is completed at this very point. The meaning is: "This is indeed painful. *Aho* expresses wonder; *nu* indicates deliberation; *khalu* denotes what is well-known; *bhoḥ* is used as an address. "O heart, I deliberate that this is indeed a wonderful and wicked sport of Fate"—this is the sense. He describes that very same wicked sport: "As if toward a friend," and so on.

This fate, at first like a dear friend, manifested a favorable disposition—uniform, of that same single nature, devoid of any other mode, and consistent with the task at hand; yet that very same fate, suddenly and without occasion, through its reversal—that is, its contrary behavior and acting with hostility—is a cruel fate. It intensifies the mental affliction, the disease of the heart; the meaning is that it shatters the purpose and leaves behind only excessive suffering. Through this censure of fate, despondency is revealed. //7//

Mālatī: O noble one, you who bring joy to my eyes, this is how much of you has been seen; you shall not be seen again, for the implication is that my life will cease to exist. You have brought joy only to my eyes, but to my mind you have inflicted great agony—this is the suggested meaning (*dhvani*). And this is the dramatic element (*aṅga*) called "the thunderbolt" (*vajra*), because of its direct harshness, as it is said: "The thunderbolt is direct harshness. Lavaṅgikā: Alas! Our dear friend has been placed by the minister in a state where her very body is in peril.

Therefore, my lady, the intention is this: setting aside the wishes of your elders, you yourself must now strive with haste to save Mālatī’s life. Mālatī: Now the fruit of my thirst for life has ripened; and through his cruelty, my father’s status as a Kāpālika has been fully realized. For it is only a Kāpālika who is merciless in the slaughter of women, children, and others. By this, something of the action of the fifth act has also been slightly indicated.

The outcome of this wretched man’s cruel undertaking has reached its conclusion and come to an end. Alas, unfortunate as I am, whom shall I blame? Or, being without refuge, to whom shall I turn for protection? By this [speech], it is indicated that one should undertake appropriate efforts toward Mādhava and Kāmandakī, as in: "How is it that even while you two are present, I have experienced such a state? Thus, let the proper exertion be commenced.

It should be understood that for this very reason, although she was anxious, Mālatī, having become shameless even in the presence of Mādhava, uttered her lamentation. Lavaṅgikā: "Friend, this way, this way; please come," is the ellipsis to be supplied. Mādhava: "Surely... How indeed could the Holy Lady accomplish her purpose by opposing the King, who is our adversary? Therefore, the meaning is that her words were intended solely for the sake of consolation. I have become one whose success in life—characterized by the attainment of Mālatī—is now rendered uncertain.

In this context, by stating that "the attainment of Mālatī alone is the fulfillment of life," the dramatic element named *puṣpa*—which consists of speech characterized by excellence—is expressed through the proclamation of her passion and the preeminence of her virtues. As it is said: "The *puṣpa* is speech that is exceedingly excellent. Now, reflecting that the purpose must be accomplished even by means of the sale of human flesh—a deed well-known in external scriptures, performed by reckless people, which yields immediate results despite being unsuitable for his caste—he resolves: "Not indeed... [na khalu...].

"Mahāmāṃsa" means human flesh. This should also be understood as the second stage. "Friend" (*vayasya*)—here it is used in the sense of an inquiry. "Utkaṇṭhate" means he becomes eager or longing. Makaranda: "Then what? (atha kim) means "Indeed, I am very much longing. He says that very thing with the word "tat" (that): seeing me with my fresh wound and my blood-stained claws from the tiger's bite, she—without hesitation, her garment covering her breasts slipping away—by this, her beauty at that moment is described.

She whose gaze is as tremulous as that of a frightened one-year-old deer—by this, her extreme passion is revealed through the perception of agitation even in her. With limbs infused with nectar, as if drenched in the essence of ambrosia—by this, it is stated that the touch of her body is the cause of supreme satisfaction. That she "embraced," meaning she performed an embrace—that very act of embracing is what agitates my mind; the meaning is that it causes me distress. //8//

Mādhava: "No. [She says this] to reassure Makaranda that Buddharakṣitā’s dear friend is not difficult for him to obtain. He determines her ease of attainment through reasoning, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*). Regarding the phrase "having crushed": having crushed—that is, having slain—the flesh-eating tiger at the time of her death, when her life was in peril; and having thus rendered assistance characterized by saving her life during such a calamity, how could she—having received your embrace, that is, a spontaneous embrace—ever find delight elsewhere, that is, in anyone other than you, with her heart so devoted?

For it was at that very moment, by the embrace of her own initiative, that she declared: "My life and body have been surrendered to you, who gave me my life. Therefore, the sense is this: having surrendered her life to you, she will not find affection elsewhere.

Just as it has been determined by me, so too her gaze upon you was exactly in accordance with that—it was manifestly affectionate, revealing an excess of love, charming and captivating due to its steadiness and its immersion in you alone through non-contact with other objects; for it is determined by that very look of affection that her attachment is fixed on you alone. This is the limb of dramatic structure called *upanyāsa* (introduction), which consists of a conclusion reached through reasoning, according to the rule: "That matter which is established by means of reasoning is desired as *upanyāsa*. //9//

"Varadā" and "Sindhu" are the names of two rivers; their *saṃbheda* is their confluence. Makaranda says: "That very same [confluence] is also a *vyatikara* (an encounter). As for "this which..."—it refers to this confluence of the two rivers. "With water... means that its banks are surrounded—that is, its riverbanks are pervaded—by all the city women who have come to bathe because it is a sacred bathing place (*puṇyatīrtha*). The word "is seen" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He describes these women: "by those who have just risen from their bath," meaning those who have emerged immediately after bathing.

Therefore, they are those women whose bodily configurations—the depressions and elevations such as the navel, the waist, the orb of the breasts, the hips, and the loins—are made manifest and clearly discernible by means of a garment that has been thoroughly saturated and tightly adhered to them by water.

Likewise, the phrase "by those who have placed their hands in the form of a *svastika* upon breasts that are lovely with the luster of golden jars, lofty, and full in their expanse" is a description of the natural state (*svabhāvokti*) of brides who have just risen from bathing at that moment. Furthermore, by the expression "by the brides who had come for the purpose of bathing," various women from different castes and cities are perceived; thus, this should be understood as the figure of speech called *varṇasaṃhāra* (the gathering of descriptions), which is a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the *pratimukha-sandhi* (the intermediate juncture).
As it is said: "The combination of various castes is called varṇasaṃhāra. //10//

Victorious are the words of the poet Bhavabhūti, which possess diverse verbal ornaments, are devoid of harshness, and are charming with praiseworthy sound and sense; they shine with ever-new brilliance.

Thus ends the commentary on the fourth act of the *Mālatīmādhava-bhāvapradīpikā*, composed by the venerable Tripurāri Sūri, the son of Parvatanātha Yāyajūka, the ornament of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Act Five.
May that splendor—the unity of the heroic and the erotic sentiments—flash within my heart; it is the left and right limbs of the friend and the enemy of the five-arrowed god [Kāma].

Now, he begins the pure *viṣkambhaka* (interlude), to be performed by a single character, in order to indicate the narrative concerning the sale of human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*) previously hinted at in the first act—beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). A pure *viṣkambhaka* may indeed be composed with even a single middle-ranking character; as it is said: "A pure [interlude] is joined with either many or a single middle-ranking character. She travels through the air because, being a *yoginī*, she possesses the perfection of supernatural powers such as moving through the sky. Her attire is both terrifying and formidable, as well as brilliant and radiant.

*Kapālakuṇḍalā* is a name whose meaning corresponds to its form. "The Lord of the Six" (*ṣaḍadhika*) means the master or the impeller of the powers (*śakti*), which consist of the essential movements characterized by knowledge, will, and action; therefore, he is "enveloped" or pervaded by them, meaning he is the independent creator of the diverse movements of the universe. Alternatively, it refers to the Lord of the powers such as Brāhmī and the others.

For this very reason, the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*), who is propounded by the Kāpālika system, is victorious—meaning he shines with supreme excellence—as he is embraced by those [sixteen channels] with the thought that they are his own mistress and is entwined by them out of affection. This is because only such a one is worthy of salutation. To the question "Of what nature is he?", the author says: "Having sixteen... He is one whose self, or essential nature, resides in the heart—the center of that wheel or mandala which consists of the sixteen channels (*nāḍī*).

Although the channels (*nāḍī*) are infinite, it is said that there are "ten plus six" because the principal channels, beginning with *iḍā*, number sixteen. These channels, beginning with *iḍā*, are as follows: "*Iḍā* and *Piṅgalā*, and *Suṣumnā* is remembered as the supreme; *Gāndhārī*, *Hastijihvā*, *Pūṣā*, and likewise *Vasuvahā*; *Alambuṣā*, *Kuhū*, and *Śaṅkhinī* is remembered as the tenth; *Tālujihvā*, *Jihvā*, *Vijayā*, and the supreme *Kāmadā*; *Amṛtā*, and the one named *Bahulā*—these are the channels impelled by the vital air (*vāyu*). Thus [it is stated].

The path of yoga holds that the body—designated by the term *piṇḍa* (the mass)—is a collection of sixteen principal channels accompanied by immeasurable subtle channels, filled with the elements of blood, fat, flesh, and so forth, and covered by skin. Alternatively, it refers to the "wheel of ten channels," which consists of ten channels and takes the form of the navel-lotus; that is, [the wheel] belonging to the seventh [center], which is in addition to the six wheels. Or else:

The wheel of sixteen channels consists of sixteen channels among the sixteen plus six channels (twenty-two); it is the wheel consisting of sixteen channels located in the cavity of the throat, known as the *anāhata*. The meaning is: one whose self—that is, whose true nature—is stationed there, having been brought into proximity for the sake of a specific form of worship. Regarding those wheels, it is said in the Yoga scriptures: "There should be a four-petalled [wheel] in the *ādhāra*, and a six-petalled one in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; in the navel there is one endowed with ten petals, and in the heart one with the number of the sun (twelve) petals; in the throat there should be a sixteen-petalled one, and between the eyebrows one numbering eighty."

"The lotus known as the thousand-petaled one is located in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). These seven lotuses are said to be situated within the wheels (cakras). Thus, the petals of these lotuses, which consist of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), are the channels themselves. By this [statement], their doctrine is that the individual soul (jīva) is subtle, or has the size of a thumb. He whose form is placed in the hearts of those yogins who know that—that is, who perceive the nature of the Self in such a way—is the bestower of perfection, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

"He is sought and pursued by practitioners, yogis, and his own devotees, whose minds are unwavering due to the renunciation of other objects and who are focused solely on their own [inner] unity. Regarding this, they say that although terms such as "the wheel of channels" (*nāḍīcakra*) and so forth are well-known only in the specialized treatises on yoga and are thus unfamiliar [to ordinary people], this lack of common recognition is not a defect in the contemplation of one's own self; rather, it is indeed a merit. //1//

"‘This’ and so forth. ‘Constantly’: daily, at the time of beginning the recitation (*japa*), that which has been deposited as a constituent part of the mantra to be performed—deposited in those respective locations according to the method of the six-limbed deposition (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) such as ‘*namaḥ* to the heart, *svāhā* to the head,” and so on—the ‘wheel’ (*cakra*) of the six limbs, namely the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon, is placed there; that is, it is meditated upon as being situated in the center of that [wheel].”

"The scripture states: 'One should practice the mantra while meditating upon oneself as being identical with the presiding deity of the mantra. For this very reason, she beholds her own self in the form of Śiva, shining forth in the center of the heart-lotus. This [state] is *laya*, well-known in the Yoga scriptures, which consists of the cessation of the movement of the breath drawn upward by the power of *laya* into its various locations within the channels (*nāḍīs*), and which serves as the cause for traveling through the sky."

By virtue of that cause, through the sequence of the arising, equilibrium, and dissolution of the specific channels known as the earthly, watery, fiery, airy, and ethereal—which are composed of the five elements—and by means of drawing in the portions of those respective elements, there occurs the extraction of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). These are the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) which do not die—that is, they do not utterly perish—because they exist at all times in the form of both effect and cause; [this extraction is performed] for the sake of the world of moving beings, the multitude of living creatures, by means of those [nectars].

Alternatively: "Feces, urine, blood, marrow, and semen are known as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Because she has drawn these [substances] out, she is free from the exhaustion of attempting to fly—that is, the effort of rising into the sky—which would otherwise have arisen. Truly, she has now arrived at the very front of the sky (*nabhas*), dispelling and driving away the clouds (*ambhomucaḥ*) ahead of her. The meaning is that she has reached her destination, the temple of Karālā. //2//

"Uddhṛttā" means tossed upward, scattered, and then fallen. That necklace for the neck (*kaṇṭhamālā*), which is strung together with skulls, is where there is a clashing—the mutual striking of the skulls—by which they are made to ring, that is, they have produced a ringing sound; "śabdāyamāna" means making a sound. It is where there are "karālāḥ," meaning jagged, small bells (*kiṃkiṇyaḥ*) placed upon the neck-garland.
The speed of my journey through the expanse of the sky produces—that is, brings about—a full, complete, delightful, and captivating ferocity (*ḍāmaratvam*) or boldness. This is the meaning. //3//

That very quality of being both beautiful and formidable is revealed by the word "viṣvak": that mass of matted hair (*jaṭābhāra*), whose existence and position extend in every direction (*viṣvak*), though firmly bound with tight knots, trembles due to the force of his movement. Likewise, the bell fastened to the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) resounds for a long time through its *kvāṇa*—the ringing sound produced by an intensity resulting from the momentum of the impact that generates the sound, which is conceived solely as an effect. It is clear (*paṭu*).

"Kṛtāvṛttiḥ" (performed repeatedly), "punaḥpunarabhyāsaḥ" (repeated practice), and "yathā syāt tathā" (in such a manner)—these three are adverbs qualifying the action. "Raṭati" means it resounds. Likewise, in the bowers (*kuñjeṣu*)—the hollow cavities (*sarandhrakuhareṣu*)—of the rows of severed heads (*vivṛta-śava-śiraḥ-śreṇī*), the wind (*anilaḥ*) produced by the force of the breeze, humming (*guñjan*) and sounding, violent (*uttāla*) and fierce (*udbhaṭa*), being the cause of the incessant tinkling (*anavarata-raṇatkāra*) and continuous jingling (*avicchinna-nikvāṇa*) of the small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*), shakes (*dhūnoti*) and causes to tremble the banner (*patākām*) fastened to the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), so that it stands upright (*ūrdhvam*). //4//

"Having walked around," and so forth. And this is that temple of Karālā. Of what sort is it? It is very close (*nedīyaḥ*), being situated in the immediate vicinity of the cemetery enclosure (*śmaśānavāṭa*), that is, the area of the cremation ground. He describes the cemetery enclosure: [it is near] garlic (*rasonaka*)—that is, garlic (*laśuna*)—"garlic, *gṛñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, and *rasonaka*," according to Amara; which has been smeared with old neem oil and is being fried.

With those funeral pyre-smokes—which reach the sky and possess a fragrance like that of resinous exudate (niryāsa)—the vast and great [pyre] situated below upon the surface of the earth is made manifest, that is, inferred. There, in the temple of Karālā, the collection of offerings—the entire array of ritual implements—must be brought forth and placed in readiness, so that the accomplishment of the mantra, having been completed and the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa) finished, may be performed with special distinction, that is, accompanied by a specific excellence relative to what preceded.

In response to the inquiry, "What is the distinction? he says: "It was promised. Previously, when this mantra had been mastered, a vow (*upayācita*) was made—that is, it was previously requested and resolved that a jewel among women (*strīratna*) would be offered as a gift (*upahāra*) to the Blessed Lady. This gift was to be brought forth. And that jewel among women was well-known—meaning it was famous among all people—right here in this very city. [The phrase] "with curiosity" means:

"How is it that one with such a delicate and sweet appearance wanders here in the night without apparent cause?"—thus [he asked] with curiosity. "One whose form is exceedingly profound and sweet" means one whose appearance is characterized by the qualities of profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) and sweetness (*mādhurya*). Regarding these: "Profundity is the absence of outward change in fear, grief, anger, or joy; sweetness is the gentle conduct toward loved ones in all circumstances. "One whose mass of curly, formidable locks of hair is bound up in a topknot" means one whose tangle of hair is tied together and fastened as a crest.

With sword in hand and blade in grasp, he descends into the cremation ground. Thus, although he is of a gentle nature, for some reason he has recently undertaken acts of daring; therefore, he must be investigated—this is the intention. He describes him specifically: "He who... [beginning with] "kuvalaya... etc.

By his very nature, although blue as the petal of a blue lotus, he possesses a body that is pale and discolored due to the absence of the habitual impressions (*saṃskāra*) caused by separation from his beloved and other such factors; likewise, because of his status as a great leader, characterized by modesty, profundity, and fortitude, even here in this cremation ground, his placement of feet is graceful, captivating in its depth, and fearless.

This person who is seen here—possessed of a distinguished luster that manifests great fortune and glory, with a face like the moon and a countenance resembling the full orb of the moon—it is not fitting for him to perform such an act. Rather, the implication is that he has resorted to this rashness in order to accomplish some desired object that must be achieved even at the cost of his life, according to the maxim: "A man does not behold auspicious things without venturing into danger."

His left hand alone—wherein there is a mire of flowing blood from his mouth, dangling human limbs, and glistening pieces of human flesh, manifesting sheer audacity—removes his modesty and reveals his lack of restraint. From the sight of that left hand with its pieces of flesh, his audacity is perceived; but upon seeing any other part of his body, he appears peaceful and composed in demeanor. The meaning is that no audacity is perceived [in those other parts]. //5//

"Having observed and ascertained: 'This is he'—meaning that very person who was seen by us as a mere child, the son of Devarāta, the friend of Kāmandakī and minister to the Lord of Kuṇḍina; it is he who, having undertaken a rash act to accomplish some exceedingly difficult task, has come here on account of his mission and wanders about as a seller of human flesh. And this deed, so difficult for a mortal to perform, is fitting for him, because he is the son of a friend of the great yoginī Kāmandakī"—this is the sense.

A "paṇayitṛ" is one who deals in trade; that is to say, a seller. The form "paṇayitṛ" is derived from the root *paṇ* (meaning "to deal in trade" and "to praise") with the suffix *tṛc*. What is the point of this? The meaning is: "Let him also accomplish his own task, and I too shall fulfill my desired purpose. He says, "The time for carrying out the teacher's command has also arrived," using the word "vigalitaprāya," which means "almost completed" or "nearly finished. [He refers to] "of the sky."

The horizons of the sky, appearing like curtains bent down at the edges of the earth’s surface, are being enveloped—covered—as it were by creepers of darkness, like rows of tamāla clusters or garlands of tamāla blossoms. Thus, through its movement across the earth's periphery, as if sinking into the surrounding regions, it seems to be plunging into fresh, turbid water; one imagines that, shrouded in darkness, it has become submerged in a vast ocean of water.

Likewise, at the onset of the three-watch night, or even at the time of its commencement, the sky makes its own darkness appear youthful—that is, it brings the profound blackness of the gloom to its prime—at that moment when the light of a thick, abundant, and encircled wreath of smoke (dhūmyā) spreads out in all directions with great force from whirlwinds (vātyā) in the form of circular gusts. //6//

Having thus indicated Mādhava’s entry for the purpose of selling human flesh, Aghoraghaṇṭa’s presence in the temple of Karālā for the sake of worship, and the bringing of Mālatī there, Kapālakuṇḍalā exits. This concludes the Pure Interlude (śuddhaviṣkambhaḥ). Then, "thereafter," etc.; Mādhava is as previously described, his form having been defined by Kapālakuṇḍalā. [Mādhava speaks] with longing: [End of section]

The meaning is that he speaks preceded by a hope for the purpose for which the act known as the sale of "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa) was intended. Regarding "love" (prema): love is said to be a specific state characterized by excellence belonging to *rati*, the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). Love, honor, affection, endearment, and passion are merely different states of *rati*. As it has been said: "This [love] sprouts from *prema*, becomes leafed through *māna* (pride), possesses buds through *praṇaya* (intimacy), and becomes flowered through *sneha* (endearment)."

"Because of passion (*rāga*), this [woman] is enjoyed with affection (*anurāga*) as if she were bearing fruit. And: "The bond of emotion (*bhāvabandhana*) that is firmly established through a dense mutual dependence, and which has as its limiting condition subservience to one another—that is called love (*prema*). Therefore, they are "moist" (*ārdrāḥ*), meaning full of sapidity (*sarasāḥ*) and characterized by favorability. As it has been said: "Whatever their beloved says to her, the promptness with which she acts upon each of those things—this they call 'fitness' (*yogyatā*) and 'moisture' (*ārdratā*), which destroys the turbidity of the mind."

Thus, they are called "touching upon affection" (*praṇayaspṛśaḥ*) because they touch upon affection and thereby become colored by it. As for affection (*praṇaya*), it is defined as follows: "When love between two youths has been brought to its highest excellence through mutual outward and inward gestures, that alone is remembered as affection. Likewise, from familiarity—that is, from the further nourishment of that very affection through repeated glances, conversation, touch, and so forth—as in the case of [the verse]: "When the rival is abroad, dead, or weak..."

"That which causes affliction toward the object of affection (dharmī) is called 'mature love' (prauḍhasneha). When such a state consisting of mature love has been attained, there arises from that a deep, intense, and never-ceasing passion known as *māñjiṣṭha*—an excellence of affection that colors the mind. Regarding this passion (*rāga*), as it is said: "If this [passion] exists in the heart through qualities, substances, place, time, and so forth..."

That which is colored and illuminated within the mind is called *rāga* (passion/attachment). As for the *māñjiṣṭha-rāga* (the madder-dye passion): "That which shines exceedingly and does not fade even when washed is called by all poets the *māñjiṣṭha-rāga*. This alone is the best kind of *rāga*. As it is said: "The *māñjiṣṭha-rāga* is the best; the *nīlī-rāga* (indigo-dye passion) is middling; the *kusumbha-rāga* (safflower-dye passion) is proclaimed by poets to be the lowest. Thus, the *nīlī-rāga*, though stable, is unattractive.

The dye of safflower is delightful at first sight but fleeting; however, those various gestures of that lovely-eyed girl—experienced in their respective ways as naturally sweet and inherently charming—possess experience alone as their essence. These bodily movements, such as the casting of side-glances, the play of the eyebrows, and the twisting of the limbs, are conducive to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). As it is said: "Playfulness (*līlā*), coquetry (*vilāsa*), grace (*vicchitti*), bewilderment (*vibhrama*), the mingled emotion (*kilakiñcita*), affected indifference (*moṭṭāyita*), feigned anger (*kuṭṭamita*), affectation (*vivvoka*), and charm (*lalita*)."

"And the *vihṛta* (the playful embrace)—thus are the ten gestures born of the limbs to be known. This [verse] uses the optative mood (*liṅ*) in the sense of a wish, meaning: "May they be thus enumerated by me through subtle observation. Even regarding those gestures which are merely imagined through such a wish—how might I become the object of her affectionate side-glances; how might I hear her words of endearment, sweet with the essence of nectar and pregnant with intention; and how might I [immerse] myself in the lake of the nectar-essence of the satisfaction of her firm embrace?

Even when [the objects of desire] are presented merely as mental constructs in the form of "I would immerse myself [in them]," and are not yet being experienced in ultimate reality, there occurs a dissolution (*laya*)—that is, a state of absorption or being submerged solely in that [object], reaching the point of becoming identified with it, according to the analogy of molten iron merging into water. What need is there to mention [the intensity of this state] when they are being experienced as actual realities? Of what nature is this dissolution?

The term [saṃhṛtendriyavṛtti] means that which has the nature of obstructing the activity of the external organs, such as the eyes and so forth, which consists of the power to grasp their respective objects. Because they have dissolved precisely into the activities of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the sense organs become indeed inactive due to the absence of their substrate. To distinguish this from the dissolution occurring in states such as fainting, it says "dense with bliss" (ānandasāndra), meaning abounding solely in bliss. The meaning is that it is like the dissolution into the blissful Brahman, as in the case of the inner self (pratyagātman) during the state of liberation (mokṣa).

And here, since the *śṛṅgāra* rasa of longing-in-separation (*abhilāṣavipralambha*) is primarily suggested, this is a case of *dhvani* consisting of a suggested meaning whose sequence is discernible, rooted in denotation (*abhidhāmūla*). //7//

And here, regarding the seed that was first seen through the account of the garden of Śaṅkara’s city, which immediately thereafter seemed lost due to the decision to bestow Mālatī upon Nandana—from the verse beginning with "moistened by love" (*premārdrāḥ*) up to "as if merged, as if reflected" (*līneva pratibimbiteva*), and then from "it is indeed appropriate" (*upapannastāvat*) until the conclusion of each respective act—the process of reconnection (*anusaṃdhāna*) occurs through repeated searching, starting from the time of Mālatī’s first sight in the sixth act up to [the verse] "spreading wide" (*vistāriṇaḥ*).

From the passage beginning with these words up to the end of the first act, there is the *prāptyāśā* (hope of attainment) being delineated; and from the passage beginning with "Child Makaranda, dressed in Mālatī’s attire, proceed toward your own marriage" up to the conclusion of that same act, there is the *patākā* (the secondary plot), which consists of the actions of the supporting hero Makaranda—who assumes the form of Mālatī—and which serves as a means for the primary narrative (*adhikārikavṛttānta*).

It should be understood that the poet has delineated the *garbhasandhi* (the juncture of development) as the connection between those narrative segments—which are characterized by artificial marriages and consist of the three acts (*aṅga*) to be presented, namely: the sale of human flesh, the saving of Mālatī’s life, the slaying of Aghoraghaṇṭa, the events within the inner sanctum of the city goddess, and the assumed role of Makaranda in the guise of Mālatī—and which are endowed with the eleven constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as the "seizing of the living being" (*bhūtāharaṇa*) that will be manifested here and there.

The characteristics of the *garbha* (embryo) juncture are as follows: "The *garbha*, however, consists of the repeated searching for a seed that was seen and then lost; it arises from a connection with the banner (*patākā*) of hope for attainment. These are the eleven members of this *garbha* juncture in their proper order. "In the midst of the hero's narrative, a story concerning someone similar to him, involving the consideration of means and obstacles, which gives rise to the possibility of attaining hope for attainment, and which is connected to the non-occurrence of the fruit—that is proclaimed as the *patākā* (banner). This is the summary.

Now, among all activities, he requests that very best activity, which consists of an embrace—beginning with the words "atimuktakaiḥ. "Atimuktakaiḥ" refers to vāsantī flowers. As Amara states: "Atimukta is puṇḍraka; vāsantī is the mādhavī creeper."

The phrase is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṇa*) describing the action in which my breasts—rendered fragrant by the constant perfuming of a garland woven from clusters of filaments and abundant with *bakula* flowers, and placed upon my chest—are deposited. [The garland] is strung together at intervals by being set within it. "In the hollow of the neck" (*kaṇṭhajāhe*) means at the base of my neck. According to the rule "after words such as *pīlu* and *karṇa*, the suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are added to denote the root or base," the suffix *jāhac* is applied to the word *kaṇṭha* because it belongs to the *karṇa*-class.

I am he whose own face was placed there [upon her lap]. At the time of embracing, it is the nature of innocent women to rest their heads, bent down, against the base of the neck of their beloved; therefore, may I attain a "parivṛtti" (exchange) of my body with her body. The meaning is that by virtue of the embrace, her body should come under my control and my body should come under hers. *Parivṛtti* itself is the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).

Some, reading "avimuktaka," explain it as follows: "The *avimuktaka* [filaments]—the series of filaments (*kesarāvalī*) which, because they were never abandoned by me through being strung together, have been held with great respect. //8//

Alternatively: according to the maxim that "there is no way for mere wishes to be realized," this is merely prayed for; because it is exceedingly difficult to attain, it is not considered possible. However, since this [other thing] is possible, I first pray for that alone. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Having come together... and so forth.

When the path of sight falls upon the face of the beloved as it enters the range of vision, all the joys that exist in the world and all the means of happiness, arising from the experience of them all, gather together as if into a single mass; they spread forth in the heart a supreme, unsurpassed abundance—an exceeding plenitude produced by their mutual union. This is the "festival for the eyes," the activity of the observer's two eyes which serves as the cause of joy.

Because it has been stated: "That which generates joy is proclaimed as a festival (utsava)," [the text] extols—that is, brings forth—the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of a specific desire for pleasure (*rati*), which is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). For it has been said: "Pleasure (*rati*) is the desire of two youths, consisting of mutual longing. The meaning is that by the mere sight [of one another], there arises unsurpassed bliss and *rati* in the form of the heroine's longing.

Furthermore, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): that [face] was as if produced from the accumulated essences—the finest portions—gathered from the collection, that is, the mass, of the digits of the young moon, which are charming due to their delicacy and freedom from spots, being generated one by one month after month. Because it is the cause of unsurpassed delight and possesses qualities such as purity and clarity, it is the auspicious abode (*maṅgalagṛha*) of the bodiless god of love (*anaṅga*); for through its presiding presence, the bodiless one attains the auspiciousness characterized by victory over the three worlds.

"May I behold once again that face of my beloved; by the ripening of my merit, let this much at least be granted—by this alone, I shall have achieved my life's purpose. This is the underlying intention (*āśaya*). The expressed ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*) are hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and metaphor (*rūpaka*). Here, the figure of "peculiar causation" (*vibhāvanā*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), as all that happiness arises from another cause despite the absence of the well-known means for such pleasure. This is further manifested by the phrase "as if they were combined" (*saṃbhūyeva*).

This face does not have material elements as its constituent cause like other bodies; rather, its constituent cause is something else entirely, transcendent—this is the *apahnava* (concealment). Because it is composed of the essence of the spotless [light], there is the cognition of its superiority over the lunar orb; this is *vyatireka* (distinction). Since the moon and so forth are unfit to be its standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and no other exists, this very face is its own comparison; this is *ananvaya* (self-comparison), which is suggested by the phrase "the digit of the young moon," and so forth should be analyzed by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). As for the suggestion of aesthetic flavor (*rasadhvani*), it has already been discussed, so enough with further elaboration. //9//

One might object: "Since you are beholding your beloved incessantly through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why do you still pray for a reunion? Anticipating this doubt, he states the distinction between a vision produced by cultivation and the vision that is to be prayed for, beginning with the word "yad" (that which): "Even though the beloved is seen now exactly as she was previously experienced, without any deficiency or excess..."

In this regard, although there is some distinction, nevertheless, the vision now being presented—the vision produced by meditative cultivation—is not the truth in the ultimate sense. However, there is at least this slight distinction: the difference between the vision to be sought and the present vision is that the former is the truth. Therefore, the meaning is that it is for that [truth] which is sought.

Now, one might raise the objection: "How can there be such a distinction [between the two], given that at present perception itself is absent? He pacifies this doubt by presenting the fact of identification (*tanmayībhāva*) as established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), saying: "For me, indeed, at present... The "prior apprehension" (*prāktana upalambhaḥ*) refers to a previous experience accompanied by an "excellent quality" (*sātiśaya*), characterized by the capacity to instill a firmer latent impression (*saṃskāra*). For a mere superficial glance might sometimes not instill a latent impression at all; or, even if a latent impression were instilled, it would not produce memory due to a lack of firmness.

However, an experience produced preceded by the desire to know is more effective, as it is invariably productive of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); and the impression produced by that [experience], being firm, necessarily generates memory—thus it is said to be "superior."

From the continuous awakening—that is, the constant arousal—of such a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as *bhāvanā*, which has its nature (*ātman*) brought about and generated by that [repeated experience], and which consists in a state of readiness to produce its own effect; from that awakening which is the cause for the uninterrupted persistence of reflection (*cintā*), [the memory] extends itself, ascending to a state of expansion in a continuous, stream-like manner. In this context, such a latent impression is produced with a superior intensity by the previous experience.

That which, having produced a single memory, does not itself perish, but rather produces an effect in the form of a continuous stream—like the cause of a reverberating sound in the case of a jar or similar object; or as in the view of the author of the *Līlāvatī*, where the initial velocity residing in an arrow or other object, produced by the first action and characterized by excellence, generates a succession of subsequent actions until the moment of falling—that is what is meant by "of the latent impression" (*saṃskāra*). The singular number is used with reference to the genus.

By that [cause], a collection of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) capable of producing a continuous stream of memory has arisen, which exists as a potentiality (*karmabhāvī*). It must be explained that their awakening occurs precisely in a sequence, inferred from the observation of sequential effects, due to the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is by other cognitions (*pratyaya*), such as those consisting of the memory of *mālatī* or those directed toward other objects, which are dissimilar to it. The mutual dissimilarity of cognitions consists precisely in their engagement with different objects. Its flow is "unobstructed," meaning uninterrupted.

The meaning is "unmixed with heterogeneous cognitions. The cognitions (pratyayas) are precisely the memories (smṛtis) concerning the beloved; their "stream of production" refers to those memory-cognitions arising as they continue in succession. It makes my consciousness—the self whose nature is pure awareness—consist of that [the beloved], as if made of Mālatī herself, as if having attained identity with her. Why? Because of the conformity of its mental state (vṛtti-sārūpyataḥ).

The meaning is this: there is a similarity between the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)—which consists of the memory directed toward Mālatī—and [the external object]; that is, it is produced in the form of Mālatī. Indeed, the Vedāntins say this: when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, the internal organ, which is by nature subject to transformation, transforms itself into the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). And the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*), delimited by the internal organ, is reflected within that modification as well. That very consciousness, reflected in the modification, is called the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that mental modification (vṛtti), having gone to the location of the object and assumed the form of the object, removes—by way of mutual opposition—the ignorance that veils the consciousness residing in the substrate of the object, just as a lamp dispels darkness. Consequently, the consciousness residing in the substrate of the object, having attained oneness with the consciousness of the knower reflected in the mental modification through the analogy of water from a well flowing into a canal and then into a basin, shines forth. Yet, because there is no superimposition of identity between the substrate-consciousness and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), there is no cognition of it as "I."

However, because of the superimposition of identity with the object, this [consciousness] appears in the form of the object as "this" alone. Thus, in the present case as well, since memory is produced in the form of Mālatī, the consciousness reflected therein attains unity with the consciousness of the object and shines forth in the form of that object. [Objection: If that is so, then the cognition should be "that is Mālatī," and not "identity with her. [Reply: True.

However, when the state of being a continuum has been thoroughly examined by you, this [object] appears in perceptual experience as being present before one, due to the gradual dissolving of the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) as it is remembered in uninterrupted succession. Furthermore, through such contemplation (*bhāvanā*) over a long period, even the aspect of "this-ness" (idantā) dissolves, and the object is perceived as having attained identity with the consciousness of the knower; this alone is the greatness of contemplation. For it is well known in the scriptures that there is a direct perception of a beloved woman by one afflicted with passion.

For this very reason, the use of the word *iva* (as if) occurs everywhere—in expressions such as "consisting of that as it were" (*tanmayam iva*) or "merged as it were" (*līneva*)—in order to indicate the lack of ultimate reality. Therefore, the sense is that even though such a vision exists, it is entirely appropriate to pray for the ultimate vision. He clarifies what was stated as "consisting of that" with the words "merged as it were," and so forth.

That beloved who manifested in the Madana garden those experiences revealing her prior passion for my person—she, such a jewel among women, was already attached to me even before I was to her; "Oh, what good fortune mine!"—thus attributing greatness to himself, he uses the plural number [in "our"]. She is "fixed in his heart. To the inquiry of how she is fixed, he imagines the specific manner of her fixation: "as if merged," and so forth.

The phrase "as if dissolved" (layaṃ gatā) means that she has vanished, like drops of water fallen into a heap of dust. One might object: "In that case, her manifestation would not even occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "as if reflected" (pratibimbateva). Just as the orb of the moon is reflected in a reservoir of pure water, she is reflected in my mind; thus, her internal manifestation is logically established. One might further object: "In the absence of the original object (bimba), how can there be a reflection? To this, he says: "as if inscribed" (likhiteva).

She appears as if painted upon the canvas of my heart by the painter Manmatha himself, using the brush of anxiety and the pigment of passion; thus, the meaning is that she shines forth visibly. Now, one might object: since a painting consists of specific arrangements of lines and contours, and therefore lacks the actual form [of the subject], it would be merely a portrait of Mālatī that has been fixed in my mind, and not Mālatī herself. To this, he replies: "as if carved in relief" (*utkīrṇarūpā iva*).

Just as a stone statue is carved from a block of stone by a craftsman using a chisel, so too has my own mind—its form already engraved by the artisan Madana with his arrows—been carved into the likeness of my beloved; this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: since the mind is extremely subtle and partless, how could the beloved be carved there? To this, he says: "as if inlaid."

Just as diamonds and other gems are set within gold ornaments, so too, because my mind has been ignited by the fire of separation, it resembles a glowing mass of refined gold; and thus, having melted, the jewel of a woman was set therein by the goldsmith Madana. Now, one might object that since the addition of an alloy (prativāpa) is a specific type of conjunction, there would also be a separation [of the parts]; therefore, he states a specific method to ensure the firmness of the union: "vajra" (diamond). A coating of lime (sudhālepa) impregnated with substances such as molasses, black gram juice, and so forth, is called "vajralepa" (diamond-paste).

The meaning is that just as an object fashioned from it becomes more solid, so too does the beloved. [Objection: In that case, there would be no contact between the mind and the beloved, because she is constructed upon the mind which is like a coating of adamant; to this he says, "as if buried within. Just as something is buried in the earth as a treasure, so too is the beloved buried in the pit of the mind. [Objection: If that were so, there would be no perception of her at all; to this he says, "as if nailed down."

Just as two pieces of wood become pinned together when pierced by iron pins, so too my beloved is, as it were, nailed to my heart by the five extremely sharp arrows, which, being directed toward both, have passed through them—this is the meaning.

Here, although his own mind is capable of enduring the pain of being pierced by needles because of its hardness, he expresses a lack of interest in how the beloved—one whose limbs are exceedingly delicate and who suffers even from the touch of a flower—could possibly endure the pain of being pierced by needles; thus, he states another way [of describing her state]: "Cintā" (anxiety). A continuous stream of anxiety, consisting of thoughts such as "How might I obtain her?", is itself a web of threads; by this, she is densely sewn, bound, or stuck—as the connection is made with every subsequent term.

Regarding this, some learned scholars explain that because the example begins with "merged" (*līnā*)—which suggests absolute non-difference—and since difference is perceived in each subsequent stage, there is a falling away from excellence (*patatprakarsatva*). Fearing that this would be an instance of a falling excellence of meaning, they argue that, according to the maxim "the sequence of meaning is stronger than the sequence of recitation," one must follow the method of descending a staircase; thus, from "the stream of thought" (*cintāsaṃtati*) up to "as if merged" (*līneva*), there is a perception of an increasing intensity of union, and therefore it does not constitute a falling excellence.

The essential point here is that this is a *bhāvotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature of a substance) based on the action [of the lover], where the primary subject—the beloved, who is the actual topic (*prakṛta*) and is indicated as the *lagna* (the point of contact)—is identified with the non-primary object (*aprakṛta-vastu*), such as time, which serves as the cause for actions like her disappearance (*laya*). As the rule states: "Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the imagining of the primary subject as a non-primary thing, due to its connection with the qualities or actions of a non-primary thing. Furthermore, because a single entity is identified in multiple ways, this is a *mālā-utprekṣā* (garland-like poetic fancy). //10//

A tumultuous noise arises from behind the scenes; the implication is that it has arisen from the *piśācas*. The *kauṇapas* are *rākṣasas*. "Raudratā" means terror-inspiring quality. For here, in this cremation ground (*śmaśāna-pradeśa*), the darkness—as the agent—manifests the brilliance of the funeral pyres' lights through their secondary excellence (*parabhāga*), that is, through the superiority of their color. Indeed, in the presence of darkness characterized by obscurity, light characterized by radiance shines forth brilliantly. Of what nature is this darkness? It is such that its habit is to obstruct the lights at their periphery, that is, in the bordering regions of the flames.

The meaning is that it exists enveloping everything up to the vicinity of the light. By that [light], it is *medura*—plump, dense, thick, solid, and massed together; the meaning is that it is pierceable even by a needle. Furthermore, it is *bhīma*—terrible—due to its *bhoga*, which is its breadth or its pervasion over many regions. Moreover, they are those whose play (*kelī*) is *saṃsakta* (joined), *avicchinna* (uninterrupted), and *ākula* (tumultuous); they are *uttāla*, meaning formidable.

The *kaṭapūtanas* are a specific class of *piśācas*; these and other *piśācas*, out of joy, raise a clamor in the form of shouts of "kila-kila" and a widespread outcry on all sides. The word *sāṃrāviṇam* is derived from the root *ru* (meaning "to sound") preceded by the prefix *sam-*. The suffix *inuṇ* is applied according to the rule *abhividhau bhāve inuṇ*, and the nominal suffix *aṇ* is added to that form according to the rule *tadantādaṇ*, being a suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*). //11//

"I proclaim" means "I announce for the purpose of selling at a high price. "O, O! is an address used out of urgency. "Unwounded by weapons" (aśastra) means not touched by a weapon; that is, free from wounds caused by weapons. For since that which is touched by a weapon cannot be grasped by *piśācas* due to its purity, the absence of such contact is stated here to demonstrate that it is easily seized by them.

"Without guile" (avyāja) means without deceit; that is to say, it was brought specifically for the purpose of sale, and not brought under the pretext of selling meat in order to inspire confidence and then strike. Alternatively, "guile" (vyāja) refers to artificial defects such as goiters (*gaḍu*) and other specific diseases that spoil meat; [the meat] is prepared from a human limb free from such [defects]. For meat spoiled by artificial defects like goiters would be tasteless and thus unfit for consumption. The mention of "human" is intended to highlight the superiority of human flesh over the flesh of women.

For it is said in the Kāpālika Āgama: "That which is not cut by a weapon, belongs to a woman, is fresh human flesh from which drops of blood are trickling. Others, however, say: "Human flesh is proclaimed to be that which is acquired through daring even at the risk of one's own life, purified by no weapon, and free from deceit. This very thing is expressed by the term *mahāmāṃsa* (great flesh).

The repetition in "Let it be taken! Let it be taken! (*gṛhyatāṃ gṛhyatām*) is for the sake of indicating an excess of urgency, because such a thing is difficult to obtain; it applies only to the first who arrives, not to one who comes later. //12//

The cremation ground was as if shaken—disturbed by a clamor that rose from all sides, tumultuous, terrifying, chaotic, distinct, and clearly manifest; crowded and congested with spirits that appeared and became visible at that very moment. The meaning is that it seemed to tremble because the activity of the Piśācas moving about within it was perceived as being inherent to the ground itself. [Regarding the phrase] "near the ears":...

The sky was filled—became overspread—with the faces of those specific types of *piśācas* known as *ulkāmukhas* (fire-mouths), whose names correspond to their appearance; for by virtue of the blazing torches held in their mouths, their targets were slightly visible, yet by virtue of the darkness, they were clearly invisible, and specifically, their bodies were dry, emaciated, tall, and exceedingly high. Of what kind were these faces?

With their ears reaching to the vicinity—that is, as far as—the split and torn corners of the mouth (*sṛkkaṇī*), which are the edges of the lips; with those [faces] in which fire blazes and shines forth through that formidable gaping, the opening of the cavity of the mouth; with the tips of their fangs, which are jagged and disordered; and with faces whose hair resembles a mass of lightning, they are said to flee because only their mouths are visible due to the connection with blazing torches as they run here and there. //13//

"Etad" means this: the host (*cakra*) of *pūtanās*, a specific class of *piśācas*, is being observed—that is, seen. Of what sort? "Paritaḥ," meaning on all sides; "ādardaram," meaning somewhat gurgling (*īṣad-ghargharam*). In some places, the reading is "āghargharam."

He was nourishing himself with the remnants—the food-leavings—of human flesh that had fallen to the ground after being half-eaten from mouthfuls seized all at once, out of excessive greed, by howling wolves—specific types of carnivorous beasts—as they cried out; [he was thus] growing fat. His shanks were as tall as date-palm trees, reaching that very height.

Bound by black skin, covered and spread on all sides—meaning pervaded everywhere—by knots of sinews and knots of veins, its skeletal frame is dense and compact; it consists merely of bones that have become a cage due to being devoid of blood, flesh, marrow, and so forth.
