Furthermore, it belongs to one who is "aged," meaning worn out by extreme longevity, such that his body-bones have become mere skeletons (*kaṅkāla*). This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *kaṅkāla* refers to the bones of the body in the masculine. (14)

"Having looked all around and smiled"—the word "said" is to be understood as the ellipsis. By means of the smile, even in the face of such a terrifying sight, his freedom from apprehension is indicated, thereby expressing the hero's extreme self-confidence (*atimanasvitā*). [The phrase] "broadly moving" (*pṛthucala*)...

Those *piśācas* whose bodies are "completely shattered" (*viśīrṇā*)—meaning they are especially decayed, fragmented due to many afflictions such as scars from wounds and swellings, and withered because they are devoid of flesh, blood, and so forth; and who have a wide (*pṛthu*), vast (*viśāla*), and trembling (*calayā*) tongue, which makes their mouths fierce (*ugram*). In the reading "pṛthutararasanogram," it means the mouth-cavity is fierce because of the extreme thickness of the tongue. This is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). Precisely because of this similarity within the compound, when the word expressing the comparison is omitted, it constitutes a *luptopamā* (elliptical simile).

Having split and torn them open, they remain there; possessing hollows that are terrifying because of the great serpents (*ajagara*)—which are moving, restless, and (in the reading "galat") emerging from the cavities—those [trees] bear the splendor and beauty of ancient *rohiṇa* sandalwood trees. The word "ancient" (*purāṇa*) is used to indicate their state of being worn out, dry, and riddled with holes. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The *rohiṇa* is the sandalwood tree. They possess radiance and loveliness.

The mention of sandalwood is intended to establish a point of similarity (*sādharmya*) between it and the python, on account of its natural lack of flowers and the like, its saplessness, and its being the refuge of pythons and similar creatures—just as this pit possesses a hollow where the tongue moves like a python. Thus, the ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is *nidarśanā* (illustration). For one thing cannot possess the splendor residing in another; since the splendor residing in the sandalwood tree cannot possibly exist in the *piśācas*, there is an implied comparison (*upamā*) through the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*), based on the underlying connection.

As it has been said: "Where, due to the impossibility of the connection of attributes between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, the process of reflection is understood, that should be *nidarśanā*. (15)

"Exceedingly loathsome" means having an object that is intensely disgusting. "Having cut up"—the *pretaraṅka* is a particularly wretched type of *piśāca*. Having first repeatedly cut and torn off the skin (*kṛtti*), and immediately thereafter, with a broad elevation—that is, with the height of the body—he [displays] the most abundant [flesh].

Having devoured—meaning, having eaten—the flesh that is easily obtained and acquired without effort from the shoulders, the tops of the arms, the buttocks, the expanse of the hips, the surface of the back, and other fleshy parts, which is intensely putrid and possesses an unbearable stench; he is such a person by whom, immediately thereafter, tendons, entrails, and eyes have been taken up. "Tendon" (*snāyu*) refers to fat (*vasā*); "entrail" (*āntra*) refers to the small intestine (*purītat*). The mention of the tendons and so forth is for the purpose of including the flesh contained within them.

Immediately thereafter, from the fleshless skeletal cage—a corpse-body—situated nearby upon his lap, he extracts the flesh (*kravya*) residing within the bones, even that which is located in the hollows, the protrusions, and the uneven regions of the bone structure. Being one whose teeth are displayed for the purpose of pulling out the flesh situated in those jagged and hard places, he devours it without agitation and without haste.
Here, through the nourishment of the sentiment of disgust (*jugupsā*), the aesthetic flavor of the loathsome (*bībhatsa-rasa*) is suggested. //16//

He describes this very flavor in another way: "Moreover, *niṣṭāpeti*. *Kuṇapabhujaḥ* refers to the *piśācas* who consume corpses. By *niṣṭāpa*, meaning complete burning (*niḥśeṣeṇa tāpaḥ*), those whose bones have marrow oozing from them due to that thorough heating are meant.

Likewise, having dragged from many funeral pyres—those heaps of fuel for burning dead bodies where the corpses were being consumed by fire amidst clinging smoke—their very bodies, whose fat was melting and trickling away on all sides due to the boiling and turning, [he took them]. Their flesh was thoroughly cooked and thus sloughing off and dripping; their limbs moved independently, as they were no longer attached to the main body.

The *jaṅghānalaka* (the lower leg-shaft) is that which is detached from those two joints at the upper and lower ends; having drawn it out—that is, having separated it from the body—nearby. In the reading "niścūṣya" (having sucked), they first perform suction like [sucking] fat and so forth because the flesh has become liquid and is oozing, and afterwards they drink the streams of marrow—the specific substances filling the cavities of the bones—which emerge therefrom without obstruction.

Regarding the phrase *niḥśabdapānāsecanam*, "āsecanam" means a slight sprinkling (*īṣat-secanam*). Because the state of being slight is prescribed by means of a sprinkling distinct from that [ordinary one], there is the substitution of *ṣ* in *niṣṭāpana*. This is because in examples such as *niṣṭaptaṃ rakṣaḥ* ("the demon is completely scorched"), what is intended to be expressed is indeed total heating. Since the eating of flesh was mentioned in the preceding verse, the description here of the act of drinking nourishes the *bībhatsa-rasa* (the sentiment of disgust). //17//

“*Prādoṣikaḥ*”: it refers to the intense joy (*pramoda*) arising at the onset of night; the sense is that because they are night-walkers (*rātriṃcara*), their great delight is appropriate when the time of *pradoṣa* has arrived. “*Āntraiḥ*”: previously, the account of the *piśācas* was told; now, the stretching out (*vijṛmbhaṇa*) of those who possess prosperous brides is described. They are those for whom protective amulets (*pratisarā*)—bracelets made of red thread and the like—are fashioned from intestines for the sake of auspiciousness.

The female Piśācas are so described because they bear as manifest ear-ornaments (*uttaṃsa*) nothing other than the very hands of deceased women, which are like red lotuses (*raktotpala*). They are likewise characterized by frequenting—that is, enjoying—the saffron that is nothing other than the mire of blood (*śoṇitapaṅka*). With their own hearts serving as white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), they have suddenly fashioned garlands. In the reading *pinahya śirasā*, it means having fastened them upon their own heads.

Thus adorned with beloved skull-cups—the cranium-bowls of corpses—as their drinking vessels, they joyfully drink the wine of bone-fat and marrow; here the ornament is a *sāvayava-rūpaka* (a metaphor with parts) existing in a single location. This is because the status of the Piśācas as the *nāyaka* (hero) of the enjoyment and the status of their female companions as the *nāyikā* (heroine) are not established through direct verbal superimposition (*śruti*), but are understood through implication (*artha*). As it has been said: "That is *rūpaka* where there is non-difference between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*)."

"That in which [the object] is both based on Vedic usage (*śrauta*) and based on meaning (*ārtha*), and where [the superimposition] occurs in part, is *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest). Furthermore, in the verse "With entrails fashioned as auspicious amulets" (*āntraiḥ kalpitamaṅgalapratisarāḥ*), there is *pariṇāma* (transformation/metaphorical identification). This is because the state of being an entrail-amulet is superimposed for the sake of serving the context. As it has been said: "When that which is being superimposed serves the purpose of the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma*. And: "That which is being superimposed, existing as the very nature of the locus of superimposition, is cited as *pariṇāma* because of its utility to the subject at hand."

By the phrase "because of its utility to the subject at hand," the distinction from *rūpaka* (metaphor) is stated: in that case (*rūpaka*), the superimposed object is merely a coloring agent for the subject; here, however, it is merely useful to it. Here, because there is the perception of a heroine adorned with garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, engaged in drinking wine together with her beloveds, the *saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra* (erotic rasa of union) is suggested as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the primary, expressed *bībhatsa-rasa* (rasa of disgust); thus, it is the *rasavad-alaṃkāra* (the figure of speech consisting of rasa).

Furthermore, the contradiction between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) is resolved through their relationship as primary and subordinate elements, as in the verse beginning "This is he who pulls up the girdle," where [the loathsome] serves as a subordinate element to the pathetic (*karuṇa*). As the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated: "When the intended rasa has attained its established footing, there is no fault in the mention of its opposites, provided they have become subordinate elements or are subject to suppression."

In this context, one should not suspect a contradiction between the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa, which is nourished from the words "moist with love" (*premārdrāḥ*) up to "as if dissolved" (*līneva*), and the *bībhatsa* (disgusting) rasa expressed by the word "intestines" (*āntraiḥ*). This is because the insertion of the *vismaya* (wonder) rasa through the phrase "turning here and there" (*itastataḥ parivartamāna-*) and the *adbhuta* (marvelous) rasa through the phrase "near the ears" (*karṇābhyarṇa-*) serves precisely to avoid the contradiction caused by their immediate succession. As it is said: "Even when two rasas are situated within the same sentence, provided they are separated by another rasa..."

"For hostility ceases upon the coexistence of two sentiments"—this means that even in the case of two [sentiments] situated within a single sentence, their conflict indeed ceases when there is an intervention by another sentiment; how much more so, then, in the case of those situated in different sentences? Furthermore, one should not suspect a conflict here based on having a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*), because it has already been established that there is no suspicion of conflict, since it is impossible for Mādhava, who is characterized by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārin*), to be the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsa-rasa*).

Nor is there a lack of contradiction here because the nourishment [of the subordinate rasa] has not been carried as far as that of the primary rasa; for it has been said: "Whether non-contradictory or contradictory, a rasa should not be brought to full nourishment when another rasa is the principal element; thus there will be no contradiction. It must be asked: "If there is no full nourishment, how can it be considered a *rasa*? For the intended meaning of this verse by Dhvanikāra is simply that the degree of nourishment which is given to the principal *rasa* should not be applied here [to the subordinate one]. Enough of this prolixity. //18//

The reading beginning with "punaraśastra-" is for the purpose of informing even those who arrived later. "Vibhīṣikās" refers to terrifying displays; by those *piśācas* who possess such transformations as distorted dress and speech intended to produce fear in another, [the place] was abandoned—meaning they fled quickly. "Niḥsattvāḥ" means devoid of courage or vigor. Regarding the phrase "sanirvedam": all the *piśācas* retreated out of sheer terror; they did not approach me with audacity to sell their flesh.

"The failure of my purpose because this [body] has not been purchased is the cause of my despondency. The entire cemetery enclosure—the whole area of the cremation ground—has been searched and scrutinized. Beyond this, there is no further portion of the cemetery land where buyers can be found. Thus, the sense is: "Alas, how adverse fate is toward me! Even though I have engaged in an act of daring that was improper, my purpose has not been achieved."

Thereafter, he states the very absence of the cremation ground area: "Indeed, right here in front, beyond the cremation ground (pāreśmaśānam), there flows a river"—this is the grammatical connection. Regarding the word *guñjat*: *pāreśmaśānam* means "at the limit" (*paryante*) of the cremation ground. The compound is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*. The river exists as the boundary, precisely at the edge. Therefore, the sense is that there is no cremation ground territory beyond this point. What kind of river is it?

It is characterized by banks that are terrifying due to a mass of howling jackals and fierce, imitative *dhātkṛti* sounds, which are intensified and augmented by the *dhūtkāra* cries of groups of owls (*ulūka*) dwelling in bower-cottages—the interior spaces of which are concealed by creepers and the like—while they are hooting and screeching.

Likewise, the *saṃrodhi* (obstructing) [current] is that which has its obstruction within the skulls—that is, the cranial fragments—of the fleshless skeletal remains of corpses; because it flows with excessive force after having gathered together in one place from that very spot, it is *kūlaṃkaṣa*, meaning it erodes the banks. [The form is derived thus: by the rule "the root *kaṣ* takes the suffix *khac* after the words *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*," there is the addition of the augment *mum*.

"Such" refers to that stream; "from its exit" means by that [exit], it is "ghora," meaning terrifying; likewise, she is "tādṛśī" (of such a kind) whose sound is "gharghara"—harsh and grating to the ear. Here, although there is an absence of rasa (sentiment) due to the presence of owls and other creatures, one should observe that because the river—the expressed subject—is terrifying, the *paruṣa* (harsh) meter is employed in accordance with that quality. //19//

"From behind the scenes"—the sense is that such a voice has arisen. "Alas, pitiless father! This person, who is now the very instrument for gratifying the heart of the king, is perishing. "Father," the implication is: you are merely a biological progenitor (*janaka*), but you do not possess conduct worthy of a progenitor. Therefore, "pitiless one"—devoid of compassion toward me—you have killed me yourself by giving me to Nandana instead of giving me to Mādhava. As for this exhaustion, it is merely the pretext for my death.

The sense is that death is otherwise certain. "This one" (eṣa) is a reference to herself. The meaning is that she has the notion of me as merely some person or creature, and not even a trace of affection such as thinking, "He is my child. She considers herself useful to the king only as an instrument for pleasing his mind, like jewels, gold, and so forth; she is not, however, his offspring—this is how it should be understood here. Mādhava [speaks] with significance, with a specific intention. "The cry" (nāda)... [is used].

This sound—sweet, soft, and high-pitched like the cry of a female osprey or a female curlew distressed by fear—is heart-stealing and captivating like the call of the *mālatī* bird. First of all, it reaches the state of being recognized as something familiar, as if previously experienced; it goes to the range of recognition, such that one thinks: "This is indeed that very same sound which I previously heard from Mālatī when she was overwhelmed by the calamity of Makaranda during the tiger's attack. It produces a correspondence with my former hearing, as if it were known from before.

Furthermore, immediately after hearing the sound, my heart, having been split and torn asunder within its very center, remains whirling and unsettled. Likewise, every limb—every member of the body, such as the hands and feet—becomes agitated and despondent. Moreover, the stiffness and immobility of the body, which is the great composite whole, causes one's movement and gait to falter. Therefore, what could this manner of distressful crying be? What indeed is this?

Is it that Mālatī herself has been brought by the power of illusion by some sorcerer seeking difficult-to-attain supernatural powers, to be offered as a sacrifice to the Great Goddess named Karālā—who resides in a nearby sanctuary, is renowned for her fondness for various living offerings, and is expert at bestowing all desired accomplishments upon practitioners—and is she thus crying piteously along the path? Or is this sound similar to her cry, or perhaps belongs to someone else? Such is the doubt.

If this sound belongs to another, then what could be the cause of the mental agitation, dizziness, trembling of the hands and other limbs, and the paralysis of my body that has arisen within me? Indeed, this unbearable pain of mine cannot result from the calamity of another. Therefore, by the maxim that "the functions of the internal organ are the authority," I believe this is the cry of distress of my beloved herself.

For she is my life-breaths moving outside; thus, Mādhava’s conjecture—containing the certainty that "this state of mine is due solely to the apprehension of her misfortune"—is entirely appropriate. //20//

"How is it known that this sound belongs to Kālī, who has been offered as a sacrifice by someone for the sake of her beloved? To this he replies: "Terrible" (*karālā*). The sound of lamentation (*karuṇadhvani*) is perceived as rising and emerging from the place of the goddess named Karālā-Kālī. For that is indeed the site of such undesirable acts as the sacrifice of living beings; therefore, the meaning is that this [sound] is quite probable [to originate there]. //21//

Having reflected thus, he resolves upon what must be done: "Let it be exactly as I have surmised. Nevertheless, I shall go and see the site of Kālī and witness the source of this cry of compassion. If, in truth, my beloved is the cause of it, then even at the cost of my own life, if she can be rescued from this calamity, I shall have attained the full fruit of living by saving her life."

If it cannot be done, then even by giving up my life right there, I shall attain [reunion with] you, my most beloved, in another world—this is her intention. Mālatī: Oh father, merciless one! This person, who was now the instrument for pleasing the heart of the king, is perishing. Oh mother! You are struck in your heart by the irresistible and wicked sport of fate. (In some readings, the word "matsnehamaye" is used as an adjective qualifying "hṛdaya"; in that case, the meaning is: "O father, you are indeed merciless, but—" )

(Ambā: "Because she is so fond of me, she will not survive the fire of grief at being separated from me; this alone is the cause of my sorrow, and not the separation from my own life. For it is her [life] that is dear to me, as she has not yet obtained Mādhava"—this is the sense. Alas, O you whose life consists of Mālatī! O you whose every activity is solely for the sake of accomplishing my welfare! [The analysis of the compound is: "She whose entire activity has as its sole fruit to be accomplished the very accomplishment of my marriage."

O venerable Kāmandakī, after a long time you have been made aware of my suffering through your affection; the meaning is that your very affection for me has become the cause of my sorrow. Alas, dear friend Lavaṅgikā, I have become for you merely one seen in a dream! Mādhava: "Hanta" expresses grief. The sense is: "It is true that I, your dearest, have been brought by someone for the sake of execution"—thus the axe has been wielded for my own ruin at the very root of the tree of my life. The interpretation "hanta expresses joy" is inappropriate.

At the moment of her being impaled upon the stake of execution—she who was my very life and all-in-all—what room is there for joy? Nor is there any certainty that my beloved will be released by me, for at that time even my own life is in doubt; it is for this reason he says, "Perhaps I might find her still alive. In every way, even by her death, my own abandonment of life is certain.

Nevertheless, there is the hope: "If I honor her while she is still alive through efforts such as seeing her, conversing with her, and protecting her, then my life will have attained its fulfillment. By the two particles *api* and *nāma*, both the possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and the eagerness (*autsukya*) are expressed. As for the interpretation offered by some—who claim that this collection of particles has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and thus explains it as "I would honor her only while she is alive" or "she exists only while alive"—that too should be disregarded because it does not accord with the context.

"Indeed, even now her life is not certain; or, if it were certain, how could the optative suffix (*liṅ*) be justified in the expression of hope, 'I might imagine [her survival]'? Enough of this. [Kāpālikas: Kapālakuṇḍalā and Aghoraghaṇṭa. [The compound is formed] by the rule "pumān striyā" (when a male and a female are mentioned, the masculine remains), resulting in a single remainder. [Regarding the passage beginning with] "The Goddess," etc.: having placed the offering of blood before her, one should present it preceded by praise and prostration; thus, the praise of the Goddess is performed—beginning with "She who is resolute," etc.

With pride and arrogance, [she was shaken] by the agitation caused by the humiliation characterized by the kick from Niśumbha’s foot. In the reading "niśumbhanirbhara," it means: the terrestrial globe (the earth's structure) bows down excessively (*nirbharam*) because of Niśumbha; the resulting compression, due to its extreme weight and the difficulty of bearing it, causes the exhaustion of the Tortoise’s power of support. From the back of such a Tortoise—whose shell (*karpara*), meaning the bony plate of the back, is bent down and sinking due to that pressure—[the water] trickles down, [caused] by its trembling.

I praise your celebrated dance-drama performance (*lāsya*), which is well-known in the assembly of the blue-throated Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*) who is ever-joyful and gratified—a performance in which the seven oceans were cast into the hollows of your cheeks, which were like rival or opposing chambers of the netherworld (*pātāla*), such that the very stability of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) seemed to tremble as you played. (Note: *Sraṃsamānā* is understood here as a variant or scribal error for *saṃsramamāṇā*; *pratimallayoḥ* means "of the two rivals"; *adhobhuvanakuharasadṛśayoḥ* means "resembling the cavities of the subterranean realm"; *gallavivarayoḥ* means "of the hollows of the cheeks"; *prakṣiptāḥ* means "cast into"; *tattādṛśam* means "such as that"; *nanditasya* means "of the one who is gladdened"; *vyaktam* means "manifest" or "well-known.")

Even here, although there is an absence of a sentiment (rasa) appropriate for a complex composition (*vikaṭabandha*), the harsh style (*paruṣavṛtti*) is consistent with the nature of the expressed meaning; therefore, the defect known as "discordant phonemes" (*pratikūlavarṇatva*) should not be suspected. This should be understood similarly in what follows. Although it has been stated that the word *galla* is vulgar (*grāmya*) because it is established solely by worldly convention, nevertheless, in the speech of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), vulgarity is indeed a merit (*guṇa*) and not a defect. As it is said: "Vulgarity is a merit in the utterances of low-natured persons. //22//

Regarding the word *pracalita*: "O Goddess," the term *vaḥ* is used in the plural for the sake of honor. "May our *tāṇḍava* lead to *ariṣṭi*—the absence of inauspiciousness—and to *hṛṣṭi*—joy"—this is a benediction. Of what nature is that *tāṇḍava*?

It proceeded from the many spirits who were terrified by her fierce, loud laughter—laughter that was released by those numerous beings who had regained their lives through the dripping of nectar flowing from the moon, which was split asunder by the impact of her flickering claws upon the edges of the elephant hide that served as her upper garment, the hide being tossed about due to the agitation of her moving limbs.

His praise is such that it arises from the pedestal of the hoods—which are wide, blossoming, and expanding—of the black serpents (asitabhujaṅga), who hiss (śvasatām) due to extreme exhaustion; these hoods are those whose coils (bhoga) serve as the knots of their armlets (aṅgada), the knots of their bracelets (keyūra), and the fastenings of their arm-rings, through the pressure of which they have opened wide. "From the pedestal" means, in effect, from the neck.

That [place] in which the mountains were cast down and scattered on all sides by the multitude of his arms—which were emerging, issuing forth, blazing with fiery luster, formidable in their expansion, terrifying, detached, tossed about, wide-reaching, and outstretched.

Likewise, his head—terrible and fearsome due to the weight of the flickering, tawny flashes from his eyes, that is, the streams of his gaze—was whirling; by that whirling, there was set in motion the action of a firebrand-wheel (*alātacakra*). A burning stick, when whirled with great speed, appears like a wheel and is called a *alātacakra*. In that [action], the quarters of space—the circle of directions—were as if sewn together, fixed therein.
Likewise, it is that place where the clusters of stars are scattered and shattered by the waving and tossing of the banner atop the lofty peak—the very summit—of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).

Likewise, by the rhythmic clapping of the palms (*tāla*) of the delighted *kaṭapūtanas*—a specific class of *piśācas*—who are leaping, fierce, and terrifying *vetālas* and *bhettālas*, Gaurī’s ears burst and the cavities of her hearing split asunder; thus she becomes utterly bewildered. For the Three-Eyed Lord (*Tryambaka*), whose mind rejoices through that dense embrace—the firm embrace—of such a Gaurī, there is bliss (*ānanda*). This is the *daṇḍaka* meter, according to the rule: "In the *daṇḍaka*, *na*, *u*, and *ra* [are the feet]. //23//

Mādhava: Seeing that Mālatī herself has been brought here for the purpose of execution, he cries out, "Alas! Woe!"—meaning, shame on the negligence of her parents and the lack of vigilance of Kāmandakī and the others. The sense is that she has been brought by this cruel man for execution, unobserved by anyone, and dressed in the garb of one condemned to death. He expresses this very point with the words beginning "nyasta-": she upon whom red lac has been applied as an ointment, and who is clad in red garlands and garments; and [he refers to] those two [executioners] who possess the undertaking—the act of killing—which belongs to the wicked, the doers of evil.

The two heretics are indeed Buddhists, and they are like *caṇḍālas* because they perform the deeds of *caṇḍālas* and because they associate with them. Of those two, the term "the two" (*tayoḥ*) is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) formed according to the rule "a male [remains] after a female. She has come within the range—the domain—of these two, who are like wolves, meaning cruel creatures such as tigers, just as a doe might fall into the grasp of a deer-hunter. She is timid by her very nature. She is the daughter of the minister Bhūrivasu, who is like one of the eight Vasus—or rather, like the Vasu Agni himself—endowed with prowess and equal to a god; yet she stands in the jaws of death. Alas! (expressing grief).

"Shame!"—the ellipsis is "shame upon my hope for life beyond this point. "Alas! This undesirable calamity has befallen me. What is this course of action of Fate, devoid of compassion and lacking mercy? How is it that the wretched god of fate has begun such an utterly improper act? It should be understood that although there is no significant difference in meaning between the words *hā*, *dhik*, *kaṣṭam*, and *aniṣṭam*, there is no suspicion of tautology because they serve to manifest an excess of pathos (*anukampā*). As it is said: "If something is employed to express an excess of pity and so forth, there is no fault in tautology and the like; on the contrary, it is an ornament (*alaṃkāra*). //24//

Kapālakuṇḍalā: "That one, my dear. At this moment of death, remember that deity who was your beloved and desired one. According to the sacred tradition (*āgama*), the remembrance of one's chosen deity at the time of death leads to prosperity in the hereafter. By saying "now," the meaning is that death is imminent. Mālatī: "Alas, Lord Mādhava! Even though you have gone to the other world, this person should be remembered by you. By addressing you as 'Lord,' [I mean] you alone are the very embodiment of my chosen deity; therefore, even in the state of death, I shall remember only you."

The sense is: "May my union with you occur in another birth. Indeed, he does not pass away for whom a beloved person remembers him; here, the genitive case in *yasya* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is that because the person who is the object of his beloved's remembrance dwells constantly in his mind, he does not cease to exist [for her]. *Hanta* expresses dejection. This poor girl (*tapasvinī*) is worthy of compassion; being thus devoted to Mādhava, he now wanders right here for the purpose of selling human flesh.

"Or perhaps by chance he might come and release him. Then there is despondency, thinking, "Alas, an obstacle to the accomplishment of the mantra is likely. Regarding the second half of the verse beginning with "O auspicious one": "O Blessed Cāmuṇḍā!"—enjoy this worship, an offering of a jewel among women, which was intended and resolved upon at the time of the commencement of the mantra-achievement, and is now presented and offered at its conclusion. (25)

Mādhava: [Waving away the raised sword of the Kāpālika with his forearm and wrist] Begone, begone! You are struck down; by this very reversal, you yourself are slain! Mālatī: May the noble sir protect me! Mādhava: [Thinking, "It is the hour of death"] That action in which all apprehension has been abandoned is described as such. In this kind of *pralāpa*—the utterance of meaningless words, such as "I shall destroy him this very moment"—he is unrestrained and unimpeded.

The meaning is this: those of great power indeed perform a service spontaneously, without first uttering words; thus, speech is superfluous. Although one should not say, "I shall do this," but rather simply act, nevertheless, because my mind was overcome by a weight of joy at having achieved such extreme success for my birth by saving the life of my beloved in such a dire situation, I have uttered some senseless prattle, casting aside even the fear of being thought light-minded.

Thus, this friend of yours—by whom his own innate and natural affection has been made manifest—stands right before you. Therefore, O fair-limbed one, cast off this trembling, a quivering caused by fear. Even now, that wicked evildoer experiences here, right before you, the fruit of such an evil deed whose ripening and commencement of result were contrary and perverse; the meaning is that he has been destroyed by his own very attempt to kill you. //26//

Aghoraghaṇṭa: An obstacle, an impediment. Kapālakuṇḍalā: By the phrase "she is the ground of this affection, the sole object of reliance," it is indicated that she must certainly be protected. By the phrase "the friend's son of Kāmandakī," it is indicated that through the grace of that great Yoginī, our jewels, mantras, and magical powers have no effect upon him. By the phrase "bargaining for human flesh," he shows that because of his extreme heroism, he cannot be overcome even by prowess. Mādhava: [With tears].

The state of being "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) arises from joy and dejection. What does this mean? It means: how can this be the occurrence of misfortune? Mālatī: Noble sir, I too do not know; I know only this much: I woke up here while still asleep upon the upper veranda. But as for you—where [have you] come together? (The word "come" is to be supplied. Mādhava: (With shame. Shame is the cause [of his emotion], because he has become compelled to report his own improper deed—the sale of human flesh—which he himself committed.

Adopting audacity and saying, "I have done what was improper out of hope for attaining you," he speaks with the words beginning with *tvat*: "O timid one (*bhīru*), being tormented by this obsession—the persistent longing that 'may I become one whose birth is blessed through the grasping of your lotus-hand'—and thus having my fortitude cast aside and rendered futile by the provocation of my own fickleness, I was wandering in the cremation ground (*paretabhūmi*) to offer myself as a stake of human flesh for sale; it is there that I have come upon hearing your weeping."

The suffix *krūṅ* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) by the rule *bhiyaḥ kruklukanau*. Then, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied because the word ends in the vowel *ū* and denotes a class of humans (*manuṣyajāti*), according to the rule *ūṅutaḥ*. Subsequently, the shortening occurs by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ*. Since the word *bhīru* invariably denotes a female, its denotation of a human class is established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Alternatively, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. //27//

Mālatī—(Aside: "The 'aside' (apavāritaka) is to be performed with the hand having three fingers extended," so it is said. This "concealment" (apavāraṇa) is the physical manifestation (anubhāva) of the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) consisting of the concealment of excessive shame and joy. How is it that they are wandering about regardless of their own safety solely for my sake? For the sake of me, who am merely a woman, how has he begun this deed, disregarding his own life, directed toward such a great task?

The meaning is this: "In this matter, I alone am the offender, for I have not approached him even by force; alas, how cruel my heart is! Mādhava: "Oh, indeed! This has been explained previously. Regarding "this very thing": this meeting with my beloved is called "the crow-and-the-palm-fruit" (*kākatālīya*). The sense is that, by chance, it is like the falling of a palm fruit at the very moment a crow arrives.

As for the establishment of its own form (*svarūpasiddhi*): within the section on the meaning of *iva* under the rule *ive pratikṛtau*, while the suffix *cha* is being carried over from the rule *kuśāgrācchaḥ*, the word *tat* in the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* refers back to the meaning of *iva*. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is: "The suffix *cha* occurs after a compound that has as its object the meaning of *iva*, provided that the meaning of *iva* itself is intended. If one objects: "Since the meaning of *iva* is already expressed by the compound itself when it has that as its object, what is the purpose of the suffix?"—it is not so. The suffix arises for the meaning of *iva* other than that which is already the object of the compound.

For instance, the arrival of the crow and the falling of the palm fruit were both accidental. By that falling palm fruit, the killing of the crow was effected; likewise, Mādhava’s arrival there by chance and Mālatī’s arrival there in the same manner occurred. The compound *kākatala* is formed from this very statement as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) through the analysis *kākāgamanatālapatanam iva* ("like the arrival of the crow and the falling of the palm fruit"). And in the context of its usage, the words *kāka* and *tāla* come to signify the actions of "arrival" and "falling."

Then, by the word *kākatāla* (the crow and the palm fruit), the meaning of the phrase is that the protection of his beloved was achieved through Mādhava’s chance arrival—which, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, resulted in the killing of the Kāpālika—just as the term *kākatālīya* denotes an unexpected occurrence or a marvelous event. This is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. Since there is no other specific rule [prescribing such a formation], its derivation follows this path because it applies to many instances; enough said on this point. The word *samprati* is an embellishment (*upaskāra*). Regarding *rāhoḥ*: she who moves in the mouth of Rāhu is *ānanacarī*.

*Tām* means "situated within her mouth. The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule *careṣṭaḥ*, with the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) as the *upapada*. Because of the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Such a beloved woman is like a digit of the moon. From the word *priya*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau*; when that suffix follows, the substitution of *preya-* for *priya-* occurs by the rule *priyasthira-*, etc. Finally, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*.

Having by chance, through fate, encountered and fallen within the range of the falling sword of this wretched Kāpālika thief—who is forcibly seizing me—I am struck with such terror at the thought: "How has my beloved, possessing such extreme delicacy like a digit of the moon, come into the range of the falling sword of this exceedingly cruel thief, as if she were the moon itself?"

If even a moment’s delay had occurred for me after this point, a great calamity would have ensued; from such a state of the permanent emotion (*sthāyībhāva*) of fear—a terrifying sentiment characterized by the definition: "Fear is known as a mental agitation produced by the terrible" (*raudra*)—he was "distraught," meaning bewildered regarding what ought to be done due to that fear. Likewise, through compassion (*karuṇā*)—the permanent emotion of the sentiment of pathos (*śoka*)—born from the contemplation of his beloved’s condition, namely that she was as if already dead even with a moment's interval, and that she has now been restored as if risen from death, he was "melted," meaning dissolved.

Likewise, from a state of wonder (*vismaya*)—the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*) characterized by such thoughts as, "Oh, how inconceivable is the power of the play of destiny! For today, my arrival here for the purpose of selling human flesh coincides with my reaching this very place by the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya-nyāya*), and the recovery of my beloved; this is a great marvel"—the mind is agitated and the marvelous rasa is produced, according to the definition stated: "Wonder is the expansion of the mind caused by the extraordinary nature of objects and the like."

Likewise, [it is] inflamed by the heroic sentiment (raudrarasa), ignited by the emotion of wrath characterized as follows: "Wrath is defined as the intensity of sharpness directed toward adversaries," and consisting of the thought: "How can this evildoer, now prepared to kill even her—who is innocent and a jewel of the three worlds—be allowed to live? Therefore, he must certainly be slain. Thus, it is kindled by the heroic sentiment.

Thus, her mind—expanded by the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and blossomed through the predominant erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), whose stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is love (*rati*) in its many forms such as "I shall have fulfilled my purpose by protecting my beloved, who is dearer to me than even my own life"—is filled with joy. How does she exist? In what manner? The sense is that it is impossible to determine how she is situated in such a state.

And here, Mādhava’s love directed toward Mālatī—which has been unfolding throughout the play—is suggested primarily as a *dhvani* (implied meaning). This love is manifested by the *ālambana-vibhāva* (the objective basis) designated as his beloved; it is excited by her glances and other such factors; it is experienced through *anubhāvas* (consequent effects) consisting of mental expansion, affectionate speech, and efforts to protect her; and it is intensified by *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory states) such as intoxication, fatigue, joy, anxiety, and recollection, which arise from seeing her. Thus, having attained the state of *rasa*, it is preeminently suggested.

As a subordinate element (*tadaṅga*), however, there arises the *bhayānaka-rasa* (the sentiment of fear), which is based on the apprehension of a terrifying Kāpālika—suggested by the simile "like the digit of the moon moving in Rāhu’s mouth"—and is intensified by the contemplation of his true nature; its permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is fear, indicated by the word *ātaṅka*; its consequent manifestations (*anubhāvas*) are the mental agitation suggested by the word *vikala* and the corresponding physical and vocal actions; and it is augmented by the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as trembling, apprehension, despondency, exhaustion, stupor, wretchedness, agitation, despair, madness, anxiety, and delusion, all of which are implied.

Likewise, the rasa of *karuṇa* (pathos) is indicated by the phrase "from the range of the robber’s sword-stroke"; it has the dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of grief, which is suggested by the beloved who is nearly dead as the objective basis (*ālambana*), and is kindled by the contemplation of her miserable state; this grief reaches its full development through the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as tears, change of color, loss of voice, stupor, agitation, delusion, madness, and despondency, which are manifested through the "quickly" mentioned mental melting (*cittadravībhāva*) and the corresponding physical and verbal expressions.

Likewise, the *adbhuta-rasa* (the marvelous sentiment) is produced: it is suggested by the phrase "having thus encountered by chance," with its determinants (*ālambana*) being a fortuitous meeting and its excitants (*uddīpana*) being the contemplation of the wonderful diversity of fate; its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is indicated as "astonishment" (*vismaya*); its consequents (*anubhāva*) are the agitation of the mind and the corresponding physical and verbal manifestations; and it is intensified by the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) invariably associated with it, such as paralysis, fainting, perspiration, joy, pride, recollection, deliberation, awakening, and anxiety.

Thus, the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*)—indicated by the words "and so he cut," which suggest the object of focus as one intent on killing his beloved, kindled by the contemplation of her wickedness, and ignited like a blazing fire; characterized by the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as trembling, horripilation, perspiration, joy, agitation, delusion, madness, intoxication, pride, fickleness, envy, exhaustion, and resentment, all of which are indicated by the phrase "how does he behave? and manifested through the consequent actions of speech appropriate to that state—is intensified. These sentiments [of the other types] likewise exist only from afar, by virtue of their reduction to a subordinate status (*aṅgabhāvāpatti*).

When mutual contradictions have been set aside, there is no conflict in view of the predominance of the primary rasa. In view of the nourishment of the primary rasa, because of the nourishment of subordinate rasas, they are described in conjunction with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) through the process of "blending" (*melanagati*), which is termed "non-conflict" (*avyatikara*) and "beauty" (*śobhana*) due to the presence of praiseworthy propriety. As it has been said: "When three rasas arise simultaneously, or even two, if the rasa is blended [with them], it is known as 'equal blending' (*samavyatikara*)."
"He who shines by his own majesty even amidst the conflict of friends and enemies, or even in the mixture of flavors, is called 'Śobhana' (the Beautiful). Enough with excessive talk. //28//

Aghoraghaṇṭa: "O Brahmin boy! By virtue of being a Brahmin and a child, you are devoid of manliness due to your timid nature—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase 'smelled by a tiger' and so forth: when a doe, a female deer, has been smelled—that is, seized—by a tiger, one who is overwhelmed with pity (kṛpākula), that is, compassionate, [would act]; by that same logic, for me, who take pleasure in violence and am constantly intent on killing, there is the site (ketana), the assembly hall (āsthāna), namely Karālāsthāna; of him who frequents (juṣaḥ), that is, dwells in, that place, my range (gocara) or domain."

"You have arrived; you are lost. The sense is: just as a compassionate deer is slain by a tiger while pursuing a doe, so too are you, being compassionate, to be killed by me now that she has been brought here by me as a sacrificial offering. The address "O sinner" is used to call Mādhava by name because he acts as an obstacle to the fruition of his own past karma (*prārabdha-karma*).

Thus, by you yourself—who previously described how a headless trunk (kabandha), with its shoulders shattered and limbs cast asunder from the blow of a sword, pours forth and rains down a mass of blood and streams of gore from its orifices—I shall satisfy and please Bhadrakālī, the mother and progenitor of all beings; [I shall do so] afterwards by means of this [blood], is the sense. //29//

Mādhava: "It is worthless! Ah, you evil-souled, heretical outcaste! How can you resolve upon and strive to do such a thing? To the question "What is it you intend to do?", he replies: [you intend] to sever the world-process (*prapañca*), which—extending from the smallest insect up to Brahmā (*ākiraṭam āvirañcam*)—is a continuous flow of activities consisting of the birth, life, and death of the diverse and manifold classes of living beings, such as gods, animals, and humans; the assumption of bodies appropriate to various places and times; and the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth corresponding to those respective bodies; and thus, by cutting this flow, [you claim] the world is worthless.

The phrase "how have you resolved to make [this world] devoid of its most excellent substance? is to be connected with every subsequent clause. For this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), despite the presence of objects such as sandalwood and gold, possesses no essence through them; rather, it possesses essence only through her. And if she is slain by you, this world would become utterly essence-less, like mere dregs. Therefore, the meaning is that by striving to kill her, you are striving to make the very cycle of existence itself devoid of essence.

In this passage, because the quality of being the sole essence of the entire world is superimposed upon Mālatī through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object, there is the figure of speech *adhyavasita-prayatnātiśayokti* (hyperbole of effort resulting in identification), according to the definition: "That is [identification] when one thing is swallowed up and another is superimposed upon it. Furthermore, because the act of determination (*vyavasāya*)—which is presented as an accomplished fact—is connected to everything [mentioned], there is also the verbal ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*) known as *kriyādīpaka* (the illuminator of action). The quality of being the essence (*sāratva*) in sandalwood, gold, and so forth does not exist in reality, but is based solely on the common consensus of the vulgar folk.

The suggestion (*vyaṅgya*) here is both the concealment (*apahnava*)—that "this alone is the essence"—and the contrast (*vyatireka*)—that "this alone is the essence even when compared to all other things that possess essence. This should be understood to apply in all such cases. Likewise, *tribhuvana* is a collective noun for the three worlds (*trayāṇāṃ bhuvanānāṃ samāhāraḥ*). According to the rule, "A prohibition must be stated [to prevent the suffix] after words beginning with *pātra*," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* (as prescribed by the rule *dvigoḥ*) does not occur. [The phrase *tatkartum* means] to act so as to have its jewels plundered or stolen.

Even though the Kaustubha jewel, gold, and other treasures exist, they do not make the three worlds a treasury of jewels, nor are they jewels in reality; rather, it is only for the undiscriminating that there is the designation of "jewel" and the established reputation of being comparable to excellent objects. This very [Earth] alone is the one jewel of the three worlds, possessing qualities that surpass all jewels—this is a *nigīryādhyavasāna* (a poetic identification by suppressing the literal meaning). "He has set out to kill her" means: you have set out to make the world entirely devoid of jewels. The application of the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is as before.

In this way, one seeks to render the world—which travels upon the path of the six means of valid cognition—a mere void of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), devoid of light, empty of illumination, and overcome solely by darkness. Indeed, this world is not truly illuminated by the lights of the sun and other such sources, because those things, being insentient in nature, are themselves manifestations that must be illumined by another light. Rather, it is this very flame of the supreme jewel-lamp within the palace of the three worlds—consisting of the light whose essence is consciousness, the singular flavor of bliss—that shines forth, illuminating this world along with the splendors of the sun, moon, and other luminaries.

The meaning is: "You desire to extinguish this [fire]; you desire to make the world blind. Likewise, [you wish] to make even the entire circle of kinsmen—that group of relatives whose sole life-force is this [child], for whom death alone is the refuge, and who are capable of dispelling the sorrow born of such a calamity—into that very state. And this intermediate sentence is a *sahacarabhinna* (one where the correlative is displaced).

For here, in this verse consisting of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), by means of subordinate sentences such as "transmigration is essence-less," it is established—through the variety of stylistic turns and the logic of bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*)—that Mālatī possesses qualities such as beauty that surpass all the world, and thus she constitutes the excellence of all things; furthermore, through her presence and absence alone, the presence and absence of the world’s worthiness of being accepted are demonstrated. Yet, by this particular sentence, the excellence of Mālatī herself is not what is being propounded.

For even when one's kinsmen—whether blind, hunchbacked, ill-behaved, or deceased—are lost, people take refuge in death; yet the world's worthiness of being accepted is never dependent upon their lineage, nor is its unworthiness dependent upon their absence, since the attainment of that worthiness is established simply through the abundance of many excellent things.

Furthermore, in the midst of a series of statements establishing extreme excellence, this sentence—which is distinct from its companions because it refers to his being a member of the twice-born (dvijāti) and is thus inferior—is contradictory; like a cowrie shell inserted as a central gem in a necklace of pearls strung together for six months, it does not deserve to be placed there as the principal ornament, and it would constitute a break in the sequence (prakramabhaṅga). This is because there is an untimely interruption of the figures of speech, such as hyperbole (atiśayokti), that were being successively constructed.

However, some explain that by using the word *jana* (people), which denotes those who are indifferent, Mādhava indicates himself as one who, seeing no other means to cross over the sorrow caused by the destruction of his beloved, perceives death itself as that very means. They argue that because he thus declares that his own death would follow her destruction, this serves to manifest the excellence of her beauty, and therefore the aforementioned fault does not apply. This is incorrect; for when one says "the circle of kinsmen" (*bāndhavajana*), the indication of oneself is not perceived in any way whatsoever, and even if it were perceived, her excellence is not established by such a statement alone.

Everyone blinded by passion considers only that object which is dear to their own heart to be superior to all the world, even if it is actually base. For instance, it is said: "Whomever a person finds desirable in this world, she appears to him as the most beautiful of forms. It is well known even among animals that for this very reason, the *cakravāka* bird, perceiving the entire world as empty during the absence of its beloved, regards her alone as possessing supermundane beauty.

Nor should it be said that even in this case, her transcendence of the world is established merely by Mādhava’s own pride; for otherwise, there would be a disruption of the aesthetic relish (*rasāsvāda*) due to the discerning connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) who experience a contrary state and perceive an incongruity (*anaucitya*). Nor should it be disregarded on the grounds that, although she may be praiseworthy through his own pride, the existence or non-existence of such a being makes no difference whatsoever to the world.

Therefore, the connoisseurs who know the essence of poetry, such as Kuntaka and others, should read: "Everything is the play of Fate and is fruitless. For in this way, there is not even a trace of fault. Indeed, in this beginningless and worthless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the "play"—meaning the creative activity—of Fate engaged in the production of most enchanting objects does not have the moon and other such things as its fruit; for because those [objects] are trivial, they cannot possibly be the fruit of such an exertion by Fate. Rather, it is this very [creation of poetry] that is its fruit; thus, there is a poetic identification (*adhyavasāna*) through the suppression (*nigīrya*) of the literal meaning.

Thus, you are prepared to destroy this very fruit out of season; the meaning is that you are intent on rendering the very operation of the Creator fruitless. Likewise, you seek to render Kandarpa devoid of pride—that is, stripped of arrogance. For even though conditions such as gentle breezes, sandalwood, and moonlight exist, he possesses no pride based upon them, thinking, "Relying on these, I shall conquer the three worlds up to the limit of the Three-eyed One," because those factors lack the power to act as his auxiliaries.

However, his pride consists in thinking, "Relying solely on this unimpeded power of my own, there is no rival to me in the three worlds; I alone am the hero. You desire to destroy that pride—meaning you wish to render even Kandarpa devoid of pride and lacking in energy—and likewise you wish to make the creation of people's eyes fruitless and devoid of purpose, for the very sight of an object possessing unsurpassed beauty is indeed the fruit of the creation of eyes.

Nor is the sight of another object the fruit of that [creation], for there exists nothing else possessing such beauty. This very limit of the essence of loveliness is its fruit; thus, the meaning is that upon her destruction, the very creation of eyes would be in vain. Likewise, it is to turn the world into a withered forest—a wilderness terrifying with cruel beasts, Rākṣasas, Pulindas, and the like, filled with trees difficult to behold due to their decayed trunks and hollows.

For by this very splendor of the springtime in the pleasure-grove of this world-jungle, which has been made fragrant by the scent of various exceedingly delicate trees and creepers in bloom, and which serves as the sole ground for the experience of bliss while warding off all distress, this world became a pleasure-garden; it was not so through other states of being, however radiant they may be with such a multitude of qualities. Therefore, the meaning is that he who wishes to leave this world as nothing more than a mere story intends to turn this entire universe into nothing but a terrifying wilderness that causes extreme agitation.

In this regard, King Bhoja resolved the objection of tautology by arguing that since the excellence [of the hero] is established by one sentence, there is no redundancy in establishing that very same excellence through subsequent sentences either; for the speaker, impelled by the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*), employs profound adjectives through the variety of bold poetic assertion (*prauḍhokti*). As he said: "If an adjective previously mentioned is stated yet again, it has the same meaning as before; however, when impelled by *rasa*, it is therefore not a defect."
Alliteration (*cchekānuprāsa*) is the verbal ornament (*śabdālaṃkāra*) here; enough, then, with this prolixity regarding the treatises on poetics. //30//

"Out of affection!"—by that [word]. Even by blows from *śirīṣa* flowers—which are exceedingly delicate and obtained by one's own will through the passion and delight found in the playful jests and specific sports of dear friends (*praṇayasakhīnām ālīnām*), who are the objects of love—even by such blows, how much more so by any other hard substance, does that body wither and fade instantly; yet upon that very body, you suddenly cast down and strike a weapon for the purpose of killing! Upon your head, [this curse] shall fall.

"Let this left arm fall like the staff of Yama, the staff of Time!"—this is the commencement of speech by Mādhava, whose anger is fully kindled and who is suited to the sentiment of the Fierce (raudra-rasa). //31//

Aghoraghaṇṭa: "Strike! Strike!"—this is a speech imbued with derision, meaning "I shall witness your prowess. Because Mādhava is so close by, he is referred to by the word *idam* (this) through a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) based on the predominance of the quality of being present before one's eyes, as in the thought, "This [person] is not you. Since their mutual slaughter is nearly accomplished and thus rendered certain, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in both instances to denote immediate proximity to the present. Mālatī: Be gracious, O Lord, you reckless one! This wretched man is indeed cruel; therefore, protect me!

"Turn back from this calamitous danger! For my sake alone—a mere woman—you, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, must not commit such a rash act. Since this [demon] is so cruel, what else could he do? Therefore, turn back"—this is the intended meaning. Kapālakuṇḍalā: "Be vigilant," that is, be careful. Mādhava and Aghoraghaṇṭa both speak simultaneously to Mālatī and Kapālakuṇḍalā respectively, using a single verse with identical meaning for both: Mādhava and Aghoraghaṇṭa: [Verse follows]

"O timid one"—this address is directed by each toward the other. "Fortitude": O timid one, you whose fear is natural to the female disposition, place fortitude in your heart; do not yield to cowardice. "This sinner is slain"—this refers to both [the speaker] by both [of them]. He is indeed slain! Why do you suspect negligence on my part even here?

Behold: has there ever been, by anyone at all, any negligence on the part of Hari—who is habitually a crusher of the multitude of the frontal globes of elephants in the act of slaughtering deer—to be experienced? [The suffix] *ṣākan* is applied in the sense of habitual action according to the rule "after the roots *jalpa*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭh*, and *vṛṅ*, [the suffix] *ṣākan* [is added]. For such a Hari, whose hand is itself a thunderbolt (*kuliśa*)—that is, one whose hand is like a thunderbolt—was any lapse ever experienced? The meaning is that it was not experienced by anyone.

In this context, regarding the sentence-meaning characterized by the impossibility [of negligence]—namely, "negligence is not possible for me on the path of minor adversaries"—the sentence-meaning characterized by the impossibility of negligence in Hari, the Lord of Beasts (the lion), is superimposed. By means of the possibility of negligence in a lion during the killing of a deer, the possibility of negligence in my own killing of this [creature] is established; thus, it fashions a relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*). Consequently, this is the figure of speech *nidarśanā*, defined as "the connection with an impossible attribute that brings about a constructed simile."
And one should not entertain the delusion that there is a *śleṣa* (pun) here, because both sentences are recited simultaneously by both [reciters]. //32//

The tumultuous noise is a great clamor. She who comforts [others] by means of auspicious omens and the like, thereby loosening their suffering; she whose vision is unimpeded and unblunted wisdom itself—that venerable lady Kāmandakī commands or issues this order. What is it? "Let this temple of Karālā be surrounded and besieged. To the question "For what purpose?", she says: "Not so."

This act of abducting Mālatī did not originate from anyone other than the fierce and terrifying Aghoraghaṇṭa; nor is any result for his ritual activity—other than the offering of Karālā for the purpose of accomplishing a mantra—perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that the Blessed Lady commands: "Let that very place be searched, for it was there that the Goddess was offered as a sacrifice by him for the sake of the *bali* along with Kapālakuṇḍalā. //33//

Kapālakuṇḍalā: "O Blessed One, we are hemmed in and surrounded by soldiers! What is to be done beyond this?"—this is an utterance of despondency. Aghoraghaṇṭa: "At this very moment."—this is a statement of consolation, meaning: "I shall slay them right before those who have come for the purpose of protection; therefore, you must not fear. Mālatī: "Alas, Father! Alas, Blessed One! Mādhava: [He enters.]

Having placed her comfortably in the assembly—that is, the gathering—of her kinsmen who have arrived for her protection, I shall afterwards kill her before them with effortless effort. The intention is this: by reporting to the minister that "just as he alone, for the sake of saving Mālatī's life, killed this wicked soul right before our eyes and performed a great service," I shall inspire in him the desire to give Mālatī to me.

Both of them employ the same single expression for both purposes—namely, "re re" (ho there!). [The term] "kaṭhora" means hard; those which are hard and firm bone-joints, the projections of the bones (*kīkasakūṭa*), by their conjunction—that is, by the impact produced by them—is generated a *ghaṇātkāra*, an onomatopoeic sound, by which it is resonant (*mukhara*). Likewise, it is that in which the cessation of momentum—the momentary rest—produced by the cutting of the harsh tendons (*snāyu*) has occurred.

Likewise, let such a sword—moving without fear or obstruction through pieces of flesh from which the bones and sinews have been removed, as if through mud—suddenly cut your body limb by limb and member by member into small bits and fragments, and scatter them, dispersing them in all directions. Here, the Furious sentiment (*raudra-rasa*) is manifested, refined by the Disgusting (*bībhatsa*). A direct description of combat has not been employed because it is prohibited; its result, however, will be indicated later.

As it has been said: "One should not point out things that are directly perceived, such as a long journey, killing, battle, the ruin of a kingdom or country and so forth, imprisonment, eating, bathing, sexual intercourse, the application of ointments, or the taking up of garments. (34)
They have gone forth for the purpose of battle.
I have here explained the intention of Bhavabhūti according to my own understanding;
may those possessed of discernment be capable of fully comprehending all its meanings.

Thus ends the commentary on the fifth act of the *Mālatīmādhava-bhāvapradīpikā*, composed by the venerable Tripurāri Sūri, the son of Parvatanātha Yāyajūka, the ornament of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Act Six.
I take refuge in innate speech, which is noble through qualities that need not be acquired, adorned with ornaments that are not adventitious, and whose essence is perfected without effort.

Now, the poet, beginning another act, introduces a *śuddhaviṣkambha*—an introductory scene involving a single character used to indicate matters already past and those yet to come—with the words "Then," and so forth. [She is] Kapālakuṇḍalā; [she refers to him] as one by whom our preceptor was caused to perish for the sake of Mālatī.

By such an address, it is indicated that Mādhava slew Aghoraghaṇṭa in battle; for you killed our preceptor on account of Mālatī, and thus I shall repay that kindness by carrying off Mālatī herself—this being the intention of Kapālakuṇḍalā. At that moment, during the heat of battle, while she was striking mercilessly and casting aside the timidity inherent to her female nature, she struck with pitiless fury out of anger at the murder of her teacher; yet I, though a woman, was treated with contempt and disregarded by you.

"Therefore, you shall certainly experience the fruit of your contempt for me. Regarding the meaning of this sentence—"How can there be happiness while I, who am bound by enmity due to the sin of murdering my preceptor, remain awake?"—he speaks the words "Peace [is impossible]" (*śāntiḥ*), superimposing upon it another meaning consisting of an impossible connection between things, through the shadow of the *nidarśanā* ornament, which conceives of a relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison: "How can there be peace—that is, happiness—for that slayer of the serpent-enemy, the venomous snake?"

Wherever a female serpent—whose latent enmity is firmly bound, whose tips of fangs are exceedingly sharp, and who is terrifying as she vomits poison—remains awake and vigilant for the sake of biting, there happiness is impossible; the sense is that because of her lack of happiness, happiness is likewise impossible for you. //1//

He indicates what is about to happen with the words "O, Kings!"—O kings, you feudal lords who have accepted the status of servants for the purpose of serving at the feet of the Great King whose edicts rest upon the ends of all the quarters; by the command of the elders, who are advanced in years and have witnessed the conduct of both the higher and the lower, proceed to your duties which you know how to perform. And let the Brahmins recite so as to make the hearing of the Veda auspicious.

The word "āśīrvādamantrān" (benedictory mantras) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Accompanied by various collections of words—meaning various specific languages such as Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and so forth—the wondrous and marvelous singing, instrumental music, dancing, and other such performances are for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgalebhyo maṅgalārtham*); the dative case is used here in the sense of purpose. Let these be performed; let them be undertaken. Then, the arrival (*praveśa*) of the bridegroom's party (*janyānām*), meaning the people related to the groom—"those who are the groom’s dear friends are called *janya*s"—according to Amarasimha—hurries, that is, generates haste for the procession (*yātrāyāḥ*), the act of going from the groom’s house to the bride’s house. //2//

They do not arrive nor do they assemble; he by whom the special adornment has been taken—that is to say, he who is properly decorated. The retinue (*anuyātrika*), the attendants of Mālatī, should be awaited—that is, they should be protected; the meaning is that they should be summoned quickly. Alternatively, the *anuyātrika* refers to the circle of friends who follow the bridegroom. He by whom the special adornment—such as ornaments, garments, and so forth—has been taken: such a person should be awaited and honored with rising to meet him and other marks of respect.

Kapālakuṇḍalā: "Let it be," and so forth. The meaning is that Mālatī cannot now be abducted by him. I shall become intent—that is, one of even firmer resolve—regarding the injury to Mādhava, which consists of the abduction of Mālatī, arising from the confusion of the thronging crowd. Thus she exits. This concludes the *śuddhaviṣkambha*. [Enter] Kalahaṃsa.

"I have been commanded by the tutelary deity of the city, who is with Makaranda in the inner sanctum: 'Find out whether or not Mālatī has set out in this direction. Therefore, I shall now gladden him—[the sense being] by the pleasant report that Mālatī has indeed set out in this direction."

By this statement, the *abhūtāharaṇa* (the introduction of what was not previously present), which is a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the *garbhasandhi* (the development of the plot), is indicated; for it suggests that Mādhava and Makaranda had already entered and remained hidden in the inner sanctum of the city goddess’s temple for the purpose of their feigned marriage. As it is said: "The *abhūtāharaṇa* is that speech which relies upon a deception. This very [statement] also serves as the introductory scene (*praveśaka*) for the two of them. Mādhava: "By means of Mālatī..."

"The continuous succession of the exhaustion of passion, the persistence of the agony of love—surely today this will reach its conclusion by determining one of two alternatives through the attainment of Mālatī. This is called the *mārga* (path), a limb of the *garbha-saṃdhi* (the juncture of development), because it consists in the proclamation of the true state of affairs (*tattvārthakīrtana*). As it is said: "The path is the proclamation of the true state of affairs."

In response to the inquiry, "How is one of the two alternatives to be determined here? he says: "By the success or failure of the means employed by the Illustrious Lady. [He explains: Let the policy of the Illustrious Kāmandakī—by way of the artifice of a feigned marriage—accomplish a good result, namely, the taking of Mālatī’s hand in marriage. If that occurs, the end of Madayantikā’s distress will come about through the very attainment of that goal. Or else, due to the deficiency of my own fortune, let it turn out otherwise; let it become the opposite.

Nevertheless, since the means already employed have failed and there is no other means, once it is certain that she cannot be obtained, my ruin is inevitable; thus, due to the absence of any other recourse, my suffering from love will surely come to an end—this is the meaning. In response to the question as to what kind of suffering from love this is, he says: "of that which has been spreading and increasing ever since the moment of first beholding Mālatī."

Likewise, it should be understood that [the hero] has been brought to the highest, unsurpassed limit of excellence by the gestures of that deer-eyed woman which indicate affection, such as her intentional glances and so forth. This is the third stage of the action, known as "hope for attainment" (*prāptyāśā*). As it is said: "Hope for attainment is the possibility of attainment through the consideration of means and obstacles. (3)

Makaranda: She will be reversed; she will become the opposite. Kalahamsa: My lord, congratulations! Mālatī has indeed set out in this direction. Mādhava: Is that so? [Is it really true? This is a question from one who cannot believe that she has truly set out in this direction. Makaranda: Disbelieving, lacking trust. "Of us" [refers to our situation].

The deep sound produced by thousands of drums for the sake of auspiciousness—which imitates the rumbling of that mass of clouds scattered and torn asunder by the powerful wind of the Maruts—suddenly deprives us of our capacity to hear any sound other than itself. The meaning is: "Having come near me, he says... (4).

Kalahaṃsa: My Lord, look! The construction of the sentence is as follows: "First, these multitudes of auspicious white parasols are seen. Of what kind? [They are like] a lake in the courtyard of the sky—that is, the expanse of the heavens—made wavy by a row of banners (*kadalikāvalī*) moving upward with overflowing force due to the breeze from the chowries, which are beautiful with the grace of royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*) as if they had flown up; and in that [lake], there is a mass of dense, upright white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).

"Carrying confusion, yet possessing [grace]"—here, the upward-facing nature of the courtyard of the sky is intended to suggest its depth; for it is only in a deep lake that the stalks of white lotuses stand erect, not elsewhere. "With grace":

by those who created a clamor through the singing of auspicious songs such as the *Gaurī-kalyāṇa*, which was sweet and faltering due to the contact (*vyatikara*) between the syllables of the song and the expansive fullness of their cheeks filled with gracefully chewed betel.

The female elephants—whose celestial dwellings in the sky were overspread and filled with clusters of courtesans who imitated fragments of great Indra’s rainbows with the rows of rays from various jeweled ornaments—are seen, making a jingling *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound with their tinkling golden bells. (Makaranda: "Swinging... [and so forth].

Such are the canopies formed by the spreading, multi-colored lights of jewels directed upward and extending toward the quarters. Of what nature are they? They are mingled with the shadows of the wings—the "chadas"—of blue jays (*cāṣas*) and sparrows (*kuliṅgas*) that are prone to opening and fluttering about in the wind; these shadows are blended and intermingled, swirling and diffusing. Furthermore, at their edges, they are interspersed with the clusters of iridescent eye-spots (*mecaka-cayas*) from the plumage of many swaying, trembling peacocks.

They appear as if completely surrounded on all sides by the surrounding regions; likewise, they appear as if possessing clearly manifested rainbows; and likewise, they appear as if covered and overspread by a carpeting or spreading of Chinese silks (aṃśuka) painted with pictures—thus the abundance of jewel ornaments is indicated. Therefore, the sense is that the sovereignty of the minister Bhūrivasu possesses a splendor exceeding even that of Indra. //5//

Kalahamsa: How is it that such a multitude of chamberlains, carrying canes in their hands, have arrived in such haste? They form a circle, and by means of cane-staffs variegated with intervals of bright gold, silver, and white metal—all bent and lowered—they have demarcated a boundary on the ground, declaring that the line thus drawn must not be transgressed. Forming a circle created by that boundary, those people stand apart, remaining at a distance.

And she was like the night, bearing in her hand the female elephant (*kareṇu*)—that is, the night likened to the female elephant through an *upamita-samāsa* (appositional compound), where the simile is explicitly expressed. Her face was reddened by a profusion of vermilion as if by the glow of twilight; and upon its appearance, she wore as an ornament a "bearer" (*dhāriṇī*) of a "star-garland" (*nakṣatramālā*)—meaning a specific kind of necklace as well as the row of stars beginning with Aśvinī—which was swaying and shining in a sweet and captivating manner. The simile is thus to be understood through this appositional compound.

Adorning herself right here, her beautiful, pale, and emaciated body—visible to all the people whose faces were blossoming with curiosity—revealed the agony of the god of love; thus, by the force of these two adjectives, Mālatī, bearing the grace of the first digit of the new moon, moved a short distance away from the circle of her attendants and proceeded to another place.

How could one woman bear the delusion of another? Thus, because such a thing is impossible, Mālatī—pale and emaciated from the contemplation of separation, yet the object of the gaze of all the world who look up with curiosity—is like the crescent moon at the beginning of the night: she is adorned by a row of stars reddened by the glow of twilight; she is pale and thin due to her natural state and her youth; and she graces the scene like an elephant adorned with a trunk decorated by a necklace of pearls reddened by vermilion. This is how she appears.

Because there is a superimposition of a different object through the relationship of an image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), this is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), supported by a simile conveyed by the words "elephant" (*kareṇu*) and "moon" (*rajanīśa*), which are embellished by the pun (*śleṣa*) expressed by the words "face" (*mukha*) and "garland of stars" (*nakṣatramālā*). [Commentary on Makaranda’s verse: "This one"—this refers to the heroine, the most excellent of beautiful women (*varārohottamā*). She is one whose ornaments and decorations are, on the contrary, adorned by her very limbs, which—though naturally possessed of loveliness—are now pale and emaciated due to the power of separation. There is no excellence whatsoever in her [external] ornaments; rather, it is her limbs that constitute the true adornment.

However, the meaning is that their very presence upon her body is seen to produce an extraordinary beauty. Being such as she is, she merely carries outwardly—due to the insistence of her elders—the marriage festival’s splendor, which is appropriate and made lovely by being endowed with auspicious ornaments; yet, she manifests through the very paleness and emaciation of her limbs that mental anguish, the pain of love, which is now exceedingly increasing and accumulating moment by moment.

The meaning is that it reveals an internal, unconditioned, and unbearable transformation caused by the pangs of love. How so? It is like a young creeper that withers from within due to defects such as insects, even while bearing blossoms on the outside; this constitutes the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). Furthermore, this heroine (*nāyikā*) is of the *dhīrā* (self-controlled/resolute) type. //6//

"Niṣāditā" means seated. Regarding the phrase "then she enters": since this has already been indicated by the preceding sentence through the continuation of the narrative of Mādhava and Makaranda—specifically because Kāmandakī and the others are signaled for entry there, and because they stand in the relationship of attendants (*parijana*) to Kāmandakī as her disciples—some commentator explains that this portion of the text is an *praveśaka* (interlude), according to the definition stated: "An *praveśaka* is to be known as one where there is a connection with the narrative of attendants. That [commentator] must be addressed [as follows].

How can an *praveśaka*—which indicates solely through pure representation (*abhinaya*) and suggests a matter to be conveyed by a single character—be inserted in the midst of an act (*aṅka*) whose form consists of direct representation (*pratyakṣābhinaya*)? Or how can it be that imagining the principal hero—who is in fact a disciple—to be a character of the *praveśaka* or a mere attendant results in a lapse of propriety? Furthermore, have you not seen the verse following your own statement: "Having made a break in the act, [one may represent] what was done in a month or even accumulated over a year"?
