Then the maiden Buddharakṣitā, awakening Madayantika who was bewildered as to what should be done due to the modesty natural to young women, raised her face and, urging her to loosen her bashfulness, sets forth the reasons why this very moment is the time to choose Makaranda: "The beloved," she says. "He whom you previously chose with a thousand desires—this very beloved, that person who is the object of unsurpassed love—is present here. And this is the minister’s house, where the guards are asleep and unheeding."

Therefore, there is not even the slightest suspicion that anyone might see us here; it is thick darkness. By this, even the fear of the city guards is dispelled. Thus, out of gratitude, perform the auspicious ceremony of Makaranda’s marriage. Immediately thereafter, let us go in such a way that our jeweled anklets are raised high [above the ground]. Come! Let us go quickly and unobserved by anyone to where Mālatī and Mādhava are, raising [the feet] so high that the sound of the anklets cannot be heard by others. Do not be bashful—this is the meaning. //3//

Madayantikā: Friend Buddharakṣitā, where indeed must we go now? Buddharakṣitā: To the very place where Mālatī has gone. Madayantikā: Has Mālatī committed a rash act? A "rash act" (sāhasa) means the offering of herself by her own hand. Buddharakṣitā: Indeed so; the meaning is that she has certainly committed a rash act. Furthermore, you say, "Who am I to him? and so forth—you should do what is appropriate to what you have said.

Madayantikā sheds tears of her own accord, as if the formal bestowal of herself were being performed by her elders. Buddharakṣitā, perceiving her self-surrender through the very shedding of tears of joy, says: "O noble one, my dear friend has indeed given herself away"—the implication being that she has done so preceded by tears of joy. Makaranda: "Today!"—today, through the attainment of my beloved, strength has been restored such that supreme victory has truly been achieved.

What else remains to be comforted beyond this? The meaning is: nothing at all. Thus, today is the festival and auspicious day for my youth, which has now become fruitful through the very attainment of my beloved. For by the God of Love (Makaradhvaja), with his face brightened by favor, having fulfilled what Mādhava desired, he has also fulfilled my own desire, thereby performing the duty of a kinsman and establishing me in a position worthy of the bond of kinship. //4//

Let us proceed and go out through the side door at the end of the wing; for at midnight, when there is no movement on the royal road, its beauty is conducive to our departure. Regarding "of the palaces": having entered the pathways of the balconies and the lattice windows on the upper stories of the mansions, one has attained delight. In the reading "returned by wandering," it means that after wandering upon the palace roofs through the window-paths, one has returned again.

Therefore, the breeze—infused with the lingering impressions produced by the scent of fermented liquor, fragrant with garlands, and repeatedly permeated by the wafting aroma of camphor—reveals the presence of young women, which is desired by youths; thus, through the drinking of wine, the wearing of garlands, and so forth, the enjoyment of sexual union and other pleasures is suggested. //5//
May the wise savor for a long time this nectar of aesthetic flavor manifested from the ocean of Bhavabhūti’s words, churned by the churning-stick of my commentary.

Thus ends the commentary on the seventh act in the *Bhāvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Mālatīmādhava* composed by the venerable Tripurāri Sūri, the son of Parvatanātha Yāyajūka, the ornament of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage.
The Eighth Act:
*Vibudharatnāvalī*.

Now follows the entrance of Avalokitā for the purpose of performing actions conducive to accomplishing the tasks of Mālatī and Mādhava, who are staying at Kāmandakī’s residence. Avalokitā: I have paid my respects to the Venerable Lady, who has just returned from the residence of Nandana. Therefore, I shall now go to Mālatī and Mādhava. (Walking about; the word "looks" is to be supplied. Here they are, adorning the stone slab on the bank of the pond, having just finished their bath at the end of the summer day. So, I will approach them. Mādhava: [He speaks.]

The night is the powerful friend of the God of Love (*manmatha*), as will be described through the rising of the moon; its status as a friend to the God of Love arises from its acting in accordance with what is to be accomplished by him. At that time, Vātsyāyana states: "Women become possessed of both joy and trepidation when intent upon sexual union. Thinking "it is indeed so," he reveals the cause for the excellence of that very youthfulness of the night—namely, that it "shatters" [the darkness].

The rising lunar light, pale like the color of a drying palm leaf, pierces the mass of darkness; it is like the pollen of a *ketakī* flower scattered by the force of the wind, appearing vast and expansive as if it were moving upward with its face turned toward the sky—such is the metaphor for the light. //1//

"Since she is a maiden of noble family and her conduct has been so strictly observed, she will approach me in a manner consistent with my intentions; thus, by acting as if she were perverse (vāmaśīlā), I shall win over this girl who is like one perverse, making her mind inclined toward the accomplishment of my desired end. The word "let it be" (*bhavatu*) is used here to recall the strategic means. Having thus resolved his mind with the intention, "I shall strive to win her over by employing the methods for winning the confidence of a maiden as taught in the *Kāmasūtra*," he speaks aloud: "My dear one" (*priya*).

By stating here, "for the sake of quelling the heat of summer," he demonstrates a modesty imbued with love, implying: "I petition you for the sake of seeking union with your limbs not out of mere passion, but with the intent of counteracting my distress. Regarding the word "niścyotante" (flowing forth): by addressing her as "O fair-limbed one" (*sutanu*), he displays the extreme loveliness of the heroine’s body, which is so perfectly suited for an embrace, [asking]: "Why do you not honor me, who am worthy of being seen in such a state?"

The intention is this: "This very moment is exactly like that occasion when you were united with me in the cremation ground. One should consider the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) form *niścyotante* as requiring reflection [in this context]. Give me an embrace while these drops of water clinging to your braided hair, loosened by bathing, are still falling; while the space between your two breasts remains moist from the bath-water; and while your skin has reached a state of dense horripilation due to the coolness of the bath—be gracious!

By this, Mādhava’s intention is as follows: "Let Mālatī know that what is truly desired by him for the sake of allaying the fever of his touch is only the coolness produced by immersion in my limbs; he does not wish to do anything else while disregarding the marriage arrangement and ignoring the intentions of Kāmandakī, Lavaṅgikā, and others. Having reflected thus, let Mālatī bestow herself upon me with the thought of it being a service rendered by the killing of the Kāpālika.

In reality, however, having observed that momentary luster or beauty produced by immersion in water—which Bharata Muni recognizes as an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) pertaining to *kānti* (loveliness)—he proceeded to request an embrace out of intense passion. "The beauty of the limbs, augmented by the enjoyment of form, youth, and charm, is proclaimed as *śobhā* (splendor). That same splendor, when love is not yet fully realized, is called *kānti*. Likewise:

"May the body of Lakṣmī purify you—her body which, as she rose at the end of lovemaking, rested one hand upon the lord of serpents for support while holding her garment with the other, and bore upon her shoulder the weight of her disheveled tresses; a body embraced by Śauri on their bed, his arms trembling with passion, as he felt his love for the amorous dalliance redoubled by her beauty at that very moment. (2)

Then Mādhava, an expert in the *Kāmasūtra*, even regarding those words [of Mālatī], placing her upon the second stage—beginning with the verse from the *Ṛgveda*, "And having perceived the unsurpassed..."—said, "O friend! By the expression "cruel one," he displayed a threat to Mālatī through the manifestation of anger. As Vātsyāyana said: "In this way, following the girl's mind, one should appease her by means of skillful methods; for thus she becomes both full of affection and confident. One achieves success with maidens neither by excessive compliance nor by excessive opposition; therefore, one should succeed through the middle path."

"He who knows how to produce joy in himself, increase the pride of women, and inspire confidence in maidens shall become beloved by them. But he who neglects a maiden thinking only that she is possessed of excessive modesty is a man ignorant of her intentions, and is thus treated with contempt like a beast. And so forth. "Reviving me": as if reviving me, who am nearly dead, let this arm—manifesting the involuntary emotion (*sāttvikabhāva*) of perspiration born of agitation—be placed of its own accord around my neck, upon my throat.

The intention is this: "Just as I have acquired this forearm upon you for the purpose of removing the Kāpālika, so it shall be. It is like the play of a necklace of moonstones, which has the quality of trickling when kissed by the rays of the moon; that too is offered around the neck for the sake of quelling the fever. Here, by means of two requests—"give me an embrace" and "let the arm be placed around the neck"—he recalls the method taught in the *Kāmasūtra* for approaching a maiden without causing her agitation:
"And the approach should be made with the upper body because it is more tolerable. //3//

Or rather, let alone the offering of one's neck or arms, which is extremely difficult to obtain; for what reason is a person of little merit an unfit vessel for even a share of conversation—the nectar of words that reveals affection? As for the word "burned": my body has long been as if burned by the breezes from Mount Malaya and other such excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of love, even as I strove solely for the sake of attaining you. That which is burned, if it were embraced, would not be extinguished; it would certainly not be brought to relief.

That itself was a great impropriety; that impropriety was not accepted by me. Then my hearing, pained and rendered sorrowful by the *kuhū* cooing of the cuckoo blinded by passion—which intensely kindles desire—[says]: "O you with the throat of a *kiṃnara*, drink [the nectar of] your speech, which is heart-pleasing and captivating to the heart. Here, the two *tu* particles signify sequence and "again" respectively; the word *nāma* has the sense of "as it were. Because your voice possesses the sweetness of a *kiṃnara*'s throat, the sound of the cuckoo is not as pleasing as your words—this is a form of flattery. (4)

Avalokitā: O you who are habitually unable to bring matters to a conclusion! You speak before me with a heavy heart, saying, "Mādhava has been separated from me for only a moment," and "That Mādhava has been separated from me for only a moment"—the analysis of the compound being thus. "The noble son is delaying; perhaps I shall see him after some time. How long, indeed, will it be?

Furthermore, since she has increased all her trepidation, I shall speak in such a way that she perceives even the closing of her eyes—which would otherwise be hindered by the obstacle of blinking—as itself an obstacle; thus, with a double-fold embrace, I shall honor her. The intention is that this is now the fulfillment of that very opportunity for an embrace which was already consented to before me, and that even though we have conversed, there is still wit [in this]. The intention is that Mālatī looks as if with indignation, but not indeed with actual indignation.

Envy (*asūyā*) and anger (*kopa*) are to be understood [here]; for the reason that she has revealed such a secret of his through her display of anger. In reality, however, the intention is that he looks upon her with joy, thinking: "The desire shown previously out of affection has been made manifest by her on this occasion. — Mādhava.

By the expression "to the first female disciple," the intention is this: has Kāmandakī properly instructed her even in such a role as that of a female messenger (*dūtī*), since she acted to disclose the secret at this juncture in accordance with what I require? "Inexhaustible" means undiminishable; "jewels" refers to her utterances, which are beautiful due to their ever-new flashes of inspiration. Their "circulation" (*saṃcāra*) consists of placing them elsewhere—even beyond their primary application—in a manner conducive to the task at hand. "Refinement" (*saṃskaraṇa*) means bringing about a state of non-vulgarity. "Publicly" (*prakāśam*); the word "asks" (*pṛcchati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The intention behind the question—"Does Avalokitā speak only what is true, or does she speak having fabricated something?"—is as follows: if, when questioned, she does not provide an answer, then her consent will be inferred from that very intention; whereas if she does provide an answer, one will gain the benefit of hearing her words. Thus, according to Vātsyāyana’s teaching on the employment of conversation, the purpose of the question is included within the art of initiating discourse. Therefore he says: "And having placed a favorable female friend, who is trusted by both parties, in between, one should initiate the conversation."

She should laugh with her face turned downward at him; and she should insult and dispute with him who speaks excessively. She should say, even if it was not said, "This was spoken by her for the sake of jest. There, having set him aside, she should remain silent with the meaning of the sentence incomplete for the sake of a reply. But when pressed, she should speak words with indistinct syllables and unfinished meaning, saying, "I do not speak thus."

"And she should look at the hero with smiles and side-long glances," and so forth; here, "incomplete sentence-meaning" (*asaṃpūrṇavākyārtha*) refers to that whose meaning is not yet concluded. Mālatī shakes her head in opposition to establish that she did not speak in this manner. Vātsyāyana states: "When being pressed for an answer, however, she gives a reply by shaking her head. Mādhava:

By saying, "You are bound by oath upon the lives of Lavaṅgikā and Avalokitā," the intention is that Lavaṅgikā and Avalokitā are ever intent on her welfare and their words are not to be transgressed. Mālatī, by saying, "I know nothing at all," displays a semblance of modesty—much like actual modesty—in order to establish her status as a young maiden; for natural modesty would be impossible through the performance of such a rash act while disregarding one's elders. Mādhava: The beauty of speech lies in its charm when its meaning remains unsaid.

"Having observed"—the word "says" is to be understood as the ellipsis. By this, it is understood that the meaning [of her speech] was not fully concluded. This recalls what Vātsyāyana stated: "And being thus pressed by him, she might utter words of unfinished meaning, saying, 'I do not speak thus. Then it is understood that Mālatī, resting her cheek upon one hand, sheds tears. Therefore, Mādhava asks Avalokitā for the cause of the shedding of tears: "Avalokitā, why is this shedding of tears so inappropriate? The implication is: "You are the one who knows her secret."

"By tears? [She asks: "Why is the face of this fawn-eyed one, which is naturally free from impurity, being washed? Immediately—meaning, at the very moment after our speech—on which cheek the moon shines with its rays reflected, due both to its natural purity and its being cleansed by the water of tears? Desiring to drink the nectar from this lake of her face's nectar, he is like a lotus stalk whose fibers are scattered; thus, it is fitting that the washing of one cheek occurs through the application of tears to that single cheek. //5//

Avalokitā: Friend, why do you weep now with such a gushing flood of tears? Mālatī: Friend, for how much longer must I endure the pain of Lavaṅgikā’s absence? Even news of her is difficult to obtain. (The word "thus she weeps" is to be supplied. Avalokitā: It is precisely because of your words that she remembers Lavaṅgikā and is distressed by the lack of news concerning her. Mādhava: "Api nāma" expresses a hope or possibility.

Regarding the role of the messenger with respect to Madayantika: since the ultimate fruit has already been obtained through that very [first success], the repeated use of the word "fruit" (*phala*) is for the purpose of establishing the present fruit. Avalokitā: Noble sir, by you who were commissioned by the Blessed One when she first reported the recovery from fainting of Makaranda—who was adorned with the claws of a tiger—you have graciously bestowed both life and heart upon Mālatī. Now, some acquisition of Madayantika will further increase this joy.

"What reward will he have now? Mādhava: "I am indeed being asked what ought to be asked. Is it that the deed performed by you is not to be accepted as a worthy object? [This is the implied meaning, because the root *pṛcch* (to ask) takes two objects. Now, since my heart and life were already given away as rewards, nothing remains for me on my chest except this garland of *kesara* flowers. [The implied meaning is: 'Look at my heart; here is the reward.'"

She who was a witness to my passion at the first sight of Mālatī—considering it a favorable omen that had reached its fruition in the sight of my beloved while I remained below her—[is the one addressed]. The two qualifiers "adornments of the forest of Love" and "possessing fortune" refer to that very *kesara* tree. [The phrase] "strung with flowers" means up to that point. She expresses the manifestation of her own intense longing through the verse beginning with "with love" (*premṇā*). Regarding "with love":

The garland of flowers that was brought into her hand by the hand of her dear friend, and which was honored—rendered weighty by being the very means for accomplishing her desired purpose—by being placed upon the lap of that expansive and broad mass of jar-like bud-breasts; here, by the word *kumbha* (jar), the stoutness [of the breasts] is indicated, and by the word *kuḍmala* (bud)—a synonym for a flower-bud—their increasing fullness is suggested.

Then, immediately after the occasion for taking her hand in marriage with Nandana had arrived, out of despair regarding me, she gave me this flower-garland, Lavangikā, as if it were her entire possession; by this she implies: "Previously your passion was such as this, but now the time has passed through the accomplishment of my desired object. //6//

Avalokitā: Friend Mālatī, this Bakula garland is indeed dear to you; now it shall pass into the hand of another who will announce pleasant news on your behalf. Therefore, the intention is that you yourself should be the bearer of pleasant news today. Mālatī: [Listens.]

Having observed that [the garland] has gone from Mālatī’s own beloved’s neck to her own neck, and again from her own neck back to her beloved’s neck, she reflects: "This [garland] is the means for accomplishing our unprecedented love and desired union; thus, by way of it, this [garland] serves as a thread of affection to strengthen the bond between our hearts. Thinking thus, out of intense emotion, she instructs her dear friend regarding her beloved; hence the repetition [of the instruction]. "Avalokitā, you yourself must instruct on both matters," with the underlying intention: "Tell me how it may pass into another's hand—what shall I say?"

Avalokitā: How is it that a sound like footsteps is heard? (This is the ellipsis. Mādhava: Ah! (The word "aye" expresses wonder. Mālatī: By good fortune, you are gladdened by the joy of obtaining Madayantikā. Mādhava: (Embracing her.)

"First, having embraced [Makaranda] out of mere circumstance due to my longing for Madayantika, that which has since become our beloved—like a noose of passion—is the very attainment of Madayantika herself. Having said this, she places a kesara garland, like a noose of the thread of love, around Malati’s neck. Avalokita: The burden of the venerable lady’s expectations has been successfully fulfilled by Buddharakshita; the "burden of expectations" refers to the mission of acting as a messenger between Madayantika and Makaranda. Malati:

We too see our dear friend Lavaṅgikā. "Api" is used here in the sense of possibility; the remainder of the sense is that "this too is possible. All: May the noble one protect us! Indeed, midway along the path, Makaranda was confronted by the city guards. "Abhiyoga" means an attack or obstruction. Thereupon, we were sent after him together with Kalahaṃsaka, who had emerged from the crowd around Makaranda at that moment and joined us to report what had happened. Kalahaṃsaka: [speaks].

Since we have heard the clamor of the battle from this very opening, I infer that another hostile force has also arrived. "Hostile" (*pārakya*) means an enemy army; it is a regional term, as "pāra" is used in common parlance. Mālatī and Avalokitā: A simultaneous mixture of joy and agitation has arisen and come upon us. Mādhava:

By saying, "Our home has been graced by you," the intention is that through the acceptance of Makaranda, our very house has been adorned by you as if he were no different from yourself. Even for a hero who is alone, there may be an attack by many; however, for Makaranda—who has witnessed his own prowess in such encounters with tigers, who is my companion, and whose valor is equal to mine—this [attack] is nothing at all. It should not cause any cause for fear in his mind.

The meaning is: "May they be well. Regarding the word *hareḥ* (of the lion): when a solitary lion must perform a daring feat, his own paw alone becomes his companion. Of what nature is it? It is such that it possesses a longing (*lālasā*), that is, a desire, for the affection (*praṇaya*) found in incomparable (*atula*), extraordinary valor (*vikrama*). Likewise, it is fierce (*pracaṇḍa*) with its claws (*kararuha*), which are resonant (*kvaṇantaḥ*), making a sound as they strike the joints of elephant bones and the like.

Likewise, the frontal globe (*gaṇḍa*) of that lordly elephant (*dvipendra*) was bursting and expanding due to the pressure of his claws; from the hollow at its tip, ichor (*dāna*) flowed forth and drenched his face. He is a singular hero (*ekavīra*)—an excellent hero or a peerless hero—in the crushing of the bone that is firm and solid upon the head of that elephant. By this, it is stated for the purpose of dispelling Madayantika’s fear that Makaranda has no need even for weapons in crushing the enemy army. //7//

Therefore, I too shall become his immediate companion—acting as a second—to fight with them in a manner that is both playful and full of disdain, yet rendered pure by my valor and prowess. (Avalokitā and the others: [The word] "they say" is to be supplied. "Perhaps the two noble ones, Mādhava and Makaranda, will turn back unimpeded. Mālatī: "Friends Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā, go quickly and report this news to the Holy Lady."

"You too, friend Lavaṅgikā, must quickly inform the noble son: 'If we are indeed worthy of your compassion, then proceed with such care that you remain vigilant. Mālatī: Alas! How is this great delay to be accounted for? What means is there by which it may be passed? Very well; I shall remain here, watching the path of return—the way back—of my dear friend Lavaṅgikā.

The intention is that watching the path by which her friend has returned is the only means to pass the time. My left [eye] throbbed; that is, my right eye (the "non-left" eye) throbbed in an unfavorable manner, for among women, the throbbing of the right eye is considered a bad omen. The intention is that this ill omen indicates the imminent calamity of Mālatī. Now follows the entrance of Kapālakuṇḍalā, who harbors enmity toward Mālatī for the purpose of abducting her while she is alone and devoid of all attendants.

"O you sinner! Hearing these words of Kapālakuṇḍalā, Mālatī weeps in terror. "O noble son! she cries. This is the paralysis of speech known as *gadgada*, which is a form of the *sāttvika* emotion (*bhāva*). It is caused by sudden and great fear. Its definition is: "The paralysis of speech arising from intoxication, negligence, shame, and so forth, is known as *gadgada*. By the word "and so forth," fear and other such causes are also understood to be triggers for *gadgada*. Kapālakuṇḍalā says: "He is your beloved. He is called a *pati* because he protects (*pāti*).

A seducer of virgins, a defiler of maidens, and a destroyer specifically of ascetics, not of heroes—like a young quail whose face is startled and distracted by the swoop of a hawk, a specific kind of meat-eating bird, you do not even perceive that you have been swallowed by me; if you have the power, then protect yourself! //8//

The word *yāvat* is used here as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇe*). "Having led her to Śrīparvata" means exactly that. "At every joint" (*pratiparvam*) means at every articulation; it signifies "at each connection. "Piece by piece" (*tilaśaḥ*) means having cut the flesh into pieces the size of sesame seeds, I shall cause her a painful death by a cruel execution (*citravadhena*). Thus, taking Mālatī without her circle of kinsmen knowing, Kapālakuṇḍalā exits. Madayantikā: I too shall follow Mālatī alone. Now, mistaking Madayantikā for Mālatī, [she] calls for Lavaṅgikā.

"Friend, Mālatī! [Entering] Lavaṅgikā [speaks—this is the ellipsis]. "Friend Madayantikā, I am indeed Lavaṅgikā; the implication is that I am not Mālatī. Madayantikā: "O dear one"—used here as a gentle address—"have you seen that noble-souled one? [The meaning is: Mādhava. Lavaṅgikā: "No, no!"

Indeed, upon merely exiting the garden enclosure, he heard the tumultuous clamor; with a harshness born of his own formidable thigh-staff being cast out impetuously, he rushed forward and entered the enemy host. "Impetuously" means with angry words. "Cast out" (*apaviddha*) means struck; one by whom his own formidable thigh-staff (*nijorudaṇḍa*) was so cast is described as such. *Vāṭa* refers to a fence or enclosure—meaning a rampart—or a path. From there, I, unfortunate as I am, have returned.

And I hear in every house the lamentations of the citizens, who are overflowing with affection for his virtues: "Alas, Mādhava, O noble one! Alas, Makaranda, you reckless one! It is said that the Great King, having heard the account of the deception regarding the two ministers' daughters, was seized by a surge of indignation; at that very moment, he dispatched a multitude of many seasoned foot-soldiers and, standing upon the roof-peak of the palace which was radiant with moonlight, he is said to be watching. Madayantika: Alas, I am destroyed, I of meager fortune! Lavaṅgikā: [She faints.]

Friend, where is Mālatī now? Madayantikā: Friend, she indeed set out first to look for your path; afterwards, I lost sight of her. She must have entered the thicket of the garden—*nāma* is used here to express a supposition. Lavaṅgikā: Friend, let us go quickly! My dear friend is extremely distressed while staying in the grove; at this moment, she cannot sustain herself. (Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā.)

"Friend Mālatī! Indeed, I say, 'Friend Mālatī'! Kalahamsa: By good fortune, I have emerged safely from the path of collision. (With joy) How wonderful! "Himāṇahe" [expresses] fear and joy; such is the local dialect (*deśī*).

I seem to behold a sight both terrifying and golden-hued, blazing with the rays of the moon reflected in the streams of pure, continuous, and surging water; resembling the waters of the Yamunā tossed upward and agitated by the effortless tossing of the plow from the massive arms of Kāmapāla as he sported in his intoxication; and filled with a swelling clamor that pervades the entire expanse of the courtyard of the sky, as it rises up unrestrained, agitated by the merciless joy of Makaranda, and turns back in its attempt to check its own momentum.

Even now, I seem to see that multitude of enemies. Retreat means flight; and I remember the various weapons snatched away and wrested from the hands of those great warriors who, having turned their backs on battle, were cast down and scattered because they were confined within a cage formed by his terrifying arms like thunderbolts. By the wide-open path left vacant by the complete rout and flight of the enemy host thus obstructed and struck down, he moved along.

"I remember Mādhava as one who has turned back from reckless violence"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. Oh, how great is the King's affection for virtue! For now, having descended from the palace roof, having pacified their conflict through the humble entreaties of the doorkeeper, and having repeatedly extended his affectionate eyes upon beholding the moon-like faces of Mādhava and Makaranda—who have been brought before him with a singular gentleness and have emerged from their peril—he has heard of their noble lineage from Kalahaṃsaka and has bestowed upon them a most precious and profound honor.

Having consoled Bhūrivasu and Nandana—whose faces were stained by the soot of throbbing envy, resentment, and embarrassment—with sweet words, saying, "What satisfaction could there be now for you two, who are ornaments to the expanse of the world, for these two noble sons-in-law who are delightful with the virtues of fresh youth," the King then retired into his inner apartments. Here, *matsara* is anger (*krodha*), and agitation is envy (*īrṣyā*); these two stand in the place of soot, by which Nandana’s face was stained.

The discernment is this: the embarrassment of Bhūrivasu is like ink. "These two, Mādhava and Makaranda, are also arriving; therefore, I too shall report this news to the Blessed Lady. Mādhava: [Regarding] my dear friend Makaranda—his natural, unfeigned, and intense (ūrjita) splendor is powerful. Regarding the phrase "by the crushing of his arms": for thus, first of all, as this dear friend was subduing the heroes...

In response to the question "How did they tear them apart?", [the answer is: "By means of that very crushing and pulverizing with his two arms, so that their skeletons might shatter and break asunder"—this is an adverbial modifier of the action. Furthermore, he snatched away their other weapons there and then, as they were displaying their prowess, performing feats of valor.

For such a beloved one, the path—the front line—of that ocean of battle, which was like a sea of countless hosts, became vast and formidable in the front due to the ranks of foot soldiers who stood motionless and paralyzed on both flanks (the *pārṣṇis*). It was further characterized by being strewn with heaps of mangled and severed limbs that were tossing and dangling upward; this describes the "ocean of number" as being covered and filled with them. //9//

Friend, alas! This worldly business of war is a place of lingering resentment and a cause for remorse. Consider this: those great warriors who, at midnight during the enjoyment of moonlight, drank wine that remained from their beloveds' drinking, which was thus mingled with the rays of the moon and beautiful with fragments of lunar radiance—now, with their very bodies whose bones are shattered by your activities, they describe transmigrating men as being essence-less, trivial, fragile, and incomplete. 10.

Right here before Mālatī, Kalahaṃsaka is describing in detail our activities for the sake of Madayantikā; we are experiencing these events as they unfold unexpectedly. (Looking ahead) How is it that these regions appear empty, as if deserted by Mālatī? (The ellipsis implies: "They are seen thus. Makaranda: I suspect that, due to the agitation and distress caused by the perilous conflict between us, Mālatī and the others have been wandering here and there in their anxiety, and are now diverting themselves right here in this deep spot of the garden. Mādhava: He tells it so.

Friend Makaranda, while you are recounting the story of our equally perilous encounter, Mālatī’s friend Madayantikā—seeing that these two preeminent men have come to such physical danger on my account—will, out of extreme exhaustion, lower her own face with eyes fixed and motionless, her modesty manifest through bashfulness, as she has no further duty to perform. Furthermore, how will she do so?

"Smiling Mālatī"—by those moving side-long glances (*kaṭākṣa*) of hers, [he was] as if struck; "struck" (*parāhata*) means that he was looked upon with such side-glances that it was like an act of loathing (*jugupsā*). Such a cause is an extremely grave cause; this is the reason for Mālatī’s smiling and for her striking him with her side-glances. (11)

Then, having heard the sound of footsteps and knowing that Mālatī has arrived, Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā—distraught by their separation from her—[speak]. (The word "speak" is to be supplied. "Friend Mālatī! [They say this] upon seeing that Mādhava and Makaranda have arrived immediately thereafter, and they speak with joy: "By good fortune, those two noble ones are seen once again!"

Then, having heard the words "Friend Mālatī" from Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā, Mādhava and Makaranda—suspicious because of an ill omen that had just occurred—asked, "Where is that Mālatī? Both [replied]: "From where? Where is she, Mālatī? The suffix *-tas* in *kutaḥ* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī-arthe*). By this, the meaning is that Mālatī is not there at all. By the word "here" (*pada*), they mean: "We two, unfortunate as we are, have been deceived by you both."

Having perceived the word "your ladyship" (bhavat-pada) as the word "Mālatī" (mālatī-pada)—the meaning being that it is joined with "Mālatī"—Mādhava says: "O ladies" (*bhavatyau*) is the vocative. "By some means or other" (*kathaṃ katham api*) means by whatever manner possible; [this state] which is impossible even to speak of, my heart is shattered in a thousand ways. Therefore, let this be said: "For mine... (*mama hi*...).

"But as for me, this inner self of mine—my mind, clearly directed toward the lotus-eyed Mālatī—is habituated to contemplating only undesirable things, thinking, 'Love perceives dangers even where there is no cause. Therefore, my heart is seized by trembling because of the memory of their words: 'In this matter, you yourself shall surely experience the manifestation of Kapālakuṇḍalā’s wrath. Furthermore, the throbbing of my left eye is a source of distress; likewise, such speech from my two friends is distressing. Thus, I am destroyed by that wretched, cursed fate. (12)

Madayantikā: Indeed, since you of great power have departed from here, Lavaṅgikā was sent with the message: "Having dismissed Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā to the presence of the noble lady, inform the noble son [Mādhava] that he must remain vigilant. Then Mālatī, becoming anxious, went forward to look for her path; the meaning is that I followed behind her. After that, I did not see her; therefore, we searched here until the two of you were seen. Mādhava:

"Something or other": O fierce one, O excessively wrathful one, let this jest—which consists of concealing one's true nature—cease; abandon your joking. Therefore, I suspect that in you there is something, something indeed, which cannot even be spoken of, and which is inauspicious and other than auspicious things; for this reason, I am eager to behold you.

Or, if you wish to discern whether I am full of passion or devoid of passion by means of my outward form, then I have already been discerned by you through such acts as the sale of human flesh. Therefore, O beloved, grant me a word; for my heart is agitated and distressed, finding no rest within itself, and you remain thus merciless. (13)

Makaranda: Without knowing—that is, without ascertaining—his intention is that it refers to his misfortune. Mādhava: First of all, another person who is indifferent does not know; do you also not know her to be Mālatī? He reminds [her] of Mālatī’s resolution to abandon her own body during the occasion of the secret marriage, and what was done by her, distressed and trembling with affection for me upon my arrival. Both: This too is possible; she may have gone to perform service at the feet of the Holy Lady (the Goddess). Mādhava:

"Let it be so named. The word "nāma" (named) is used here in the sense of possibility or assumption. Makaranda: "She has gone. Because she was the object of Mādhava’s love for all of us, and because she was the object of our boundless affection due to her own exceptional qualities, Mālatī was like a friend; thus, she has gone. I am apprehensive as to whether she will return again to that venerable lady’s residence alive—truly maintaining her life—even though there was the agitation caused by the encounter with the city magistrate’s men and the siege of the inner apartments.

Aghoraghaṇṭa, Vyāghrapāda, Rājaviruddha, and Virūpākṣa—these are the tokens [of her fate] that cast doubt upon Mālatī’s life. Now, having ascertained Mālatī’s calamity through this, he establishes the instability of worldly pleasure with the second half of the verse, beginning with "prāyeṇa" (generally). The happiness of union with kinsmen and others is as flickering as a flash of lightning; this is the sense. That happiness of which the association with kinsmen and so forth is the primary instance is of such a nature.

Nevertheless, keeping in mind that the remedy for Mālatī’s calamity and the removal of Mādhava’s suffering would have as their sole cause the flash—the manifestation or a specific activity—of Saudāminī, who was indicated in the *mukha-sandhi* of the first act, the author of this play has inserted the word "Saudāminī" in the verse at the end of the act to signal her entrance in the subsequent act. //14//

Out of devotion to Śabarasvāmin, the learned author has fashioned this Mandara mountain of commentary for the extraction of the essence from Bhavabhūti’s *Prakaraṇaratnākara*; no other could have done so.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*, in the *Bibudharatnāvalī* composed by the venerable Nānyadeva.

Act Nine. At Śrīparvata, Saudāminī, having snatched Mālatī away from Kapālakuṇḍalā and placed her in a secure location, fears for Mālatī’s life. Anticipating that Mādhava—who suspects Mālatī’s death—will surely perish, she takes the Bakulāvalī garland from Mālatī’s neck and flies up swiftly so that Mādhava may believe she is alive and will return. This marks the beginning of the ninth act. Then, Saudāminī reflects to herself on what she must do: "Here I am."

"I am that very Saudāminī and no other, who was favored by the venerable Kāmandakī through her instruction in the practice of yoga and brought to this state. Therefore, since Mālatī and Mādhava—whom Kāmandakī must protect even at the cost of her own life—must have their calamities averted, I must perform this remedy even at the sacrifice of my own life; such is the intent of the words 'I am here. Having come from the venerable Śrīparvata, I have arrived at Padmāvatī."

In that city of Padmāvatī, having heard that Mādhava—who is separated from Mālatī—is about to enter that region, the forest and difficult path on the mountain characterized by the Great Tank (Bṛhaddroṇī), I shall now proceed toward him. Let it be; what does his entry into the forest matter? Such is the intention.

Of what sort is Mādhava? He is one for whom the region familiarized through its role as the setting for play and other activities with Mālatī is now, in her absence, unable to endure being beheld. To the two expectations—"How can there be an entry into the forest? and "Of what nature is it?"—the two phrases "together with his circle of friends" (*saha suhṛdvargeṇa*) and "having abandoned his dwelling" (*saṃstyāyaṃ gṛhaṃ parityajya*) are to be applied. Furthermore, the venerability expressed by the word *bhagavat* (Lord) applies to Śrīparvata because it is a field for the accomplishment of many mantras. Likewise, [he says] "I."

Likewise, by means of that extraordinary velocity, or by resorting to ascending to such a high place, one who has flown up contemplates his own bodily lightness—accompanied by the excellence of its perfection—as a sign of the maturation of yoga, as well as his own swiftness of movement as a cause for wonder. "Lightness" (*laghimā*) is that by which one becomes light, whereby, having grasped the rays of the sun, one enters its orb; and there is the ascent to the lofty sky so that one may clearly behold the mountain valley of Mādhava and even Śrīparvata.

*Vyatikara* means a distinction or a collection. The eye is "enveloped" (*pariṣicyate*), meaning it is perceived by being pervaded by the circle of rays. "Excellent, excellent!"—the repetition of the word "excellent" is the cause for [indicating] that Padmāvatī has been quickly reached and that prosperity is near. Regarding "Padmāvatī": the city of Padmāvatī supports the atmosphere as if it were the sky itself. In response to the question "Why?", there is a specific river named Sindhū, which is vast and expansive with its pure waters. Of what nature is that atmosphere?

The meaning is that the sky, which was previously split by the collision of those lofty palaces, appears as if it has subsequently released [its fragments]. Here, "the sky" should be understood as that which appears in the upper region in the form of a blue expanse; otherwise, since space is all-pervading (vibhu), any report of its falling or similar movement would be untenable. //1//

This is the river named Lavaṇā. By the word "janapada" (country), the people of the country are intended. For their delight, the pregnant cows—which are dear [to them] and which possess the nature of bearing fresh rows of grass—are shining like forest-dwellers; such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Here, the word *mālā* takes its short form according to the rule: "In the case of *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā*, [the final vowel is shortened] before words meaning 'built,' 'reed-mat,' and 'bearer' respectively."

Regarding the form *gogarbhiṇī*, by the rule "catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.71), when it is a *jāti* compound, one obtains *gogarbhiṇī* and *ajāgarbhiṇī*. However, even for that which is not a quadruped, one would have *mānuṣīgarbhiṇī*; and even when it is not a genus (*ajāti*), one would obtain the form *kālākṣigarbhiṇī*. //2//

This very river is familiar from before. By the word *bhagavatī*, which denotes venerability, he indicates the sacredness (*tīrthatva*) of the stream named Sindhu. A *prapāta* is a fall from a high place onto lower peaks; it is that which has split the surface of the earth due to its lofty descent. "Where it flows" (*yatrayeti*): where this tumultuous roar was produced, manifesting with many modulations and as fierce as the thunder of fresh clouds; and this roar, being reflected by the nearby mountains, has attained a resemblance to the throat-roar of Gaṇapati.

And here, regarding the present sound which is charming due to its similarity to the thundering of fresh clouds, the description of it as "fierce" (pracaṇḍatva) is for the reason that it might cause harm by giving rise to the suspicion: "Perhaps this [sound], entering the range of Mādhava’s hearing while he is separated from Mālatī, appears like the roar of a new rain-cloud. //3//

"Etāḥ" (these): these forest lands, by the visualization of groves and forests abounding in sandalwood and other trees, cause one to recall the great southern forest mountains; that is to say, by virtue of their similarity to them. Of what nature are these forest lands? They are fragrant with the scent of ripe bilva fruits.

In response to the inquiry as to what kind of mountains [they were], the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "The broad regions of their girdles (*mekhalā*) were made resonant by the Godāvarī river, which issues forth with a primary current characterized by a faltering sound and is humming—that is, making noise—within the thickets (*nikuñja*), which are specific caves covered by creepers and the like, and which are heavy with the darkness firmly established and intensified by forests of young *kadamba* trees and others. Regarding the word "this" (*ayam*): it refers to a specific river called Madhumatī; "confluence" (*saṃbheda*) means a meeting point, and "purifying" (*pāvana*) means that which produces sanctity.

The name of that Blessed One is Svarṇabindu; he is established as non-human (apauruṣeya), his installation is not produced by human effort, and his greatness is proclaimed by the Śruti. "Victory! O Creator of the worlds, O progenitor of the fourteen worlds; O Giver of all boons, O bestower of the desires of all who bow; O Treasure of the Vedas, O treasure of the entirety of speech! And his status as the Primordial Teacher (Ādiguru) is due to his being the instructor even of Brahmā at the beginning of creation. //4//

"This" refers to the following grammatical connection (*anvaya*): "This mountain, being easily visible to the eyes, produces pleasure. Its qualifiers are as follows: its lofty ridges are darkened by fresh clouds; for this very reason, it possesses uninterrupted cries from peacocks filled with joy. Furthermore, its body is glossy due to those nesting trees (*nokaha*) which are variegated and mottled (*śabala*) by birds (*śakuni*); here, the birds to be understood are the cranes (*balākā*) and the peacocks (*kekinaḥ*), for it is precisely they who are beginning their nest-building at that time.

By those very white and dark [spots], there may be a variegated appearance of the nests. Regarding the word "dadhati" (they bear): here, the young bears—those who have eaten the "ambūkṛta" (moistened) [substances] along with their saliva, which are enhanced by the quality of resonance within the hollows—are the agents that "bear" (*dadhati*) solidity (*styāna*, *styānatva*).

Just as the resinous exudation (*niṣyanda*, *drava*, *kṣaraṇa*) from the joints of *sallakī* trees—which were first crushed and later scattered and dispersed—is solidified (*styāyate*), becoming concentrated on all sides; the meaning is that it spreads forth. //6//

"Kāśmaryāḥ": *kāśmarya* is the *madhuparṇī* tree; at that time, it was leafless (*niṣpatrāt*). "Udgatadalam" means a young, fresh leaf. "Kṛtamālacchāyam": the *koyaṣṭika* is a particular kind of bird; because it is found in the forest, it "ṭīkate," meaning it runs. Likewise, on the riverbank, there were plants called *aśmantaka*, synonyms for *atasī*; their "mouths" (tips) were merely touched by its seed-pods (*tac-chimbicumbita-mukhāḥ*), meaning they were just grazed by the tips. The intention of the word "cumbita" is not that they ate them out of thirst.

The *pūrṇikās*—a species of bird also known by the name *aśoka*—move through the water. The *dātyūhas* remain hidden at the base or trunk of the *tiniśa* tree (also known as *syandana*), due to their innate nature. Likewise, in the lower region, the *kukkubhas* mimic the warbling of the pigeons residing in nests within the creepers. The *kukkubha* is a specific species of bird resembling a village sparrow. As it has been said: "The *kukkubha* has a tail white like the autumnal moonlight, a blue throat, and the form of a village sparrow;
it cries out like a cock, is land-dwelling, and is red in color. //7//

Thus ends the Pure Interlude (*śuddhaviṣkambha*). Makaranda, sighing piteously, speaks to himself: "Where not... Here, we—all of us—though endowed with intelligence, prowess, and energy, find ourselves existing, remaining in that very calamity. In that calamity, the mind (as the agent) does not even descend upon, nor does it take hold of, that hope in the form of Kāmandakī’s consolation which serves as the cause for attaining him; for that consolation has ceased to exist precisely because its object no longer exists.

Nor does that [hope], though rejected and rendered hopeless, abandon or cause one to lose the expectation of attaining it; for even after many encounters with Aghoraghaṇṭa and others, its attainment is seen again and again. One enters only the darkness of delusion (*moha*); and here, "delusion" refers to the failure to discern what ought not to be done. Remaining inactive—doing nothing whatsoever appropriate for counteracting the calamity—and occupied only with the act of eating, we are like cattle.
And in this matter, the intention is that the sole cause is the play of adverse fate, not any deficiency in our own human effort (*puruṣakāra*). //8//

Mādhava: You have come to your end, having reached destruction in such a way that the true nature of things remained unknown and the cause of your ruin was not perceived. This is indeed marvelous! As for "dear one": she whose dear one is Mādhava is "Priyamādhavā"; having been so by her very nature, why has she now become affectionate toward him only because of this [present] occasion?

And I am not another; rather, I am that very Mādhava who, for your sake, engaged in such an action as was appropriate for the occasion of the proposed sale of human flesh. Having thus reflected in his mind upon Mālatī’s affection for him and his own role as the one who has countered such a calamity, he says: "He who gladdened me... Your hand, like a personified great festival, gladdened me. To the question of what kind of hand it was, [he replies]: "Having taken up a beautiful bracelet. To the question of how it gladdened him, [he replies]: "Of its own accord."

For, since my throat was rendered motionless by the sight of you, I offered Bakulāvalī with my own hand under the mistaken impression that it was Lavaṅgikā; thus, this act is to be understood as being even more significant than the gift of one's own body. //9//

"Friend," [he says]. "Rare indeed"—the meaning is that from the time she began with the mention of the Madana garden, the degree of affection she has shown toward me is impossible to find elsewhere in this world except for Mālatī; the sense is that no other heroine has been shown to possess such passion. He describes that very excellence of her affection: "Full of sap..."—[she] endured for a long time, incessantly, one whose nature is to agitate with limbs as delicate and tender as fresh jasmine flowers moistened with honey.

Regarding the word *kṣāma* (emaciated), its meaning is both "delicate" and "unable to endure being overcome"; in both senses, the seed [of my suffering] is "mine alone," which serves as the specific cause for death that is harsh at every moment—this is the qualification of the fever. Immediately after that, when there was the apprehension of losing my pride, I resolved and established my mind to renounce even those very life-breaths, which are like blades of grass, out of a sense of "mine-ness."

Let all this rest: that this noble maiden, disregarding her elders out of passion, carried through and brought to completion the audacity of offering her hand and the audacity of taking his hand; beyond this, what more can we say? Such is the intention. //10//

Thinking "and moreover," he says "mayi" (in me), composing the stage for the seventh state called "insanity" by means of the signs of the fourth state of love through the praise of Mālatī’s other virtues.

Do you remember how, prior to the occasion of your marriage in the Nandana grove, when all hope of attaining me had vanished, she—distraught by the pain of that severance of her vitals and as if agitated by those heart-rending, distressing sobs—nevertheless extended toward me an intention of affection, a disposition dominated by love, even in that state? And as for me, you yourself remember everything exactly as it was, how I became, and what I was, with my mind rippled by waves of agony. This is the syntactical connection. //11//

With agitation and haste: the word *aho* expresses wonder; *nu* indicates deliberation; *bhoḥ* is a term of address. Regarding "it splits" (*dalati*), this is used in the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*). Having itself made my heart the object of the effort of splitting—even exceeding that [effort]—since it has split due to intense longing, why is it not perceived? To this, the answer is "in two parts" (*dvidhā*). For he reveals to Makaranda that the pain existing in the heart is exactly like the pain that would occur during the actual splitting within.

Just as the body—the physical frame—is distressed and agitated when the heart is elsewhere, it carries delusion (*moha*) and mental distraction (*vaicittya*); if there is delusion, how is it that you know this? To this, the answer is: the intention is that she does not indeed abandon consciousness, which is the knowledge of the pain of separation from Mālatī. Likewise, the internal burning—taking the form of the fire of grief fanned by the wind of love—consumes her body. If so, since the meaning of the verbal root *dah* is "to reduce to ashes," why is the state of being ashes not seen? To this, the answer is: she does not reduce [herself] to ashes.

It reveals that the harshness [of his condition] is such as that experienced when the body is being burned. Likewise, Fate, acting unfavorably, strikes as if with a weapon that severs the vital organs. If it is asked, "How then do you live?", the answer here is: "He does not cut [the thread of life]. The reason for not severing his life is the thought, "Let him experience this torment for a long time. //12//

Makaranda: Unrestrained, unchecked, or free from delusion—or "unrestrained" (*niravagraham*) may be used as an adverb. Even the sun, with its fierce rays, burns you at midday like our own past karma, which is divine and irresistible. This [state] is a sign of having entered such an insurmountable condition. A lotus-lake (*padmasaras*) is a lake where lotuses predominate. Regarding "with upraised stalks" (*unnāla*): here in this lake, the wind will sustain you when you have fallen into such a state. He states the qualifiers of the wind: "with upraised stalks."

Those young lotuses which have upraised stalks and are freshly blossoming—their source is their place of origin; therein, that which is the *mākaranda* (honey), the outflow, the flow—that is to say, the protection—is by it "intermingled," meaning mixed together. That which is the "dense" (*māṃsala*), i.e., the abundant fragrance, is its "companion" (*bandhu*), meaning its associate. Likewise, those waves (*kallola*) revolving in front, their sprays (*śīkara*) are like frost (*tuṣāra*); by them it is "chilled" (*jaḍa*), meaning slow-moving. //13//

Then Makaranda, his mind distracted by the sight of his friend’s impending end, forgets the role of the "kindling" (uddīpana) factor in the state of separation; instead, he presents those very same things in order to cause Mādhava to turn his attention elsewhere. "I distract him" means I make him change his mind. "In this"—that is, let the regions of the earth be seen in this lake.

He describes the characteristics of the regions: those areas where there are *puṇḍarīka* lotuses whose broad stalks—shaken by the wings of *mallikākṣa* swans (a specific kind of goose) emitting joyful, deep-toned cries—throb first and then last. To the question of how they might be seen given that his eyes are filled with tears of grief, he replies: "In the interval between the falling of one tear and the rising of another. 14.

For Mādhava, Makaranda’s very instruction on diversion became the cause of his agitation. Makaranda: [He says this] because, due to my inability to respond—stemming from my failure to grasp the meaning of his words—his heart has become utterly desolate. Thus rising up, he is unable to look upon the means for his own diversion suggested by Makaranda, suspecting them to be the opposite of what they were intended to be; the meaning is that, having risen, he has set out to go from this place to another location.

Then Makaranda, unable to counteract his friend’s onset of such unbearable distress, sighed and said: "Be gracious; abandon the longing of your heart—or rather, be comforted. Vānīrā! Look at the water of the rivers, which has acquired fragrance through the *vetasa* flowers growing along their banks. Here, divert your mind"—this is the intended meaning. "At the edges" means on the riverbanks.

The intention is: "Behold that [mountain] which has blossomed—that is, burst open—with the clusters and buds of *yūthikā* flowers. Furthermore, having taken hold of the ridges—that is, having made the peaks their support—the clouds act as a canopy (*vitāna*) for the sake of the wild dance of the peacocks; they are spread out like a cloth-made dancing pavilion. In which regions? He says: "On the slopes"—that is, on the mountain sides—which possess a pre-eminent smile in the form of blooming *kuṭaja* flowers. //15//

"Jṛmbhā" means blossoming; by that [blossoming], the *jarjara*—meaning having a loosened compactness—is the mass of buds (*ḍimbaḍambara*). By means of this, the regions at the foot of the mountains possess the dense beauty of *kadamba* trees. The intention is: "Behold these for the sake of diverting the mind. Here, the mountain regions are the subject (*anuvādya*) and the *kadamba* trees are the predicate (*vidheya*). Likewise, the quarters of the sky become dark with rows of clouds. Behold those directions as a means of mental diversion. Such is the relationship between the subject and the predicate in both cases.

Likewise, let the mind be diverted even by those riverbanks—which are marshy regions where kandalī plants are sprouting and which bear lovely ketakī flowers—these being well-known [sources of pleasure]. Similarly, let it be diverted by the rows of forests, which appear as if smiling with the blossoms of śilīndhra and lodhra trees whose fragrance has manifested; this is the intention that these serve as causes for the diversion of the mind. By this composition, the approaching rainy season is indicated, which is an extremely undesirable cause for those separated from their lovers.

*Śilīndhras* are a specific type of *puṃnāga* tree; others say they are *rambhās*. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *śilīndhra* refers to the flower of the *kandalī*, and to the two types of *karatripuṭaka*. *Tripuṭaka* is a specific kind of *vicikala*. //16//

Mādhava: Out of respect for the words of the Blessed One, I shall look. The distinction is this: in her present state, she is difficult to behold because she inflames the god of love; yet her beauty is delightful only to those who are happy and free from separation, such as those dwelling in forests and mountain regions. Therefore, in the general statement "What is this?", the neuter gender is used. The intention is: what kind of sequence of presenting objects that are utterly adverse to me is this, on the part of my all-knowing friend, for the sake of pacifying my grief? Or rather—

"What other cause for my friend's altered fortune need be sought in the sequence of events?"—thus he conceals his own internal thoughts. Or rather, he is reflecting on the reason why those who are so lovely are now difficult to behold. Or else, "What other days have arrived that serve as the cause for this difficulty in beholding her?"—to the question of what kind of days these are, he says: "with blossoming [lotuses]," and so forth.

Those days were such that a fierce east wind, blowing along and scented by the blossoms of the *kakubha* and *sāla* trees in full bloom, caused the rows of clouds—glossy like fragments of sapphire—to tremble and waver, displaced from their positions; likewise, they were fragrant with the scent of the earth moistened by fresh showers;

and they possessed a beauty characterized by a mingling of two states: the disappearance of perspiration due to the coolness of the shower-wind, and its simultaneous manifestation due to the intense heat of the sun. (17)

"Hā" is an indeclinable particle indicating despondency. "O young woman!"—O beloved, if even you remain alive, separated from me, then how can these quarters of the sky be looked upon now? How could I gaze upon them? To the question of what the directions are like, he says: they are those in which the clouds are as dark as the mature *tāpiñcha* tree, dense and numerous, and likewise rising upward; furthermore, they are shaken by cool breezes that carry fresh droplets, and they possess Indra’s weapon, the rainbow.

Likewise, they are resonant with the quarrels of peacocks (*nīlakaṇṭha*) made melodious by intoxication and joy; and here, pervaded by rainbows and accompanied by harsh sounds from the quarrels of peacocks blinded by passion—how can such [clouds] be beheld now in this present state? Thus, sound (*dhvani*) is the cause for their being difficult to behold, while the meaning [of the words] serves as the excitant determinant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*). //18//

"How can those things most undesirable to people separated from their beloveds—such as rising clouds and the like—which now pervade [the sky], be beheld by those like me? This is grief (*śoka*), which is the distress of the mind. "Affliction" (*ārti*) means pain. "He enacts" refers to the actor who has assumed the role of Mādhava, and not Mādhava himself; for dramatic performance (*nāṭya*) is defined as the imitation of a state of being. And it is not logical that Mādhava would be imitating his own current state. Makaranda: An indescribable transformation of condition, taking the form of a state bordering on death, caused by something made of adamant.

The fact that he still lives even in this state of witnessing the destruction of his friend is proof of his adamantine nature. "Distracting" refers to a means of warding off suffering; [Mālatī] sighs and reflects that it is a means for Mādhava’s survival—thinking, "If this is so... Because there is no means of consolation, she feels as if her life has already ended or is nearly finished. She addresses her friend as "sakhi" (friend) because of her beloved's status as a friend. What further purpose is served by speaking of your many faults? By merely saying, "You are pitiless" or "You are merciless," you should understand that all your own faults have been exposed.

Just as your husband—who was not even looked upon by you, yet who saved your life through the occasion of his undertaking the sale of human flesh for the sake of obtaining you—was thus protected, why do you not likewise protect the life of Mādhava, arriving unexpectedly from somewhere? Thus, you are merciless. By saying "you have cast [him] aside," she implies that you have disregarded the consent of your mother, father, and others.
Since you committed this rash act of offering your own hand to this Mādhava out of greed at that time, what is this cruel course of action, this conduct, toward one who is innocent? (19)

"O Mother! [He says: "It splits, it bursts asunder; it crumbles, it breaks apart—the bond of the body, the joints and locations of the limbs of the physical frame. Without such a preeminent man, I perceive the world to be empty. Thus, with an unbroken flame, I seem to blaze, I am as if burning within my heart. Likewise, the inner self, sinking and becoming exhausted, makes me blind; I am as if drowning in this darkness. On all sides, delusion obstructs and veils the functions of all the senses."

"Distressed" means agitated. "How can I, unfortunate as I am, [perform] the protection of his life?"—this is the ellipsis. Alternatively, "how" (*katham*) is an indeclinable used in the sense of "what" (*kim*); thus the meaning is, "What shall I do now? //20//

"Bandhutā" means a group of kinsmen; for her heart, it is like the Kaumudī festival (the full moon festival). The word *maha* refers to a celebration. For Mālatī’s eyes, he is like the new moon (*pratipaccandra*); because his appearance is not yet complete, the description of him as a "delightful moon" (*mugdha-candra*) is used to evoke longing, based on the thought: "When will he become the proper object of my vision? He is the son of Makaranda, who, for the sake of Makaranda's joy, is like an ornament (*tilaka*) to the world of living beings. A *tilaka* is a specific kind of decoration.
[The word] *pralīyate* means "perishes" or "vanishes. //21//

"Upon the limbs," etc. Sandalwood paste upon the limbs as he is embraced; the autumn moon in his sight as he is beheld; bliss itself incarnate in his heart as it is perceived—by you, who are exceedingly desirable and naturally charming, by one who rescues [him], leading him to another world as if rescuing his very life. And all this, because it is a form of lamentation, does not for the moment bring about the nourishment of a specific aesthetic flavor (rasa). //22//

"Touching the body of Mādhava—O merciless one! Grant me a gaze that is radiant and stainless, accompanied by a smile; likewise, give me speech that is exceedingly harsh yet made radiant by a smile. O you for whom Makaranda is dear—addressing him thus—how do you not consider, how do you not know me, your companion whose heart is devoted [to you], and not merely through outward affection? The sense is: 'How could I ever have a mind colored by passion [for another]? "

The reason for describing her as "cruel" is the thought: "Now, my life would be sustained by the mere gift of a glance from you; why then do you show such aversion and lack of compassion even toward that alone? //23//
Makaranda: A fresh rain-cloud, possessing a luster that is as beautiful and full-bodied as a newly polished, dark royal turban or a specific kind of black stone; "āsāra" refers to a downpour of rain.

Here, in Mādhava’s sigh as one separated from his beloved, Makaranda’s prayer for the rain-cloud’s downpour—which is exceedingly difficult for those in the state of separation to endure—should be understood as arising from a delusion (bhrānti), since he identifies himself with others who are likewise separated from their beloveds and perceives that even for others, the clouds and other elements produce pleasure. "By good fortune" (diṣṭyā) means by luck, both for me and for himself; the intention is that this event has occurred such that he has now sighed, having released the breath that was previously suppressed. Mādhava says: "That... [referring to what follows].

The sense is that even the words of Vālmīki, "Joy comes to one who lives," provide a basis for hope. One must supply the phrase "having approached him after a long time. As for why the word *sāmānyajāti* (general class) is used in the neuter gender: it refers to the bearer of the news of my welfare to my beloved. Regarding the phrase "with a burden of fruit": a fresh cloud rests upon the mountain peak; the intention is, "I shall make this very cloud the messenger of news. To the question "Where?", the answer "to the river" (*sravantīm*) is to be connected with what follows.

In the northern direction of the flowing river, not far away, there is a bower surrounded by *jambū* creepers that are dark with the ripening—that is, the maturation—of their fruit-laden burden; she is one whose waves are thinned by the stumbling, that is, the striking against, [the banks] of that bower. Likewise, the specific description of the cloud is "dark like *tāpiñcha* trees," meaning those which possess dense, thick, and continuous rows. //24//

"Kaccit" (I hope): the word *kaccit* is used to express a wish. The meaning is: "Please tell me your own wish or desire. "Saumye" (O gentle one) is a form of address; it is used because you have rendered assistance even to those who are enemies to the class of separated lovers by immediately dispelling their delusion with your showers of spray. Your dear companion, the lightning, embraces you. The intention is: "Like Mālatī, who has gone away somewhere leaving me behind," [the cātakas do so]. Furthermore, the cātakas, whose faces are bright and cheerful due to that manifest affection and joy, attend upon you.

"Having abandoned me like Makaranda and others, she has gone somewhere"—this is said by one who, due to the force of madness, does not see Makaranda even while looking at him, as if he were invisible. "The east wind, acting as a messenger, brings you well-being and makes you happy. Addressing the cloud: "Bearing that very mark, the rainbow of the Lord of the Gods, on all sides. To the question of what kind of mark it is, [the answer is] "possessing beauty," meaning radiant. //25//

Mādhava, anticipating a response from this sound of the clouds, speaks again: "This cloud gives me its consent"—meaning it grants me permission to speak what I desire. To the question "By what does it give consent?", the phrase "by a deep *huṃ*-utterance" is supplied. The construction is as follows: it is connected with that which is accompanied by, or equal to, the sweet and deep *kekā* cries of those blue-throated peacocks whose throats are raised in joy and longing within the caves filled with echoes.

He has already given his consent; therefore, I now entreat him. The word *yāvat* is used here as a particle of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As Amara states: "The words *yāvat* and *tāvat* are used for totality, limit, measure, and restriction. Thus, the meaning is: "Entreat him indeed. The term *bhagavan* means "one worthy of worship. The word *bhagavat* is used in the sense of veneration; even one who is venerable may be entreated. As it is said: "A request made to one of superior merit is not in vain, whereas a wish fulfilled by a base person is worthless. The phrase *daivāt* [means "by fate"].

If, while wandering at will in this world, you should by chance behold your beloved Mālatī—according to the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit—then, like Hanumān consoling Sītā, you should first comfort her with words such as "Your beloved lives," and thereafter describe the condition of Mādhava; he will even mention his own name in the course of conversation, saying, "I am Mādhava."

When asked, "How can one live in such a state?", you, by describing that condition, must not utterly sever the thread of hope—the expectation of attaining me—which serves as the very support for her life. The meaning is: by such words as, "In separation from you, your beloved will not survive," [you must preserve her]. For that single thread of hope alone protects the life of that large-eyed woman. As it has been said elsewhere: "The bond of hope in women is generally like a flower. (26)

"Aha! He has set out to search for my beloved, having fixed his attention on my words"—this is the reason for his joy. "Therefore, I shall seek him elsewhere"—thus he wanders off in such a manner for the sake of searching for him. Makaranda: It is madness itself that acts as an eclipse—a seizing by Rāhu—over Mādhava, who is like the moon; it overwhelms him. The utterance of the names of father and mother, beginning with "O Father," indicates that Makaranda has passed beyond childhood and entered the first stage of youth.

"Bhagavatī" is the mention of Kāmandakī’s name for the purpose of dispelling [any doubt regarding her identity]. Mādhava: Shame! What negligence and lack of attention on the part of people like us! Regarding the word "naveṣu" (in the new...): since my beloved has been clearly and manifestly divided by these cruel ones—having been torn apart and broken in this forest—among these things: her luster is in the new *lodhra* blossoms; likewise, her eyes are in the deer; likewise, her gait is in the elephants; likewise, her gracefulness is in the creepers. The word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) is to be supplied everywhere.
The particle "iti" indicates the manner [of division]. //27//

Makaranda: "In a friend"—that is, in a well-wishing companion, one endowed with virtue, an object of affection, and a lord of life, without whom one cannot sustain one's breath; likewise, in one who has been a close confidant since our childhood games—while he, bearing the intensity of that very malady which is the mental anguish born of separation from his beloved, O wretched heart, why do you not shatter, break asunder, and split into two? //28//

Mādhava: [His] intensity of madness has somewhat subsided; the meaning is that he recognizes this as an illusion based on resemblance, thinking, "It is my beloved, separated from me," among the blooming *lodhra* flowers and the like. "Let it be so"—let it be thus for now. "May she live"—the meaning is that she is still living somewhere. "Loudly"—the word "speaks" is to be supplied. "I, having first bowed to the mountain, address these forest-dwelling creatures, such as lions and other beasts: may they go and favor me for a moment merely by their attention."

The meaning is: "I do not request much at all. Regarding the phrase "by you": by those staying here, meaning those residing in this forest. "A lady of noble family" (*kulavadhū*) was seen; by the term *kulavadhū*, the exclusion of a courtesan (*vārāṅganā*) is indicated, and her unique, virtuous characteristics (*sādhvī-liṅga*) are signaled. "Beautiful by nature in all her limbs": the beauty inherent in every part of her body is meant, not a beauty produced by ornaments or the like; this is her unique quality. Her definition has thus been stated.

Now, if she has not been seen, then she is known only through her authority [as a description]. If you wish to know what happened to her, or what stage of youth she was in, then listen: in that state, Love (Madana) operates with full maturity within her heart, while her body is both beautiful and charmingly innocent (*mugdha*). By this, her stage of early youth (*prathamayauvana*) is also indicated. Its definition is given by Bharata: "With full thighs, cheeks, hips, and lower lip; with breasts firm and pleasing to her husband..."
"Kāma is that first youth which is full of enthusiasm for sexual union"—thus it has been said. (29)

"Alas! Oh!"—this expresses unbearable suffering born of despair due to the absence of any means to regain his beloved. "With cries of *kekā*": "To whom shall I appeal? To whom shall I pray?"—the remainder of the sense being "for news of my beloved's welfare. Just as my state of being a petitioner, my very act of seeking, has been seized and cast aside by creatures such as peacocks through their lack of occasion—that is, their lack of opportunity.

For instance, the peacock (nīlakaṇṭha), with his crest raised high and his plumage burdened aloft due to his frantic dancing—the tāṇḍava—ignores my words and does not listen. The cakora bird, out of inner joy, hastens toward its beloved; it does not hold my speech in high regard. And the golāṅgūla—a specific type of monkey with a black face—is smearing the cheek of his beloved with pollen. Thus, these reasons are stated for the lack of opportunity. //30//

"Having teeth": this one with a wrinkled face and red lips kisses his beloved’s face after lifting it up. He describes the specific quality of the face: that face wherein the lovely row of teeth is reddened by the crimson glow of the lower lip; likewise, that wherein the edge of the cheek is pale-red like the fruit of the *rocanikā* plant; and that wherein the face possesses the luster of a pomegranate that is red from ripening and split open by the swelling of its seeds—this is the meaning. //31//

This is an elephant; the word "stands" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. With his neck resting at the foot of a *rohiṇa* tree—the *rohiṇa* being a banyan tree—he provides no occasion for my words. Regarding the phrase "with eyes closed due to itching": this is some other wild elephant practicing proficiency in the art of catering to his mate; in response to the question "What is he doing?", [the answer is that] he is scratching his beloved, whose eyes are closed from itching, with the tip of his tusk.

Likewise, fanning his companion with ears that were alternately and successively tossed about by those delightful, pleasure-inducing breezes; and thus providing sustenance for his friend the female elephant with half-chewed fresh sallakī sprouts. //32//

Not so; there is another reason. I suspect that the elephant, distressed by separation from his beloved who is as dear to him as his own life, is languishing. For, though the clouds are thundering, he neither increases nor manifests his own roar; likewise, he does not take mouthfuls of the moss drawn from the nearby lake.

Likewise, due to the loss—that is, the diminution—of his intoxication, there arose a dejection from the absence of drinking liquor; by that dejection, those who were drinking honey-wine became silent. Their intense attachment (*vyāsaṅga*), which took the form of a dissolution (*laya*) characterized by immobility so as not to taste the liquor, rendered his face wretched and joyless. //33//

"This one shares my same distress; therefore, enough with this exhaustion caused by the door of conversation. This other leader of the herd is worthy of conversation"—this is the intention. His qualification is "with joy" (*sānanda*): he whose distinguished sound is being heard by his beloved who is full of joy. The grammatical construction is: "having plunged into the lake, which has become the object [of the action], he sports. He states the qualifiers of the lake: "freshly blossomed," and so forth.

It was like a lake whose expanse was covered with mud produced by the thick, abundant, and overflowing flow from the temples—[a flow] which was rich and dense with a fragrance as sweet and cool as a cluster of freshly blossomed *kadamba* flowers; and it was a lake from which filaments and other parts were scattered about from the heaps of lotus clusters that had been uprooted.

[The lake] is such that the curlews and cranes—two species of birds—are terrified by the mists and spray emerging from the waves shattered by the fierce flapping of their ears, which are engaged in an incessant, uninterrupted, and charming wild dance. Very well; he is composed in mind and fit for conversation. Therefore, I shall address him. [O you] whose youth is praiseworthy, yet whose youth is devoid of separation from a beloved!

Your skill in following your beloved is indeed accompanied by a flaw; that very skill is revealed by the word "playfully" (*līlayā*). Those mouthfuls of lotus stalks which were playfully uprooted—upon their severance and completion, splashes of water fragrant with blooming lotuses were transferred, meaning they were poured from the mouthfuls onto her chin. By this, the hero’s role at the commencement of lovemaking is described. Through the word "mouthfuls" (*gaṇḍūṣa*), the act of giving water after having drunk it oneself is suggested.

Likewise, a sprinkling was performed with a thick hand holding drops of water; this pair of actions is indeed quite appropriate. He states the fault: "At the cessation of love-making, the umbrella of lotus petals with their curved stalks was not held [over her] out of affection. The meaning is that this is improper; thus, the implication is that you do not know how to comply with your beloved. //34//

"Disregard" means the failure to give a reply; the sense is that he proceeds in such a way as to be devoid of interest. "Alas! expresses despondency. By the phrase "suitable for my dear friend Makaranda," having remembered Makaranda through this association, he says, "O dear friend!
