"Fie!"—fie upon this very "breathing," which is the calamity and suffering of maintaining life, since you are gone and I am left alone; fie upon that which was once so delightful!

Fie upon the charm of sense-objects, which are born in vain because their arising is fruitless! Here, the word "fie" (dhik) indicates the realization of the absence of any experience of charm in those objects. May that day pass you by—along with Mālatī—which does not go by; may it perish and be utterly destroyed. Likewise, fie upon that burden of joy and delight, which is but a mirage, should it ever be directed toward any other human being besides Mālatī and Makaranda! (35)

Makaranda: This latent impression of natural affection belonging to Mādhava, which serves as the seed for the knowledge of memory, has been awakened by some stimulus—such as a similar object, a past experience, or reflection—that awakens the seeds of memory; though it was previously obscured by madness and delusion, and though it had faded, it has now been fully revived from its manifestor. Thus, upon seeing Makaranda, Mādhava says: Mādhava: Embrace me! I have lost all hope regarding my beloved. Makaranda: [Embracing him] I honor you as the lord of my life, the master of my existence.

"How is it that he remains thus, longing to behold me while my intoxication has arisen? He is senseless, devoid of consciousness. Enough of this miserable obsession with a futile hope for life; for life exists only for the experience of suffering. My intention is this: 'Now I shall abandon that life. *Pariccheda* is the resolve made in the absence of companions. As for the words 'by whose affection' (*yatsneha*): by whose affection you were tormented, so that your heart was bound with trembling, and in that very manner, the fear was experienced."

To the question "How did she become bound with trembling?", he says: "even without a cause. That is, even without that which was present as the cause for her trembling; for it has been said, "Love perceives dangers even where there is no occasion. Furthermore, with what kind of heart? With one reflecting upon such states [of fear] regarding you. All that fear vanished instantly, at once, when you became unconscious. //36//

Those moments that have passed were indeed better than the present moments; the meaning is that they were "auspicious" (*bhadrāḥ*). According to Amara, the word *vara* is an indeclinable meaning "good" (*bhadram*), as seen in such usages as "even enmity with the great-souled is better. In those moments, while he was experiencing such unbearable and manifold sufferings, Makaranda—using the present participle form *cetayan* (meaning "being conscious")—now reflects within himself, having manifested through the power of detachment a direct realization of the Self as distinct from the body: "It is a burden," and so forth.

Just as one who is burdened by a load becomes free from suffering by casting it off, so too do I become free from affliction by abandoning this body and life; thus, the body is described as a "burden. That life which does not depart even upon the destruction of such a lord of life is like a "vajra-stake" (*vajrakīla*). By describing it as a vajra-stake, its firmness is expressed, and the capacity of life to produce unbearable suffering is also stated. From the knowledge of your departure, all of this appears clearly to me.

Therefore, now all the directions are as if empty and void, their purposes unfulfilled; the eleven sense-faculties are fruitless, for each respective object of perception is no longer grasped by its corresponding faculty. Because all activities have ceased, time has become bitter. When it was necessary to say "death" regarding your departure, he was unable to utter that word because its meaning is inauspicious; thus, he spoke instead with the term "departure," which conveys a sense of auspiciousness.

As it is said: "When Devavrata desires the long sleep, and when Droṇa and Karṇa remain as mere remnants of their fame, O child, even so is this son of Droṇa a companion to you, who have Lakṣmī for your aid. Here, by means of words such as "long sleep" (*dīrghanidrā*), which are mere semblances of conveying meaning, the poet has expressed things that are inauspicious. In this context, the word "long sleep" signifies death; "remaining as a mere remnant of fame" signifies being dead; "of him who has Lakṣmī for his aid" implies being alone; and "possessing affection" (*vātsalyavān*) implies having affection as one's only companion—that is, being solitary.

The world of living beings is a world of extinguished light; by the phrase "a world of extinguished radiance," he demonstrates that the world of living beings is composed of darkness, thereby demonstrating that his own self is composed of delusion. //37//

"The sun is setting"—this very knowledge of Mādhava’s death is the sole fruit of my life. The intention is: "In that case, I shall make an effort to abandon my life. The meaning is: "As soon as Mādhava dies by falling from the mountain peak into the river named Pāṭalāvatī, at that very moment I shall give up my life. "This very thing" refers to this body of Mādhava, which possesses the luster of a blue lotus petal; even with firm embraces, no satisfaction—that is, no contentment—has arisen in me regarding it.

When her limbs—which were previously drunk in by the eyes of Mālatī, agitated by the play of fresh passion and filled with wondrous beauty—were gazed upon with constant devotion; "batā" expresses grief. //38//

Regarding the term "fully filled" (*āpūrṇa*): just as the stainless moon, though full of its digits and bringing joy, is seized by Rāhu; or just as a rain-cloud, having only just formed and ready to pour forth rain, is shattered by the force of a violent wind; or just as [a fire] that has not yet accomplished the cooling of the distress of the earth and other elements dissolves away due to a fierce gale.

Or rather, just as a mango tree laden with fruit, which has not yet satisfied the group of travelers and others with its own fruits, is consumed by a forest fire, so too you—having attained the status of the crest-jewel of the world through your extraordinary collection of virtues, yet having failed to derive benefit from that collection of virtues—have fallen under the power of death; this is the meaning. //39//

This very object in the form of an embrace was requested and entreated; for it was only just now, by means of this passage—“Friend, honor me; embrace me; as for my beloved Mālatī, I am hopeless”—that he was shown to be heavy with virtues, rather than with physical bulk. Likewise, that specific act consisting of the surrender of her own person—namely, Mālatī’s self-choice (*svayaṃgrāha*) which disregarded her elders and was based solely on her passion for Mādhava—is the very cause of his life.

The intention is that, at this moment of Mādhava’s misfortune, there is no cause for Mālatī’s grief other than her unsurpassed affection for him. By the phrase "one who brings joy to Kāmandakī and Makaranda," the intention is that since I too have either already provided or am currently providing a remedy for the calamity along with Kāmandakī, I shall remain submissive because my efforts would otherwise be rendered ineffective. "Apaścima" means first; because there will be no further embrace from me, this is the final and rarest one. "Paścimāvasthā" means the final state. "From birth" [refers to the duration of their relationship].

It is improper that you alone, having drunk even the mother’s milk while accompanying her since birth, now drink the funeral offering (*nivāpa*) given by your kinsmen as a group who have cast you out—setting aside the nectar (*makaranda*). *Nivāpa* refers to the libation offered to the ancestors. (40)

"Of the beloved": in whatever place there may be the birth or origin of my beloved—that is, my friend who is the object of my affection—in that very place may my own birth also occur. Likewise, in the next world, "may I become his very follower"; such is the twofold prayer. //41//

Makaranda: [He utters] the word "Ambā" upon seeing her dress, friendliness, and age, which resemble those of Kāmandakī. He is "pratiṣiddhaḥ," meaning restrained or forbidden. Having heard from afar the words of prayer, "May I continue to follow him," Saudāminī asks: "Is it Makaranda? Saudāminī: "Indeed so. This means he is alive. "Atyāhitam" refers to great danger. Her intention is: "Has some calamity befallen Mādhava? You have resolved upon an undesirable act in the form of abandoning your own body. Makaranda: [He speaks.]

*Pramugdham*: seized by intense delusion; that is to say, having reached the state of unconsciousness. *Makaranda*: his consciousness restored; one whose awareness has reappeared. Saudāminī, who had previously not seen the physical forms of Mādhava and Makaranda, now beholds both and says, "It corresponds": the meaning is that the appearance of both is exactly as Mālatī described it. *Mādhava*: "Nūnam" means I suspect or am certain. "Vyāpāraḥ" refers to an action conducive to severing my delusion.

The intention is that, in this state, for the wind-god *Prabhañjana*, delusion (*moha*) alone is the adversary to his experience of the final stage. Having identified *Prabhañjana* as the cause for severing his own delusion, [the poet] addresses him with words of reproach: "Make them whirl. Cause the clouds to whirl hither and thither; by the whirling of the rain-clouds, the heat shall be pacified. And because they are filled with water, gladden the *cātaka* birds, whose desires are fulfilled and who are afflicted by thirst for the waters that are free from old age and death.

Likewise, for this very reason, make the peacocks full of longing for their cries; likewise, harden the *ketaka* flowers by making them mature through the process of watering. While a person like me, separated from his beloved, has fallen into a swoon by fate and is thus dispelling his own suffering by casting it out [upon others], what do you intend to achieve today by inflicting upon him this disease in the form of consciousness—the very nature of awareness? Is it for your own sake, or for the sake of another? Such is the intention. (42)

Makaranda: Well-arranged; made auspicious. [The world's] state of being a forest for all living beings [is due to its] being the life-breath of the universe. "These"—meaning these monsoon winds—draw away people whose nature is to suffer from separation. To the question of what they are like: they carry the fragrance of the *ketaka* flower; likewise, under the pretext of swaying their creeper-like tresses of hair, they have enjoyed the faces of bold city women; and furthermore, they are enchanting with the humming of swarms of bees clinging to the pollen within the blossoming buds of the *kadamba*. //43//

Mādhava: Even though you have caused this affliction in the form of a delusion, nevertheless, I entreat you precisely because you are a deity. Regarding the word *vikasat*: "Carry away my life-breaths along with the pollen to that place where my beloved resides"—here, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case. Or, send some object cooled by contact with her limbs to wherever I am staying. The intention is: "Without you, who now shall be my refuge in the forest? (44)

"Very well-composed" means exceedingly auspicious. That very same *añjali* which Mādhava formed during his first salutation, he offers there as a garland of recognition (*abhijñānasraj*). Mādhava: With an uplifted [gesture], his form becomes playful through its upward turning. Others say that "unnāha" means height or elevation. It is a garland of filaments in the courtyard of the temple of Love. Here, the word "anaṅgamandira" (temple of the bodiless one) is used in the sense of something loathsome. What doubt can there be? The meaning is: "This is indeed that very same [garland]. For such is the very division of this garland. "O charming one... [he says].

Although the flowers were arranged by them in a manner that was ill-placed and rendered inauspicious, they nevertheless produced and extended satisfaction for Lavaṅgikā; indeed, it was precisely because they were fashioned from ill-placed flowers that the arrangement was unevenly knotted. He states the reason for their being ill-placed: in order to conceal the curiosity toward Mādhava—which was unrestrained and intense due to the *helā* (a specific emotion born of the erotic sentiment) arising from beholding her face, which is as beautiful as the charming moon. The meaning is: for the sake of hiding it from Mālatī’s attendants. //45//

Then, thinking that Mālatī was nearby yet concealed due to the attainment of extraordinary supernatural powers (*asādhāraṇābhijñāna*), he—driven by the madness of untimely calamity—spoke as if in anger: "Indeed, jesting is practiced when one is in a state of well-being. You, however, are currently ignorant of my condition. For instance: 'They depart'—the vital breaths seem to be escaping; the heart seems to burst; the limbs seem to burn; and darkness, delusion, seems to spread. Therefore, this is the opportunity for me to act with haste in order to preserve my life."

Furthermore, you are not an object of derision in the form of concealing your own body; rather, grant joy to my eyes by manifesting your true self-form. The meaning is: "Become free from illusion. //46//

Then, not seeing Mālatī and regarding the garland of kesara flowers as if it were her own consciousness returned from madness, he said: "Niṣpratyūhāḥ" (unimpeded). Just as the impulses of the intoxication of love had arisen for her at that time, so too did an embrace resembling my own embrace occur, serving as a means to save her life. To the question of what kind of impulses of the intoxication of love they were, [the answer is]: "niṣpratyūhāḥ," meaning unobstructed; that is to say, they were unhindered. Likewise, they were heavy due to the exhaustion of her body.
This is the intended meaning: that which was the cause of her life at that time—namely, you—she does not live now even though she has been abandoned by you as well. //47//

"O Bakulamālā, I remember your comings and goings upon my neck with such intensity that it was truly painful. He describes the specific qualities of those comings and goings: they were 'gladdening,' meaning they inflamed the fever of passion; likewise, they 'expressed the essence' of deep affection—that is, attachment—and were 'thick with tenderness. (48)

The "attainment by one's own hand" is the attainment of the unique token of recognition belonging to Mālatī. The intention of the phrase "how do you think? is this: since she is indeed alive, how could her separation from her neck be possible? Makaranda: Then Makaranda expresses his intent regarding Mādhava’s discovery with the words, "She who brought [the token]... Saudāminī: She lives; she is not dead. The intention is that she has reached some place. Mādhava and Makaranda: Now, this news—where does it exist? Where is she?

Mādhava: "And this garland of hers has been obtained"—such was the form [of his thought]. Now, because he saw the report that the Kāpālika Aghoraghaṇṭa had been slain by Mādhava in the past, Mādhava speaks—having shattered the vow of Kapālakuṇḍalā which had been recalled [by Saudāminī’s words] without waiting for their completion, saying: "Noble lady, desist! Enough of this exertion. The news of Mālatī has been learned. Makaranda: *Note: The text provided contains a fragment of a dramatic dialogue from Bhavabhūti's *Mālatīmādhava*. The translation reflects the specific context of the characters' interaction.*

Then Makaranda, having heard Kapālakuṇḍalā’s vow, asks: "Who indeed? Makaranda—having determined from the words "Kapālakuṇḍalā has her desire fulfilled" that they were intended to convey Mālatī’s destruction, and thus finding consolation in the thought that Mālatī lives—he asks Saudāminī: "Noble lady, is it truly so? Saudāminī—intending to show that she was fulfilled by the abduction of Mālatī rather than by her murder—says: "It is exactly as the dear boy has reported. Makaranda:

Then Makaranda, having understood from the words of the young man—"as it was reported"—that Mālatī was not there, being intent on reaching a conclusion, said: "Alas! How painful! [He continues: "O Night-lily! If the moonlight, for the sake of the quality of its loveliness, by chance (*daiva*) met and joined with the cluster of night-lilies, then that was indeed a virtuous and auspicious act performed by the moonlight. But what kind of decree is this—the expansion of an untimely cloud—that has separated the night-lily bed? It has torn them asunder.
In this context, Mālatī is the moonlight, Mādhava is the bed of white water-lilies, and Kapālakuṇḍalā is the mass of untimely clouds; such is the intended meaning. //49//

Then Mādhava, reflecting on the state of Mālatī’s being killed, says: "Exceedingly loathsome" means utterly contemptible due to such an unworthy slaughter. The word *api* is used in the sense of *iva* (as if). The implication is: "In what manner would you be [compared] if you were swallowed by Kapālakuṇḍalā? The meaning is that even if a single digit of the moon were ever swallowed by a streak of smoke portending a cosmic calamity (*utpāta*), that might serve as a metaphor for you. //50//

"Bhagavatī": the word *bhagavat* refers to one who possesses excellence of knowledge; thus, she is one endowed with preeminent wisdom. "Nirmāṇam" (creation): this refers to the nature of sweetness that must be nurtured with great effort in the body of Mālatī, which is otherwise of a nature so cruel as to be fit for nurturing by a Rākṣasa or similar being. "Do not become a Pūtanā, do not become a Rākṣasī"—this is the meaning. Here, her loveliness is the cause for nurturing; he provides an illustration for this, saying "inherent" (*naisargikī*).

It is well known that the natural state of a fragrant flower is to remain upon the head; alas, how painful it is that it is not merely crushed by pestles! However, because Kapālakuṇḍalā possesses supreme knowledge, the intention here is as follows: since you, with such superior insight, have considered the matter, Mālatī herself has not directly wronged you, nor does she have any teacher for whose sake she was slain—she would only be one whose enmity must be extinguished. Having understood her purpose, Mālatī is now extremely distressed; therefore, comfort her—this is the underlying thought. (51)

"She would have done it"—this means that Kapālakuṇḍalā would have committed the sinful act of killing Mālatī; thus she is indeed utterly merciless. "In that case, had I not been her obstacle and adversary"—by this she consoles [Mālatī], implying that she merely carried her away, but did not actually kill her. //52//

Saudāminī: "You shall know me by the very result," such is my intention. Regarding the word *guru*: it refers to practice distinguished by the conduct of a preceptor; *tapas* refers to penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*; *tantra* refers to the drawing of mandalas and so forth; *mantra* refers to the spells of goddesses such as Tārā, or the mantra of the *tantra* itself; and *yoga* refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Through the application and cultivation of these, I shall extend this power of attraction (*ākarṣiṇī-siddhi*) for your well-being. (53)

"Unobserved by Makaranda, along with Mādhava. Regarding "the confusion" (*vyatikara*): *vyatikara* means a transformation or a mingling. "Terrible" (*bhīma*) means fearsome. "Consisting of darkness" (*tamomaya*) means that, as if consisting of lightning, it impaired the functioning of the eyes, destroying their power to discern objects. It arose and vanished in a mere moment. The meaning is that through the power of his knowledge (*vidyā*), this great blinding darkness became a great light. When the confusion had subsided, not seeing Mādhava, he says: "How is it that my friend is not here?"

The fact that Kapālakuṇḍalā was dispatched and led Mādhava to Śrīparvata is the seed of her state of fear. "What else?"—she prevails through her majesty in the form of a perfected yogic power as the Mistress of Yogis (Yogīśvarī). The underlying intention is that she acted in order to abduct Mādhava. //54//

The meaning is: Is this action, consisting of the abduction of Mādhava, appropriate as being of the nature of a reunion with Mālatī? Or is it something never before mentioned, in that it accomplishes a most incongruous deed? Regarding the word *astoka* (not small): it undergoes a state of variegation through joy and sorrow, and a state of non-distinction between them.

It is indeed a great marvel that, upon witnessing such an event, his mind remains so unaffected by the power of that wonder; that he has not forgotten the past experiences such as Mālatī’s attempted murder; that he suffers from the fever of fear and anguish born from the sudden suspicion of some misfortune to Mādhava; and that within a single moment, his mind is characterized by a delusion first severed by Saudāminī’s words regarding Mālatī’s calamity, and then reassembled through the sight of Mādhava. //55//
Since Kāmandakī alone is capable of perceiving matters beyond the senses and of investigating such unprecedented wonders, I shall inform her.
Out of devotion to Śabarasvāmin, the learned author has fashioned this commentary on Bhavabhūti’s *Prakaraṇaratnākara*—an extraction of its essence—as Mount Mandara; no other could have done so.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*, the *Vibudharatnāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Nānyadeva.

The Tenth Act. Now, following the abduction of Mālatī, an act characterized by the *nirvarṇana-sandhi* (the juncture of description) begins, intended to describe the activities corresponding to the conditions of Mādhava and Makaranda, and to set forth the specific tasks of Kāmandakī and other trusted persons. "Then enters... [is said]. "With tears" is a sign of the *karuṇa-rasa* (the sentiment of pathos). "From birth... [is said].

O child, the actions performed by you since birth—your natural movements of the limbs and so forth, which were auspicious, and especially those endearments that became increasingly delightful moment by moment, producing affection, charming and generating pleasure for the eyes, and sweet and thus gladdening the mind—when remembered, burn the body and tear the heart asunder. By this, the affliction of both body and mind is expressed. (1)

"Unsteady": I remember that lotus-face of yours, my child, when you were still a little girl. Its qualifiers are "unsteady" and so forth. It was such that its signs of dejection and joy—tears and smiles—were unsteady and unstable. Likewise, it possessed the sprouts of a few shining, charming bud-like teeth. Furthermore, it was accompanied by charming prattle that conveyed meanings characterized by complete expectancy, semantic fitness, and proximity. //2//

The others—Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā—speak with tears as if addressing the air; this is the meaning. "Alas, dear friend, you whose moon-like face was so beautiful and serene, where have you gone? What fate, resulting from the cruel play of destiny, has befallen your body while you were all alone? Alas, noble Mādhava! The world of the living has become one where the great festival of sunrise and sunset has ceased. Kāmandakī: "The two children—the girl and the boy"—meaning Mālatī and Mādhava. "Abhinava... [etc.]

The embrace of you two has been thwarted by a whirlwind—a gust of wind in the form of destiny or fate. Of what nature was that embrace? It was one in which passion (*rāga*) was the very essence (*rasa*). For according to the *Kāmasūtra*, "passion, agitation, and consummation" [are the stages]; thus, passion itself is the essence. Others maintain that "essence" (*rasa*) refers to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), based on the etymological derivation from the root *ras* (to be tasted/enjoyed). He performed the auspicious rites; he made the marriage-thread binding.

He states the simile: just as at the time of a simulated marriage arranged by a clever heroine and hero for the *lavalī* and *lavaṅga* trees in a garden, their embrace—performed with festive joy—is struck down by a whirlwind; such is the meaning. //3//

Lavaṅgikā: O you of ruined hopes! O you whose heart is made of adamant! You are altogether cruel. Madayantikā: Friend Lavaṅgikā, surely I am saying this: take heart for even a single moment! Lavaṅgikā: Madayantikā, what can I do? My life does not leave me, as if it were fixed and motionless by a firm cement of adamant. Kāmandakī: Her life is rising up; her vital breaths are departing. She is radiant!

This Lavaṅgikā is affectionate and full of love for you; her face has withered solely from the pain of separation from you. Abandoned by you, who possess a radiant appearance (*ujjvaladarśana*), she does not shine. The meaning is that just as a wick of thread and oil, though moistened and filled with oil, does not gleam when abandoned by a brightly glowing flame because its tip has been scorched by contact with that flame, so too is she. According to Amara: "The two words *āloka* mean both 'sight' and 'illumination. //4//

The meaning is that your limbs, having grown large through dwelling in my lap for so long, have now attained further growth by the warmth of the hem of my garment. Regarding the word "stanya" (breast-milk): from the time you ceased drinking your mother’s milk, it was I alone who brought you to the practice of playing with children's toys, and thereafter led you to the attainment of training in the arts and sciences, and thus brought you to maturity. The intention is that you, possessing such qualities as being born of a lineage superior to the world, were established by me alone in this excellent husband, and not by your parents.

By that collection of reasons, it would be appropriate for you as well to have an affection exceeding that toward your own mother. Just as an ivory doll (*pāñcālikā*), being regarded as a daughter (*putrikā*) and established as possessing virtues (*guṇavatī*)—that is, as having praiseworthy qualities—is led away for the sake of children's play and so forth, and subsequently placed with a bridegroom; this is the meaning. *Vinaya* refers to the determination of the scriptures. //5//

"Without cause": deprived of the fortune of being fit for enjoyment, I did not behold my son as he went to the lap of Lavaṅgikā today. He describes the son with these epithets: his face was charming because of a smile whose cause was unperceived; furthermore, white mustard seeds had been placed upon his crest and forehead for protection. An alternative reading is *manoharānana* (charming-faced) due to his affection toward his father and others, even though it was without [visible] cause. //6//

Lavaṅgikā: "O Blessed One, be gracious! I am unable to sustain my life. Therefore, having cast myself down from this mountain precipice, I shall find peace. May the Blessed One grant me such a blessing that even in another birth I may behold my dear friend once more. [The word] *saṃgama* (meeting) implies the hope that there will be a meeting even in the contemplation of death; for although, due to the distinction between auspicious and inauspicious karmas which cause one to reach different worlds, a meeting might perhaps occur or might not, [she hopes it will].
May that fruit be the fruit of death; the meaning is that it will take the form of the cessation of the suffering characterized by Mālatī’s death. //7//

Lavaṅgikā: "As you command. (She rises; the phrase "to fall" is understood as the remainder of the sentence. Kāmandakī: (Looking at Lavaṅgikā with compassion, unable to say "Hold Lavaṅgikā," she calls for Madayantika. Madayantika, however, unable to endure the sorrow of separation from Mālatī and likewise incapable of witnessing the destruction of Lavaṅgikā, says: Madayantika: "What do you command? [The other character replies: "Go before Lavaṅgikā. "I am attentive; I am on my guard regarding that task."

Lavaṅgikā: "Friend, be gracious! Desist from this attempt at self-destruction! Do not forget this person [yourself] for the sake of yourself. Madayantikā: Having resolved to throw herself from the peak, she says to Lavaṅgikā as if in anger: "Begone! I am not under your control. Her intention is: "I shall certainly die"; her further implication is: "Only she who is truly under your control will remember [this]. Kāmandakī: "She has certainly resolved upon the act of casting down her body"—this is said out of compassion for the poor girl.

Madayantikā—having mentally surrendered her life, which was purchased by the prowess of Makaranda’s essence (makaranda), and acknowledging that her life is dependent upon him, she bows to Makaranda, the lord of her life. Madayantikā: "O Lord Makaranda, salutations to you! Lavaṅgikā: "Venerable lady, this very mountain peak is the 'Pavitramekhala' (Holy Girdle) because it is joined to the stream of the Madhumatī river. According to Amarasimha, 'viṭaṅka' refers to a pigeon-cot (a niche or ledge on a building wall), and is used in both masculine and neuter genders. [The Madhumatī is a river. Kāmandakī: [She speaks.]

Death has been introduced; its obstacle consists in the form of a delay in time. The verse beginning with "vyatikara" has already been explained. Kāmandakī [speaks] with wonder and joy—the word "speaks" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. How else could such a conjunction (vyatikara) be possible, other than through my own pupil, which indicates a preeminent prosperity arising from a meditative concentration (samādhi) fully ripened by mutual instruction in the traditional lineage? The sense is that the sight of this conjunction is the cause of both wonder and joy.

"How then is my dear Makaranda to be seen?"—this is the ellipsis [of the sentence]. The intention is that since the fruit of seeing him has already been manifested through this auspicious omen in the form of the current event, the cause of that event must also be understood from this very source. Regarding the partial question of Kāmandakī, "What is this?", Makaranda, perceiving her desire to know the story, enters and says: "What else could it be? This is some Yoginī of preeminent yogic power.

The intended meaning is that this event has occurred due to her power. Furthermore, the implied sense is that Kāmandakī and the others have determined that Mālatī is well along with Mādhava, based on Makaranda’s gestures and the state of his eyes being filled with intense joy. For this very reason, they all desist from their falling [down]. //8//

"Behind the scenes": Because her fall produces such terrible suffering, there is a great crush of spectators. "Mālatī": Having understood and realized in a general sense that she has once again been carried off in that same manner, her mind turns away from worldly objects and lives; and having ascertained that very same calamity once more, she approaches the temple of Śiva known as Suvarṇabindu in order to enter the fire—thus [ends] the speech of the attendants: "We are undone! //9//

Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā: Instantly, the rise of fortune for Mālatī and Mādhava has occurred as if it were already accomplished; yet instantly, there is also great peril and intense fear due to the apprehension of Bhūrivasu’s destruction. Kāmandakī and Makaranda: [They are] filled with joy by the success of Mālatī and Mādhava, yet distressed by Bhūrivasu’s entry into the house of death. "What is this? they ask.

Is this encounter with Mālatī and Mādhava, occurring upon hearing that Bhūrivasu’s daughter has entered [the fire], to be inferred as a shower of sword-blades and sandalwood paste? This applies likewise to the latter half of the verse: Is this encounter, occurring without a cloud, a rain of nectar that causes the burning of the body? (10)

Regarding the term *saṃjīvana*: today fate acts as the agent for us, imitating the union of two things that produce opposite effects—sorrow and joy—by bringing together two objects that cause agitation and bliss. Just as there is a commingling or mixture of the life-restoring herb (*saṃjīvanauṣadhi*) and poison, so too is this a confluence or meeting of light and darkness; likewise, it is a blending of the thunderbolt and the moonbeams. //11//

[Offstage: Alas, father! Desist! I am longing to behold the lotus of your face; be gracious! Have regard for me! Why, on my account, do you abandon yourself—who are like a single, stainless lamp of auspiciousness that illuminates the entire expanse between the worlds? As for me, shameless and pitiless as I am, I have abandoned all of you. Kāmandakī: [To herself] "Birth... [She reflects.]

Another calamity, in the form of entering the fire—which is the cause of Bhūrivasu’s destruction—is about to swallow you, just as it did Kapālakuṇḍalā. The meaning is that because she has been worn away by the distress of being humiliated by the Kāpālikas, she is now like a mere sliver of the moon; thus, this misfortune is like an eclipse. //12//

Mādhava: "This one"—that is to say, for a living being (*jantu*), a creature, [it is] of destiny (*daiva*), meaning of previously performed action (*purākṛta-karma*). When that action is "facing fruition," meaning inclined toward the bestowal of its results in the form of imminent pleasure, pain, and so forth, he is able to set aside those visible secondary causes for the arising of suffering and the like—which act as doors, as it were, to that fruition, and which appear to be distinct from the previously performed action itself. The meaning is that he has the power [to do so]. //13//

Makaranda: Where has she gone who departed taking you with her? [Mādhava: "From Śrīparvata. [Makaranda: "I have come here in haste from Śrīparvata along with that very Yoginī, so that it might happen exactly thus. [Mādhava: This was the statement of the forest-dweller: "Bhūrivasu is approaching Suvarṇabindu in order to cast himself into the fire. Immediately after that, I no longer saw her as she vanished. (14)

Kāmandakī and Makaranda: For what reason have you vanished? The meaning is: "By means of the removal of Mālatī’s distress—now, moreover, by the removal of that distress through the destruction of Bhūrivasu—save us once again! Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā: Friend Mālatī! Indeed, I am saying, "Friend Mālatī! This is a variety of lamentation. Blessed One, save her! Her heart has become motionless due to a long-suppressed breath.

"Alas, Minister! Alas, dear friend! You two have both become the cause of each other's end; that is, you are the cause of the destruction of both—this is the intended meaning. Kāmandakī: "As if being split apart... This is a statement caused by the falling of water that has begun unexpectedly, distinct from natural rain. It "pleases," meaning it satisfies or, in other words, restores life. Mādhava: "As if her consciousness has returned," meaning as if her life has returned. He states the signs of this: "She is... [She] was first obstructed.

Her heart was such that her breasts were pushed back by the expansion of her breath drawn out and spread wide; "unnāha" means height or swelling. Furthermore, her eyes, which had been harsh due to the power of her delusion, became lovely as they returned to their natural state—their own inherent nature. Here, the word *nija* (own) is redundant, as its meaning is already implied.
Immediately thereafter, her face, now free from delusion, became clear and radiant with the quality of serenity, like a lotus at dawn enveloped in beauty and splendor. //15//

[From behind the scenes: "O noble lady, save me once more! Hearing this most piteous cry from Kāmandakī, Saudāminī, standing in the sky, prevents Bhūrivasu from entering the fire and says: "Disregarding... [Verse 16]. Disregarding the King, who was accompanied by Nandana and had prostrated at his feet to dissuade him from entering the flames, Bhūrivasu—his intense joy and wonder instantly dispelled by my words, namely, "Mālatī certainly lives"—is such a person.
*Saṃmada* means great joy. //16//

Mādhava and Makaranda: By good fortune! With joy! That Yoginī—by whom Mālatī was protected through her own power and speed—is coming from the sky where the clouds have been rent asunder; she whose downpour of the nectar-stream of speech excels all and triumphs. It should be inferred that, by means of protecting Bhūrivasu and Mālatī, she is the savior of the lives of all her kinsmen. //17//

Kāmandakī: "It is not pleasing," she says; "she approaches"—this is an exclamation of agitation. Mālatī: By good fortune, I have been restored to life after a long time! Mālatī: Oh, how is it that the Venerable Lady is here? Kāmandakī: Live! May you live! For this very reason, grant life to Mādhava; and may your circle of friends, including Madayantikā, live as well. The meaning is: "With your limbs, cooled by contact with the snow, restore life to me and my dear friend. The implication is that she should do so by offering her embrace. (18)

The others: "Dear friend, since you have appeared beyond our wildest dreams, honor us with an embrace. Mālatī: "Alas, my dear friends! Kāmandakī: (To Mādhava and Makaranda) "What is this?"—this is her question. Then follows their reply: "Venerable lady, [we were rescued] by Kapālakuṇḍalā. We, who were in danger from the calamity consisting of the abduction of Mālatī, have been drawn out from that perilous situation with great effort and persistence. (19)

Kāmandakī: Since Aghoraghaṇṭa has been slain by Mādhava, that operation of his female disciple—consisting of the abduction of Mālatī as a means of retaliation against Mādhava—is indeed the manifestation of Aghoraghaṇṭa’s own destruction. Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā: Oh, what a marvel! How the dispensation of Fate turns from repeated cruelty into a delightful conclusion! What was like a repetition—a repeated abduction of Mālatī—has become, through the recovery of Mālatī unharmed at the end, a conclusion that is truly beautiful. Saudāminī: [Listens.]

By the masculine designation "disciple" (*antevāsī janaḥ*) for himself, he indicates his own accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in the form of rescuing Mālatī from the grasp of Kapālakuṇḍalā. "Ancient" (*ciraṃtanaḥ*) means one who first received initiation; the intention is that because of his status as an excellent disciple, he was the first to receive the most eminent mantra from the teacher whose mantras are proven effective. Regarding Mādhava and Makaranda: the word "how" (*katham*) expresses wonder. It calls to mind Saudāminī, his former disciple, who is a worthy object of partiality.

In independent circumstances, all this—which consists of the recollection of the lightning-flash and so forth, and which takes the form of activity directed toward remedying Mālatī’s misfortune—becomes consistent; that is to say, it is appropriate. [The phrase] "Come, come" refers to the accumulation of merit resulting from the gift of life to Bhūrivasu; and that gift of life is mediated by the prevention of the calamity of both Mālatī and Bhūrivasu. "Hanta" expresses joy.

Therefore, although my body has already been granted joy by the fulfillment of these two most cherished desires, please gladden it further with an embrace. Cease from prostrating; for my intention is that you alone are worthy of being saluted by me, both because you are the giver of my life and because of your superior excellence. This is in accordance with such sayings as: "Virtues are the ground of honor among the virtuous, neither gender nor age. //20//

He clarifies this very point with the following verse, beginning with "Vandyā": by such playful activities (*vilasita*) whose fruit is the benefit of others—activities belonging to those who are "exceedingly Bodhisattvas," that is, those who have transcended the [ordinary] Bodhisattva stage; and in the mental scriptures (*manogatāgama*), even here, Brahmā’s *māyā* has been described by means of this excellent composition on awakening (*bodhasadgrantha*).

O you who are devoted solely to the accomplishment of the welfare of others even at the cost of your own life, you alone are worthy of the world’s worship through your glorious deeds; therefore, the meaning is that you should desist from my prostrations. That mantra-attainment (*mantrasiddhi*) whose success is so desirable is likewise desirable for us as well. By the manifestation of such activity on your part, that seed—which was the source for the spreading of the *Mālatīmādhava* tree—has become possessed of wonderful and abundant fruit. What kind of seed?

In former times, at the time of receiving my education, there was a bond of affection between us in the form of a vow that we must certainly establish a relationship through offspring; it is my hope that today, by means of such a true act, this vow may become a form of deliverance for both of us. //21//

Mālatī: "Certainly. This means that she is indeed Saudāminī. For by her—who is partial toward our connection with the Holy Lady (Bhagavatī)—I was rebuked, led to her own dwelling, and comforted. Having arrived here with the *kesarāvalī* [garland] as a token of recognition in her hand, all of you were sustained; that is to say, these kinsmen were saved from death. The others: "How very gracious is the Holy Lady toward her youngest [niece]! Makaranda and Mādhava: The word *aho* expresses wonder. *Bhoḥ* is used as a form of address. *Api*... [is used here].

Even the wish-fulfilling gem requires the exertion of thought from the seeker; yet this [act] consists of saving the life of Mālatī. How then could it have been conceived by me? Nevertheless, it was performed by the Noble Lady—something that could not have been done even by others such as the Kalpavṛkṣa tree. Therefore, it is truly marvelous. //22//

Saudāminī: The intention here is that this [message] is for the gratification of Lavaṅgikā and the others; however, for Madayantika, it is a cause for joy because of the news regarding the attainment of her husband. Regarding the word "ślāghya" (praiseworthy): the mention of the "son-in-law" is the underlying reason. Based on the conviction arising from Bhūrivasu’s words, "The Great King has authority over his own daughters," the thought that Madayantika is indeed his own daughter is present. The intention is that affection for you—a son-in-law of such eminent qualities, free from calamity, and born of a great lineage—is entirely appropriate.

For that reason—due to our former affection and for the sake of bringing about [your] life—even though she has been united [with him], she is being given by us to your friend Makaranda for the purpose of pleasing you; such is the meaning. //23//

Addressing Mādhava, Kāmandakī says: "Let it be heard. [The meaning is: Mādhava; the word "in all matters" (*nikhilārthe*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The sense is: "I am entirely fulfilled by the son of the king and others. Mālatī: "By good fortune! Even this thorn of doubt in my heart has now been removed. Lavaṅgikā: "Now the desires of the illustrious Mādhava have been fulfilled without exception. [Note on grammar: Since there is no fixed rule regarding the position of words in Prakrit, the word *śrī* (illustrious) appears after the name, which is contrary to the usual rule of its preceding placement.

By the word *kāryanidhāna* (repository of effects) followed by the suffix *-āp*, it is meant that the entire collection of effects, whose nature is their connection to a repository, has been accomplished by you alone; thus, you yourself are the treasure-trove (*nidhi*) of all effects. "Victory to you, Mādhava, the joy of Makaranda, the full moon!"—the expression "joy of Makaranda" is used because the attainment of Mālatī by Mādhava brings even greater bliss than the attainment of Madayantī by Makaranda. He is called the "full moon" because he reaches the limit of increasing his own excellence (*pāpavṛddhi-pakṣa*).

The description of him as a "full moon" is due to his having attained his unbroken desires. "By good fortune you prosper"—she looks at them with a smile; the ellipsis here is that they are dancing out of joy. The reason for her smiling is that the venerable disciple Avalokitā is dancing. Therefore Lavaṅgikā says: "Lavaṅgikā! His purpose too has been fulfilled in this matter; thus she dances in this great festival in every respect. Kāmandakī: "It is exactly as Lavaṅgikā says."

Or is there perhaps anywhere such a dramatic work—a *mahotsava-prakaraṇa*? This is the poet’s intention: that somewhere, some poet has indeed composed a work of this kind, similar to the *Mālatīmādhava*, which generates the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta-rasa*), possesses invented subject matter, is variegated and beautiful, enchanting through its diverse arrangement, radiant, endowed with the quality of nectar-like flavor, and possessed of poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*). Herein, the poet now brings together in the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture) the entire collection of matters indicated in the *mukha-sandhi* (opening juncture).

Or rather, just as this vow—"We two must certainly form a matrimonial alliance"—was made by Bhūrivasu and Devarāta in our presence, Saudāminī, and was indicated there, it has now been brought back to mind at the conclusion of the play through the very arrangement of Saudāminī’s words. Mālatī: How, then, can this be pleasing here? For what is the intention [behind] such a manner of ultimate outcome for my father Bhūrivasu and Devarāta? Makaranda and Mādhava: [They speak.]

That matter which took the form of taking her hand has turned out otherwise; the sequence of words and the manner of speech have become unmanifest—this is the meaning. Lavaṅgikā: "O Blessed One, now that the true nature of the hidden statement has been understood through your explicit words, what should be done regarding that which was brought about by the circumstances? Kāmandakī: [The remainder is: "She speaks in that very same way, but only aside from the people."

The intention is that the favorable turn of events for Nandana is caused solely by the connection between Madayantikā and Makaranda. "Free from apprehension" means devoid of doubt. To the statement made by Mādhava and Makaranda—that the matter has unfolded otherwise—he speaks the following reply aloud: "O children," and "Indeed not. During the time of his instruction in the stage of a disciple, there was an association with people residing in various directions for the sake of gathering [disciples] through affection. "In the presence of Saudāminī."

Therefore, Saudāminī alone is the witness here; for while his mere presence was pleasing to him by virtue of his actions and conduct, she has now performed a remedy for his misfortune—this is the underlying intention. She asks about the courtesan’s role, which was determined as the proper time for her own engagement in the thought that "we must certainly establish a connection with offspring," and which was carried out publicly before all the world. By this very act, a direct prohibition would lead to anger; thus, she reminds [him] of this means for the sake of the conclusion, thinking, "This is a propitious expedient."

Mālatī: Oh, what a concealment! Oh, what an exaggeration! For that was indeed a concealment, especially because of her youth, and so forth—this is what she has kept in mind. Makaranda and Mādhava: [These words] are inconsistent and deceptive; yet they are convincing, being endowed with conviction. Since the word *pratyaya* is a synonym for *prabhāva* (power), and power is to be inferred from the sudden accomplishment of even a difficult task, they are auspicious and beautiful.

"How could the wisdom of one as intelligent as you be subverted, both in victory and in praise? This should be understood as having been indicated by the *mukhasandhi* (the opening juncture). Kāmandakī says: "That which was previously... [The auspiciousness] in the form of taking her hand has borne fruit through merits performed in the past, and by my own efforts acting from afar—that is, by my mental operations (*buddhivyāpāra*) serving as the instrumental causes, those causal factors have come together to produce that auspicious result.

Likewise, the divisions born of such anxieties as "may the marriage of the two disciples, Bhūrivasu and Devarāta, take place according to their wishes," have borne fruit. Similarly, a meeting with his beloved Madayantika has been skillfully arranged for my dear friend Makaranda. Furthermore, those two princes who were previously considered worthy of trust are now filled with joy and united in their affection. (24)

Therefore, let it be told what else could be more dear than this? By means of such words as "I shall accomplish [it]," the four castes, beginning with the Brahmins and ending with the Śūdras, are successively made the objects of his aspiration. //25//
Out of devotion to Śabarasvāmin, the learned author has fashioned this commentary on Bhavabhūti’s *Prakaraṇaratnākara* as a Mandara mountain for extracting its essence; no other could do so.

Indeed, this ocean of treatises— which is exceedingly difficult to cross for those of small intellect, yet which clarifies purifying deeds— has been crossed with joy by me, having relied upon the commentary as my boat, pulling it stroke by stroke.

Thus ends the commentary on the tenth act in the *Mālatīmādhava-ṭīkā*, composed by the illustrious Nānyadeva—the son of the illustrious Haricandra, who belonged to the lineage of the illustrious Śilābhaṭṭīya, and whose mind acted as a bee at the lotus feet of the enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
